attempts.paper_title: Physiological Properties and Behavioral Correlates of Hippocampal Granule Cells and Mossy Cells
attempts.entry_title: Granule cells and mossy cells of the dentate gyrus (Senzai and Buzsaki 2017)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Senzai and Buzsaki (2017) on dandiset 000003, which holds silicon probe recordings of the dentate gyrus and CA3 in 16 mice, in 101 files from 94 recording days, with labelled granule cells, mossy cells, CA3 pyramidal cells and interneurons, sleep states, dentate spikes, light pulses, and positions on a circular T-maze and in open fields. It covers firing by brain state, theta and gamma phase locking, recruitment by dentate spikes, optogenetic tagging, monosynaptic transmission, place fields and remapping, and, on the 17 files that give each unit's shank, depth and the classification of granule and mossy cells.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Senzai and Buzsaki (2017) from dandiset 000003

outcomes.statement: The second-stage classification divided dentate excitatory neurons into 586 putative granule cells (GC) and 500 putative mossy cells (MC).
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells; Figure 1F
outcomes.notes: The files hold 609 GC (paper 586, within tolerance) and 568 MC (paper 500, outside the tolerance of 450 to 550), from all 16 mice, counting each of the 101 files once.
deviations: Counts come from the dandiset's labels; the paper's classification was not re-run on all files.

outcomes.statement: Narrow-waveform interneurons have a trough-to-peak latency below 0.425 ms, and among wide-waveform units the excitatory cells have a burst index above the threshold separating them from wide-waveform interneurons.
outcomes.notes: Under both burst thresholds (1.2 in the Methods, 1.8 in the Figure 1A legend), 98.2% of GC and MC are wide-waveform and bursty and 91.7% or 93.3% of wide-waveform interneurons are wide and not bursty, but 82.5% of narrow-waveform interneurons have a latency below 0.425 ms (40% to 100% by mouse), short of the 90% criterion. The labels pool dentate and CA3 interneurons; 92.7% are below 0.525 ms, the paper's CA3 threshold, and in the 17 files that give the shank 94.4% of the 71 narrow-waveform interneurons on shanks with GC or MC and no CA3 unit are below 0.425 ms (variants). The stored waveforms have their trough at 0.80 ms, so latencies above about 0.75 ms cannot be measured. On the wide-band signal of the 17 files, 64.7% (unfiltered) or 88.5% (300 Hz high-pass) of narrow-waveform interneurons are below 0.425 ms.
deviations: Latency measured on the mean of the first 200 stored waveforms (1.6 ms long, filtering not stated in the files); the paper used unfiltered waveforms.
The Methods and the Figure 1A legend give different burst thresholds (1.2 and 1.8); both were tested.

outcomes.statement: Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform interneurons (medians 7.97 and 2.11 Hz; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001).
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells
outcomes.notes: Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform ones (Kruskal-Wallis P = 5.3e-17 over the recording span, 1.4e-15 in awake periods), but the medians are outside tolerance under both readings (5.96 and 2.57 Hz over the recording; 8.75 and 3.08 Hz awake). In the 17 files that give the shank, interneurons on shanks with GC or MC and no CA3 unit have medians of 8.56 and 2.29 Hz over the recording, both within tolerance (P = 3.7e-08); this variant does not decide the outcome.
deviations: The interneuron labels include CA3 interneurons, which the paper counts apart, and the files do not say which region an interneuron is in.
The paper does not define the rate; two readings were tested.

outcomes.statement: The waveform of granule cells is narrower than that of mossy cells.
outcomes.source: Results, end of Identification of granule cells and mossy cells; Figure 1E
outcomes.notes: GC median trough-to-peak latency 0.710 ms against MC 0.740 ms (Mann-Whitney P = 2.3e-14). The stored waveforms have their trough at 0.80 ms of 1.6 ms, and 43% of GC and 67% of MC have their peak at the end, so the result partly reflects how often each type is cut off; among units with the peak inside the window GC are not narrower (0.660 against 0.645 ms, P = 0.057). On the wide-band signal of the 17 files (window to 2.4 ms), the unfiltered waveform the Methods use gives GC 0.755 against MC 0.840 ms (P = 0.017); after a 300 Hz high-pass they do not differ (0.710 against 0.720 ms, P = 0.4).
deviations: Measured as trough-to-peak latency on the stored waveforms, where the paper describes the waveform shape through a PCA of its second derivative.

outcomes.statement: In DRD2-Cre::Ai35 mice, 29 of 107 putative mossy cells were suppressed by green light, against none of 202 putative granule cells, 8 of 68 wide-waveform and none of 69 narrow-waveform interneurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Optogenetic validation; Figure 1H; STAR Methods, Optogenetic tagging
outcomes.notes: In 26 DRD2-Cre::Ai35 sessions with 20 ms pulses (4 mice), 68 of 106 MC (0.642) are suppressed by at least 20% with the baseline before the pulse and 71 (0.670) with the baseline later in the cycle, against 6 (0.030) and 13 (0.066) of 198 GC. Wide-waveform interneurons 20 of 88, narrow-waveform 14 of 132. The MC fraction is far above the paper's 29 of 107 and GC are not zero; MC exceed four times the GC fraction under both readings. At a 50% threshold the MC fraction is 0.066. Adding a one-sided Poisson test (P < 0.05) to the 20% rule keeps all 68 MC and 5 GC. The 37 units of the Figure 1H legend equal the 29 MC and 8 wide-waveform interneurons of the text.
deviations: The Methods do not define the baseline of the light-pulse histogram; two readings were tested.
The fifth DRD2 mouse (YutaMouse45) has no 20 ms pulses and is not included.

outcomes.statement: Mossy cells are more active than granule cells during both waking and NREM sleep (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for each).
outcomes.notes: MC median 0.736 Hz against GC 0.077 Hz in awake periods (Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.8e-114), 0.727 against 0.083 Hz with quiet wake, and 0.913 against 0.391 Hz in NREM (P = 2e-29). With home-cage awake time as wake (a variant), 0.692 against 0.077 Hz (P = 8.1e-102).
deviations: Wake is read as the `awake` periods, or `awake` with `quiet`; the states table does not describe its labels.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells fire most during NREM sleep and at similar rates during wake and REM.
outcomes.notes: GC fire most in NREM (median 0.391 Hz against 0.077 Hz awake and 0.198 Hz REM; adjusted P 1.3e-86 and 8.7e-31), but REM rates exceed wake rates (adjusted P = 1.4e-25 with awake periods, 6.3e-23 with quiet wake), so wake and REM are not similar by the paper's test. With home-cage awake time as wake (a variant), wake and REM still differ (adjusted P = 3.3e-24).
deviations: The post hoc test is taken as Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney tests; the paper names Kruskal-Wallis only.

outcomes.statement: CA3 pyramidal neurons are most active during wake and least active during REM.
outcomes.notes: CA3 pyramidal cells fire least in REM (0.287 Hz; adjusted P = 1.1e-15 against NREM and 5.4e-09 against wake), but the NREM median (0.459 Hz) is above the wake median (0.441 Hz awake, 0.433 Hz with quiet wake) and the two do not differ (adjusted P = 0.77 and 0.59). The REM part of the claim holds. With home-cage awake time as wake (a variant), the wake median is 0.412 Hz and NREM against wake gives adjusted P = 0.14; CA3 units fire at similar rates awake in the home cage and during behaviour (0.424 and 0.415 Hz).
deviations: The paper's CA3 units come from a separate classification (Figure S2); here the dandiset's `pyramidal cell` label is used.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells increase their firing in NREM sleep compared with waking, while mossy cells fire at equivalent rates in the two states.
outcomes.notes: Median NREM to wake ratio 4.63 for GC and 1.11 for MC (Mann-Whitney P = 3.9e-141; 4.28 and 1.11 with quiet wake), and the GC ratio is above the MC ratio in every mouse with both. The part saying MC fire at equivalent rates does not fully hold, as MC NREM rates are slightly above wake rates (Wilcoxon P = 1.4e-06). With home-cage awake time, 4.56 and 1.10.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by theta oscillations than mossy cells and fire at later theta phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
outcomes.notes: Modulated units 483 GC and 532 MC. Theta MRL GC 0.422 against MC 0.339 (Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.5e-20); GC fire later (circular means 30.8 and 12.0 degrees from the peak; P = 1e-17 with phases on (-pi, pi], 0.82 on [0, 2 pi)). After subtracting the uniform-phase expectation for the spike count (GC have fewer spikes), GC are still higher, at P = 0.00056. The bias-corrected MRL comparison (P = 0.00056) does not reach the paper's P < 0.0001. In the 17 files where it can be checked the theta-reference channel has a positive DS2 (+459 to +786 uV), so it lies below the DS2 reversal.
deviations: Phases from the theta-reference channel the conversion flagged, during up to an hour of awake periods per file; the paper's periods and reference channel are not stated.
Phase comparisons depend on where the cycle is cut; both cuts are shown and the claim holds on one.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by gamma oscillations than mossy cells and fire at earlier gamma phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
outcomes.notes: Modulated units 345 GC and 475 MC. Gamma MRL GC 0.319 against MC 0.212 (P = 4.8e-43; 0.219 against 0.166, P = 4.1e-18, after subtracting the uniform-phase expectation); GC fire earlier (circular means -20.2 and 1.7 degrees; P = 1.2e-23 on (-pi, pi], 0.18 on [0, 2 pi)).
deviations: As theta-modulation.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing neurons are more strongly coupled to gamma than fast-firing ones (GC r = -0.176, MC r = -0.184, P < 0.0001 for each).
outcomes.notes: Over all units with a gamma MRL, GC r = -0.177 (P = 3.6e-05, within tolerance) and MC r = -0.161 (P = 0.00013, just outside the tolerance and above P = 0.0001). Over modulated units, GC -0.397 and MC -0.253, both P below 0.0001 and outside tolerance.
deviations: The paper does not say which units or which rate the correlation uses; two unit sets were tested with the rate over the recording span.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells are more effectively recruited by type 2 dentate spikes than mossy cells and fire earlier (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
outcomes.notes: Median DS2 peak ratio GC 6.88 against MC 4.82 (Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.1e-10); median peak time -3.0 against +1.0 ms (P = 2.2e-09). 10 GC and 14 MC dropped for a zero baseline.
deviations: The DS2 events are those stored in the files; the peak-ratio baseline (50 to 100 ms on both sides) is a choice, as the paper does not give it.

outcomes.statement: 5.5% of granule cells monosynaptically excite mossy cells (32 pairs), whereas no mossy cell significantly excites a granule cell.
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission; Figure 3B and 3C
outcomes.notes: Among 4713 GC-MC pairs the automatic test finds 65 GC to MC pairs and 8 MC to GC pairs. The fraction is 0.107 (pairs over GC), 0.0805 (GC with a target over GC) or 0.0138 (pairs over tested pairs), none within 0.0495 to 0.0605. GC to MC pairs outnumber MC to GC pairs 65 to 8. Stricter thresholds lower both counts (56 and 6 at the 99.99999th percentile). For 22 GC to MC pairs the largest bin is the first of the window (1.5 to 2 ms); without them 43 pairs remain (0.0706 of GC). Of the 8 MC to GC pairs, 6 are in YutaMouse33, 4 involve one GC (unit 3 of YutaMouse33-150224) that is also synchronous with each of those MC, and 5 are also detected as GC to MC pairs, which fits common input. In the 17 files that give the shank, 17 of 39 GC to MC pairs are on one shank.
deviations: The paper inspected and refined each detection by hand; the automatic test alone is used here.
The fraction 5.5% can be read three ways; all are shown.

outcomes.statement: Spike transmission probability from granule cells to mossy cells increases from the first to the second spike of a granule cell burst (P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission; Figure 3E to 3G
outcomes.notes: For the 65 detected pairs, the median transmission probability is 0.0066 for first and 0.0334 for second burst spikes, higher in 58 pairs (Wilcoxon P = 1.2e-09); it holds with bursts at 4 ms (P = 4.4e-08) and 10 ms (P = 5.5e-10). The detected pairs are partly reproduced (see monosyn-gc-to-mc) and number 65 against the paper's 32. It also holds with only burst intervals of 3.5 to 6 ms, where the two response windows do not overlap (58 of 65, P = 7.6e-10), with a baseline hollowed by 60% (P = 1.2e-09), and without the 22 first-bin pairs (41 of 43, P = 3.8e-11). First spikes transmit less than single spikes (0.0066 against 0.0147), which the outputs do not explain.
deviations: Bursts are spikes at most 6 ms apart, a choice; the paper does not define them.
Transmission is the excess over the plain Gaussian baseline of the Methods.

outcomes.statement: GC to MC spike transmission is lower during NREM sleep than during waking (n = 31, P < 0.005).
outcomes.notes: For 65 detected pairs, median transmission 0.0125 from GC spikes in awake periods and 0.0108 in NREM, lower in NREM for 34 pairs; Wilcoxon P = 0.39. The pairs are the automatic detections (see monosyn-gc-to-mc), not the paper's 31. Without the 22 first-bin pairs NREM is lower in 24 of 43 (P = 0.27); in the 17 files that give the shank, in 20 of 39 (P = 0.86).
deviations: Uses the automatic pair detections in place of the paper's curated pairs.

outcomes.statement: Synchronous co-activation within 1 ms is found in 23% of mossy cells and 9% of CA3 pyramidal cells, but in fewer than 0.2% of granule cell pairs.
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission
outcomes.notes: GC pairs 4 of 3155 (0.0013, within the claim). MC 0.0766 of pairs or 0.433 of cells; CA3 0.0120 of pairs or 0.102 of cells; none within the tolerance of 0.23 and 0.09. Read as cells, MC and CA3 exceed the GC pair fraction more than ten times. In the 17 files that give the shank no synchronous pair is on one shank (0 of 160 MC, 0 of 51 CA3), so leaving out same-shank pairs changes little (cells MC 0.494, CA3 0.267 there); 143 of 160 synchronous MC pairs are on neighbouring shanks. No synchronous pair shares more than 15% of the sparser unit's spikes within 0.5 ms (MC at most 5.8%), so none looks like one neuron sorted twice.
deviations: Automatic detections without the paper's manual refinement.
Pairs recorded on one shank cannot be left out in 83 of 101 files, which do not give the shank; in the other 17 files none of the synchronous pairs is on one shank.

outcomes.statement: On the circular T-maze, the fraction of active neurons (above 1 Hz) is higher in the central arm than in the side arms, for granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001 for each).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 5B
outcomes.notes: The central-arm median fraction of active units is above the side-arm median for GC (0.020 against 0.018, P = 0.043), MC (0.314 against 0.272, P = 2.2e-06) and CA3 (0.214 against 0.189, P = 0.048); only MC reach P < 0.00001. The bin-wise test treats smoothed, neighbouring bins as independent; compared unit by unit (a variant) the central arm is more active for MC (P = 2.8e-05) but not for GC (higher in 17, lower in 31 of 253 units, P = 0.83) or CA3 (P = 0.21).
deviations: T-maze runs are taken from the start of the central arm to 10 cm before the reward port in trials without light; the paper uses the time from gate opening to arrival at the reward.
The meaning of the linearised T-maze positions is inferred from the values and the maze dimensions.

outcomes.statement: Few granule cells have two or more place fields on the T-maze (6.6%), against 57.8% of mossy cells and 36.1% of CA3 pyramidal cells (Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 5C and 5D
outcomes.notes: Of all units, 4.3% of GC (253), 63.7% of MC (303) and 43.1% of CA3 (341) have two or more fields; of units with a field, 24.4%, 78.1% and 66.8%. No reading puts all three in tolerance (MC misses by 0.001 under reading a). GC have the fewest fields (KS P = 3.2e-53 against MC). The units come from 7 mice; the paper reports 213, 225 and 249 units from 9 mice.
deviations: Fields are counted on a map of the central arm from all runs plus each side arm, smoothed per segment; the paper builds left and right choice maps without saying how fields are combined.
The 'local maximum' of the field rule is taken iteratively from the highest unassigned bin.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells have the lowest within-field peak firing rates (GC against MC, Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.003) and the lowest spatial information of the three types (P < 0.0005).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 5E and 5F
outcomes.notes: Within-field peak GC 2.63 Hz against MC 5.68 Hz (KS P = 4.5e-05); spatial information GC 0.035 bits/s against MC 0.603 (P = 1.6e-49) and CA3 0.293 (P = 1.5e-29).
deviations: As tmaze-multiple-fields.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of splitter cells, whose central-arm firing predicts the coming turn, is comparable in granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells.
outcomes.notes: Splitters 0 of 17 GC, 4 of 179 MC and 4 of 141 CA3 with a central-arm field; chi-square P = 0.76. Fisher's exact test gives P = 1 for GC against MC and against CA3 and 0.73 for MC against CA3. Under equal fractions 0.40 GC splitters would be expected, so the GC comparison has almost no power.
deviations: The paper names no test for comparing the fractions; a chi-square test was fixed in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: For neurons with stable place fields, the remapping index between open fields A and B is above zero in each group (Wilcoxon signed-rank; GC P < 0.05, MC and CA3 P < 0.00001).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 6C and 6D
outcomes.notes: Place cells GC 27, MC 116, CA3 145 (paper 30, 111, 144), of which 27, 116 and 143 have a remapping index; median remapping index 0.128 (P = 0.0013), 0.293 (P = 1.5e-13) and 0.207 (P = 8.6e-14). Units per type 246, 182 and 317 in 5 mice (paper 247, 181, 317 in 5 mice).
deviations: The place-field 'local maximum' is the map's peak; the speed is from positions smoothed over 0.25 s.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells with stable place fields remap less than mossy cells (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.034; post hoc GC against MC P = 0.028).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 6D
outcomes.notes: The GC median index (0.128) is below the MC median (0.293) but neither test is significant (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.306; GC against MC P = 0.114, 0.342 after Bonferroni). With the variant place-cell rule, GC against MC P = 0.0648.
deviations: The paper's post hoc test is not named; Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney tests are used.

outcomes.statement: Only 36.7% of granule cells with place fields (11 of 30) remap, against 61.3% of mossy cells (68 of 111) and 55.6% of CA3 pyramidal cells (80 of 144).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 6C
outcomes.notes: 11 of 27 GC (0.407), 65 of 116 MC (0.560) and 73 of 143 CA3 (0.510) place cells remap. MC and CA3 are within tolerance; GC is 0.003 above it. GC remap least at every threshold shown (0.1 to 0.3).

outcomes.statement: Population-vector remapping is smaller for granule cells than for mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells, for populations of 5, 10, 15 and 20 place cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties; Figure 6E to 6G
outcomes.notes: For 5, 10, 15 and 20 cells, the GC median index (0.162 to 0.210) is below the MC (0.253 to 0.302) and CA3 (0.251 to 0.352) medians, Kruskal-Wallis P from 5.8e-35 to 8.1e-190. 71% to 89% of GC draws fall below the MC median. These P values treat 1000 overlapping draws from the same 27 GC as independent and do not measure the evidence. With all place cells together the index is 0.22 for GC and 0.25 for MC, and permuting the GC and MC labels gives P = 0.32 for that difference.
deviations: Place cells pooled across sessions and mice for the draws; the paper does not say whether it pooled.

outcomes.statement: Mossy cells rarely inherit place fields from single presynaptic granule cells; of 10 place fields of connected granule cells, only 2 overlapped a field of the postsynaptic mossy cell.
outcomes.source: Results, Transmission of place information; Figure 7A and 7B
outcomes.notes: 5 of 16 GC fields (0.31) of GC with a detected MC partner overlap a partner MC field, within the criterion of at most a third; 15 of 23 GC partners have no T-maze field (paper 11 of 18). The result is close to the criterion's limit and uses the automatic pair detections (see monosyn-gc-to-mc). With the partner replaced by a random other MC of the session (1000 draws), the overlap is 0.38 (5th to 95th percentile 0.19 to 0.62) and 33% of draws are at or below 0.31, so the overlap with the connected MC is at the chance level.
deviations: "Rarely" was fixed as at most a third of GC fields; the paper gives 2 of 10.
Pairs are automatic detections, not the paper's curated pairs.

outcomes.statement: In the open fields, the rate maps of connected granule cells and mossy cells are not correlated within the granule cell's place field (median near 0, n = 19, Wilcoxon P = 0.60).
outcomes.source: Results, Transmission of place information; Figure 7J
outcomes.notes: 18 comparisons from 6 pairs in 4 sessions; median r = -0.038, Wilcoxon P = 0.67; 5 of 18 above 0.5 (paper 2 of 19). The 18 comparisons come from only 6 pairs, so they are not independent.
deviations: Pairs are automatic detections; the open-field sessions include the curtain sessions, as the paper's five sessions per pair do.

outcomes.statement: Mossy cells are located deeper than granule cells relative to the reversal of the type 2 dentate spike (DS2) (Mann-Whitney P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Figure 1G; Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells
outcomes.notes: In the 17 files with the wide-band signal and shanks (4 mice; 139 GC, 226 MC with at least 20 spikes in the wide-band window), the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, read from the wide-band signal, has a median of +580 uV for MC and +232 uV for GC (Mann-Whitney P = 2e-40); 100% of MC (to two decimals) and 80% of GC sit where DS2 is positive, and MC are deeper in each of the 4 mice. With the site the electrodes table gives (a variant), +271 against -38 uV (P = 5.7e-09), with YutaMouse33 reversed; the two sites share the LFP column for 9% of units and the DS2 sign for 63%.
deviations: Depth is read from the DS2 amplitude at the site, as the files give no site coordinates; the paper measures distance from the DS2 reversal.

17 of 101 files only. The site is the wide-band column where the unit's spike is largest (300 Hz high-pass, about 150 s of signal per file), as the electrodes table's channel map disagrees with the wide-band signal; the criterion's shank channel taken through the table is shown as a variant.
DS2 amplitude from about 220 s of LFP per file (the two LFP chunks with the most DS2 peaks).

outcomes.statement: K-means clustering on the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, the NREM to wake rate ratio and two principal components of the waveform's second derivative separates excitatory dentate units into granule cells and mossy cells.
outcomes.source: Results; Figure 1D to 1F; STAR Methods, Unit classification
outcomes.notes: On 364 GC and MC of the 17 files (32 dropped for fewer than 20 spikes in the wide-band window, no DS2 site or a zero awake rate), k-means on the DS2 amplitude at the wide-band site, the Methods' NREM to wake ratio and two components of the second derivative of the unfiltered wide-band waveform agrees with the labels for 95.3% of units (93% to 97% by mouse). Without the DS2 amplitude 89.0%, without the first waveform component 88.5%, without the ratio 94.2%. With the log ratio 95.6%, with home-cage awake time 94.8%, with the stored waveforms and the table's site 92.8%.
deviations: Run on 17 of 101 files (364 of 1177 GC and MC); the paper ran it on all excitatory units.
The site and the waveform are read from the wide-band signal (about 150 s per file), as the electrodes table's channel map disagrees with it; the stored waveforms with the table's site are a variant.
Wake is the `awake` periods, as fixed in the criterion; the Methods name awake time in the home cage, shown as a variant.
The four features are standardised and clustered directly; the paper took a second PCA before k-means, which does not change k-means on all components.
The second-derivative window starts at the trough; the Methods say 0 to 0.8 ms without naming the origin.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells reside 59 +- 35 um above the mossy cells they drive.
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission; Figure 3D
outcomes.notes: Needs the positions of the recording sites in um. The electrodes tables give x, y and z as NaN in every file, the order of sites along a shank is not stated, and 83 of 101 files do not say which shank a unit was on. The paper's own monosynaptic pairs were not converted either. The Methods give 8 sites per shank on the 8-shank probes and 10 on the 6-shank probes, staggered with 20 um vertical separation, but the table's site numbers do not follow depth (the DS2 profile along them crosses zero more than once on 43 of 64 shanks with a crossing), and a unit's largest wide-band column lies on the shank the table gives for only 45% of units. In the 17 files that give the shank, the order of each shank's stored waveform channels can be recovered from the units' spikes in the wide-band signal, and along it the DS2 profile crosses zero once on 43 of the 51 shanks that cross, so it is consistent with depth. This attempt wrote no criterion for the claim and ran no test on that order; a new attempt could test it on these 17 files (39 detected GC to MC pairs).

outcomes.statement: Granule cell spikes show a delay from the soma to the proximal dendrites, absent in mossy cells.
outcomes.notes: Needs each unit's waveform along the shank with the sites' vertical positions; the files give no site coordinates (x, y, z are NaN) and the stored waveforms span 1.6 ms at the channels of the shank without their positions. In 83 files the shank itself is not given. The wide-band signal gives each unit's spike on every column, and in those 17 files the order of each shank's stored channels, recovered from the units' spikes, is consistent with depth (see gc-mc-distance). This attempt wrote no criterion for the claim and ran no test of a delay along that order; a new attempt could.

findings.statement: In 24 files the end index of the first unit in the units table is short by a multiple of 65,536 spikes (k = 1 to 7). The missing spikes open the second unit's spike train, which then restarts at the beginning of the recording, so the second unit's times are not sorted. The first moved spike follows the first unit's last stored spike by 2 ms to 0.5 s. This looks like an integer overflow at conversion; the waveforms follow the same boundaries.
The genotypes in the files (6 SST-Cre, 5 Drd2-Cre::Ai35, 4 POMC-Cre::Arch, 1 POMC-Cre::Ai35) do not match the paper's 16 mice (7 SST-Cre, 5 DRD2-Cre::Ai35, 3 POMC-Cre::Ai35 and 1 wild type).

83 of 101 files do not say which shank each unit was recorded on (`shank_id` is a cluster number, and there is no `electrode_group`), and no file gives site coordinates (x, y, z are NaN). The paper's depth measures can be computed for 17 files only, and distances between cells not at all.

The T-maze position series (`twhl_linearized`, `twhl_norm`) are not described. The values show column 0 of `twhl_linearized` runs along the central arm (0 to 2) and column 1 is an angle along the circular side arms, negative for the left arm, which fits the maze in the Methods but is not stated.
The states table holds `awake`, `quiet`, `nrem`, `rem` and `transit` without a description; the paper names wake, NREM and REM, and whether `quiet` counts as wake is not stated.

The interneuron labels (narrow-waveform, wide-waveform) do not say whether the unit is in the dentate gyrus or CA3, which the paper separates; only the excitatory label was split by region (granule cell or CA3 pyramidal cell).

The monosynaptic connections the authors detected and curated (`MonoSynConvClick.mat`) were not converted (the conversion code comments them out), so the pair-based results (Figures 3, 4 and 7) cannot be checked on the authors' pairs.
The dandiset holds 568 mossy cells and 609 granule cells against the paper's 500 and 586, and 237 units labelled `missing` (units of the spike sorting with no row in the authors' unit summary).
The light-pulse series PulseStim_5V_20ms_LD12 of YutaMouse57-161006 holds 89,086 times of which 24,286 are duplicates, and its times decrease once.

The units table has two layouts. 18 files (mice 33, 41, 42 and 54) carry an `electrode_group` column naming each unit's shank, one of them without waveforms (YutaMouse33-150218, which the conversion script lists as excluded); the other 83 files do not.

Seven dates hold two files of one mouse (the second named with `b`). They share no spike trains, so they are different recordings, but the metadata do not say whether they come from a second probe or a second session.
The Methods give a burst index threshold of 1.2 for excitatory cells, and the Figure 1A legend gives 1.8.

In the 17 files with the wide-band signal and each unit's shank, the electrodes table's assignment of columns to shanks and sites disagrees with the data. The column where a unit's spike is largest in the wide-band signal lies on the shank the units table gives for 45% of units (11% to 79% by file) and is the table's own site for 9%, and the DS2 amplitude along the table's site numbers crosses zero more than once on 43 of 64 shanks where it crosses at all. The wide-band and LFP columns match each other. The units' shanks (`electrode_group`) and stored waveform channels fit the wide-band signal under one fixed map of columns, the same in all 4 mice (a map from three mice gives the column of a unit's largest spike for 78% to 89% of units in the fourth, against 5% to 13% for the table), so the error is in the table, whose blocks of 8 rows do not match the probe's columns.

The stored spike waveforms are about 5 times larger than the same spikes in the wide-band signal (median peak-to-peak 421 against 81 uV, 300 Hz high-pass), and their filtering and scaling are not described. They match the wide-band spike best after a 300 Hz high-pass (median correlation 0.987, against 0.981 unfiltered and 0.867 at 800 Hz), with a gain of 5.08, close to 5.13, the inverse of the wide-band conversion of 0.195 uV per count, which is consistent with waveforms stored in ADC counts and read as microvolts. Each holds 1.6 ms with the trough at 0.8 ms, which cuts off the peak of 43% of GC, 67% of MC and 78% of CA3 waveforms.

attempts.paper_title: A NWB-based dataset and processing pipeline of human single-neuron activity during a declarative memory task
attempts.entry_title: Human single neurons during a recognition memory task (Chandravadia et al. 2020)
attempts.description: Tests the data descriptor of Chandravadia et al. (2020) on dandiset 000004, which holds 87 sessions of 59 epilepsy patients with single units from the amygdala and hippocampus during a new/old recognition task. It checks the files against the paper's description of the data records and subjects, and repeats the behavioural results (AUC, ROC asymmetry, accuracy by confidence) and the proportions of visually and memory selective cells of Figure 5.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Chandravadia et al. (2020) from dandiset 000004

outcomes.statement: The dataset holds 1863 single neurons recorded from the medial temporal lobes of 59 subjects.
outcomes.source: Abstract; Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells
outcomes.notes: 1864 unit rows over 87 files (paper 1863, one more) and 59 subjects. With the 55 units of sessions 44 and 55 counted once, as their spike trains repeat those of sessions 43 and 54, 1809. Both readings are within tolerance. CS sessions hold 1787 units and TWH sessions 77. The paper gives no count per session or site, so the extra unit cannot be identified; no unit is empty (the fewest spikes is 22).
deviations: The exact count differs from the paper's by one unit; the tolerance is the protocol's 10%.

outcomes.statement: The patients performed 87 sessions, listed by subject and session id in Online-only Table 1 (the Methods give 89).
outcomes.notes: The 87 (subject, session) pairs of the files equal those of Online-only Table 1, none missing and none extra. The Methods' 89 sessions disagree with the table and the files. Every task variant of the table corresponds to one stimulus set in the files.

outcomes.statement: Online-only Table 1 gives the age and sex of every subject; there are 25 female and 34 male subjects.
outcomes.notes: Age and sex match for 56 of 59 subjects. C24 is 57 in the files and 47 in the table, H33 is 30 and 29, and H48 is female aged 32 in the files and male aged 54 in the table. The files have 26 female and 33 male subjects (table 25 and 34), within tolerance. Each subject has one age and one sex across its files. The diagnosis text differs for 19 of 59 subjects. For 8 the files give a broader category; for 6 (H10, H16, H17, H19, C58, T89) they give Lateral Frontal, which adds Lateral to the table's Frontal except for H17 (Left Inferior Frontal in the table). Five differ in substance, C61 (Left Lateral Frontal in the files, Left Mesial Temporal in the table), C34 (Bilateral Independent Temporal against Bilateral Mesial Temporal), C56 and H51, where the files leave out part of the table's diagnosis (orbitofrontal, temporal), and T90, where they add Bilateral. All 87 files have the age and sex of their section in the code's session list, defineNOsessions_release.ini, as printed in the notebook.

outcomes.statement: Each session has 100 encoding trials showing 100 novel images and 100 recognition trials, of which 50 show new and 50 old images, and the images come from 5 visual categories.
outcomes.source: Methods, Task; Data Records, stimuli group; Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells
outcomes.notes: All 87 sessions have 100 recognition trials with 50 per label, 5 categories (ids and names) and one stored image per trial timestamped at its onset. 79 sessions have 100 encoding trials with 100 distinct images; sessions 18, 20, 21, 23, 26, 27 and 44 have 50 and session 123 has 97. In these eight sessions 2% to 48% of the images shown as old have no encoding trial in the file. The images are stored as one ImageSeries per file, not as stimuli_learn_x and stimuli_recog_x.

outcomes.statement: In the trials table, new_old_labels_recog is 0 for old stimuli (seen during encoding) and 1 for new stimuli.
outcomes.notes: The labels are coded the other way. In 79 of 87 sessions every label-1 image and no label-0 image was shown during encoding; in no session do label-0 images match the encoding block. Label 1 draws "old" responses (4 to 6) more often than label 0 in 86 of 87 sessions (medians 0.70 and 0.24, sign test p = 1.1e-24). In the 8 sessions with short encoding blocks, 52% to 98% of the label-1 images are among the stored encoding trials and no label-0 image is. The paper's code reads 1 as old, and every analysis here does the same; with the stated coding the mean AUC is 0.247.

outcomes.statement: The events stream holds the TTL markers 55, 1, 2, 3, 20 or 21, 31 to 36, 6 and 66 with the meanings of Table 1, and the events and experiment_ids streams have one entry each, in the same order.
outcomes.notes: Events and experiment_ids have the same length and timestamps in all 87 files, and 17019 of 17047 trials show the codes 1, 2, 3, a response and 6 in order. 78 files meet every condition. Codes not in Table 1 occur in sessions 43 (98, 99), 58 (23), 93 (99), 123 (0), 127 (0), 128 (4), 2001 (22, 23), 2002 (23) and 2003 (23). Seven files (sessions 92, 93, 96, 97, 99, 100, 101) have no start code 55 and session 2001 has a third end code 66; these do not enter the criterion. In every trial that shows the sequence the response is of its phase's kind (20 or 21 in learning, 31 to 36 in recognition), 17019 of 17019. In 6 files 1 to 18 trials have a response event that differs from the trials table's response_value; the analysis uses response_value.
deviations: The criterion did not give a number for most files in a partial result; 78 of 87 was taken as most.

outcomes.statement: The learning block is labelled with one of 80, 83 or 88 and the recognition block with one of 81, 84 or 89.
outcomes.notes: 83 of 87 files use the ids of Table 2. Session 55 uses 80 and 82, session 77 uses 81 and 82, and sessions 100 and 105 use 82 and 83 (learning and recognition, identified by their responses). The files' data_collection field states the same ids.

outcomes.statement: To protect patient information, session_start_time keeps only the year and month of the experiment, with the day set to the first of the month for all sessions.
outcomes.source: Data Records, structure of the NWB file
outcomes.notes: 86 of 87 files start on the first of a month; session 48 starts on 2010-03-13. Session 68 is dated 2000-01-01, outside the 2006 to 2019 span of the others.

outcomes.statement: The units table holds spike_times, waveform_mean_encoding, waveform_mean_recognition (sampled at 100 kHz), origClusterID, SNR, IsolDist and electrodes, with one electrode per neuron.
outcomes.notes: All 87 files hold every column (IsolDist is named IsolationDist) and link each unit to one electrode. The stated waveform sampling rate is 98400 Hz, within tolerance of 100 kHz, with 256 samples. SNR is finite for 1778 of 1864 units (11 infinite, 75 NaN); the isolation distance is NaN for 493 units and above 1e4 for 4 (up to 8.08e+32). Spike times are not in increasing order for 13 units in sessions 21, 58, 68, 70, 73, 77 and 128, and units 35 and 37 of session 58 hold every spike time twice.

outcomes.statement: The electrodes table gives each electrode's brain area, MNI coordinates, impedance, the filter applied before spike sorting (300 to 3000 Hz) and the original hardware channel.
outcomes.source: Data Records, general group; Methods, data acquisition
outcomes.notes: Location, filtering (300-3000Hz for all) and origChannel are filled for all 887 electrodes. The impedance column is stored as NaN (float64) for all 887. Coordinates are missing for 99 electrodes in sessions 7, 20, 21, 23, 24, 50, 52 and 2004; where given, the sign of x matches the hemisphere of the location for all 788.

outcomes.statement: Clusters were accepted as units only when fewer than 3% of their interspike intervals were shorter than 3 ms.
outcomes.notes: 1858 of 1864 units (99.7%) have fewer than 3% of interspike intervals below 3 ms (median 0.19%). Six units are at or above 3%, four at or above 5% and two above 20% (maximum 50.1%); the two above 20% are the session 58 units whose spike times repeat. With the spike times as stored, 1860 units pass. All 77 TWH units pass.

outcomes.statement: All neurons were recorded from the medial temporal lobe, in the amygdala and the hippocampus.
outcomes.notes: All 1864 units are on electrodes in the right amygdala (594), left amygdala (498), right hippocampus (407) or left hippocampus (365).

outcomes.statement: Subjects distinguished new from old images; the behavioural AUC averaged over all sessions is 0.74 ± 0.10.
outcomes.notes: Mean AUC 0.753, SD 0.094 over 87 sessions (range 0.445 to 0.919; 6 sessions below 0.6, one at or below 0.5). Against chance (0.5), t = 25.1, p = 2.2e-41. With sessions 44 and 55 dropped, 0.754 and 0.095. Recomputed with the label coding the paper states (0 = old), the mean AUC is 0.247 (0.081 to 0.555).
deviations: The tolerance of the mean is the stated spread (0.10), as the protocol prescribes; the spread itself was held to 10%.

outcomes.statement: Performance was similar at the two study sites, with an average AUC of 0.74 ± 0.09 for CS sessions and 0.69 ± 0.13 for TWH sessions.
outcomes.notes: CS 0.760 ± 0.085 over 78 sessions and TWH 0.688 ± 0.138 over 9, all within tolerance. Welch's t-test between sites p = 0.161 (difference 0.072).

outcomes.statement: The ROC curve is asymmetric (p < 0.05), as expected for declarative memory.
outcomes.notes: Six sessions (59, 60, 93, 99, 119, 2008) have all five interior z(FA) or z(H) points equal, so their fitted slope is not an estimate (negative in four, 0 in one); they are left out. Over the other 81 sessions the z-ROC slope has mean 0.792, median 0.795, SD 0.289, and is below 1 in 64. One-sample t-test against 1, t = -6.49, p = 6.6e-09; Wilcoxon W = 487, p = 3.3e-08. With all 87 sessions, mean 0.726, below 1 in 70, t-test p = 1.631e-09, Wilcoxon p = 1.586e-09. The pooled ROC has slope 0.816. Per-session AUC and slopes are printed.
deviations: The paper names no measure or test for asymmetry; the z-ROC slope of the paper's code and a t-test against 1 were fixed in the criterion.
Sessions whose interior z-ROC points do not allow a fit are left out of the mean and the tests, after the second verification round; all 87 sessions are a variant.

outcomes.statement: Accuracy is significantly higher in high than in low confidence trials (P < 0.001, paired t test) across all sessions.
outcomes.notes: Fixed split, high 80.1% against low 60.9% over 84 sessions, high above low in 73, paired t-test p = 3.2e-16. Dynamic split, 78.3% against 60.4%, paired p = 1.2e-13. Sessions 93, 99 and 2008 have no responses in one group and are left out. The unpaired test of the code gives p = 3.4e-17 and 1.3e-15.
deviations: Three sessions without responses in one confidence group are left out; the paper says all sessions.

outcomes.statement: 343 of the 1863 cells (18.4%) are visually selective, by a one-way ANOVA (P < 0.05) of the firing rate in recognition trials, in a 1 s window starting 200 ms after stimulus onset, across the 5 visual categories.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells; Figure 5f
outcomes.notes: Methods' window (200 to 1200 ms), 332 of 1864 units (17.8%), within tolerance. The code's window (200 to 1700 ms) gives 343 of 1864 (18.4%), the paper's count. Counting duplicated spike trains once, 326 of 1809 (18.0%). Shuffled categories give 4.7% (10 shuffles per unit). At p < 0.01, 8.6%; at p < 0.1, 25.6%. Among sessions with at least 20 units, 0.0% to 35.7%.
deviations: The main result uses the Methods' 1 s window; the paper's code uses 1.5 s, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: 146 of the 1863 cells (7.8%) are memory selective, by a two-tailed bootstrap comparison of mean firing rates (1,000 runs, P < 0.05) between the 50 novel and 50 familiar recognition trials in a 1 s window starting 200 ms after stimulus onset.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells; Figure 5f
outcomes.notes: The Methods' test (all 50 new and 50 old trials, 200 to 1200 ms) selects 110 of 1864 units (5.9%), against the paper's 146 (7.8%). With labels shuffled (10 per unit, 18640 tests) 5.39% are selected (95% CI 5.07% to 5.73%); 110 is not distinguishable from this null (one-sided binomial p = 0.18) and only just above 5% (p = 0.044). A second bootstrap seed gives 118 (6.3%), also outside tolerance; 22 units are selected under one seed only. Correct trials only in the Methods' window give 143 and 140 under the two seeds, and the code's choices (correct trials only, 200 to 1700 ms) 147 and 149, all within tolerance (147 against 5%, p = 7.1e-08). With labels shuffled among the correct trials in the code's window the null is 5.58% (95% CI 5.26% to 5.92%), and 147 exceeds it (104.1 expected, one-sided binomial p = 2.5e-05). All trials in the code's window give 108 and 109. The paper's number therefore follows its code's restriction to correct trials, which the Methods do not mention, and the outcome comes from that disagreement, not from the data. It is judged on the Methods' procedure, as the protocol requires. Per-unit p-values of the 288 units selected under some reading or seed are printed.
deviations: The paper's code restricts the test to correct trials and uses a 1.5 s window; the Methods describe all 50 and 50 trials and a 1 s window. The Methods give the main result.
The bootstrap uses the code's algorithm with a fixed seed.

outcomes.statement: 26 cells (1.4%) are both visually and memory selective.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells; Figure 5f
outcomes.notes: Under the Methods' tests 12 of 1864 units (0.6%) are both VS and MS, against 19.6 expected if the two were independent and the paper's 26 (1.4%); 14 with the second bootstrap seed. The code's choices give 26 (1.4%) under both seeds. Counting duplicated spike trains once, 11 of 1809. As for ms-cells-proportion, the outcome comes from the Methods disagreeing with the code.
deviations: Depends on ms-cells-proportion, whose main test follows the Methods and not the code.

outcomes.statement: The percentages of VS, MS and dual cells are comparable between CS sessions (18.4%, 7.7% and 1.4%) and the new TWH sessions (19.4%, 10.4% and 1.3%).
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells; Figure 5f (the values as written into plotFigure5.ipynb at commit 1d95162)
outcomes.notes: Fisher's exact test finds no difference between sites (VS p = 0.360, MS p = 0.215, dual p = 1.000). Under the Methods' tests CS has 17.6%, 5.8% and 0.7% and TWH 22.1%, 9.1% and 0.0%; only CS VS is within tolerance. The code's choices give CS 18.4%, 7.8% and 1.4% (328, 139 and 25 of 1787) and TWH 19.5%, 10.4% and 1.3% (15, 8 and 1 of 77), matching Figure 5f to within 0.1 point, so the partial outcome comes from the Methods disagreeing with the code. With 77 TWH units the 95% intervals of the TWH percentages are 13.4% to 33.0% (VS), 3.7% to 17.8% (MS) and 0.0% to 4.7% (dual), so the Fisher tests have little power.
deviations: The paper names no test for "comparable"; Fisher's exact test was fixed in the criterion.
The expected values come from plotFigure5.ipynb, which writes them into the plot as constants.

outcomes.statement: The dataset includes 9 sessions from a new institution, Toronto Western Hospital.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, proportion of selective cells; Online-only Table 1
outcomes.notes: Sessions 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2009 and 2011, from 8 subjects, with 77 units; all name Toronto Western Hospital as institution.

outcomes.statement: Neuron 132-177-4-RA (session 132, channel 177, cell 4, right amygdala) is visually selective, responding most to images of animals.
outcomes.notes: Session 132 has one unit on channel 177, at electrode row 4 in the right amygdala, which matches the label 132-177-4-RA. It is the file's unit at 0-based index 4 of 8, so the label's cell number equals both its electrode row and its 0-based unit index. ANOVA across categories p = 1.2e-22 (Methods' window) and 7.9e-19 (code's window); mean rate 6.75 Hz for animals against 0.25 to 0.85 Hz for the other four categories.

outcomes.statement: The sessions of the earlier release (Faraut et al. 2018) are found in this dandiset under the same subject, session id and task variant.
outcomes.source: Faraut et al. 2018, Scientific Data 5, 180010 (doi:10.1038/sdata.2018.10), Table 1
outcomes.notes: 64 of the 65 sessions of Table 1 of Faraut et al. 2018 (98.5%) are in the dandiset by session id, all under the same subject and task variant. Session 98 of subject H48 is not; its section in the code's session list is commented out. Age and sex agree for 39 of the 42 matched subjects; C24, H33 and H48 differ, the same three that differ from Online-only Table 1, whose values the 2018 table shares.
deviations: The claim was added after the first verification round, to link the earlier release's session list to the dandiset for previous-release-additions.

outcomes.statement: Relative to the earlier release of this task's data (Faraut et al. 2018), this release adds 23 sessions, 17 subjects and 288 neurons.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset has 23 sessions not in the earlier list (14 CS, 9 TWH) from 17 subjects with no earlier session, the paper's numbers. The new sessions hold 325 units, outside the tolerance of 288; the sessions also in the earlier release hold 1539 units, where Faraut et al. 2018 gives 1576 neurons for 65 sessions. 1576 + 288 = 1864, the dandiset's unit count, so the paper's 288 matches a difference of totals and not a count of the new sessions. The differences of the stated totals are 22 sessions, 17 subjects and 287 neurons. The link holds for 64 of 65 earlier sessions; the missing session 98 does not change which sessions or subjects are new, and may account for part of the difference in the earlier sessions' unit count.
deviations: The earlier release's session list is Table 1 of Faraut et al. 2018, not its Dryad archive, which refuses automated download (HTTP 403 on the file stream, and its API asks for a bearer token).
In the first version of this attempt the claim was blocked for want of the list; it was tested after the first verification round.

outcomes.statement: Neuron 144-140-3-RH (session 144, channel 140, cell 3, right hippocampus) is visually selective for phones.
outcomes.notes: The neuron's session id, 144, is not among the dandiset's 87 sessions, nor in Online-only Table 1 or in the session list of the paper's code. The paper's demo script (python/export/demo/export.py, printed, not run) sets NOID 144 under the comment session 'TWH103_111918', and the code's session list gives subject T103 one section, session 2009. In session 2009 two units are on channel 140 in the right hippocampus (unit indices 1 and 2, both at electrode row 1, clusters 352 and 414); unit 2 is visually selective (ANOVA p = 1.3e-09) and fires most to phones. The Figure 4 neuron's cell number 4 is its electrode row and its 0-based unit index (its 1-based index is 5); under that convention the candidate is cell 2 or 1, not 3. With neither the cell number nor a recorded mapping of 144 to 2009, the neuron cannot be identified. The candidates and the cell-number test are printed in the notebook.

findings.statement: The new_old_labels_recog column is described in every file, and in the paper, as 0 for old and 1 for new stimuli. The data have 1 for old; label-1 images are those shown during encoding and draw most "old" responses. The paper's code reads it correctly, but a user following the description gets an AUC of 0.25.

Sessions 43 and 44 (subject H23) and sessions 54 and 55 (subject H42) hold identical spike trains for every unit, 23 and 32 units. In each pair the units are the same neurons, so 55 of the 1864 units are repeats and the paper's neuron count includes them twice. Session 55 also repeats session 54's learning block trial for trial and differs only in its recognition block.

Seven sessions (18, 20, 21, 23, 26, 27, 44) have 50 encoding trials and session 123 has 97, where the paper describes 100. Only 52% to 98% of the images later shown as old are in the stored encoding blocks of these sessions.
Electrode impedance is empty for all 887 electrodes, though the paper lists it in the electrodes table. MNI coordinates are missing for 99 electrodes in 8 sessions.
The isolation distance is NaN for 493 of 1864 units and implausibly large for 4 (up to 8.08e+32), and SNR is NaN for 75 units and infinite for 11.

The spike times of 13 units in 7 sessions (21, 58, 68, 70, 73, 77, 128) are not in increasing order, and units 35 and 37 of session 58 hold every spike time twice, which doubles their firing rates and puts half their interspike intervals at zero.

Age or sex differ from the paper's Online-only Table 1 for three subjects (C24 57 against 47, H33 30 against 29, H48 female 32 against male 54). The files follow the code's session list; Table 1 of Faraut et al. 2018 gives the same values as Online-only Table 1.

Session 48 keeps the day of the experiment (2010-03-13) in session_start_time, where the paper says every day was set to the first of the month to protect patient information. Session 68 is dated 2000-01-01.

Experiment ids outside Table 2 are used in four files (sessions 55, 77, 100, 105), and event codes outside Table 1 (0, 4, 22, 23, 98, 99) occur in nine files. In six files 1 to 18 trials have a response event that differs from the trials table's response_value.
The Methods state 89 sessions; Online-only Table 1 and the dandiset have 87. The paper gives 1863 neurons; the dandiset has 1864 unit rows.

The Methods select memory selective cells by comparing all 50 novel and 50 familiar trials in a 1 s window. The paper's code uses correct trials only and a 200 to 1700 ms window for both selections. The paper's counts (343 VS, 146 MS, 26 dual) and Figure 5f follow the code; the Methods' procedure gives 332, 110 and 12.
plotFigure5.ipynb, the notebook the code provides to reproduce Figure 5, writes the per-site percentages of Figure 5f into the plot as constants and does not compute them.

The example neuron of Figure 3 is labelled as from session 144, which is not in the dandiset or in the paper's session list. The paper's code names NOID 144 as a recording of subject T103, whose one session in the dandiset is 2009, but nothing maps 144 to 2009.
Session 98 of subject H48, listed in the earlier release (Faraut et al. 2018, Table 1), is not in the dandiset or in Online-only Table 1; its section in the code's session list is commented out.
The 23 sessions that are new relative to the earlier release hold 325 units, where the paper says 288 neurons were added; 288 is the dandiset's 1864 units minus the earlier release's 1576.
The institution is written "Hunigton Memorial Hospital" in 28 files and "Hunington Memorial Hospital" in 6, and the device as "Neuralynx-cheetah" and "Neuralynx-Cheetah".

attempts.paper_title: Layer 4 fast-spiking interneurons filter thalamocortical signals during active somatosensation
attempts.entry_title: VPM and layer 4 responses to touch and whisking (Yu et al. 2016)
attempts.description: Tests the findings stated in the abstract of Yu, Gutnisky, Hires and Svoboda (2016) on dandiset 000005, which holds silicon probe recordings in VPM and single-cell recordings in layer 4 of barrel cortex of mice locating a pole with their whiskers. It measures touch responses and whisking modulation of VPM units, light-tagged GABAergic (FS) cells and broad-spiking excitatory cells, and the effect of the PV-Cre and VPM-site light. The full text is not open access.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Yu et al. (2016) from dandiset 000005

outcomes.statement: Neurons in the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) fire in response to touch in mice locating objects with their whiskers.
outcomes.notes: 20 of 24 included VPM units (0.83) fire more 0 to 25 ms after a touch onset than 25 to 0 ms before it (one-sided Wilcoxon over touches, p < 0.01); 0 of 24 with spikes moved to the next trial. Median touch response 7.5 Hz (rate 25.0 Hz after, 14.4 Hz before). At least one responsive unit in each of the 6 mice. 5 of 29 units were dropped for too few spikes or touches in trials without light.
deviations: The full text was not available; the touch window, the test and the threshold are choices made here, and no number of the paper is compared.

outcomes.statement: VPM neurons fire in response to whisker movement.
outcomes.notes: 21 of 24 VPM units (0.88) are modulated by whisking phase away from touch under the occupancy-corrected test with a trial-shift null (p < 0.01), against 0.12 with spikes moved to the next trial, so the test marks about ten times its nominal rate on the null; this does not bring 0.88 near 0.5. 23 of 24 fire more during whisking than at rest (median 12.78 against 3.78 Hz, p = 1.2e-06). With a 5 degree whisking threshold, 0.92. One mouse (2 units) has no modulated unit. The paper's measure (r2 of a sinusoid fit above 0.25) marks 0.96, but it marks 0.33 to 0.40 of L4 cells with spikes moved to the next trial. The first version of the test (Rayleigh) gave 0.92 with the true alignment and 0.88 with the wrong one.
deviations: The whisking test of the claims file (a Rayleigh test of spike phases) was replaced after the first run, because its null control marked 0.88 of units as modulated with spikes in the wrong trial; the claims file records the amendment and what had been seen. Both versions are shown.

The whisking band (6 to 30 Hz), threshold (2.5 degrees) and the measure are choices made here. The paper judges modulation by the r2 of a sinusoid fit (Supp. Fig. 2e), read after the criteria were written; it is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: L4 fast-spiking (FS) interneurons inherit the responses of VPM, firing in response to both touch and whisker movement.
outcomes.notes: 20 tagged cells (10 mice) are included; 13 (0.65) are touch-responsive, 16 (0.80) are modulated by whisking phase, 11 are both. Median touch response 34.9 Hz, whisking modulation 2.64 Hz (VPM 1.30 Hz, Mann-Whitney p = 0.085). Unchanged with tag thresholds 0.1 and 0.3. 4 of the 20 come from 2 mice flagged as lacking touch input (probably ION-transected) and none of them responds to touch; without them 0.81 of 16 are touch-responsive and 0.81 modulated. With the paper's r2 measure, 0.80 are modulated. With spikes moved to the next trial, 0 of 20 pass either test. 3 of 23 tagged cells were dropped for lack of a named principal whisker; 2 included cells have fewer than 99 null draws, so p < 0.01 was out of reach for them.
deviations: FS cells are identified here as cells spiking within 6 ms of isolated 5 ms light pulses in VGAT-ChR2 mice (23 cells, all tagged from the vS1 site or the site labelled VPM and vS1, at 1.6 to 4.6 ms latency). The paper also requires a spike waveform inside a boundary of peak-to-trough ratio and duration (Supp. Fig. 6), not given in numbers, so the tagged cells may include non-FS interneurons.
The files do not mark ION-transected mice, so their cells are in the group; leaving out the mice flagged as lacking touch input is shown as a variant.
The whisking test was amended as for vpm-whisking.

outcomes.statement: In contrast with VPM neurons and L4 FS interneurons, L4 excitatory neurons respond mainly to touch.
outcomes.notes: Touch selectivity of the 18 included excitatory cells (median 0.980) is not significantly higher than that of FS cells (0.916, one-sided Mann-Whitney p = 0.074) or VPM units (0.883, p = 0.090). The test is fragile. Selectivity rests on few spikes (median 23 in the 25 ms after touches; 8 of 18 cells at exactly 0 or 1). Without the mice flagged as lacking touch input the excitatory cells are more selective than both groups (p = 0.024 and 0.038), and so are the 12 excitatory cells with at least 20 spikes in the touch windows (p = 0.003 and 0.005). These do not decide the outcome, as the flag is inferred from touch responses and both selections favour the claim. Only isolated touches gives p = 0.084 and 0.131; widths of 0.7 ms gives 0.112 and 0.126. The measures the criterion reports go the claim's way, 0.28 of excitatory cells are modulated by whisking against 0.80 of FS cells (Fisher p = 0.0016) and 0.88 of VPM units (p = 0.00011), and a selectivity built from the whisking-minus-rest rate is higher than both (p = 0.047 and 0.032). 0.56 of excitatory cells are touch-responsive (FS 0.65, VPM 0.83). Of the 53 untagged whole-cell cells, 26 have fewer than 5 spikes and 5 more too few spikes or touches, so the group holds the cells that fire most, against the 37 whole-cell excitatory cells of the paper.
deviations: Excitatory cells are identified here as untagged whole-cell cells with action potentials at least 0.6 ms wide at half maximum (22 cells). The paper's excitatory group also holds cell-attached cells (Supplementary Table 2) and leaves out ION-transected mice, which the files do not mark.
The touch selectivity index is a choice made here; the paper's measure is not known.

outcomes.statement: FS interneurons reduce movement-related spiking in L4 excitatory neurons; silencing them increases the spiking of excitatory neurons during whisker movement.
outcomes.notes: In PV-Cre mice, inside the vS1 light window (about 0.8 to 2.3 s after the trial start), the rate of excitatory cells during non-touch whisking rises in 6 of 7 cells (median 0.05 Hz without light, 1.07 Hz with; one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.016), from 4 mice; the seventh has no spikes during whisking in either condition. The evidence is thin. 4 cells come from anm266945 (without it 3 of 3 rise, p = 0.125), and several rates rest on 0 to 10 spikes. Over the whole light window 5 of 7 rise (p = 0.188), and the phase modulation rises in 3 of 6 (p = 0.219). The mice whisk and touch about as much with light as without (0.35 against 0.29 s of whisking, 3.4 against 3.6 touches per trial). The PV-Cre juxtacellular cells not suppressed by light, mostly excitatory by Supplementary Table 2 (38 of 42 cell-attached PV-Cre cells), rise in 24 of 32 (p = 0.00042), but that selection is biased toward a rise and does not decide the outcome. The light cuts the firing of 3 PV-Cre cells by more than half, as for the 3 of 4 PV cells inhibited in Supp. Fig. 13a.
deviations: The supplement (read after the first run) states that this light drives eNpHR in PV cells; the files do not name the opsin.
7 whole-cell excitatory cells decide; the paper's PV-Cre excitatory cells are mostly cell-attached, and the juxtacellular cells are shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: By suppressing movement-related spiking, FS interneurons enhance the selectivity of L4 excitatory neurons for touch.
outcomes.notes: Touch selectivity inside the light window is lower with light in 2 of 6 excitatory cells (median 0.083 without light, 0.949 with; one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.953). The touch response rises with the light (median 0.4 to 8.62 Hz, 5 of 7) more than the whisking modulation does. Without light three cells sit at selectivity 0 because their touch response in the window is below zero, on 0 to 13 spikes after touches, so the measure is near its floor there. In the 30 juxtacellular PV-Cre cells not suppressed by light, selectivity is lower with light in 14 (median 0.885 against 0.881, p = 0.613). The first (uncorrected) version gives lower selectivity in 1 of 5.
deviations: As for fs-suppress-movement-spiking; the selectivity index is a choice made here, and the touch counts inside the light window are smaller than over whole trials.

outcomes.statement: Thalamic activity drives L4 FS interneurons.
outcomes.notes: With light at the site labelled VPM (250 pulses over 0.32 to 2.82 s, 100 Hz as in Supp. Fig. 9i), the rate of all 9 tagged FS cells falls (median 17.9 to 7.7 Hz, median ratio 0.40, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.00195), and so does their rate during non-touch whisking (9 of 9). The mice whisk less with the light (0.60 against 0.99 s per trial in the window, touches 5.13 against 4.45), so the whisking-period rate is the stronger evidence. The cells come from 2 mice. The drop is not specific to FS cells; 18 of 21 cells recorded with this light fire less.
deviations: The VPM-site light in VGAT-ChR2 mice is taken as the paper's thalamic photoinhibition, which the supplement describes as a 100 Hz train of 5 ms pulses; the files do not say what the light does, and its wavelength is given as 594 nm.

outcomes.statement: The movement-related activity of L4 FS interneurons is driven by sensory input (reafference through the thalamus), not by a corollary discharge from motor areas.
outcomes.source: Abstract; Figure 7 title; Supplementary Figures 6, 11 and 12 legends
outcomes.notes: The supplement (Supp. Figs. 6, 11 and 12) shows the test, the spike-phase relationship of FS cells in control and ION-transected mice. Supplementary Table 2 counts 9 transected VGAT-ChR2 mice with 9 whole-cell excitatory and 10 cell-attached FS cells. The files hold as many VGAT-ChR2 cells per recording mode as the table, but no file marks the transected mice; the files hold no surgery, notes or lesion field. The notebook flags 4 mice whose cells have no touch input (anm273341, anm275231, anm318530, anm318532), with a rule chosen after seeing the values. Their 4 included tagged cells respond to touch in none, are modulated by whisking in 3, with lower modulation (1.12 against 2.90 Hz in 16 cells of 8 other mice, p = 0.061) and no lower sinusoid r2 (0.50 against 0.53). This is not a test of the claim. The light at the site labelled vM1 is not part of the paper's described test.

findings.statement: No L4 file names the cell type of its neuron (excitatory or FS). The cell types the paper compares can only be inferred from the data, here from light tagging in VGAT-ChR2 mice and from action potential width.

No file marks the mice whose infraorbital nerve was transected (9 VGAT-ChR2 mice in Supplementary Table 2 of the paper), and the files hold no surgery or notes field. Their cells cannot be told from control cells except by inference; 4 mice whose cells have no touch input are probably among them. This blocks the test of Figure 7, and these cells may be mixed into any analysis of control cells.

The genotype is missing for the 6 VPM mice (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP in Supplementary Table 1) and for 3 L4 mice (anm260074 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP, anm223517 PV-IRES-Cre x Ai32, anm250509 PV-ChR2), and the 5 SOM-IRES-Cre x Ai32 mice are given as Ai32.
Every L4 file gives cortical layer 4 (depth 0.42 to 0.62 mm), though the paper's waveform analysis (Supp. Fig. 6) includes L5 cells; the layer of each cell cannot be checked.

The optogenetic conditions are not described. `photo_stim_mode` has an empty description and its labels do not map to one kind of light (VPM-site pulse trains are labelled `5ms_pulse` in early files and `shift` in later ones); `photo_stim_power` is NaN in every L4 file; no file names the opsin. The light epochs can be read only from the photostimulation series.

The session description gives the wrong recording mode for 24 of 130 L4 files, all from PV-Cre mice. 23 described as whole-cell hold traces near 0 mV with small extracellular spikes, as juxtacellular recordings do, and one described as juxtacellular sits near -65 mV. By the trace, PV-Cre has 9 whole-cell and 39 juxtacellular cells where Supplementary Table 2 has 5 and 42.

In the L4 files the trial table's `first_touch_time` is the trial start plus the true first-touch latency divided by 1000 (it matches the touch onset series within 2 ms in 0.956 of trials once multiplied by 1000). In the VPM files it is correct.

The L4 trace is sampled at 10 kHz in files up to March 2015 and at 20 kHz from late August 2015 on, with trials of 5.2 or 5.5 s at 10 kHz and 5.9 s at 20 kHz; nothing but the timestamps states the rate.
8 files name no principal whisker, and the VPM files give one principal whisker per file though the session description says each unit has its own.

The light at the site labelled VPM in VGAT-ChR2 mice is given as 594 nm, and isolated pulses at the site labelled vS1 (594 nm) evoke short-latency spikes in VGAT-ChR2 cells; these wavelengths may be worth checking against the experiment.

The paper's full text is not open access and neither it nor the dandiset links analysis code. The public supplement names the measures (a sinusoid fit of rate against phase, a waveform boundary for FS cells) but not their windows, bins or boundaries.

attempts.paper_title: Distinct descending motor cortex pathways and their roles in movement
attempts.entry_title: Two types of pyramidal tract neuron in mouse motor cortex (Economo et al. 2018)
attempts.description: Tests the findings in the abstract of Economo et al. (2018) that dandiset 000006 can test. The dandiset holds silicon probe recordings from the anterior lateral motor cortex of 12 mice in a delayed response task, with tagged PTupper and PTlower units. The notebook measures the selectivity for lick direction of the tagged units in the sample, delay and response epochs, and compares the two types. The transcriptomic and anatomical findings are not testable on it.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Economo et al. (2018) from dandiset 000006

outcomes.statement: Single-cell transcriptional profiling and axonal reconstructions identify two types of pyramidal tract (PT) neuron in motor cortex.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds electrophysiology only. The single-cell RNA-seq was described in an earlier paper, the bulk RNA-seq is at GEO (GSE119182), and Seq.zip and Axons.zip of the Figshare record hold sequencing and axon data; none is in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Both types of PT neuron project to several targets in the basal ganglia and brainstem.
outcomes.notes: No anatomy or axonal reconstructions are in the dandiset; Anatomy.zip and Axons.zip of the Figshare record hold them.

outcomes.statement: One type of PT neuron projects to thalamic regions that connect back to motor cortex.
outcomes.notes: No anatomy is in the dandiset. The files label tagged units PTupper without naming a projection target; the link to thalamus-projecting neurons comes from the paper's code.

outcomes.statement: The second type of PT neuron projects to motor centres in the medulla.
outcomes.notes: No anatomy is in the dandiset. The files label tagged units PTlower without naming a projection target; the link to medulla-projecting neurons comes from the paper's code.

outcomes.statement: Descending PT neurons in layer 5 of motor cortex carry preparatory activity, which predicts the upcoming movement before it is initiated.
outcomes.source: Abstract (stated as background to the study)
outcomes.notes: 72 of 100 included tagged units are selective for lick direction in the delay epoch (rank-sum p < 0.01); the label-shuffle null has a 99th percentile of 0.040 (p = 0.001). PTupper 29 of 44, PTlower 43 of 56; every animal 25% to 85%. 76 units at p < 0.05 and 67 at p < 0.001. The selective units lie at nominal depths of 430 to 1600 um; the files give no layer per unit, so the statement's "layer 5" is not checked. With one session per animal 26 of 36 units are selective (p = 0.001), and among the paper's 130 units from its processed data 89 are (p = 0.001).
deviations: Claims written from the abstract only; the criterion and the shuffle test of chance are this attempt's.

Epoch rates are spike counts on the file's clock; the paper's code averaged a causally smoothed PSTH of spikes already assigned to trials. Leaving out the spikes that overlap the next trial, as far as the stored order shows them, gives 73 of 100.

Units recorded on different days in one animal are counted separately, as in the code; they may be the same neurons (44 of 100 lie within 20 um of a unit of the same animal on another day, and the files hold no waveforms). A variant keeps one session per animal.

The dandiset holds 44 of the paper's 61 PTupper and 56 of its 69 PTlower units; the code's inclusion rule gives the paper's counts on its processed data and the same decision for every unit the dandiset holds.

outcomes.statement: The thalamus-projecting PT type produces early preparatory activity.
outcomes.notes: 27 of 44 included PTupper units (0.614) are selective in the sample epoch (-2.5 to -2.1 s), against a null 99th percentile of 0.045 (p = 0.001); in the baseline epoch 2 of 44 (p = 0.079). All 8 PTupper animals have sample-selective units (25% to 100%). 0.795 at p < 0.05, 0.432 at p < 0.001; 26 of 44 without flagged spikes. One session per animal gives 8 of 20 (null 99th percentile 0.100, p = 0.001); the paper's 61 PTupper units give 40 of 61 (p = 0.001).
deviations: Claims written from the abstract only; "early" is read as the code's sample epoch, the first 400 ms after the pole comes in.

outcomes.statement: The early preparatory activity of the thalamus-projecting PT type persists until the movement is initiated.
outcomes.notes: (a) 27 of 44 PTupper units are selective in the late delay (null 99th percentile 0.046, p = 0.001). (b) The cosine similarity of sample and late delay d' is 0.495, against a shuffle null median of 0.182 and 95th percentile of 0.433 (p = 0.016). The code's Pearson correlation gives r = 0.496 (p = 0.0006). 17 of the 27 sample-selective units keep the sign of their d' in the late delay. Both parts hold without flagged spikes, without the trials marked not good, with one session per animal ((a) 12 of 20, p = 0.001; (b) cosine 0.670, p = 0.006) and on the paper's 61 PTupper units ((a) 38 of 61, p = 0.001; (b) cosine 0.514, p = 0.002).
deviations: The code compares coding directions with bootstraps and plots the correlation; the shuffle test of the similarity is this attempt's.

outcomes.statement: The medulla-projecting PT type mainly produces late preparatory activity and motor commands.
outcomes.notes: Among 56 PTlower units, 0.714 are selective in the late delay and 0.482 in the sample epoch (one-sided McNemar p = 0.0096), and 0.643 in the response epoch (p = 0.088 against the sample epoch), so part (a) holds and part (b) does not. The rise rests mostly on anm369962 (0.30 in the sample epoch, 0.90 in the late delay); the other three animals stay between 0.44 and 0.77 in all three epochs. At p < 0.001 both parts hold (p = 0.0033 and 0.018), at p < 0.05 neither (0.054 and 0.14). The response epoch rate differs from baseline in 53 of 56 PTlower units and 37 of 44 PTupper units (one-sided Fisher p = 0.080). The variants give the same split. With one session per animal (16 units) part (a) holds (p = 0.016) and part (b) does not (p = 0.23). On the paper's 69 PTlower units from its processed data, (a) holds (0.507 against 0.652, p = 0.049) and (b) does not (0.551, p = 0.37); there both parts hold at p < 0.001 and neither at p < 0.05.
deviations: Claims written from the abstract only; "mainly late" is read as more units selective late than in the sample epoch, and "motor commands" as selectivity in the first 400 ms after the go cue (a change from baseline is shown as a variant).
The outcome depends on the test threshold, which the code sets at p < 0.01 for counting selective units.

outcomes.statement: The two PT types differ in when they carry information about the movement; the thalamus-projecting type carries early preparatory activity, the medulla-projecting type mainly late preparatory activity and motor commands.
outcomes.notes: (a) Sample epoch selectivity is 0.614 for PTupper and 0.482 for PTlower (one-sided Fisher p = 0.134). (b) Response epoch selectivity is 0.643 for PTlower and 0.841 for PTupper, the reverse of the claim (p = 0.99; p = 0.022 for the reverse). Over animals neither holds (Mann-Whitney p = 0.30 and 0.93). The code's coding-direction variant points the abstract's way but is not significant. The sample to late delay similarity is 0.473 +/- 0.214 for PTupper and 0.216 +/- 0.204 for PTlower, with PTupper higher in only 83 of 100 bootstraps. Without the bootstrap, PTupper's similarity is above its shuffle null (p = 0.007) and PTlower's is not (0.177, p = 0.43). On the paper's 130 units from its processed data, (a) is 0.656 against 0.507 (p = 0.062) and (b) is reversed (0.551 against 0.770, p = 0.007 for the reverse); with one session per animal, (a) p = 0.28 and (b) is reversed (0.438 against 0.800). The paper's measure of early information (Extended Data Fig. 9, single-unit decoding accuracy in the sample epoch, at least 70%) goes the abstract's way, with 7 of 44 PTupper against 1 of 56 PTlower units here (Fisher p = 0.012) and 12 of 61 against 1 of 69 on the paper's units (p = 0.0005), where the legend gives 15 of 61 against 3 of 69; the means match the legend (0.638 and 0.586 against 0.644 and 0.589), and the smaller counts are not explained. Part (a) is thus supported under the paper's measure but not under the criterion's. Part (b), selectivity for lick direction in the response epoch, is reversed in every variant. Under the variant reading of "motor commands" as a response epoch rate that differs from baseline, PTlower is ahead, 53 of 56 against 37 of 44, without reaching significance (one-sided Fisher p = 0.080). The reversal thus shows that PTlower units are less often direction-selective in the response epoch, not that they lack movement-related activity.
deviations: Claims written from the abstract only; the comparison of fractions between types is this attempt's reading of the contrast in the abstract, and the paper may compare the types differently.
Each animal holds one type (8 PTupper and 4 PTlower animals), so type and animal are confounded; the PTlower recordings include sessions in both hemispheres.
The dandiset lacks 17 of the paper's 61 PTupper and 13 of its 69 PTlower units; the variant on the paper's units gives the same outcome.

findings.statement: 11 sessions of the paper's processed data (Figshare doi:10.25378/janelia.7007846) that hold tagged units are not in the dandiset. They hold 17 of the 61 PTupper and 13 of the 69 PTlower units the paper analysed, so the dandiset holds 44 and 56. Every tagged unit the dandiset does hold is in the processed data with the same label and the same inclusion decision under the paper's code. The dandiset's description says some files were found to be broken and were left out, without naming them.

The dandiset holds the electrophysiology only. The transcriptomic and anatomical data behind four of the abstract's findings (the two PT types and their projection targets) are not in it; they are at GEO (GSE119182) and on Figshare (doi:10.25378/janelia.7007846).

Spike times are not sorted in 1120 of 1149 units. They were written trial by trial as trial start + go cue time + the spike time from the go cue. Each trial's spikes cover 6.4 s from about 0.97 s before the pole comes in, and trial starts are a median 6.4 s apart (5.4 to 7.9 s from the 1st to the 99th percentile), so consecutive trials overlap on the file's clock and some spikes of one trial lie in the next trial's early epochs (11.7% of the spikes counted in the baseline epoch, under 2% in later epochs, are detectably out of order). Trial membership of a spike cannot be recovered in full from the files.

The trial table's stop_time is NaN in every file, and pole_in_time, pole_out_time and cue_start_time are relative to the trial start without saying so. On the file's clock the go cue of a trial often falls after the next trial's start_time.

The tagged unit labels PTupper and PTlower are not described in the files or the dandiset metadata, and the projection targets (thalamus and medulla) that the paper uses to name the types are stated only in the paper's code.

Unit quality mixes two vocabularies (single, and Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and has undescribed empty values ([], 0, blank). Sex is U and genotype empty for every mouse, the electrode positions are all zero, and every electrode group gives layer 5 whatever the depth.

In the paper's processed data, in every one of the 53 sessions the dandiset holds, the spike windows of the first ten trials start later relative to the pole than those of the other trials (by about 2.7 s in the session examined in detail); the paper's code leaves out the first ten trials of each unit, which hides this. The files carry the same shift, as their spike times equal the processed ones in every unit.
