attempts.paper_title: Phenotypic variation of transcriptomic cell types in mouse motor cortex
attempts.entry_title: Patch-seq neurons of mouse motor cortex at physiological temperature (Scala, Kobak et al. 2021)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Scala, Kobak et al. (2021) that can be tested on dandiset 000035, which holds the paper's follow-up recordings at 34 degrees C (185 neurons, mostly layer 5 Sst and excitatory cells). It extracts the paper's 17 electrophysiological features from the traces, checks the cohort and the stimulus against the Methods, tests whether IT and ET neurons overlap electrophysiologically, and compares Sst t-types between temperatures using the paper's published room-temperature features. The findings on the main room-temperature data set are in dandiset 000008 and are not tested here.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Scala, Kobak et al. (2021) from dandiset 000035

outcomes.statement: After quality control, 1,227 Patch-seq neurons from mouse primary motor cortex were assigned to transcriptomic types, covering 77 of the 90 neuronal t-types of the reference taxonomy.
outcomes.source: Results, "Patch-seq of mouse primary motor cortex"; Figure 1a
outcomes.notes: The finding rests on the 1,329 cells of the main data set and their sequencing. The dandiset holds only the 185 cells of the follow-up at 34 degrees, with their t-type labels but no gene counts. The main data set's recordings are in dandiset 000008, its sequencing data at NeMO (dat-kq04hua) and GEO (GSE163764), and its processed tables in the paper's repository.

outcomes.statement: A sparse reduced-rank regression of 17 electrophysiological features on gene expression, using 25 genes and a rank-5 latent space, reached a cross-validated R2 of 0.38, with cross-validated correlations of 0.90, 0.74 and 0.67 between the first three pairs of projections.
outcomes.source: Results, "Distinct phenotypes of major families"; Figure 2
outcomes.notes: Needs gene expression and features of the main data set. The dandiset holds no gene counts and none of the main data set's cells; they are in dandiset 000008 and at NeMO and GEO.

outcomes.statement: A reduced-rank regression restricted to ion channel genes did not perform much worse than the full model, with a cross-validated R2 of 0.33 and correlations of 0.86, 0.71 and 0.56.
outcomes.source: Results, "Distinct phenotypes of major families"; Extended Data Figure 5e-f
outcomes.notes: As fig2-rrr-prediction.

outcomes.statement: In a k-nearest-neighbour classification of cells into seven transcriptomic families from electrophysiological features, the confusion matrix was mostly diagonal, with only the ET and IT subclasses strongly overlapping.
outcomes.notes: Needs the main data set's cells, which are in dandiset 000008. The same classifier was run on the 34 degree cells for ed6-it-et-overlap, where Lamp5, Vip and CT cells are absent.

outcomes.statement: Families were less separable by morphology than by electrophysiology among inhibitory neurons, and most separable when electrophysiological and morphological features were combined.
outcomes.notes: Needs morphological reconstructions, which are not in the dandiset (none were recovered in the 34 degree experiments). They are in the Brain Image Library, with features in the paper's repository.

outcomes.statement: Across 200 pairs of t-types from the same family, the transcriptomic distance and the electrophysiological distance between t-types were correlated with r = 0.60.
outcomes.notes: Needs the main data set's cells (dandiset 000008) and the reference 10x expression data.

outcomes.statement: Among IT t-types, transcriptomic distances were strongly correlated with differences in average soma depth, r = 0.70.
outcomes.notes: Needs the main data set's IT cells (their soma depths are in the paper's repository and dandiset 000008) and the reference 10x expression data.

outcomes.statement: Most t-types were classified into their own family from electrophysiology, but some, such as Sst Pvalb Calb2, Lamp5 Egln3_1 and Vip Mybpc1, were often classified into another family.
outcomes.notes: Needs the main data set's cells, in dandiset 000008. The t-types named in the claim are not among the 34 degree cells except Sst Pvalb Calb2.

outcomes.statement: Many t-types had a normalized total variance of electrophysiological features well above that of k-means clusters, while some, such as Pvalb Vipr2_2, appeared homogeneous.
outcomes.notes: Needs the main data set's cells, in dandiset 000008.

outcomes.statement: At physiological temperature, 185 neurons were sequenced from 8 adult mice (7 Sst-Cre/Ai9 and 1 Pvalb-Cre/Ai9); 177 got a t-type (110 Sst, 43 IT, 12 ET, 10 Pvalb, 2 NP); 175 were in layer 5; electrophysiological features were extracted for 184.
outcomes.notes: Every count matches the Methods. All 17 features are defined for 185 cells against 184 in the paper, within the 10% tolerance. Families are read from the t-type names in the files; the 12 ET cells are named L5 PT_1 to L5 PT_4 there.
deviations: The number of cells with features comes from the re-implemented extraction here; the paper's table has no row for 20200406_sample_4.

outcomes.statement: Cells at physiological temperature were stimulated with the same paradigm as the main data set, 600 ms current pulses from -200 pA upwards in 20 pA steps up to 1,380 pA, sometimes stopped earlier.
outcomes.source: Methods, "Patch-seq recording procedures" and "Experiments at physiological temperature"
outcomes.notes: In all 185 cells every step lasts 600 ms and consecutive steps differ by 20 pA; all 14,054 sweeps with a nonzero step start at 0.1 s and end at 0.7 s, and 139 cells end at 1,380 pA. 174 of 185 (94.1%) conform to the whole ladder. Nine cells of mouse_UEQOU end at 1,400 to 1,580 pA, and two cells of other mice start at -180 pA and -100 pA and end above 1,380 pA. The intervals of 1.3 or 1.4 s between pulses cannot be checked because every series has an undefined starting time.

outcomes.statement: Follow-up experiments at 34 degrees C confirmed the electrophysiological overlap between IT and ET neurons seen at room temperature.
outcomes.source: Results, "Distinct phenotypes of major families"; Extended Data Figure 6a-g
outcomes.notes: With the paper's kNN classifier (k = 10, leave-one-out, 17-feature representation, all 185 cells), 58.3% of ET cells (7 of 12) are classified as IT and no IT cell as ET; Sst cells are classified as Sst 100% of the time and Pvalb cells 60%. ET cells go to IT in both mice with ET cells (1 of 3 and 6 of 9). The overlap is one-sided and partly reflects that IT cells are 78% of IT and ET cells. With IT subsampled to 12 cells and an odd k (no ties), 10.5% (k = 9) and 12.4% (k = 11) of ET cells go to IT and 33.4% and 36.5% of IT cells to ET; a class-balanced logistic regression separates layer 5 IT from ET with a balanced accuracy of 0.83 against a shuffled-label null of 0.50 (p = 0.005). The result on layer 5 cells alone, and without 20200406_sample_4 (the paper's 184 cells), is the same as on all cells (58.3% and 0%). All ET cells come from two mice. Within mouse_UEQOU alone (10 IT, 9 ET), the kNN classifies 33.3% of ET cells as IT and 20.0% of IT cells as ET, and the logistic regression reaches 0.78 (p = 0.025). The criterion does not require a test within mouse.
deviations: The paper shows the 34 degree comparison as feature distributions and two-feature scatter plots (Extended Data Fig. 6a-g); it reports no classifier at 34 degrees. The test applies the room-temperature classifier of Fig. 3d to the 34 degree cells, with four families present instead of seven.
Features are computed by the re-implementation here; link-features shows they agree with the paper's.
The main test uses all 185 cells, including 20200406_sample_4 (layer 5 IT), which the paper leaves out; the 184-cell result is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: At 34 degrees C, the AP threshold showed a prominent difference between layer 5 IT and ET neurons.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 6e and its legend
outcomes.notes: Layer 5 IT median -27.0 mV (43 cells) against ET -33.1 mV (12 cells), Mann-Whitney p = 0.00035, area under the curve 0.84; second of 17 features after input resistance (p = 0.0001). Without 20200406_sample_4, p = 0.00026 (42 IT cells). Same sign in both mice with both subclasses, but within mouse_UEQOU alone the gap is smaller and not significant (-29.3 against -31.8 mV, area under the curve 0.73, p = 0.094, 10 IT and 9 ET cells). All ET cells come from two mice, so a difference between mice may contribute; the criterion does not require a test within mouse. The ranking of the first two features is the one the paper's code prints for 34 degrees.
deviations: The ranking covers the 17 features used here, not all 29 the paper's code ranks.
The main test uses all 185 cells, including 20200406_sample_4, which the paper leaves out; the 184-cell result is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's recordings are the cells of the paper's published table of the 34 degree cohort, with the same t-type, layer and soma depth.
outcomes.notes: All 185 files match a row of the paper's table by cell id and no row lacks a file. Family, layer, soma depth and mouse agree for every cell; the files' inferred layer equals the layer the paper's code computes from soma depth and cortical thickness. The t-type name agrees for 93.5% of cells, below the criterion's 95%, only because the 12 ET cells are named L5 PT_1 to L5 PT_4 in the files and L5 ET_1 to L5 ET_4 in the table, one to one; with that renaming the agreement is 100%. The partial outcome reflects the names, not a mismatch of cells. The verifier of round 1 would call this reproduced; the outcome is kept because the criterion, written before the analysis, compares t-type names.
deviations: The criterion did not anticipate renamed t-types and was applied as written, to the names.

outcomes.statement: The electrophysiological features computed here from the dandiset's traces agree with the paper's published features for the same cells.
outcomes.notes: 184 of the 185 cells are in the paper's feature table. The Spearman correlation between the features computed here and the published ones is at least 0.9 for 16 of 17 features and 0.877 for the lowest, the AP coefficient of variation. The median absolute difference is zero to three decimals for all features but the AHP (0.011 mV). By mouse, 0.895 (mouse_UEQOU) to 0.995 of values are within 10% of the paper's. The maximum number of APs differs between the Methods' and the code's definitions for 3 cells.
deviations: The extraction is a re-implementation of the paper's methods and code (scala34.py), not the paper's code, which is under the Allen Institute's license.
The maximum number of APs follows the Methods (sweeps with spikes in the 100 ms before or the 200 ms after the step are excluded before taking the maximum); the code's version is shown.

outcomes.statement: For layer 5 Sst t-types, AP amplitude and AP width changed the most between room temperature and 34 degrees C, but the relative differences between t-types stayed roughly the same; AHP, input resistance, rebound and sag ratio changed little, and the relative differences between t-types stayed the same.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 6h and its legend
outcomes.notes: 147 layer 5 Sst cells at 25 degrees (published features) and 101 at 34 degrees (computed here); seven t-types have at least 5 cells in both. Shifts in units of the 25 degree SD are AP width -1.78, AP amplitude -1.66, input resistance -0.61, rebound -0.33, AHP -0.25 and sag ratio -0.02, so AP width and amplitude change most. Spearman correlations of t-type medians between temperatures are 0.75 (AP amplitude), 0.88 (AP width), 0.93 (AHP, input resistance, rebound) and 0.96 (sag ratio), median 0.93. The same holds with the paper's published 34 degree features and with t-type means. In each of the 7 mice with such cells, the 34 degree medians of AP amplitude and width lie below the room-temperature medians.
deviations: The room-temperature side uses the paper's published features of dandiset 000008's cells, not features recomputed from that dandiset.
The legend says the relative differences "stayed roughly the same"; the criterion turns this into Spearman correlations of t-type medians and a shift measured in standard deviations.

outcomes.statement: At physiological temperature, as at room temperature, morpho-electric properties of layer 5 Sst neurons varied continuously across the transcriptomic landscape, and the electrophysiological distance between Sst t-types correlated with their transcriptomic distance.
outcomes.source: Results, "Continuous phenotypic variation"; Extended Data Figure 6i
outcomes.notes: The transcriptomic distance between Sst t-types needs the average expression of each t-type in the single-cell 10x v2 reference data (Yao et al. 2021). The paper's code reads it from reduced-allen-data.zip on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.5118962), member 10X_cells_v2_AIBS.pickle. The notebook reads the archive's directory (87.9 MB compressed, 517.0 MB uncompressed) and times a 1 MB range request. In the delivered run the rate was 62 kB/s, about 24 minutes for the member. The rate varies between runs; in the earlier runs of this attempt (not in the delivered notebook) it was 27, 114, 44, 149 and 58 kB/s, about 55, 13, 33, 10 and 25 minutes. A run that fetched the member would have exceeded the 30 minute limit in two of these six runs and fitted in the others, so the claim was not tested. The reference is public, and the verifier of round 2 holds that the claim is testable; the block reflects this attempt's choice not to make the run depend on Zenodo's rate. Proposed change for another round, fetch the member in the run, write a criterion for the claim (it has none), and test it. The original reference data at NeMO are much larger. The electrophysiological half is computed from the dandiset as in the paper's code (cell 19 of physiological-temperature.ipynb), for 9 layer 5 Sst t-types with at least 5 cells (Sst Chodl left out), as the paper's code prints, with distances between their mean standardized features of 1.54 to 5.24. It tests nothing without the transcriptomic half. A proxy transcriptomic distance from the paper's own 34 degree Patch-seq counts was not computed, as it differs from the paper's method. The paper reports the correlation and its p-value only inside the figure.

findings.statement: Every voltage series states the unit volts and every stimulus series amperes, with a conversion of 1, but the values are in millivolts (-150 to 67) and picoamperes (-200 to 1,580).

Every series has an undefined (NaN) starting time, so the timing of sweeps relative to each other is not recorded. Within a sweep the response and the stimulus share a clock (onset at 0.1 s, offset at 0.7 s).

The t-type of the 12 ET cells is stored under the older names L5 PT_1 to L5 PT_4, which differ from the paper's and its tables' L5 ET_1 to L5 ET_4; no mapping is given. All other t-type names match the paper's table.
The dandiset's description repeats the main data set's "over 1300 neurons"; the dandiset holds 185 neurons of the follow-up at 34 degrees.

In the published version the contributor list has a placeholder "Last, First" with Zizhen Yao's ORCID, the brain region is typed as a disorder, and the assets summary gives no approach or measurement technique. The unpublished draft corrects these.
Eleven cells were stimulated beyond the 1,380 pA the Methods give (up to 1,580 pA), and two of them started at -180 pA and -100 pA, not -200 pA. Nine of the eleven are from one mouse (mouse_UEQOU).

The paper's code takes the maximum number of APs before excluding sweeps with spikes outside the step, and looks for those spikes over the whole trace before and after the step; the Methods exclude such sweeps first and look 100 ms before and 200 ms after. The two definitions differ for 3 of the 185 cells.

The Methods build the electrophysiological representation from 17 principal components of 17 features and later call it "the 16-dimensional electrophysiological representation"; the paper's code uses all 17.

The legend of Extended Data Fig. 6j describes it as "the same analysis as in (c)", but in the paper's code panel j is the 34 degree version of panel i (the Sst overlay and the transcriptomic-distance correlation), not of panel c.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier listed the version's assets through the DANDI API and ran synthetic checks of the helper functions (input resistance, time constant, sag, rebound, spike counts, rheobase, family_of, layer_from_depth, knn_family_confusion).

disagreements.reason: 185 of 185 cells match, and layer, soma depth and mouse agree 100%. Literal t-type agreement is 93.5% because the files say L5 PT_k where the table says L5 ET_k. The mapping is one-to-one, and after renaming agreement is 100%. The claims file itself treats PT as ET.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The full executed notebook of the first revision, with its conclusions and summary, the helper module, the claims file, the README and this attempt record, with the paper.

disagreements.reason: As in round 1. The only mismatch is the one-to-one PT/ET renaming. After renaming, agreement is 1.000 (cell 26), and the claims file itself treats PT as ET. The record states the disagreement correctly.

attempts.paper_title: Network Homeostasis and State Dynamics of Neocortical Sleep
attempts.entry_title: Firing rates across sleep states in rat frontal cortex (Watson et al. 2016)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Watson, Levenstein, Greene, Gelinas and Buzsaki (2016) on dandiset 000041, which holds silicon probe recordings of units, LFP and sleep states from the frontal cortex of 10 rats in their home cage. It compares firing rates and bursting across WAKE, nonREM and REM, how rates of fast and slow firing cells change over sleep and within nonREM packets, how they relate to LFP band power, and the rate changes across state triplets. UP and DOWN state and spindle analyses are blocked, as their methods are in the unavailable supplement.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Watson et al. (2016) from dandiset 000041

outcomes.statement: The recordings come from 11 rats and 27 sessions of 294 plus or minus 137 min, yielding 995 putative pyramidal cells and 126 putative interneurons.
outcomes.source: Results, identification of brain states and assessment of firing patterns; Experimental Procedures
outcomes.notes: Two of five values are within tolerance, 10 rats and a mean session duration of 286.8 min (SD 150.2). The files hold 22 sessions, 826 excitatory and 96 inhibitory units (and 23 of unknown type); the 21 usable sessions hold 812 pE and 89 pI cells. Per session the pE count is close to the paper's (mean 38.7, range 10 to 105, against 36.9 and 10 to 104).
deviations: Counted on the files as deposited, with session duration from the state table.

outcomes.statement: Median firing rates of pE cells are 0.76 Hz in WAKE, 0.69 Hz in nonREM and 0.88 Hz in REM; of pI cells 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2A
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) the three pE medians are within tolerance (0.755, 0.662 and 0.825 Hz) and the three pI medians are below it (3.92, 2.73 and 3.06 Hz, against 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25). Reading (b) gives the same counts (pE WAKE 0.748). The pI sample is 89 cells in 9 subjects, with per-subject medians from 0.07 to 13.4 Hz across subjects and states.
deviations: 812 pE and 89 pI cells from 21 sessions, against 995 and 126 from 27.
WAKE excludes microarousals derived from the Awake label, not the paper's scored MAs.

outcomes.statement: The distribution of pE firing rates is strongly positively skewed and spans three orders of magnitude, from 0.05 to 5 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2A
outcomes.notes: WAKE rates have skewness 4.57 and a 97.5th percentile of 7.17 Hz (within a factor of 2 of 5 Hz), but the 2.5th percentile is 0.0124 Hz, about four times below 0.05 Hz. 13 of 812 cells have a WAKE rate of zero. The log10 rates are skewed to the left (-0.74).
deviations: The paper's range is read from a log axis; the factor-of-2 tolerance was fixed in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of pE cells firing above 2 Hz is 19.2% in WAKE, 19.2% in REM and 8.8% in nonREM (chi-square, p < 1e-10).
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2A
outcomes.notes: REM (18.7%) and nonREM (9.1%) are within tolerance, WAKE (17.0%) is not. nonREM is lower than WAKE (chi-square 21.5, p = 3.5e-06) and REM (30.5, p = 3.4e-08), but neither test reaches p < 1e-10, which the criterion requires. The direction of the effect is as in the paper, with fewer cells than the paper had. Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes, WAKE is 20.2% (within tolerance) and both tests still miss p < 1e-10.

outcomes.statement: Per-cell nonREM and WAKE rates are highly correlated (R = 0.82), and the slope of their relation is below 1 (95% confidence interval 0.66 to 0.71), so state transitions act differently across the rate spectrum.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2B
outcomes.notes: On log10 rates (799 cells, 13 with a zero rate left out), R = 0.862 and the slope of nonREM on WAKE is 0.757 (95% CI 0.727 to 0.788). In Hz the slope is 0.583 (0.560 to 0.607), outside the widened interval. The reverse regression on log10 rates gives 0.982 (0.942 to 1.022), so the slope below 1 may in part be regression to the mean. Per subject the slope ranges from 0.41 to 0.91. A split-half control (alternate WAKE epochs of each cell) gives a slope of 0.936 between halves and a reliability of 0.961 for the log10 WAKE rate; corrected for this noise the slope is 0.788 (0.756 to 0.821), still below 1. The rest of the gap to 1 comes from the WAKE-nonREM correlation being below 1, which is also regression to the mean. The ratio of the SDs of log10 rates, nonREM over WAKE, is 0.878 (Pitman-Morgan p = 9.8e-13, 95% interval resampling sessions 0.777 to 0.971), so the spread of rates is narrower in nonREM.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the slope is on log or linear rates; both readings are shown and the log reading matches.

outcomes.statement: The burst index (fraction of spikes with inter-spike intervals under 15 ms) is highest in nonREM (median 11.8%), lowest in WAKE (4.0%), with REM (5.5%) slightly above WAKE (Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.05).
outcomes.notes: The order nonREM > REM > WAKE holds under both readings, with Kruskal-Wallis p = 5.7e-36 (a) and 7.3e-38 (b), and REM above WAKE (paired Wilcoxon p = 1e-32). Reading (a), the fraction of intervals under 15 ms, gives medians of 6.35, 2.64 and 3.65%, none within tolerance; reading (b), the fraction of spikes in such an interval, gives 11.67% in nonREM (within tolerance), 4.95% in WAKE and 6.71% in REM (above). The measured values are those of reading (a), the first listed. The paired Friedman test over the 753 cells with all three values gives p = 3.9e-151.
deviations: The definition "fraction of spikes with ISIs under 15 ms" can be read two ways; both are shown and neither matches all three medians.

outcomes.statement: The average spike autocorrelogram of pE cells peaks near 8 ms in nonREM, with a smaller peak near 125 ms (theta) in REM and WAKE.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2C
outcomes.notes: The nonREM autocorrelogram peaks at 8.5 ms. The smoothed REM and WAKE autocorrelograms are highest at the 60 ms edge of the 60 to 250 ms window, so the criterion finds no theta peak. In a variant that divides the 21 ms smoothing by a 101 ms one, WAKE has a maximum at 118.5 ms (ratio 1.016) and REM at 142.5 ms (1.017). Per subject the REM maximum falls within 112.5 to 137.5 ms in two subjects (Bogey 135.5, Dino 125.5). Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked, the nonREM peak is at 6.5 ms, outside 7 to 9 ms, so the nonREM part rests on the sample as well as on the method. A fix to the binning (lags rounded to 1 ns, so that float error does not move a lag on a bin edge) moved the nonREM peak from 7.5 to 8.5 ms.
deviations: The peak location criteria (windows, 21 ms smoothing) were fixed here; the paper shows the peaks in a figure only.

outcomes.statement: The autocorrelogram of pE cells decays faster in nonREM than in WAKE and REM (decay fit exponent medians -1.35, -0.83 and -0.80; Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2C
outcomes.notes: The main text gives decay fit exponents but not what is fitted (function, lag range); the Supplemental Experimental Procedures, which would say, could not be retrieved (PubMed Central and the publisher answer with a browser check). The autocorrelograms themselves are computed for fig2c-acg-peaks.

outcomes.statement: In nonREM, pairs of fast-firing pE cells are positively correlated, while pairs of one slow and one fast cell are negatively correlated.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2F
outcomes.notes: Over 20764 same-session pE pairs (169 without a defined correlation), the (6,6) mean correlation of 100 ms counts in nonREM is 0.0424, the largest of the 21 group combinations, and correlations rise with the rates of both cells. The (1,6) mean is 0.0089, above zero (t = 10.85, p = 8.7e-26); 22.8% of all pairs are negative, but no group combination has a negative mean. Reading (b) gives the same pattern ((6,6) 0.0401, (1,6) 0.0087).
deviations: The correlation measure is Pearson correlation of raw counts in 100 ms bins; the paper's measure and test are in the unavailable supplement and may differ (for example a correction for the shared UP/DOWN modulation).

outcomes.statement: Microarousals have a median duration of 15.9 plus or minus 3.3 s, occur 0.32 plus or minus 0.12 times per minute and occupy 9.1 plus or minus 3.5% of SLEEP (790 in total).
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), median MA duration 19.0 s (within the spread), 0.096 MAs per minute of SLEEP and 3.22% of SLEEP time; reading (b) gives 19.0 s, 0.127 per min and 4.23%. The paper reports 0.32 and 9.1%. 391 MAs in 21 sessions (262 inside SLEEP periods), against 790 in 27. Looser rules raise the counts but none reaches both values: Non-REM on at least one side and under 60 s gives 0.177 per min and 7.63% of SLEEP; every Awake epoch inside SLEEP gives 0.245 per min and 13.66%. Of the short Awake epochs left as WAKE, 186 lie between REM and Non-REM and 120 between two REM epochs.
deviations: The dandiset has no microarousal label. MAs are derived from Awake epochs under 40 s between two Non-REM epochs, without the paper's EMG and theta criteria; 345 short Awake epochs elsewhere are left as WAKE.
The state table has 1 s resolution and may not be the scoring the paper used.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of time occupied by MAs decreases over the course of nonREM episodes (R = -0.85, p < 1e-10).
outcomes.notes: Over 243 episodes with an MA, pooled episode bins give R = -0.087 (p = 1.7e-05); the bin means give R = -0.451 (p = 0.19). Neither reaches -0.85 or p < 1e-10. The mean fraction rises from 0.067 to 0.157 over the first six bins and falls to 0.010 in the last. With a looser MA rule (Awake under 60 s with Non-REM on at least one side, 757 MAs) the bin means give R = -0.602 (p = 0.066) and pooled bins R = -0.111 (p = 2.8e-08), the same judgment.
deviations: MAs derived from the Awake label (see ma-statistics); the binning was fixed here.

outcomes.statement: The duration of nonREM packets spans two orders of magnitude, with a median of 111 s.
outcomes.notes: Over all 1069 Non-REM epochs the median is 108 s (5th to 95th percentile 12 to 484 s, range 6 to 1199 s). Inside SLEEP periods (685 epochs) the median is 128 s, outside tolerance. Per subject medians range from 76 to 219 s.
deviations: A packet is one Non-REM epoch of the dandiset's state table.

outcomes.statement: The dataset holds 54 WAKE-SLEEP episodes (at least 7 min of WAKE followed by at least 20 min of SLEEP), an average of 2.0 per session, and sessions without one were discarded.
outcomes.source: Results, identification of brain states and firing pattern changes across sleep
outcomes.notes: 30 cycles in 21 sessions, 1.43 per session, and 3 sessions (BWRat18-020513, BWRat19-032413, BWRat20-101013) have none. Accepting SLEEP ended by the end of the recording gives 34 cycles (1.62 per session) and one session without a cycle. In the three sessions without a cycle, the long sleep segments fail because the Awake before them lasts 3.6 or 5.0 min, under 7 min, or because the recording ends them (BWRat18-020513 and BWRat20-101013).
deviations: SLEEP and cycles are rebuilt from the Results' definitions on the dandiset's state table; the paper's Table 1 was not available, and its state scoring and MAs may differ.

outcomes.statement: The mean firing rate of pE cells declines over the course of SLEEP, restricted to nonREM (R = -0.11, p < 1e-3).
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern and LFP changes across sleep; Figure 3B
outcomes.notes: Per packet R = -0.267 (p = 4.3e-06, 287 packets in 30 cycles); in 10 bins R = -0.285 (p = 7.6e-07). The decline is steeper than the reported R = -0.11. R is negative in 8 of 9 subjects with a cycle.
deviations: The paper does not give its binning or normalization; two readings were fixed in the criterion.
30 cycles from 21 sessions, against 54 from 27.

outcomes.statement: The mean pE rate is lower in the last than in the first nonREM packet of SLEEP (1.04 plus or minus 1.20 against 0.88 plus or minus 0.91 Hz; Wilcoxon p < 0.02).
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern and LFP changes across sleep
outcomes.notes: Over 1070 cell and cycle pairs, 1.0915 plus or minus 1.483 Hz in the first packet and 0.9679 plus or minus 1.241 Hz in the last (the upper bound of tolerance is 0.968), Wilcoxon p = 3.9e-06. The decrease is significant within 3 of 9 subjects. With one value per cycle the last packet is lower in 22 of 30 cycles (Wilcoxon p = 0.015). Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked, the last mean is 1.006 Hz, outside tolerance.
deviations: 30 cycles from 21 sessions, against 54 from 27.

outcomes.statement: Comparing the same neurons in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP, the regression slope departs from 1 (95% confidence interval 0.827 to 0.880), as fast cells slow down and slow cells speed up.
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern and LFP changes across sleep; Figure 3D
outcomes.notes: On log10 rates (1021 pairs, 49 with a zero rate left out) the slope of last on first is 0.801 (95% CI 0.768 to 0.834); in Hz 0.723. The reverse regression gives 0.864 (0.829 to 0.900), and the second half of the first packet regressed on its first half gives 0.855 (0.829 to 0.881), above the first-to-last slope. Corrected for the noise of the first-packet rate (reliability 0.946 from its halves), the slope is 0.846 (0.812 to 0.881), still below 1. The ratio of the SDs of log10 rates, last over first packet, is 0.963, a narrowing of about 4% that is significant over pairs (Pitman-Morgan p = 0.028) but not when cycles are resampled (95% interval 0.892 to 1.029). Most of the slope below 1 comes from the first-to-last correlation being below 1 (R = 0.832), so the claim's reading that fast cells slow down and slow cells speed up is weakly supported. The criterion, fixed before the analysis, judges the slope alone.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the regression is on log or linear rates; both are shown.

outcomes.statement: pE rates are lower in the 5 min of WAKE after SLEEP than in the 5 min before (p < 1e-6, Wilcoxon), with a decrease in the top three sextiles and an increase in the lowest.
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern changes across sleep and sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 3E
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), 1070 cell and cycle pairs, mean 1.341 Hz before and 1.180 Hz after, Wilcoxon p = 4.1e-09. Sextiles 4, 5 and 6 decrease (one-tailed p = 0.03, 0.00063, 2.4e-05); sextile 1 does not increase (mean change -0.002 Hz, p = 0.3), and sextiles 2 and 3 decrease. Reading (b), 727 cells, gives the same pattern (population p = 1.4e-09, sextile 1 p = 0.36). In 23 of 30 cycles the WAKE after SLEEP is shorter than 300 s. With the pre-sleep window cut to the length of the post-sleep one, the result is the same (population p = 1.7e-09, sextile 1 p = 0.18, sextile 6 p = 1.8e-05). With one value per cycle the population decrease holds (20 of 30 cycles, p = 0.016) and sextile 6 decreases (p = 0.048), but sextiles 4 and 5 do not (p = 0.87 and 0.12); the sextile part rests on pooling cells within cycles. With only the 7 cycles that have a full 300 s of WAKE after SLEEP, the population p is 0.055 and sextile 6 p is 0.27 (sextile 5 p = 0.0034), so the result depends on the cycles with a shorter post-sleep window.
deviations: Where the WAKE after SLEEP is shorter than 5 min, all of it is used.

outcomes.statement: Over SLEEP, restricted to nonREM, the fastest sextile decreases its rate while the slowest shows a marginal increase.
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern changes across sleep; Figure 3B
outcomes.notes: Per packet, sextile 6 R = -0.447 (p = 3.1e-11) and sextile 1 R = +0.163 (p = 0.0074); sextile 5 R = -0.341 and sextile 2 R = +0.143. In bins, sextile 6 R = -0.430 (p = 2e-11) and sextile 1 R = +0.094 (p = 0.11). Sextile 6 has a negative R in all 7 subjects where it can be computed.
deviations: Binning and normalization fixed here (see fig3b-population-decline).

outcomes.statement: The coefficient of variation of pE firing rates decreases over the course of SLEEP (R = -0.05, p < 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern changes across sleep
outcomes.notes: R = -0.026 (p = 0.66) per packet and R = -0.014 (p = 0.81) in bins.
deviations: The CV is taken across a session's pE cells at each point; the paper does not define it further.

outcomes.statement: Within both nonREM episodes and nonREM packets, the fastest sextiles decrease their rates while the slowest increase.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM; Figure 4A and 4B, panel iv
outcomes.notes: Within 622 episodes, sextile 6 R = -0.083 (p = 3.7e-08) and sextile 1 R = +0.060 (p = 6.3e-06); within 952 packets, R = -0.055 (p = 4.4e-06) and +0.061 (p = 2e-08). The signs hold with 5 or 20 bins and with a 60 s minimum. The effects are small, and per subject within packets sextile 6 increases in Rizzo (R = +0.121) and does not decrease in BWRat19 and BWRat20. With one R per session, sextile 1 increases in episodes (p = 0.049) and packets (p = 0.011) and sextile 6 decreases in episodes (p = 0.013) but not in packets (median R -0.025, 6 of 16 sessions positive, p = 0.19).
deviations: 10 bins, a 20 s minimum and normalization within each interval were fixed here.

outcomes.statement: The coefficient of variation of binned population rates decreases within nonREM episodes (R = -0.13) and packets (R = -0.12), both p < 1e-10.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM; Figure 4A and 4B, panel v
outcomes.notes: Episodes R = -0.005 (p = 0.71), packets R = 0.011 (p = 0.28); no variant exceeds an absolute R of 0.011.

outcomes.statement: The 15 ms burst index of pE cells increases within nonREM episodes (R = 0.09) and packets (R = 0.08), both p < 1e-10.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM; Figure 4A and 4B, panel vi
outcomes.notes: Episodes R = 0.029 (p = 0.022), packets R = 0.024 (p = 0.021); variants give R = 0.020 to 0.047 with p from 0.069 to 0.0008. The burst index rises in the reported direction, but far from p < 1e-10.
deviations: The burst index per bin is pooled over the session's pE cells (fraction of intervals under 15 ms).

outcomes.statement: Delta and sigma power increase over nonREM episodes and packets, while gamma power decreases over episodes but not over packets.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM; Figure 4A and 4B, panel i
outcomes.notes: Sigma rises within episodes (R = 0.135) and packets (R = 0.104), both p < 1e-20. Delta rises within episodes (R = 0.069, p = 1.1e-07) but not within packets (R = -0.005, p = 0.61; with a 60 s minimum R = 0.022, p = 0.063). Gamma rises within episodes (R = 0.062) and packets (R = 0.182), where the paper reports a fall over episodes. Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes the judgment is the same; delta over packets is +0.014 (p = 0.27) and gamma over episodes +0.005 (p = 0.77).
deviations: One LFP channel per session, the one the conversion flags as spindle reference, in raw units; the paper's channel choice is not stated in the main text.
The LFP of Dino-061914 is left out (scrambled samples).

outcomes.statement: Mean delta power within whole packets, normalized by nonREM delta power, is positively correlated with packet length (R = 0.31, p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM
outcomes.notes: Over 915 packets of at least 20 s, R = 0.334 (p = 2.8e-25), near the upper edge of 0.279 to 0.341; Spearman rho = 0.555. Positive in 9 of 10 subjects (Templeton -0.101). Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes the judgment is the same (R = 0.297).
deviations: One LFP channel per session; Dino-061914 left out.

outcomes.statement: Per packet, the rate of the fastest sextile is negatively correlated with delta power (R = -0.28) and positively with gamma power (R = 0.44), and the rate of the slowest sextile is positively correlated with sigma power in the last 20 s of the packet (R = 0.25), all p < 1e-10.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM; Figure 4C and 4D
outcomes.notes: All three signs as stated. Sextile 6 against delta R = -0.416 (p = 1.3e-28) and against gamma R = 0.570 (p = 4.2e-57), both stronger than reported; sextile 1 against sigma in the last 20 s R = 0.104 (p = 0.0029), weaker than 0.25 and above p < 1e-10. None within tolerance. Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes the judgment is the same (R = -0.428, 0.533 and 0.132).
deviations: One LFP channel per session; Dino-061914 left out; z-scoring per session fixed here.

outcomes.statement: An intervening nonREM packet reduces the rates of the top two sextiles from one MA to the next (both p < 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5B
outcomes.notes: 148 triplets, 6073 cell and triplet pairs. Sextile 6 mean change -0.104 Hz (p = 0.077), sextile 5 -0.011 Hz (p = 0.24). With per-cell means, sextile 6 -0.120 Hz (p = 0.029) and sextile 5 p = 0.79. With one value per triplet or per session neither sextile 5 nor 6 changes at p < 0.1. With a looser MA rule (Awake under 60 s with Non-REM on at least one side), 343 triplets, sextile 5 p = 0.14 and sextile 6 changes by +0.029 Hz (p = 0.92), the same judgment.
deviations: MAs derived from the Awake label (see ma-statistics).

outcomes.statement: An intervening WAKE episode increases the rate of the fastest sextile from one nonREM packet to the next (24 triplets).
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5B
outcomes.notes: 265 triplets (the paper had 24). Sextile 6 mean change -0.051 Hz (p = 0.092); sextiles 1 and 3 increase slightly (p = 0.0063 and 0.015). The intervening WAKE lasts 40 to 3945 s (median 102). No minimum WAKE duration from 40 to 900 s gives a sextile 6 increase at p < 0.05; at 900 s, 23 triplets remain, near the paper's 24, with a mean change of -0.185 Hz (p = 0.5).
deviations: Every Awake epoch of at least 40 s between two Non-REM epochs counts as WAKE here; the paper's 24 triplets suggest a narrower selection that the main text does not describe.

outcomes.statement: An intervening MA increases the rates of slow-firing pE cells from one packet to the next and does not affect fast-firing cells.
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5B
outcomes.notes: 391 triplets. Sextile 1 mean change +0.0034 Hz (p = 0.082); sextiles 5 and 6 decrease (p = 0.0023 and 6.8e-05), and sextile 2 increases (p = 0.00019). With one value per triplet sextile 1 increases (p = 0.037), but per session it does not (p = 0.17); the decrease of sextiles 5 and 6 holds per session (p = 0.0094 and 0.00015). With a looser MA rule (Awake under 60 s with Non-REM on at least one side), 463 triplets, sextile 1 increases (+0.0048 Hz, p = 0.016; per triplet p = 0.029, per session p = 0.11) and sextiles 5 and 6 decrease (p = 0.0041 and 5.3e-06), which would meet the partial condition. The outcome follows the MA rule fixed in the claims file before the analysis, and rests on it.
deviations: MAs derived from the Awake label (see ma-statistics).

outcomes.statement: An intervening REM episode decreases the rates of all sextiles from one packet to the next.
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5B
outcomes.notes: Only 17 triplets, as 49 of 534 REM epochs are followed directly by Non-REM. Sextiles 4 and 5 decrease (p = 0.022 and 0.011); the other four do not change significantly, and sextiles 1 and 2 have positive mean changes. With one value per triplet only sextile 4 decreases at p < 0.05.
deviations: The paper does not give its number of REM triplets; the dandiset's state table yields few.

outcomes.statement: Longer REM episodes produce a proportionally larger decrease of rates from one packet to the next (R = -0.22, p < 1e-2).
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5C
outcomes.notes: Per triplet R = -0.047 (p = 0.86, 17 triplets); per cell and triplet R = -0.061 (p = 0.21, 436 pairs). REM durations 8 to 157 s. Without BWRat21-121813, whose state labels could not be checked against the spikes, 13 triplets give R = -0.452 (p = 0.12).

outcomes.statement: Sigma power in the last 20 s of a packet between two MAs correlates with a larger increase of the slowest sextile from one MA to the next (R = 0.181, p < 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5C
outcomes.notes: Over 125 MA, packet, MA triplets with sextile 1 cells and LFP, R = 0.033 (p = 0.71). Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes the judgment is the same (R = -0.001). With a looser MA rule (Awake under 60 s with Non-REM on at least one side), 293 triplets give R = 0.110 (p = 0.06), the same judgment.
deviations: MAs derived from the Awake label; one LFP channel per session; Dino-061914 left out.

outcomes.statement: The increase of the slowest sextile's rate from one packet to the next is positively correlated with the change of delta power between the packets, regardless of the intervening state.
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5C
outcomes.notes: Over 613 consecutive packet pairs, R = 0.183 (p = 5.3e-06) for sextile 1, and R = -0.368 for sextile 6. Per subject the sextile 1 correlation is positive in 4 of 8 subjects, so the pooled result rests on some animals. With one R per session (14 sessions with at least 5 packet pairs) the median R is +0.025, positive in 7, Wilcoxon p = 0.43, so the correlation does not hold per session; the criterion uses the pooled pairs. Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes the judgment is the same (R = 0.114, p = 0.011).
deviations: One LFP channel per session; Dino-061914 left out.

outcomes.statement: Within WAKE the two fastest sextiles increase and the two slowest decrease their rates; within REM all sextiles except the fourth increase.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM, last paragraph (Figure S5A and S5B)
outcomes.notes: Within 495 WAKE epochs sextiles 5 and 6 decrease (R = -0.122 and -0.120, p < 1e-12), opposite to the claim, and sextile 2 increases (R = +0.067). Within 388 REM epochs no sextile changes at p < 0.05.
deviations: The paper's analysis for this claim is in Figure S5, which was not available; entry into WAKE may have been analysed differently (for example aligned to WAKE onset).

outcomes.statement: WAKE periods with more movement have a larger effect on the rate increase of the fastest sextile from one packet to the next (R = 0.43, p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, sleep sub-states induce lasting changes; Figure 5C
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds no movement, accelerometer, video or EMG data (acquisition is empty; the files hold units, LFP, spike waveforms and the state table), and no other public source of the movement measurements was found.

outcomes.statement: DOWN states have a median duration of 0.19 s and UP states 0.47 s.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns (Figure S4A)
outcomes.notes: UP and DOWN states were detected with spike and LFP criteria whose thresholds are given only in the Supplemental Experimental Procedures, which could not be retrieved. The spikes and LFP needed are in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Over SLEEP, the incidence of spindles (R = -0.093), UP states (R = -0.10) and DOWN states (R = -0.08) decreases and DOWN state duration increases, while spindle duration, frequency and amplitude do not change.
outcomes.source: Results, firing pattern and LFP changes across sleep; Figure 3C
outcomes.notes: Needs UP/DOWN state and spindle detection, described only in the unavailable supplement (see updown-durations); the main text says only that spindles were detected after filtering and integration.

outcomes.statement: Within packets the incidence of UP and DOWN states increases, UP states shorten and DOWN states lengthen, and spindle incidence and duration increase.
outcomes.source: Results, firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM; Figure 4A and 4B, panels ii and iii
outcomes.notes: Needs UP/DOWN state and spindle detection (see fig3c-slow-oscillation-spindles-over-sleep).

outcomes.statement: pE cells fire in stable sequences early in UP states, and the latency of a cell's first spike is negatively correlated with its firing rate.
outcomes.source: Results, assessment of firing patterns; Figure 2D and 2E
outcomes.notes: Needs UP state onsets (see updown-durations).

outcomes.statement: Within UP states, the fastest sextile and pI cells decrease and the slowest sextile increases from early to late SLEEP, and within packets the fastest sextile drops while pI cells increase.
outcomes.notes: Needs UP state detection (see updown-durations).

findings.statement: The dandiset holds 22 sessions from 10 rats, where the paper and the dandiset's own description report 27 sessions from 11 rats; the files hold 945 units (826 excitatory, 96 inhibitory, 23 unknown) against the 995 putative pyramidal cells and 126 interneurons analysed. Which sessions and units were left out, and why, is not stated.

In sub-Dino_ses-Dino-072114 the spike times are whole seconds divided by 20000 (8451 distinct values from 0 to 0.4252 s, in a recording of 7959 s). The conversion read this session's spikes from a CellExplorer file with a hard-coded 20 kHz rate. The session's spikes cannot be used.

In sub-Dino_ses-Dino-061914 the LFP has 125 columns for 128 electrodes, lasts 331.7 min against 291.9 min of states and spikes, and its samples are scrambled (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.28 on the reference channel, against 0.99 or more in every other session), consistent with a 128-channel file read as 125 channels.

The state table holds only Awake, Non-REM and REM. The paper scores microarousals as a state of their own and builds WAKE-SLEEP episodes, nonREM packets and episodes, UP/DOWN states and spindles, none of which is in the dandiset. MAs derived from short Awake epochs are fewer than the paper reports (391 in 21 sessions, against 790 in 27).

The dandiset does not say how the state table was scored. The conversion code takes it from each session's SleepState.states.mat; it yields 30 WAKE-SLEEP cycles in 21 sessions (3 sessions with none, though the paper kept only sessions with a full cycle), and only 49 of 534 REM epochs are followed directly by Non-REM, so it may not be the scoring the paper used.

The dandiset description gives 11 animals, 27 sessions and 1360 units, the paper's numbers, while the files hold 10 animals, 22 sessions and 945 units (the archive's summary counts 10 subjects). The description gives an age of 4-7 months, the files 3-7 months.
The LFP is stored as int16 with unit volts and conversion NaN, so it cannot be converted to volts.

Every electrode's location is "unknown" and every unit's region is "CTX" or "unknown", although the paper records from medial prefrontal, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate and secondary motor cortex; only the electrode groups carry a region.
23 units of sub-BWRat21_ses-BWRat21-121613 have cell type and region "unknown", with no description of what the label means.
No movement, accelerometer or EMG data are in the dandiset, though the paper uses EMG to score states and movement to define WAKE and to relate WAKE to rate changes.

The state labels are consistent with the spikes in 20 of 21 sessions (not established for BWRat21-121813), but in 14 sessions the best agreement is with the table shifted 5 to 60 s earlier, so state boundaries may lag the activity. The LFP agrees with the spikes to within 50 ms in 14 of 21 sessions. Of the other seven, three (BWRat21-121113, Bogey-012615, Dino-072414) have a clear cross-correlation extreme 56 to 64 ms from zero lag; in three (BWRat17-121912, BWRat21-121613, BWRat21-121813) the extreme is less than three times the value at plus or minus 1 s, so agreement is not established; and the LFP of Dino-061914 is scrambled.

attempts.paper_title: Diversity in neural firing dynamics supports both rigid and learned hippocampal sequences
attempts.entry_title: Rigid and plastic hippocampal sequences (Grosmark and Buzsaki 2016)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) on dandiset 000044, which holds eight sessions of CA1 units, LFP, sleep states and track positions from four rats, each with sleep before and after exploring a novel track. It decodes candidate ripple events with a Bayesian decoder, compares sequence scores across PRE, MAZE and POST, estimates each place cell's contribution to sequences, and relates firing rate and ripple gain to coactivation and replay.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) from dandiset 000044

outcomes.statement: Recordings were made in four rats, in eight novel exploration sessions, each a PRE sleep, a MAZE epoch on one of two linear tracks or a circular track, and a POST sleep.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure S1 (as cited in the text)
outcomes.notes: 4 subjects and 8 sessions, each with PRE, MAZE and POST epochs in that order (8 of 8), on a 1.6 m linear track (4 sessions), a 2 m linear track (1) and a circular track (3). PRE lasts 2.98 to 5.37 h, MAZE 34.5 to 92.7 min and POST 2.22 to 4.51 h. The rooms the paper names are not in the files.

outcomes.statement: The Bayesian decoder was built from 491 place cells over the eight sessions.
outcomes.notes: 417 of the 562 pyramidal units have a smoothed rate-map peak of 1 Hz or more on running, below 491 by more than the tolerance of 49. At 0.5 Hz the count is 480 (within tolerance), at 2 Hz 352, so the count depends strongly on the threshold; the criterion fixes 1 Hz and the other thresholds are variants that do not decide the outcome. By subject, Achilles 181, Buddy 30, Cicero 127, Gatsby 79.
deviations: The place-cell definition is a common choice (peak of 1 Hz or more on running above 5 cm/s, 2 cm bins, 4 cm smoothing); the paper's definition is in the supplementary Methods, which were not available.

outcomes.statement: Sequence scores (rZ) of candidate events are higher in POST sleep than in PRE sleep (replay).
outcomes.notes: Pooled over sessions, as the criterion fixes the test, POST does not exceed PRE (mean rZ 0.763 against 0.770, Tukey on ranks after Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.412). Within sessions it does; POST is higher in 8 of 8 sessions (sign test p = 0.0039; one-sided rank-sum p < 0.05 in 6), and with each session's PRE mean subtracted POST is higher by 0.106 (p = 2.3e-14). The pooled test is dominated by the three circular-track sessions, which score lower in every epoch (PRE 0.161 and POST 0.260 against 1.112 and 1.207 on the linear tracks, where the event takes the better of two templates) and supply 11161 of 23801 POST events but 5912 of 16448 PRE events. The same test run on each kind of track finds POST above PRE on the five linear-track sessions (Tukey on ranks p = 5.1e-07) and on the three circular-track sessions (p = 1.1e-05). By subject, POST minus PRE is +0.089 (Achilles), +0.185 (Buddy), +0.021 (Cicero) and -0.173 (Gatsby) when pooled within subject.
deviations: Candidate events are population bursts of all units holding a ripple (150 to 250 Hz envelope above 3 SD on one LFP channel per session), outside REM in PRE and POST and below 5 cm/s in MAZE; the paper's detection is in the unavailable Methods.
The rZ null is 200 column-cycle shuffles of the posterior; the paper's shuffle is not stated in the main text.
On the linear tracks each event takes the better of the two direction templates, which raises their scores over those of the single-template circular track.
The Tukey comparison is scipy's Tukey HSD on the pooled ranks, not MATLAB's Tukey-Kramer after kruskalwallis.
Immobility for MAZE candidate events is taken from the 2D head speed, while running for the rate maps is taken from the speed of the linearized position, both at 5 cm/s.

outcomes.statement: Sequence content is higher in MAZE immobility events than in PRE sleep events.
outcomes.notes: MAZE events score higher than PRE events (mean rZ 1.270 against 0.770, n = 2460 and 16448; Tukey on ranks p printed as 0), and MAZE is higher in all 8 sessions (one-sided rank-sum p from below 0.0001 to 0.0405). It holds on the linear-track sessions (p printed as 0) and on the circular-track sessions (p = 0.0007) separately. MAZE has 76 to 953 scored events per session.
deviations: Events and scores as for fig1c-post-gt-pre.

outcomes.statement: 216 neurons showed significant PCC scores in PRE or POST and were considered to contribute strongly to sequences.
outcomes.notes: The test fixed in the criterion (one-sided signed-rank test of a cell's contributions over its events, p < 0.05) finds 303 strongly contributing cells (72.7% of 417 place cells), against 216. With every rate map shifted it calls 56.1% of cells significant (0.843 on the 1.6 m tracks, 0.905 on the 2 m track, 0.140 on the circular track), so about 234 would be expected by chance. The paper calls these PCC scores significant, which implies a 5% false-positive rate; this test is far from it, so it is not the paper's procedure. The excess is on the linear tracks, where the contribution is taken on the template the event was selected for. A best-template variant of the contribution has a false-positive rate of 0.206 (0.132 in PRE, 0.118 in POST) and finds 188 cells, outside the tolerance; at alpha 0.001 its false-positive rate is 0.031 and it finds 95. The false-positive rates are measured on every fourth PRE and POST event, so on all events they would likely be higher. The best-template numbers are not identical across machines (the verifier's executed copy printed 190 cells and 0.129 in PRE); no conclusion rests on the difference. The PCC definition and its test are in the unavailable Methods.
deviations: The PCC and its significance test are choices made here, as the Methods were not available.
The 20 shifts of a cell's map are drawn afresh for every event.

outcomes.statement: Most neurons strongly contributing to PRE sequences (73%) also contributed to POST sequences.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Of 248 PRE strongly contributing cells, 235 (94.8%) also contribute in POST, against a chance level of 69.5%. With the best-template variant 72 of 102 (70.6%), within 73 +/- 7.3, against a chance level of 37.9%.

outcomes.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence score is eliminated when the place fields of the 10 to 20% of cells with the highest dPCC are shuffled, and remains after shuffling the bottom 75%.
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test of the criterion replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% (POST minus PRE -0.100, p = 1.0) and the top 20% (-0.127, p = 1.0), but also after shuffling the bottom 75% (+0.022, p = 0.21), so one of the two conditions holds. The pooled test finds no replay before shuffling either (-0.008, p = 0.916), so on all sessions it cannot show a removal. On the five linear-track sessions replay is present before shuffling (+0.101, p < 0.0001), absent after shuffling the top 10% (+0.015, p = 0.23) or 20% (-0.039, p = 0.995) and present after the bottom 75% (+0.098, p < 0.0001); shuffling a random 10% or 20% leaves it (+0.099, +0.088). dPCC is measured on the events that are decoded again. Ranking cells on the even-numbered events and measuring replay on the odd-numbered ones, on the linear tracks replay falls from +0.116 to +0.046 (p = 0.024) after the top 10% and +0.042 (p = 0.038) after the top 20%, so out of sample it is reduced but not removed.
deviations: Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.
dPCC is the difference of the criterion's PCC, whose significance test is not the paper's (fig2b-strong-contributors); the ranking does not use that test.

outcomes.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to a small number of plastic cells; removing them, unlike removing rigid cells, removes the increase.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. On the pooled test, removing plastic cells gives POST minus PRE -0.168 (p = 1.0) and removing rigid cells +0.038 (p = 0.019); removing as many random strongly contributing cells gives -0.023 (p = 0.99). On the linear-track sessions -0.060, +0.136 and +0.094. With classes from the even-numbered events and replay on the odd-numbered ones, the linear tracks give -0.009 (p = 0.54) and +0.090 (p = 0.0027). With the best-template classes, pooled, -0.125 and +0.020 (p = 0.24).

outcomes.statement: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; fig. S2 as cited
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Rate-map peaks of rigid and plastic cells do not differ by the KS test (medians 0.419 and 0.486 of the track, D = 0.145, p = 0.072); with the split over all place cells p = 0.079, with the best-template classes p = 0.12.

outcomes.statement: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields than rigid cells.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Plastic cells carry more spatial information (median 0.904 against 0.594 bits per spike, p = 1.9e-05; best-template classes p = 0.0035), but the number of fields does not differ (means 1.484 and 1.685, p = 0.073).

outcomes.statement: Plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity (in-field versus out-of-field firing ratio) steadily during the MAZE session.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Both groups raise their in-field ratio over the session (change of log10 ratio, plastic median 0.155, p = 0.0079; rigid 0.129, p = 0.030; between groups p = 0.41). With the best-template classes plastic p = 0.020 and rigid p = 0.28.

outcomes.statement: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were higher than those of plastic neurons.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Rigid cells fire somewhat faster (median 0.700 against 0.591 Hz) without significance (p = 0.062; split over all place cells p = 0.053; best-template classes p = 0.74).

outcomes.statement: Ripple-related spiking, bursting and pairwise coactivation were higher in plastic than in rigid neurons.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Ripple gain (4.489 against 3.939, p = 0.015) and bursting (0.180 against 0.147, p = 0.028) are higher in plastic cells; coactivation is not (0.028 against 0.027, p = 0.90). With the best-template classes none reaches p < 0.05 (gain p = 0.15, bursting p = 0.11).

outcomes.statement: In PRE sleep, coactivation was dominated by fast-firing neurons.
outcomes.notes: PRE coactivation rises with firing rate, from 0.0208 in the slowest window to 0.0486 in the fastest; Spearman correlation 0.861 on the averaged curve, positive in 6 of 8 sessions. The POST minus PRE change of the fastest window does not differ from 0 over sessions (sign-rank p = 0.383), which fits the statement that these correlations remain into POST.
deviations: Coactivation over whole epochs, all states; the paper's restriction, if any, is not stated in the main text.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep.
outcomes.notes: The POST minus PRE change does not fall with firing rate; Spearman correlation -0.068 on the averaged curve (p = 0.55), negative in 5 of 8 sessions. The averaged change is 0.0019 in the slowest window and -0.0007 in the fastest, with a maximum of 0.0090.
deviations: Coactivation over whole epochs, all states.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing cells showed the greatest replay, the partial correlation between RUN and POST coactivation accounting for PRE.
outcomes.notes: The partial correlation of MAZE running and POST coactivation given PRE is 0.186 in the slowest window and 0.115 in the fastest, but the Spearman correlation over windows is 0.095 and negative in only 4 of 8 sessions. By subject it is -0.588 (Achilles), -0.646 (Buddy), -0.070 (Cicero) and 0.671 (Gatsby).
deviations: MAZE coactivation is taken over running bins (above 5 cm/s on the track).

outcomes.statement: Place cells divided into equal groups by sleep firing rate have medians of 0.39 Hz (low-rate) and 1.12 Hz (high-rate).
outcomes.notes: Split by non-REM sleep rate, the low-rate median is 0.435 Hz under both readings, just outside 0.39 +/- 0.039, and the high-rate median 1.091 Hz (a, within sessions) or 1.092 (b, pooled), within 1.12 +/- 0.112. With the rate over all of PRE and POST (a variant) both are within tolerance (0.395 and 1.041 under reading a). The split is of 417 place cells, not 491.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the split is within sessions or pooled; both readings are shown and give the same medians.
Off-line sleep rate is taken as the non-REM rate in PRE and POST; the rate over all of PRE and POST is a variant.

outcomes.statement: Low-rate neurons carried more spatial information per spike on the maze, and increased their within-ripple firing-rate gain from PRE to POST more than high-rate cells.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; fig. S16 as cited
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), which the criterion selects as neither reading of rate-split-medians matched, low-rate cells carry more spatial information (median 0.975 against 0.622 bits per spike, p = 4.1e-08), but their ripple-gain change from PRE to POST is not larger (0.251 against 0.155, p = 0.948). Reading (b) gives the same.
deviations: Ripple gain is the rate within candidate events over the epoch rate; the paper's definition is in fig. S16, which was not available.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to sequences from PRE to POST sleep, in a decoding restricted to each group.
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test neither half shows replay (low-rate POST minus PRE -0.024, p = 0.964; high-rate -0.049, p = 0.9999), as for all cells (-0.008, p = 0.916). In the within-session variant both halves show replay, larger for low-rate cells (+0.116 against +0.058, p of at most 0.0001 for each), which would be the criterion's partial pattern. On the linear-track sessions alone the pooled test also finds both, larger for low-rate cells (+0.077, p = 0.0046, against +0.044, p = 0.018).
deviations: Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.

outcomes.statement: PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells with high ripple-specific recruitment (gain).
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test neither half shows replay (high-gain -0.001, p = 0.71; low-gain -0.111, p = 1.0). In the within-session variant high-gain cells show replay (+0.111, p < 0.0001) and low-gain cells do not (+0.016, p = 0.14), the paper's pattern. On the linear-track sessions alone the pooled test finds replay in neither half (+0.023, p = 0.25; +0.010, p = 0.21) and the within-session variant finds it in both (+0.045, p = 0.029; +0.050, p = 0.0028).
deviations: Gain is the rate within PRE and POST candidate events over the PRE and POST rate, split at the session median.
Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.

findings.statement: In versions 0.210812.1516 and 0.250624.0426 every position series stores its sampling period (0.0256 s) as its rate, so the positions span about 880 to 2360 hours in place of the MAZE epoch. Version 0.261005.2101 stores 39.06 Hz, which matches the epoch lengths.
In Gatsby_08022013 the POST epoch ends at 30413.6 s, while the LFP, the spikes and the sleep states run to about 32000 s.
The dandiset description lists neck EMG and head-mounted accelerometer signals, and the files hold neither; they also hold no wide-band data (acquisition is empty), only the LFP at 1250 Hz.

The paper's derived data are not deposited. There are no candidate or ripple events, no place-cell list, no sequence scores and no PCC values or rigid and plastic labels, so the paper's selections cannot be checked against the dandiset and every one must be rebuilt.

Neither the paper nor the dandiset links analysis code, and the supplementary Materials and Methods, which define the candidate events, place cells, the PCC and its test, are not openly available (PMC and Science serve them only behind a browser check).

Every electrode's location is "unknown" and no depth or layer is given, so the channel for ripple detection has to be chosen from the signals. Units carry only the hemisphere (lCA1 or rCA1). Subject age is "/".

On the circular track the animals ran toward decreasing linearized position (47 to 63% of samples against 7 to 16% the other way). The series description says the position increases clockwise but not which way the animals ran.

The verifier checked the blocked claims against the archive's file list and metadata and tested the helper functions on synthetic inputs. Report in transcripts/000044/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: This claim ranks all place cells by dPCC and does not use the strong-contributor selection, so the block reason does not apply (problem 4). By the criterion replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% or 20% but also after shuffling the bottom 75% (p = 0.35); the unmanipulated baseline has no pooled replay either (p = 0.92), so "eliminated" cannot be judged (uninformative). The within-session variant shows the paper's pattern. dPCC is computed from the same PRE and POST events that are decoded again, so the result is circular and there is no control that shuffles a random X% of cells (problem 3).

Replay is absent without plastic cells (p = 1.0) and present without rigid cells (p = 0.020). The result is circular (problem 3), and with the shift-test classes removing rigid cells leaves no replay (p = 0.11).
KS p = 0.034 (cell 37). This is fragile, p = 0.051 under reading (b) and 0.12 under the shift-test variant.
Spatial information is higher in plastic cells (p = 3e-4). The number of fields does not differ (p = 0.52) (cell 39).
Both groups increase: plastic p = 0.015, rigid p = 0.032 (cell 41).
Rigid cells have the higher median, but p = 0.059 (cell 43).
Gain is higher in plastic cells (p = 0.037). Bursting (p = 0.20) and coactivation (p = 0.79) are not (cell 45).
