attempts.paper_title: Reactivations of emotional memory in the hippocampus–amygdala system during sleep
attempts.entry_title: Hippocampus and amygdala reactivation during sleep (Girardeau et al. 2017)
attempts.description: Tests the findings stated in the abstract of Girardeau, Inema and Buzsaki (2017) on dandiset 000061, which holds sorted units of the hippocampus and the amygdala, sleep states, ripple, air-puff and reward events from four rats on an air-puff linear track task. It tests the reactivation of joint hippocampus and BLA patterns in sleep after the run, its peak at ripples, the BLA cells modulated by ripples and their weight in the patterns, and the difference between the air-puff and the safe run direction. The paper's full text was not available, so the methods are common choices fixed before the analysis.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Girardeau et al. (2017) from dandiset 000061

outcomes.statement: Coordinated hippocampus and BLA activity patterns of the training run are reactivated during non-REM sleep after training, more than during non-REM sleep before it.
outcomes.notes: 15 sessions (9 Rat08, 3 Rat10, 3 Rat11) with 341 hippocampal and 483 BLA units; every session has at least one significant joint pattern, 36 in all. Post-sleep minus pre-sleep Non-REM strength has a median of 0.0119, positive in 28 of 36, Wilcoxon p = 3.6e-05. The median is above zero in each rat (Rat08 0.0170, 18 of 21, p = 0.00013; Rat10 0.0024, 5 of 8, p = 0.74; Rat11 0.0190, 5 of 7, p = 0.11). Non-significant patterns change by a median of 0.0001. The variants (25 and 100 ms bins, the wider BLA labels over 21 sessions, the first pattern of each session) all give positive medians with p of 0.0084 or less. The comparison does not separate reactivation from slow drift of the recording, since post-sleep is next to the run in time.
deviations: The paper's methods were not available; the joint-pattern method (singular vectors of the run's hippocampus by BLA cross-correlation matrix, shuffle threshold, product of projections), the 50 ms bins and the unit criteria are common choices fixed in the claims file.
BLA is taken as the units labelled bla or BLA; other undescribed labels that may be parts of the basolateral complex are a variant only.
Sessions without sleep states or ripples, and Rat09 (no hippocampal units), are left out; which sessions and rats the paper used is not known here.
Units 0 and 1 of ten files are left out because their spike times are mixed (see findings).

outcomes.statement: The hippocampus and BLA reactivations peak during hippocampal sharp wave-ripples.
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) holds. The mean ripple-triggered strength in post-sleep Non-REM is highest in the bin of the ripple peak, 4.36 times its mean at 0.5 to 1 s; the peak bin exceeds the flanks in 30 of 36 patterns (median 0.103, p = 6e-06), with a positive median in each rat. 22 of 36 patterns have their own maximum within 100 ms of the ripple. The pre-sleep curve also peaks at ripples (0.136 against 0.223 post), and the peak over flanks is larger post than pre (23 of 36, p = 0.022). Reading (b) also holds; the post minus pre change in ripple bins exceeds that outside ripples (median difference 0.0537, 25 of 36, p = 0.0033). Much of the reading (a) peak is already present in pre-sleep, so reading (a) alone does not separate reactivation of the run from co-activation at ripples in general; the post minus pre contrasts do. At session level (15 sessions) the peak over flanks is positive in 13 (p = 0.00031), its post minus pre increase in 10 (p = 0.03), and the reading (b) difference in 10 (p = 0.03).
deviations: The abstract's "peaked during SPW-Rs" can be read in two ways; both readings were fixed in the criterion and both match.
Ripples are the dandiset's `rip` annotations, not a detection run here.

outcomes.statement: A subgroup of BLA cells is positively modulated during hippocampal sharp wave-ripples.
outcomes.notes: 103 of 822 BLA units in 17 sessions (12.5%) are positively modulated in Non-REM ripple windows, against a chance level of 0.7% (6 units) from the same procedure on windows shifted by 7 s; binomial p = 9.8e-90. Above chance in each rat (Rat08 51 of 496, Rat10 4 of 84, Rat11 48 of 242), also against each rat's own chance level (Rat10 has 0 chance units; p = 0.018 against one unit). 104 units (12.7%) are negatively modulated. At p of 0.05 or less the fraction is 16.3% against 5.6% chance, at 0.002 or less 10.8% against 0.2%. The shifted windows stay mostly in Non-REM (a median of 0.9% of randomly shifted and 1.4% of 7 s shifted ripple peaks fall outside it).
deviations: The test of modulation (spike count in ripple windows against windows shifted together by 0.5 to 5 s, one-sided p of 0.01 or less) is a common choice; the paper's test is not known here.
Units are counted once per session; a cell recorded on several days may be counted more than once, as the dandiset does not match units across days.

outcomes.statement: The hippocampus and BLA reactivations involve the subgroup of BLA cells that are positively modulated during sharp wave-ripples.
outcomes.notes: In 31 significant patterns with both kinds of BLA unit, the mean squared BLA weight of the ripple-up units exceeds that of the other BLA units (medians 0.0505 and 0.0181; difference positive in 24 of 31, Wilcoxon p = 0.0013). The ripple-up units are a median 20% of a pattern's BLA units and carry 34% of its BLA weight. It holds in Rat08 (17 of 21) and Rat11 (6 of 7) and not in Rat10 (1 of 3). In patterns whose post minus pre reactivation is positive, p = 0.0018. Firing rate accounts for part of the effect; up units fire faster in the run (median 1.66 against 0.41 Hz) and squared weight rises with rate within a pattern (median Spearman 0.46). Against other BLA units of the nearest rate, up units still carry more weight (24 of 31 patterns, p = 0.012). At session level (13 sessions) the difference holds (10 of 13, p = 0.027), the rate-matched difference does not (9 of 13, p = 0.22). The criterion is the pooled per-pattern test, which holds.
deviations: The abstract does not say how involvement was measured; the pattern weights were chosen here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: Reactivation is stronger for the hippocampus and BLA correlation patterns of the run direction that held the air puff than for those of the safe direction.
outcomes.notes: Over 15 sessions, post minus pre reactivation of the air-puff templates exceeds that of the safe templates by a median of 0.0133, in 9 of 15 sessions, Wilcoxon p = 0.11; the criterion needs p < 0.05, and p < 0.1 for a partial outcome. Positive in 6 of 9 Rat08, 2 of 3 Rat10 and 1 of 3 Rat11 sessions. Variants lean the same way with mixed strength; the first pattern of each direction gives p = 0.048 (10 of 15), the pooled per-pattern Mann-Whitney test p = 0.083, equal numbers of template bins (a random subset) p = 0.33, post-sleep strength alone p = 0.45, leaving out the two sessions with fewer than 5 puffs p = 0.15, and templates from the travel part of each lap only (its last part, as long as the session's 10th-percentile lap) p = 0.19. Laps from reward times include the time spent at the end where a lap starts; a median of 33% of the air-puff and 43% of the safe template time is in the travel part, and in the early Rat08 sessions laps last up to 2310 s, so the safe templates of some sessions rest on few bins (5610 against 66804 in Rat08-20130709).
deviations: Laps, and so run direction, come from the reward times, as the dandiset holds no position; the paper presumably used the position on the track.

The air-puff direction is the lap direction of the run holding most puffs; in the 15 sessions tested, 295 of their 304 puffs fall in laps of that direction (927 of 957 over the 31 files with units and at least 5 puffs). No minimum number of puffs was set; two sessions with 2 and 3 puffs enter the test.
Laps include the time spent at the starting end, not only running; templates from the travel part of laps are a variant.
The measure (mean over significant patterns of post minus pre strength, compared across sessions) was chosen here before the analysis; the paper's is not known here.

outcomes.statement: Rats learned the location of an aversive air puff on a linear track.
outcomes.notes: Learning the location of the puff is behaviour along the track, which needs the rat's position. The dandiset holds no position tracking. The files hold the raw video frames (360 by 640 pixels, gzip), so position could in principle be tracked, but the 40 run videos have 1920573 frames (1328 GB uncompressed) and streaming 20 frames took 7.2 s in the final run, about 190 hours for the run frames alone (the rate varies between runs); the video timestamps are also not on the session clock. No public copy of the tracking linked to the paper or the dandiset was found. As a description only, laps toward the air-puff end take longer than the other way in the run (median ratio 1.18 over 38 sessions, p = 0.0063) and about as long in the pre-run (0.95) and the post-run (1.00); lap times give no location on the track, and slower laps where puffs are given do not separate learning from the puffs themselves. No criterion was written, so this decides nothing.

findings.statement: The epochs table is stored in milliseconds although its columns say seconds; in all 40 files its last stop time is exactly 1000 times the LFP duration and the last spike time.

Video timestamps are stated in seconds but are in milliseconds and are not on the session clock. The first timestamp matches the start of the video's epoch in 1 of 114 videos, while the spans match the epoch durations in 93 of 114.

In ten files the spike_times_index is wrong at the first units. Unit 1's spike times fall back once, after 65536 times k spikes, and unit 0 stops part way through the session at the time unit 1 starts, so the first part of unit 1 is the end of unit 0. Units 0 and 1 of these files were left out.

Seven files have no units table (Rat08-20130722, five Rat09 files and Rat11-20150403), sixteen have no sleep states and fourteen have no ripple events. The Rat09 files have no hippocampal units and no ripples, so Rat09 cannot enter a hippocampus and BLA analysis.

There is no position tracking, only the raw video frames, so behaviour on the track, including the learning of the puff location, cannot be measured without tracking about 1.9 million frames; run direction can only be inferred from reward times.

Unit region labels are undescribed short codes (bla, blv, bmp, ladl, cen, den, ven, pir, plc01, PLCo1, cpu, hpc, HIP, no label), some in two cases for the same region, and Rat09-20140328 has no location column; the electrode table gives every channel as unknown. Which labels make up the paper's BLA cannot be told from the dandiset.
The `trials` table of the Rat08 and Rat09 files is described only as "experimental trials"; its intervals of 3 to 5 s fall partly outside the run and are not laps.

The ripple annotations carry a number in each label (for example "Ripple peak 156"), presumably the detection channel, with no description; ripples, puffs and rewards are stored as annotation series under stimulus presentation.
The paper is not open access and neither it (as far as the abstract shows) nor the dandiset links analysis code, so the reactivation method, unit selection and statistics had to be chosen here.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper's abstract (the full text is not open access). The verifier tested helper functions on synthetic inputs and read the archive's asset metadata for the blocked claim. Its report had no attempt record and gave its own outcome for each claim; all six agree with the record on the outcome, and it gave a different reason for the block.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook after the round-1 revision, with its conclusions and summary, the helper module, the claims file, the attempt record and the README. The verifier agreed with all six outcomes and recomputed the three session-level Wilcoxon tests of cell 35. It found five passages the printed outputs did not support. The video streaming time in the record did not match cell 11; this is corrected from the final run (7.2 s, about 192 hours). The pre-run and post-run were said to have no puffs without a count; cell 51 now prints the puffs by epoch (1195 of 1197 in the run, 2 in the pre-sleep, none in the pre-run or post-run). The 927 of 957 puffs covered only the 31 files of cell 19; cell 20 and the deviation now say so, and cell 48 prints the count for the 15 tested sessions (295 of 304). Cell 40 gave the negatively modulated units as the reason the up units are a subgroup; it now rests that on the fraction being below 1. The README run time was not printed; the notebook now prints its run time (13.9 min in the final run) and the README gives it. All round-1 points were resolved. No outcome changed, and none is proposed to change.

attempts.paper_title: Behavior-dependent short-term assembly dynamics in the medial prefrontal cortex
attempts.entry_title: Prefrontal assemblies and monosynaptic dynamics in a working memory task (Fujisawa et al. 2008)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Fujisawa, Amarasingham, Harrison and Buzsaki (2008) on dandiset 000067, which holds recordings of three rats from a 64-site prefrontal probe and a CA1 probe during an odor-place matching task. Units are placed on the probes from their waveforms in the wideband signal. It tests the population activity, field sizes and trajectory selectivity of prefrontal neurons, monosynaptic connections found with a jitter test, the cell classes and distances they imply, and the task dependence, short-term plasticity and summation of the connections. The paper's example session and fourth rat are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Fujisawa et al. (2008) from dandiset 000067

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's recording channels can be assigned to the prefrontal probe, the CA1 probe and the nose-poke sensors by the channel map of the CRCNS pfc-2 description of the same recordings (channels 1 to 64 prefrontal, 65 to 96 CA1, 97 right and 98 left nose-poke sensors), and the data agree with that map.
outcomes.source: Methods (8-shank, 64-site probe in mPFC); CRCNS pfc-2 data description, version 0.7
outcomes.notes: Records are matched by channel number. In rats EE and FF the CRCNS map holds in every session; the CA1 channels have a theta ratio 1.9 to 2.7 times that of channels 1 to 64, and the more active sensor during the nose poke is the trial's side in 0.97 to 1.00 of trials. In rat GG channels 97 and 98 are not sensors (agreement 0.35 to 0.42); the sensors are on 65 and 66 and the CA1 probe on 70 to 101, and with that correction both checks hold in every session (agreement 1.00). The sensor on 66 is active on trials labelled Right, so in GG the order of the sensors, or the side labels, is reversed relative to EE and FF. Channels 1 to 64 have a lower theta ratio than the CA1 channels in every session (0.16 to 0.27 against 0.37 to 0.54), so the prefrontal probe is placed as the description says in all three rats; every claim that uses PFC units depends on that part, which holds.
deviations: The map is used with the per-rat correction found in the data, not as published.
The sensor check of EE.088 uses its LFP only; it has no wideband signal for the theta check.

outcomes.statement: 633 well-isolated units were recorded from the mPFC of four rats.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds three rats (EE, FF, GG), against four. The eight analysed sessions hold 417 PFC single units under reading (a), 346 under (b) and 491 under (c), all outside 633 plus or minus 63. The 350 units of EE.088 cannot be placed on a probe, and EE.152, EE.165 and EE.188, working memory sessions in the CRCNS table, are not in the dandiset; the paper does not say which sessions its 633 units come from, nor whether units recorded on several days were counted once. Variants; leaving out also the first unit of each shank block gives 416. Placing EE.088's units by the conversion's block order (a block starts at each multi-unit cluster; blocks 1 to 8 taken as prefrontal), a rule that matches the waveform placement in EE.049 and EE.196 (agreement 1.000) but not in FF and GG (0.360 to 0.956), adds 214 PFC single units and gives 631, within tolerance; the count of rats still fails.
deviations: Units are counted per session; the paper's way of counting is not stated.
Well-isolated units are selected by a refractory rule chosen here.

outcomes.statement: Rats performed the odor-place matching task at 92% correct (91.9% in the recording sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Methods, Behavioral task
outcomes.notes: The trial table lists correct trials only (the CRCNS description of SessionNP, from which the conversion built the table), so the fraction of correct trials cannot be computed. The position has no y coordinate, so the choice on other trials cannot be recovered from the path. Error trials are not in the dandiset, and the CRCNS data need an account. Every listed run holds one lap found from x1, and the nine sessions hold 100 laps and 147 nose-poke bouts outside the 335 listed trials; if every lap outside a listed run were an error trial, performance would be 77.0%, and if every unlisted nose-poke bout were one, 69.5%. The files do not say which were errors, nor whether every error trial produced a lap or a bout, so these are not bounds in one direction and not a test.

outcomes.statement: About 10% (layer 2/3) and 20% (layer 5) of the recorded neurons fire at least one spike in any 100 ms window, a fraction that is relatively constant along the maze.
outcomes.notes: Per-rat medians of the session means are 10.2% (EE), 19.7% (FF) and 6.2% (GG); EE fits the layer 2/3 value and FF the layer 5 value, GG fits neither. The ratio of the largest to the smallest position-bin mean is 1.16 to 1.88 in seven sessions and 2.57 in GG.149. Neither part of the criterion holds for every rat; both hold for EE and FF. GG's sessions have 18 or 19 PFC single units each.
deviations: The layer of each rat is not known; values are matched rat by rat under the layer readings.
The threshold for "relatively constant" (a factor of 2) is chosen here.

outcomes.statement: Neurons are active over similar standardized distances of the maze, 0.27 (62 cm) plus or minus 0.17 (39 cm) (mean and s.d.), from the 50% boundaries of the peak firing rate.
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), 346 units, mean 0.270 and s.d. 0.196; (b) 0.281 and 0.206; (c) 0.331 and 0.220. The mean is within tolerance under every reading and the s.d. under none (0.17 plus or minus 0.017). No side without spikes entered reading (b); with only sides whose own peak is at least 1 Hz it gives 0.292 and 0.214. With peak thresholds from 0 to 5 Hz the mean of (a) is 0.254 to 0.330 and the s.d. 0.189 to 0.243. Per rat the means are 0.221 (EE), 0.322 (FF) and 0.272 (GG).
deviations: The mean's tolerance is the paper's stated s.d. of the neurons, as the protocol asks, which accepts a wide range of means; the s.d. carries the test.
The 1 Hz peak rule is the CRCNS "Cells" rule, not the paper's.
The paper does not say how the 50% boundaries are taken or which trajectory is used; three readings are shown.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of neurons with significantly different firing on left and right trials is 16% (layer 2/3) and 18% (layer 5) in the central arm (positions 0 to 0.3), where the trajectories overlap, and 22% (layer 2/3) and 40% (layer 5) in the side arms (0.5 to 1).
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 2b; Methods, permutation tests and global bands
outcomes.notes: Central arm, 22.9% (EE), 24.5% (FF) and 26.2% (GG) of units with a peak of at least 1 Hz (24.0% of 346 pooled), against 0.9% with relabelled trials (Fisher p = 7.3e-24; a McNemar test on the same units, 82 against 2 discordant units, p = 1.9e-22); every rat is above the 14.4 to 19.8% range. Side arms, 51.6%, 59.9% and 52.4%, above both layer values. Per session the central-arm fraction is 1.9% to 69.2%. With the s.d. band, 24.3% and 59.8% pooled. The procedure's chance rate (0.9% for each segment) is below the global 5%, as expected for a segment of the track. The selective fractions are higher than the paper's in every rat, so units selective by this test are more common here.
deviations: The number of permutations (1000) and the 101-point grid are chosen here.
Layers are matched rat by rat, as the layer of each rat is not known.
In rat GG the side labels may be swapped (see channel-region-link); this does not change a left-right test.

outcomes.statement: Left and right trajectories overlap in the central arm and begin to differ significantly at position 0.3.
outcomes.notes: The claim is about where left and right trajectories separate laterally, which would show along the y coordinate; the second LED series is zero throughout (cell 33), so the dandiset has no y coordinate. x1, the x coordinate of the first head LED, runs along the maze (about 570 px at the start, 190 px near position 0.5, back up towards the reward) on both sides. Under the criterion written in the first revision it differs between sides somewhere in 0.5 to 1 in all 9 sessions, by at most 7 to 57 px, with a median divergence point of 0.49 (8 of 9 sessions have one), which the written criterion would rate as partially reproduced. The divergence point lies within 0.08 of the position where x1 reaches its minimum (0.47 to 0.53) in the seven sessions other than GG.149 (median -0.01 over eight, cell 35), and at position 0.3 the sides differ by a median 2.8 px while x1 falls by a median 244 px from 0 to 0.3. x1 thus begins to differ where the path turns back in x and does not locate a lateral separation, and the criterion's partial rating would follow from any x1 divergence past the turn. Changed to blocked in round 3, with the verifier's agreement. The overlap of the paths in the central arm cannot be judged either; the 5 to 17 px x1 differences there in five sessions do not stand in for a two-dimensional comparison.
deviations: Only the x coordinate is available; the paper used the two-dimensional position.
The test (Welch t-test per bin of 0.02, p < 0.01, divergence from the first bin of a run up to 0.6) is chosen here; the paper's is in a supplementary figure that was not available.
The criterion was written in the first revision, after the verifier's report.

outcomes.statement: About one quarter of the neurons fire at significantly different rates (P < 0.05 per cell) during nose poking for the two odors.
outcomes.notes: 37.8% of 397 units (Mann-Whitney P < 0.05) against 4.0% with relabelled trials (Fisher p = 5.5e-35; McNemar on the same units, 142 against 8, p = 3.9e-33); outside 20 to 30%. A t-test gives 28.5%, which would be within, but the test was fixed beforehand. Per rat 34.9% (EE), 50.3% (FF), 11.1% (GG). Odor and side are the same variable here, as only correct trials are listed, so the difference can come from the odor or from the coming choice; the paper's Supplementary Figure 6 analysis of that point was not available.
deviations: The paper names no test; a Mann-Whitney test of per-trial rates was chosen.
The nose-poke period is from the start of the first nose poke to the end of the last (median 4.66 s), as the trial table gives; the paper's window is not stated in the main text.

outcomes.statement: Of all ordered pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons, 0.79% had short-latency, narrow peaks or troughs in their cross-correlograms (0.55% excitatory, 0.24% inhibitory), found with a jitter test.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 3a and 3e; Methods, identifying monosynaptic interactions
outcomes.notes: 31754 ordered pairs; connections 1.131%, excitatory 0.898%, inhibitory 0.233%. Only the inhibitory rate is within tolerance. Excitatory connections are 4.01% of same-shank pairs and 0.35% of pairs across shanks; per rat the excitatory rate is 0.84% (EE), 1.05% (FF), 0.94% (GG). The Poisson screen passed 857 unordered pairs to the Monte Carlo test, and none of the 800 unscreened pairs tested anyway was significant. 40 unordered pairs (0.252%) are connected both ways (paper 0.17%). Counting peaks of any width gives 0.938% excitatory. The excess of same-shank peaks may include pairs of clusters split from one neuron, which the paper's curated units may not contain. The inhibitory match is fragile; 34 of the 74 inhibitory connections are troughs in the reverse direction of a pair with a peak, which jittering both trains can produce (on 30 synthetic excitatory pairs with no inhibition, the criterion's rule finds such a trough in 21, and none once they are excluded). Without them the rates are 1.023%, 0.898% and 0.126%, none within tolerance, and 10 pairs (0.063%) are reciprocal.
deviations: Bins of 1 ms (not stated in the main text) and a Poisson screen before the Monte Carlo test.

A trough beside a peak in the same direction is not counted as inhibition (chosen here). Troughs that mirror a peak in the other direction are counted, as the criterion was written; the rates without them are shown as a variant.
The set of well-isolated units is selected here, not by the paper.

outcomes.statement: By their connections, 32.5% of units are putative pyramidal cells and 12.5% putative interneurons, a ratio of 2.82 plus or minus 0.51 (s.d.), and 50.7% of the postsynaptic targets of putative excitatory cells themselves inhibit other neurons.
outcomes.notes: Of 417 units, 37.9% putative pyramidal and 3.1% putative interneurons, and 21 units have outgoing connections of both kinds. The ratio is 11.92 plus or minus 7.46 over the five sessions with an interneuron (pooled 12.15, mean of rats 12.96), against 2.82 plus or minus 0.51. Of 124 targets of excitatory connections 7.3% are putative interneurons (20.2% have any inhibitory connection), against 50.7%. 54 of the 74 inhibitory connections come from units that also excite others. No value is within tolerance under any reading; the shortfall of interneurons drives the ratio and the targets. Without the troughs that mirror a peak (fig3-connection-rates), 38.6% pyramidal and 2.4% (10 units) interneurons, pooled ratio 16.10, and 4.8% of targets are interneurons, further from the paper.
deviations: Units with both kinds of connection are counted in neither class (chosen here).

outcomes.statement: Most connected pairs were recorded on the same shank, and the probability of a connection falls with the distance between the neurons, though connections were found up to 1200 micrometres apart.
outcomes.notes: Same shank 4.60% against 0.52% across shanks (Fisher p = 1.1e-89), 61.0% of connections on the same shank, and 8 connections at 1000 micrometres or more (largest 1400). The Spearman correlation over 0 to 1400 micrometres is -0.619, p = 0.102, so the second condition fails and the criterion gives not reproduced. The probability falls from 4.60% at 0 to 0.24% at 600 micrometres and is 0.17 to 0.19% from 800 to 1200; the 1400 bin (2 of 310 pairs, 0.645%) breaks the rank order. Over 0 to 1200 micrometres rho = -0.964, p = 0.00045, and over pairs connected pairs are closer than unconnected ones (Mann-Whitney p = 2.3e-87). The fall with distance is present; the outcome comes from the test fixed beforehand on eight points. The distance assumes that the channel groups are in shank order; a unit's second-largest shank is a neighbour of its largest for 47.7% of 407 units, against 25.0% for a random order, which is consistent with it.
deviations: Distance is the shank separation only; positions within a shank were not estimated.

outcomes.statement: Out of 343 excitatory monosynaptic pairs, 67 showed position dependence of their short-latency coincidences in the maze (P < 0.01), beyond what the firing rates explain.
outcomes.source: Results, third section; Figure 4; Methods, identifying position dependence
outcomes.notes: Changed from not_reproduced in the first revision. Reading (a) 10 of 285 excitatory pairs (3.5%); reading (b) 5 (1.8%); rank band 1.4% and 2.1%. The criterion's test compares coincidences with jittered trains, so it finds any excess of coincidences somewhere on the track, not a change of efficacy along it; on synthetic pairs with a constant efficacy driven by real presynaptic trains it flags 30.0% (efficacy 0.05) and 75.0% (efficacy 0.2), against the paper's P < 0.01. By the protocol's rule on stated false-positive rates the procedure is not the paper's, whose thinning step and null are defined in the supplement, which was not available. As a variant, a null of constant efficacy flags 0 of 285 real pairs, none of the constant-efficacy synthetic pairs and 6.7% of synthetic pairs driven only on 0.5 to 0.8 of the track (25.0% of those with at least 50 coincidences), so it has little power at these counts. The median pair has 7 coincidences during runs (range 0 to 442). The rank band cannot reach 0.01 in 183 of 285 pairs.
deviations: The band is mean plus c times s.d. of the surrogates, not the Methods' rank band, because the rank band cannot reach a one-sided 0.01 with 1000 surrogates on 101 points (it is empty when more than 1% of data sets reach the extreme rank somewhere). This was found after a first run of the rank version gave 1.0% and a synthetic test showed that it could not detect a strong position-limited coupling; the rank result is shown as a variant.
Event positions are kept at the original presynaptic spike in the surrogates.

outcomes.statement: About equal fractions of connected pairs show firing pattern-dependent depression (12.7%) and facilitation (10.7%), comparing the transmission of the first spike of a train with that of later spikes.
outcomes.notes: Of 284 excitatory pairs with enough spikes, 14 (4.9%) depressing and 44 (15.5%) facilitating. Facilitation is above chance (binomial p = 3.5e-11), depression is not (p = 0.56). Overall later spikes transmit more than first spikes (median 0.0099 against 0.0068, Wilcoxon p = 6.1e-08). With at least 50 or 200 spikes of each kind, 5.0 to 5.3% depressing and 15.4 to 15.9% facilitating. The paper's measure (rate-normalized peak height) was not available, and a measure that normalizes by the postsynaptic rate in each condition could give a different balance.
deviations: Transmission measured as excess spikes from 1 to 4 ms over the jitter expectation, chosen here in place of the paper's rate-normalized peak height.
Later spikes are any spike within 40 ms of the previous one (the Figure 6 legend), not only spikes inside trains that began after 200 ms of silence.

outcomes.statement: Coincident firing of two or more presynaptic neurons within 5 ms on a common target is more effective than the sum of their separate effects (supralinear), while spikes spread over windows longer than 10 ms add linearly.
outcomes.notes: 41 satellites, 40 with at least 20 two-partner events; 15 (38%) supralinear; median excess 0.0145 for one partner and 0.0197 for two; Wilcoxon p = 0.993. Two coincident partners transmit more than one, but less than twice as much. With 20 ms events, 29% supralinear (p = 0.998). The criterion's measure is biased towards sublinear (on synthetic satellites with linear summation it gives -0.0278, s.d. 0.0030). A variant against a linear prediction from each partner's one-spike events, with the response window from the first spike to the last, is unbiased there (0.0016, s.d. 0.0046) and detects supralinear input (0.198); on the data 4 of 40 satellites (10%) are above the linear prediction (median 0.0015 against 0.0239, p = 1), and 12 of 40 (30%) with 20 ms events. That variant's local baseline is biased on the data, as the post rate in the flanks is higher around two-partner events than one-partner events (median 9.44 against 7.26 Hz, 28 of 40 satellites, Wilcoxon p = 0.00022). With the post unit's mean rate as baseline (unbiased on synthetic satellites, -0.0021, s.d. 0.0068), the two-partner response is 0.0135 against a prediction of 0.0337, above it in 9 of 40 (22%), below it by Wilcoxon p = 0.00058; that baseline leaves in more background for two-partner events (median 0.0125 against 0.0074), which favours a supralinear result. No measure finds supralinear summation, and with both baselines the two-partner response is below the one-partner response (0.0135 against 0.0180 with the global one), which these measures do not explain. The paper had 14 satellites converging on interneurons; here any target with two excitatory partners is used, and its definitions of satellite and transmission probability are in the supplementary information, which was not available.
deviations: Satellites, events and the excess measure are defined here.

outcomes.statement: Large fractions of putative pyramidal cells (72.2% in layer 2/3, 84.7% in layer 5) and of interneurons (58.3% and 83%) are trajectory specific.
outcomes.notes: EE, 58.5% of 94 putative pyramidal cells and 60.0% of 5 interneurons are trajectory specific; FF, 66.7% of 57 and 62.5% of 8; GG, 14.3% of 7 and no interneuron. Chance is 0.0 to 2.5%. FF matches the layer 2/3 values within 10%, EE matches neither layer, and GG cannot meet the criterion without interneurons. Large fractions of both classes are trajectory specific in EE and FF, which is the qualitative part of the claim; the interneuron counts are small, as fig3-cell-classes found few interneurons. With the classes without mirrored troughs, EE has 4 interneurons (50.0% specific) and FF 6 (66.7%); GG still has none.
deviations: Layers are matched rat by rat; trajectory specificity is the test of fig2b-trajectory-selective over the whole track.

outcomes.statement: In the example layer 2/3 session, 117 neurons gave 1172 pairs with 48 excitatory and 30 inhibitory connections, 39 of the 117 cells formed one connected hub, 15 of 36 excitatory connections were active in particular maze segments, and the example pairs (156-136, 197-201, 49-52, 186-201, 197 and 186 onto one interneuron, a satellite on cell 135) show position-dependent, depressing, facilitating and supralinear transmission.
outcomes.notes: The CRCNS description names EE.188 (day EE0708) as the session of Figures 2a and 3d, and Figure 5 uses the same session; the dandiset has no file of that day, nor of EE.152 and EE.165. The CRCNS copy needs an account. The example cell numbers cannot be matched to the dandiset's units in any case, as its units carry no original cluster numbers.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds three rats (EE, FF, GG); the paper recorded four. Of the 13 working memory sessions in the CRCNS session table, EE.152, EE.165 and EE.188 are not in the dandiset, and EE.210 has no trial table or position. EE.188 is the paper's example session (Figures 2a, 3b to 3d, 4 and 5).

The units table holds spike times only. It has no channel, shank, brain region, cell type or quality label, and mixes prefrontal units, CA1 units, multi-unit clusters (cluster 1 of each shank, kept by the conversion) and clusters of the sensor signals. Units can be placed only from their waveforms in the wideband signal, which EE.042 and the ten sessions of 2008-06-27 (EE.080 to EE.089, among them the working memory session EE.088) do not have.

Electrode locations are "unknown", coordinates are missing and impedances are -1. The electrode groups "shank1" to "shank13" are cuts of eight consecutive channels, whatever the probe, so they do not identify the prefrontal shanks, the CA1 shanks or the sensor channels. The layer recorded in each rat is not stated.

In rat GG the channel order differs from the CRCNS description. The nose-poke sensors are on channels 65 and 66 (1-based) and the CA1 probe on 70 to 101, where the description gives 97 and 98 and 65 to 96. The sensor on 66 is active on trials labelled Right, the reverse of the order in rats EE and FF, so either the sensors or the trial side labels of rat GG are swapped.

The trial table's stop_time is the end of the last nose poke, the paper's trial start, and reward_time is the paper's trial end; the column left_or_right carries the description of reward_time ("Time when subject began consuming reward."). Only correct trials are listed, which the files do not say.

The two "(x,y) coordinates" series SpatialSeries1 and SpatialSeries2 are the x coordinates of the two head LEDs, in pixels although stated in metres, and the second is zero in every file; untracked frames are -1. The y coordinates are not in the dandiset. The linearized position is stated in metres but runs from 1 (trial start) to 2 (reward), with 0 outside trials.

In six files (EE.049, EE.088, EE.196, FF.103, FF.130, GG.069) the spike times of unit 1 are not in ascending order. In EE.049 and FF.103, examined in detail, they are two sorted runs one after the other; in the five analysed files the unit is a multi-unit cluster.
GG.063, a spontaneous alternation session in the CRCNS table, has a trial table with left and right trials like the working memory sessions; the files do not say which task a session is.

The session description of every file is the paper's abstract, and session start times are dates at midnight; the files do not say which sessions are sleep, test, spontaneous alternation or working memory sessions.

attempts.paper_title: Neural population dynamics during reaching
attempts.entry_title: Rotational dynamics of motor cortex during reaching (Churchland et al. 2012)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Churchland, Cunningham, Kaufman, Foster, Nuyujukian, Ryu and Shenoy (2012) that can be tested on dandiset 000070, which holds the paper's two Utah array datasets (monkeys J and N, 108 maze conditions each) and eight further array sessions. It runs jPCA on condition-averaged rates around movement onset and tests the consistency of rotations across conditions, the variance the jPCA planes capture, the fit of rotational dynamics, the shuffle controls, the separate PMd and M1 arrays, and simulated kinematic populations. The single-electrode datasets, EMG, leech and walking-monkey data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Churchland et al. (2012) from dandiset 000070

outcomes.statement: The two array datasets, monkey J-array recorded 2009-09-18 and monkey N-array recorded 2010-09-23, each present 108 reach conditions and comprise 146 and 218 isolations (a mix of single and multi-unit isolations).
outcomes.source: Methods, Recordings and task design; Figure 3e and 3f legend
outcomes.notes: Both sessions are in the dandiset (sub-Jenkins ses-20090918 and sub-Nitschke ses-20100923) with 108 conditions each among the selected trials. Each holds 192 units, one per electrode of the two arrays, with rates over trial time of 13.5 to 178 spikes/s, against the paper's 146 and 218 isolations. The sorted isolations are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: In the first jPCA plane the neural state rotates in the same direction for all conditions of the J-array and N-array datasets, including reaches in opposite directions.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching; Figure 3e and 3f
outcomes.notes: 102 of 108 conditions (0.944) rotate counter-clockwise in J-array and 108 of 108 in N-array; median net rotation 70.2 and 114.6 degrees over the 200 ms. Under the variants (24 ms smoothing, two other windows, 10 PCs, all successful trials) the fraction is 0.944 to 0.981 and 0.972 to 1.000. jPCA orients the plane so that the net rotation is counter-clockwise, so the fraction is also 0.963 to 0.991 after shuffles 2 and 3 and 0.926 and 0.972 for the velocity model with no lead; it shows that the conditions turn the same way, not on its own that the rotation is specific to the data.
deviations: Tested on the 192 per-electrode units, not the paper's sorted isolations.
No PC smoothing of single-unit rates; the supplement reports it has essentially no effect.
The analysis window is -50 to +150 ms from movement onset for both datasets, from the codepack's example; the paper chose a start per dataset, just before the rapid change in activity.

outcomes.statement: The rotations do not relate directly to reach curvature; the neural state rotates the same way for clockwise-curving, counter-clockwise-curving and straight reaches.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching; Figure 3e and 3f
outcomes.notes: In N-array all conditions rotate counter-clockwise in each class (44 clockwise, 53 counter-clockwise, 11 straight reaches). In J-array 0.984 of 63 counter-clockwise and 7 of 7 straight reaches do, but 0.868 (33 of 38) of clockwise reaches, under the 0.9 of the criterion and above 0.75. Spearman correlation of heading change with net neural rotation is 0.227 (p 0.018) in J-array and -0.214 (p 0.026) in N-array; the J-array logistic slope is 0.0101 per degree. The hand paths drawn by class match the classes; the five clockwise-class conditions of J-array that turn clockwise in the plane are loops of 162 to 180 degrees. With the heading taken over the unbroken run around peak speed, or thresholds of 10 or 30 degrees, the J-array clockwise class has 38 or 41 conditions, of which 0.868 to 0.878 rotate counter-clockwise.
deviations: The paper shows this by eye in Figure 3; the classes of curvature and the thresholds were fixed here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: The rotation phase follows from the preparatory state; knowing the initial state in the jPC plane, the subsequent states are reasonably predictable.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching; Figure 3
outcomes.notes: Leave-one-condition-out R2 of the +150 ms state from the -50 ms state is 0.632 in J-array and 0.748 in N-array, both above 0.5. Shuffle 3 gives 0.633 to 0.718 (median 0.671) in J-array and 0.611 to 0.689 (median 0.656) in N-array, so the data exceed the control in N-array only. Shuffle 1, which has no rotation, scores 0.82 to 0.91 in every run, so this R2 rewards any consistent map from the first state to the last and is a weak test of the claim. With jPCA refitted leaving each condition out, the R2 is 0.615 and 0.727 against shuffle 3 medians of 0.628 and 0.649, reached by 8 of 10 shuffle 3 runs in J-array and none in N-array; several runs lie within 0.02 of the J-array value, and the round-2 verifier's copy printed 0.614 and 6 of 10, so this count moves with small numerical differences between runs. A phase score (the last phase predicted as the first plus the other conditions' mean advance) is 0.763 and 0.894 for the data, against 0.236 and -0.356 for no advance; shuffle 1 scores the same with and without an advance, and shuffle 3 keeps an advance of 65 and 99 degrees and scores a median 0.811 and 0.797, so this score also separates the data from shuffle 3 in N-array only (9 of 10 shuffle 3 runs reach the data's phase score in J-array, none in N-array).
deviations: The paper gives no measure of predictability; the complex-gain prediction and its thresholds were fixed here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: The first jPCA plane captures an average of 28% of the total data variance (typically 20 to 35%).
outcomes.source: Results, Controls regarding rotational structure; Supplementary Figure 5 legend
outcomes.notes: The first jPCA plane captures 20.0% (J-array) and 23.1% (N-array), both within 18 to 38.5% (reading b, which matches). The mean, 21.6%, is outside 28 +- 2.8% (reading a). The sub-Nitschke ses-20090910 session gives 18.8%.
deviations: The paper's 28% averages nine datasets, of which the dandiset holds two; the reading of the typical range was used, as listed in the criterion.
Tested on per-electrode units, not sorted isolations.

outcomes.statement: The plane of PC2 and PC3 captures 29% of the total variance on average, about as much as the first jPCA plane, so the jPCA plane captures patterns already present in the top PCs.
outcomes.notes: PC2 and PC3 capture 21.6% (J-array) and 27.0% (N-array), mean 24.3%, outside 29 +- 2.9% under reading (a) and under reading (b) for J-array. The jPCA plane captures 0.93 and 0.86 times the variance of PC2 and PC3, so the comparison the claim makes holds.
deviations: Two datasets in place of the paper's nine.
Tested on per-electrode units, not sorted isolations.

outcomes.statement: In J-array the first three jPCA planes found within the top 10 PCs capture 22%, 19% and 12% of the variance (54% together), against 64% for the top six PCs, and each plane holds rotations coherent across conditions.
outcomes.notes: In J-array the three jPCA planes from the top 10 PCs capture 12.3%, 14.8% and 12.8% (40.0% together) against 22%, 19% and 12% (54%); only plane 3 is within tolerance. The top six PCs capture 60.5%, within 64 +- 6.4%. The planes rotate consistently (0.926 to 0.991 of conditions counter-clockwise). The lower variance may come from the per-electrode units, which carry more noise than sorted isolations, and from the missing PC smoothing; this was not tested.
deviations: Per-electrode units in place of the paper's 146 isolations; no PC smoothing.

outcomes.statement: Every dataset contains two, and usually three, planes with rotations, together capturing 50 to 70% of the variance.
outcomes.notes: The three planes capture 50.1% in N-array (within 45 to 77%) and 40.0% in J-array (below it). The first two planes have 0.954 or more of conditions rotating in their direction in both datasets. ses-20090910 gives 40.9%.
deviations: Two datasets in place of the paper's nine; per-electrode units.

outcomes.statement: The distribution of the angle between the neural state and its derivative in the first jPCA plane, over all conditions and times, peaks near pi/2 (rotation), not near 0.
outcomes.notes: The angle between the state and its derivative peaks at 0.528 pi (J-array) and 0.639 pi (N-array), medians 0.511 and 0.603 pi. Under the variants the peak lies between 0.528 and 0.639 pi, and with 24 or 48 bins between 0.542 and 0.646 pi.
deviations: The thresholds come from reading Figure 6a; the paper gives no number.

outcomes.statement: For the neural data the rotational (skew-symmetric) dynamics matrix fits the data nearly as well as the best unconstrained linear dynamics matrix, both in the 6-D space and in the first jPCA plane.
outcomes.notes: R2(M_skew)/R2(M) is 0.905 and 0.845 in 6-D and 0.957 and 0.881 in the first plane (J-array, N-array). Under the variants the 6-D ratio is 0.819 or more and the plane ratio 0.879 or more. Absolute R2 of M_skew is 0.343 and 0.517.
deviations: The thresholds come from reading Figure 6b; the paper gives no number.
M_skew is solved in closed form as in the Supplementary Derivation, where the codepack uses a gradient method for the same unique optimum.

outcomes.statement: The rotations are brief and fast, up to about 2.5 Hz; the largest eigenvalues of M_skew in the monkey A and B datasets are 8.8 to 13.5 radians/s.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching and Population-level quantification
outcomes.notes: The first plane rotates at 1.38 Hz (8.65 radians/s) in N-array, within 1.26 to 2.75 Hz, and 1.03 Hz (6.49 radians/s) in J-array, below it; the larger value is given as measured. No variant exceeds 1.68 Hz, so the upper bound holds. J-array reaches the range with the -100 to +100 ms window (1.45 Hz) or 10 PCs (1.68 Hz), variants that do not decide the outcome. The low J-array value is not the effect of a window starting before the rotation does (a synthetic 2 Hz rotation starting at movement onset reads 1.49 Hz from -50 ms), since windows starting at 0 and +50 ms give 1.04 and 1.13 Hz. The J-array plane's mean angular speed is about 1.3 Hz from -60 to +20 ms and 0.7 to 0.9 Hz by +100 ms, and windows starting at -150 or -100 ms give 1.31 and 1.45 Hz, so J-array rotates faster before movement onset than over the window used, which the paper chose per dataset.
deviations: The lower bound of the range comes from the eigenvalues the paper reports for monkeys A and B, whose data are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Three shuffle controls that keep preparatory activity and invert or reassign the peri-movement activity largely remove the rotational structure found by jPCA, so jPCA does not find rotations that are not there.
outcomes.notes: Shuffle 1 removes the rotations (median R2(M_skew) 1.0% and 0.8% of the original; fraction counter-clockwise 0.565 and 0.602). Shuffle 2 leaves 71% (J-array) and 94% (N-array) of the original R2(M_skew), shuffle 3 leaves 81% and 94%, and one shuffle 3 run in N-array exceeds the original; after both the median fraction rotating counter-clockwise is 0.963 to 0.991. Only shuffle 1 meets the criterion in N-array, and shuffles 1 and 2 in J-array. The paper expected shuffles 2 and 3 to leave part of the rotational structure and to disrupt its relation to the preparatory state, which R2(M_skew) does not measure; the criterion's choice of measure, fixed before the analysis, may not capture what the paper judged by eye.
deviations: The dividing point is one time per dataset (median go cue plus 50 ms, -301 and -320 ms from movement onset) on movement-aligned rates; the paper split each condition 50 ms after its go cue on rates aligned separately to target, go cue and movement.
The paper judged the shuffles from projections (Supplementary Figure 3); R2(M_skew) and its thresholds were fixed here.

outcomes.statement: Analysed separately, the PMd and M1 arrays each show clear rotations; the jPCA plane captures 29% (PMd) and 29% (M1) in J-array and 32% and 28% in N-array.
outcomes.notes: PMd and M1 capture 23.7% and 22.8% (J-array) and 18.1% and 25.0% (N-array) against 29, 29, 32 and 28%; none within 10% (N-array M1 misses 25.2% by 0.2 points). All lie within 18 to 38.5%, with 0.917 to 0.991 of conditions rotating counter-clockwise. ses-20090910 gives 15.4% (PMd) and 21.6% (M1) against 26% and 24% for N-9-10-2010.
deviations: 96 per-electrode units per array in place of the paper's isolations.

outcomes.statement: The angular velocity of the rotations is slightly higher for M1 than for PMd in each dataset.
outcomes.notes: M1 rotates faster than PMd in J-array (1.82 against 0.83 Hz) and N-array (1.54 against 1.02 Hz), and in ses-20090910 (1.70 against 0.89 Hz), under every variant shown. The paper calls the difference slight; here M1 is 1.5 to 2.4 times faster across the sessions and variants.

outcomes.statement: A simulated population of units tuned to hand velocity and speed, with preparatory activity tuned to reach endpoint, matched to the recorded data, shows no robust or consistent rotations; M_skew fits it poorly and its angle distribution peaks slightly above zero.
outcomes.source: Results, Rotations, kinematics and EMG; Figure 4d and 4h; Figure 6a and 6b
outcomes.notes: The velocity model's 6-D R2 ratio is 0.361 (J-array) and 0.255 (N-array), against 0.905 and 0.845 for the data, and 0.630 and 0.778 of its conditions rotate counter-clockwise. Its angle distribution peaks at 0.806 pi and 0.361 pi, not below pi/4, so the criterion fails in both datasets. With no lead the peaks are 0.194 pi and 0.417 pi and the ratios 0.362 and 0.337. The part of the claim about the poor fit of M_skew holds under every variant (6-D ratio 0.08 to 0.55). The angle peak depends on the model's open choices. A decay toward the origin peaks near pi (0.972 pi on a synthetic decay), and the preparatory tuning decays from movement onset. With the 100 ms lead the peak lies at 0.36 to 0.86 pi over five seeds and with the preparatory tuning decaying, held or absent; with no lead and preparatory tuning it lies at 0.19 to 0.42 pi; with no lead and no preparatory tuning it is 0.028 pi in both datasets, near zero as the paper reports. The outcome follows the model fixed in the criterion.
deviations: The model is simulated here from the dandiset's condition-mean hand kinematics; its lead of 100 ms, the time course of preparatory tuning and the modulation depths are choices made here, as the Methods do not give them.

outcomes.statement: A simulated population tuned to hand position, velocity, acceleration and jerk (with the Methods' sensitivities) produces multiphasic responses but no consistent rotations; M_skew fits it poorly.
outcomes.source: Results, Rotations, kinematics and EMG; Figure 4e and 4i; Figure 6a and 6b
outcomes.notes: The complex kinematic model's 6-D R2 ratio is 0.082 (J-array) and 0.132 (N-array), 0.289 and 0.207 with no lead, and 0.565 and 0.528 of its conditions rotate counter-clockwise. Its angle peaks are 0.861 pi and 0.750 pi (0.806 and 0.917 pi with no lead), not below pi/4, so the criterion fails in both datasets. The poor fit of M_skew holds as the paper reports (6-D ratio 0.06 to 0.61 across variants). With the preparatory tuning held or absent, no lead, and four more seeds, the peak lies within pi/4 of zero only in J-array with no preparatory tuning and no lead (-0.083 pi) and in one N-array seed with no lead (0.194 pi); elsewhere it lies at 0.19 to 0.97 pi or near -pi.
deviations: Simulated here with the Methods' sensitivities; the lead, the preparatory time course and hand positions read as mm are choices made here.

outcomes.statement: The population responses of the swimming leech and of premotor cortex in a walking monkey rotate in the jPCA plane, as expected for rhythmic movement.
outcomes.notes: The leech imaging and the walking-monkey recording are not in the dandiset, whose ten files are all maze-task array sessions, and the paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: Single neurons recorded with single electrodes show multiphasic, quasi-oscillatory responses lasting about 1 to 1.5 cycles, from 469 isolations in four monkeys averaging 810 trials per neuron.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching; Figure 1c and Figure 2
outcomes.notes: The 469 single-electrode isolations of monkeys A, B, J and N are not in the dandiset, and the paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: The rotations are seen in the seven single-electrode datasets (monkeys A, B, J1 to J4 and N), for example monkey B, A, J3 and N in Figure 3a to 3d.
outcomes.notes: The seven single-electrode datasets (A, B, J1 to J4, N) are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The recorded muscle populations (6 to 12 EMG recordings per dataset) show weak, inconsistent rotations, also when the neural population is down-sampled to their size.
outcomes.source: Figure 4c, 4f and 4j; Figure 6a and 6b; Supplementary Figure 6
outcomes.notes: EMG was not recorded for the array datasets (Methods), and the EMG of the single-electrode datasets is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: A generator model of two rotations of fixed frequency fits deltoid EMG with correlations of 0.97 to 0.99, and its simulated units resemble real neurons.
outcomes.notes: The generator model is fitted to deltoid EMG of the single-electrode datasets (J2, J3), which is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Rotations have similar angular velocity for instructed fast and slow reaches; the largest M_skew eigenvalues are 8.8 against 9.8 radians/s (monkey A) and 12.2 against 13.5 (monkey B), with larger amplitude for fast reaches.
outcomes.notes: The speed task of monkeys A and B is not in the dandiset, which holds sessions of monkeys J and N only.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds the paper's two array datasets but not the sorted isolations the paper analysed (146 for J-array, 218 for N-array). Its Units table has 192 units per file, one per electrode. The seven single-electrode datasets, the EMG, the leech and the walking-monkey data are not in it either, so six of the paper's main findings cannot be tested.

In nine of the ten files (all written by the first conversion) the first entry of units/spike_times_index is the true end of unit 0 modulo 65536. Unit 0 is cut short (in J-array 61030 of its 257638 spikes) and its remaining spikes open unit 1, whose times then jump from the end of the session back to its start.

In five Nitschke files (ses-20090812, 20090819, 20090910, 20090920 and 20100923) the clock restarts at recording segments after the first, as the conversion offsets only one segment. Trials overlap in time (2094 overlapping pairs in N-array), and every unit's spike times go backwards at each restart, so spikes cannot be placed in trials by time; they can be placed by their storage order, which the notebook shows decodes reach direction in every segment.

Hand position is stated in metres (with conversion NaN); its values span about -220 to +165 on the scale of the target positions (up to 145) and the median speed peaks at 600 to 730 per second during a reach, so they are in mm.

The hand position ends a median 35 mm (Jenkins) and 52 to 53 mm (Nitschke) below the reached target in y, while the cursor lands on the target; the offset between hand and screen coordinates is not described in the files.

The Units table carries only the default description ("Autogenerated by NWBFile") and does not say whether its units are sorted neurons, multi-unit activity or threshold crossings. Their number (one per electrode) and rates (8.8 to 300 spikes/s over trial time in the three sessions analysed) are consistent with channel-level activity.

The dandiset does not say which of its ten sessions are the paper's datasets. Two match the J-array and N-array dates; the other eight (27-condition and two-condition maze sessions, and one 108-condition session) are not described.

The first conversion's code sets the year of every session date to 2009. The file sub-Nitschke ses-20090910 has 108 conditions with the same reached target as N-array (2010) for all of them, and is consistent with the N-9-10-2010 dataset of Supplementary Figure 5; if so, its date is a year early. The other 2009 Nitschke dates may be affected in the same way.

attempts.paper_title: Oxytocin neurons enable social transmission of maternal behaviour
attempts.entry_title: PVN units and maternal behaviour in co-housed virgin mice (Carcea et al. 2021)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Carcea et al. (2021) that dandiset 000114 can support. The dandiset holds PVN single units and video annotations from virgin mice co-housed with a dam and litter, and fibre photometry from virgins watching dam retrievals. The entry tests the fraction of units activated during nest entry, shepherding and dam retrieval, the firing after shepherded against voluntary nest entries, and the rates of shepherding and dam retrieval. OT-PVN identity, the behavioural cohorts and the auditory cortex data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Carcea et al. (2021) from dandiset 000114

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's behaviour labels can be named through the paper's code; "Mom agressing" is shepherding, "Virgin in rest" is nest entry (a nest dwell) and "Mom retrieval" is spontaneous pup retrieval by the dam.
outcomes.source: Methods (Spike train analysis); Extended Data Fig. 7b; shepNestPup_xCorr_ForNature.m at GitHub commit 2db2a75
outcomes.notes: In V116 03122018, the one file with both naming schemes, all 7 "Mom agressing" intervals coincide with "Shepherding" intervals and both "Mom retrieval" intervals with "Self gen retrieval" intervals, and all 13 "Virgin in rest" intervals lie inside "Virgin in nest" intervals. Pooled over files, 366 of 499 "Virgin in rest" intervals (73.3%) last 40 s or less, within 70.5% +/- 7.05. By mouse the fraction is 72.2% in V110 and 89.2% in V111, but 9.9% in V116, where the label marks dwells with medians of 1103.7 to 2492.7 s, and 0 of 3 in V118 (median 64.1 s). Adding V85's "Virgin in nest" gives 77.3% of 639.
deviations: The names come from the paper's code, not from the dandiset; "Mom aggressing" in V85 is taken as the same label as "Mom agressing".

outcomes.statement: A significant fraction of virgin PVN units were activated during nest entry (6 of 21 OT-PVN and 33 of 126 PVN units; one-sided Fisher's exact test p = 0.01 and 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Fig. 2i; Extended Data Fig. 7a (middle); Source Data Fig. 2i
outcomes.notes: 42 of 194 units (21.6%) are activated during nest entry, outside the tolerance of both readings (pooled 23.9 to 29.2%, PVN only 23.6 to 28.8%); the Fisher test against zero gives p = 1.9e-14, and 7 units are suppressed. By mouse, V116 has 37 of 70 (52.9%), V110 1 of 31 and V111 4 of 93. Without the 40 s cap, as in the code, 2 of 194 (1.0%, p = 0.25). Without the 20 units above 1,048,500 spikes, 42 of 174 (24.1%), inside the tolerance of both readings, so this variant would reproduce the fraction. With q = 0.01 and 0.1, 14.4% and 28.4%. The paper's statement separates OT-PVN (6 of 21) and PVN (33 of 126) units; the OT-PVN part cannot be tested. The clock shared by spikes and annotations could not be established in any session. Poisson units with each unit's spike count and no response give 2 of 194 (1.0%) on the same episodes and test. Real episodes without spikes are left out of the mean in 116 units (median 17% of their episodes); counting them as 0, as the shuffles do, gives 31 of 194 (16.0%, p = 1.3e-10). Counting V111 once gives 38 to 40 of 132 (28.8 to 30.3%; 28.8% is inside the pooled reading's tolerance, so this variant would reproduce the fraction); without V116 03102018, whose clock is not known, 25 of 168 (14.9%, p = 1.1e-08). The baselines of 3 to 20 entries per session overlap an earlier nest dwell or a shepherding episode; the largest count is in V110 03032018 (20 of 72, all an earlier dwell) and the largest share in V116 03092018 (16 of 29, all shepherding).
deviations: Units from 4 virgins and 7 sessions (194 units), against the paper's 147 units from more animals; which sessions the paper used is not stated.
OT-PVN and PVN units are pooled and the false discovery rate is applied over each session's units, as OT identity is not in the dandiset; the Methods apply it over OT-PVN or PVN units of a day.
The baseline ends 0.5 s before the episode, from the code; the Methods do not give it.
V111's three sessions probably hold the same clusters (spike counts correlated 0.93 to 0.97) and are counted as separate units, as the paper counts units per day.
As in the code, real episodes with no spike in either window are left out of a unit's mean, while shuffled ones count as 0; counting both as 0 is shown as a variant, as is counting V111 once.

outcomes.statement: A significant fraction of virgin PVN units were activated during shepherding by the dam (5 of 21 OT-PVN and 9 of 97 PVN units; p = 0.02 and 0.001).
outcomes.source: Fig. 2e; Extended Data Fig. 7a (left); Source Data Fig. 2e
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' 10 s baseline, 3 of 194 units (1.5%) are activated during shepherding, Fisher p = 0.12, against 11.9% (pooled) or 9.3% (PVN only); 10 units are suppressed and 15 have no value. With the code's equal-duration baseline, 9 of 194 (4.6%, p = 0.0018). V116 alone, 2 of 70 (p = 0.25). Sessions hold 1 to 22 shepherding episodes, so most units are tested on few events. Poisson units with no response give 3 of 194 activated, as many as the real units. Counting empty episodes as 0 gives 1 of 194, counting V111 once 2 or 3 of 132, and leaving out V116 03102018 2 of 168, none with p < 0.05.
deviations: Units from 4 virgins and 7 sessions, OT-PVN and PVN pooled, as for nest entry.
Real episodes without spikes are left out as in the code, and V111's sessions counted separately, as for nest entry; both are also shown the other way.
The Methods' 10 s baseline is used; the code's equal-duration baseline is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Spontaneous pup retrieval by the dam, in which the virgin was not involved, activated a significant fraction of virgin PVN units (5 of 17 OT-PVN and 10 of 69 PVN units; p = 0.02 and 0.0007).
outcomes.source: Fig. 3b, c; Extended Data Fig. 7a (right); Source Data Fig. 3c
outcomes.notes: 13 of 132 units (9.8%) are activated during dam retrieval, Fisher p = 9e-05, outside the tolerance of both readings (pooled 15.7 to 19.1%, PVN only 13.1 to 16.0%). 9 of the 13 are from V111 03032018, which has one retrieval episode; over sessions with at least 2 episodes, 4 of 101 (p = 0.061). More units are suppressed (20) than activated, and the median change is -22.4. With the code's baseline, 16 of 132 (12.1%). The OT-PVN part (5 of 17) cannot be tested. The 9 units of V111 03032018 share a median 71% of their spikes pairwise within 0.1 ms (33 to 81%), against 1.7% among the session's other 22 units, so they are probably far fewer than 9 neurons. Counting V111 once gives 11 of 101 with V111 03032018 (p = 0.00037) and 4 of 101 with V111 03062018 (p = 0.061). Poisson units with no response give 3 activated and 12 suppressed of 132, so the suppressed count is not far above the test's false-positive level. Counting empty episodes as 0 gives 12 of 132 (p = 0.00019); without V116 03102018, 12 of 106 (p = 0.00018). The baseline of the single retrieval in V111 03032018 is not a recording gap (537 population spikes, more than in 43% of the session's 10 s windows; no interval over 0.22 s within 60 s), but 7 of 31 units have no spike in it and the 9 activated units fire 0 to 2.1 Hz. During the 5.2 s episode about 16 units fire at 144 to 221 Hz together (14,346 population spikes in the first 5 s against 1,838 per 5 s over the session, a size reached in 12 of 3,325 windows), so the retrieval falls on one of the session's largest synchronous bursts. The outputs cannot tell a response from a burst that coincides with the episode; the outcome follows the criterion, which counts units as given.
deviations: Units from 2 virgins and 5 sessions with 1 to 11 retrieval episodes each; OT-PVN and PVN pooled.
Real episodes without spikes are left out as in the code, and V111's sessions counted separately, as for nest entry; both are also shown the other way.
The Methods' 10 s baseline is used; the code's equal-duration baseline is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: PVN units fired more when the virgin entered the nest after being shepherded than when she entered it voluntarily (18 units, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, p = 0.0056).
outcomes.source: Fig. 2j; Extended Data Fig. 7a; Source Data Fig. 2j
outcomes.notes: Over 128 units in 5 sessions, the change is higher for shepherded than voluntary entries in 70, median difference 3.9, Wilcoxon p = 0.182. Sessions disagree; V110 03032018 (one shepherded entry) has 30 of 31 units higher (p = 4.66e-09) and V116 03102018 has 6 of 26 (p = 0.00669). With windows of 5 and 30 s, p = 0.37 and 0.166; over the 36 units activated during nest entry, median difference -7.3, p = 0.148; V116 alone, -6.0, p = 0.0732. Without V116 03102018, whose clock is not known, the median difference is 10.8 over 102 units and p = 0.0237; this variant does not decide the outcome under the criterion, and 31 of its units come from V110 03032018, compared on a single shepherded entry.
deviations: The paper does not say how a nest entry was classed as shepherded or which 18 units were used; the rule (entry starting from the start of a shepherding episode to 10 s after its end) and the unit set were fixed before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: Dams shepherded virgins more often than the 0.2 events per hour at which dams chased virgins without pups, at 3.5 +/- 0.9 events per hour with pups present.
outcomes.notes: Over 10 sessions from 5 mice the mean rate is 0.65 shepherding events per hour (s.e.m. 0.17), above 0.2 (t = 2.59, two-sided p = 0.0292), and far below 3.5 +/- 0.9. Averaged per mouse first, 0.63 per hour, p = 0.193 against 0.2. Session rates run from 0 (V118 03222018) to 1.58 (V85). Annotations of any label span each session with no gap over 0.81 h; the virgin labels run from within 0.61 h of the start to within 0.15 h of the end with gaps of up to 1.93 h. This is consistent with sessions scored in full but does not show that every shepherding episode was annotated.
deviations: Sessions are recordings of 2.5 to 15.8 h, not the paper's days of co-housing per dyad, and the dandiset does not say whether each session was annotated in full.
The comparison of 3.5 per hour comes from Extended Data Fig. 3b (N = 4 dyads); its dyads are not identified.

outcomes.statement: About once every two hours, dams dropped and then retrieved pups during co-housing (daily means 0.34 to 0.60 retrievals per hour, N = 14 dams).
outcomes.source: Results (Social transmission of maternal behaviour); Extended Data Fig. 8a
outcomes.notes: Dams retrieve 23 times in 108.4 h, 0.21 per hour (session mean 0.21, range 0 to 0.70), below 0.31 to 0.66 and close to the 0.2 +/- 0.1 per hour (N = 5) the legend of Extended Data Fig. 8a gives for singly housed dams. Two of 10 sessions are inside the range (V116 03082018 at 0.33, V118 03222018 at 0.40). The rate depends on every retrieval being annotated, which the dandiset does not state; the annotations span each session with no gap over 0.81 h, and dam retrievals are too rare (gaps of up to 9.89 h) for their spacing to show unscored stretches.
deviations: Rates from 5 cages over 10 sessions, against the paper's 14 dams over 4 days.

outcomes.statement: Optically tagged OT-PVN units (21 units) were activated by shepherding, nest entry and dam retrieval, and pairs including OT-PVN units were more correlated than PVN pairs during these behaviours.
outcomes.source: Fig. 2b, e, g-i; Fig. 3b-d; Extended Data Figs. 5, 6a, 7a, 7d, 7e
outcomes.notes: OT-PVN units were identified by optical tagging at the end of each day; the tagging recordings (laser pulse times) are not in the dandiset, the units table has no label, and the paper's code reads the identities from a spreadsheet ("Identified OXT neurons.xlsx") that is not public. The Zenodo record 5039601 holds Blackrock .nev files of the same co-housing sessions, not the identities. The unit names in the files are the indices 0 to n-1 in every session. The pooled PVN part of these responses is tested in the three ed7a claims.

outcomes.statement: Units activated during shepherding fired less when the virgin chased the dam (6 units, Wilcoxon p = 0.03).
outcomes.notes: The files have a "Virgin Agressing" label (32 events in 5 sessions with units), which may be the virgin chasing the dam, but neither the files, the Methods nor the code name it. It never overlaps "Mom agressing" and starts at least 162 s from the nearest one. Of the 3 shepherding-activated units, 2 have such episodes; one fires less over 11 episodes (change -25.3, shuffle p = 0.054), the other stops firing in its single episode. Two units cannot test the paper's 6.

outcomes.statement: During 5-minute interactions, more virgin PVN units were activated by the dam than by pups (25 of 248 against 7 of 248), and units barely responded to pup calls (1 of 71).
outcomes.notes: The 5-minute interaction periods with the dam or with pups, and the pup call playback times, are not annotated in any file.

outcomes.statement: Virgins co-housed with a dam and litter began retrieving pups earlier than virgins co-housed with pups alone (n = 14 and 10, P < 0.0001), and nest entry and shepherding on day 1 correlated with retrieval at the end of day 1 (r = 0.66 and 0.75).
outcomes.source: Fig. 1c, d, f, k; Extended Data Fig. 2
outcomes.notes: The daily retrieval tests of the 14 D+ and 10 D- virgins are not in the dandiset; only summary values are in the paper's Source Data, and the videos are on Databrary.

outcomes.statement: Chemogenetic silencing of OT-PVN neurons delayed the onset of retrieval in co-housed virgins.
outcomes.notes: The DREADD cohort's retrieval scores are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Non-co-housed virgins learned to retrieve after watching dams retrieve, with no barrier (11 of 15) or through a transparent barrier (12 of 19), but not through an opaque barrier (2 of 18) or when lacking the oxytocin receptor (3 of 10).
outcomes.notes: The observation cohorts' retrieval scores are not in the dandiset. The photometry files of six observing virgins hold retrieval tests for two of them only.

outcomes.statement: PVN units of non-co-housed virgins were activated while watching dam retrievals (15 of 65), some also during the virgin's own retrievals (15 of 41), and only in virgins that went on to retrieve (learners against non-learners, P = 0.0001).
outcomes.notes: All units in the dandiset are from co-housing sessions; no unit recording from an observation session is in it.

outcomes.statement: Auditory cortex photometry responses to pup calls increased over co-housing up to the day of retrieval onset (P = 0.003, n = 3).
outcomes.notes: No photometry file has pup call playback, and fibre location is "unknown" in every file; the photometry files are observation and retrieval sessions of Fig. 4g-i.

outcomes.statement: Single-trial PVN activity correlated with pup-call responses in auditory cortex during observation (r = 0.5, P = 0.00001, n = 4).
outcomes.notes: No file holds PVN units together with photometry.

outcomes.statement: PVN to auditory cortex projections were activated during observation of dam retrieval in virgins that learned to retrieve (P = 0.02) but not in those that did not (P = 0.5), three animals per group.
outcomes.notes: The six photometry animals (ROV40, 41, 43, 44, 45, 49) match the three learners and three non-learners of the Source Data, but only ROV40 and ROV41 have retrieval-test files, in which they retrieve on Day 1 and Day 2; whether the other four learned is not in the dandiset. The response measure is also not stated; the Source Data values (-12.1 to 65.7 per animal) are on a scale the files cannot be linked to without it, so the claim is also methods_underspecified. The mean change in the 5 s after the dam's retrievals against the 5 s before is positive in all six animals on Day 1 (0.22 to 1.85%), which does not separate the groups even if ROV40 and ROV41 are taken as learners.

outcomes.statement: An oxytocin receptor antagonist in auditory cortex prevented learning by observation (2 of 10 against 7 of 9), and stimulating OT-PVN fibres in auditory cortex enhanced it (4 of 4 against 2 of 4).
outcomes.notes: The infusion and optogenetic cohorts' retrieval scores are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Superficial superior colliculus projects to OT-PVN neurons, and stimulating this input replaced visual experience (4 of 5 against 1 of 6 virgins retrieving).
outcomes.notes: Tracing histology and the stimulation cohort's retrieval scores are not in the dandiset.

findings.statement: The behaviour labels ("Mom agressing", "Virgin in rest", "Mom retrieval", "Virgin Agressing", "Mother in nest" and others) have no description; the table's description, "events and states of pups", the same in every file, fits none of them. Shepherding, nest entry and dam retrieval can be named only from the paper's code, and "Virgin Agressing" not at all. One file (V116 03122018) carries both the code's labels and the paper's names.

The optical tagging recordings and the identity of the 21 OT-PVN units are not in the dandiset, so no oxytocin-specific result can be tested. The behavioural cohorts of Figures 1 to 4, the unit recordings during observation, and the auditory cortex photometry and units are also missing. Units are present for 4 of the paper's 17 recorded virgins.

Units in V110 and V111 have a median 7.0 to 9.2% of inter-spike intervals under 2 ms, and 79 to 90% of their spikes lie within 0.1 ms of a spike of another unit. The Methods say spikes violating a 2 to 3 ms refractory period and spikes recorded at once on 10 or more channels were removed. These units look like multi-unit clusters or one neuron split over several wires. In V111 03032018 the 9 units activated by the dam's retrieval share a median 71% of their spikes pairwise within 0.1 ms, and the retrieval falls on a synchronous burst of about 16 units at 144 to 221 Hz, one of the 12 largest of the session's 3,325 windows of 5 s.
Session start times disagree with the dates in the session ids; V116 03082018 and 03102018 start in May 2018, V116 03092018 on 11 March, and V118 03182018 on 23 March, after V118 03192018.

In V116 03102018 the raw voltage lasts 4.46 h, but spike times and annotations run to 13.4 h; in V118 03222018 annotations run to 2.52 h against 2.27 h of voltage. The spikes and events of these files cannot all come from the recording they are stored with.

The units table holds spike times and a name only, with no channel, waveform, quality or cell type, and every electrode location is "unknown". V111's three sessions hold 31 units each with spike counts correlated 0.93 to 0.97 across days, and nothing says whether they are the same units.

Every subject is described as "Virgin female co-housed with dam and pups", including the six photometry animals of the observation experiment. Photometry fibre location, fluorophore, wavelengths and gain are "unknown" or NaN; the trace is stated in watts with values near 1000; the commanded_voltage series, described as the LED command, varies from 0.07 to 482 within sessions and is not a command signal.
Which photometry animals learned to retrieve is in the dandiset for 2 of 6 (ROV40 and ROV41, from their retrieval-test files), so the learner and non-learner groups of Fig. 4i cannot be formed.
No test here established that spikes and annotations share a clock; the firing change at annotation onsets was not larger at the stated times than at shifts of up to 2 minutes in any session.

The Methods cut nest entry episodes at 40 s and use the 10 s before shepherding and dam retrieval as baseline; the paper's significance code has the cap commented out and uses an equal-duration baseline for every behaviour. On this data the cap changes the fraction of units activated during nest entry from 1.0% to 21.6%.

The dandiset holds units from 4 virgins (228 units in 8 sessions), no units for V85, V116 03122018 and three V118 sessions, and annotations limited to "Mother in nest" in two V118 files, against 17 recorded virgins and 541 units in the paper. It does not say which recordings were deposited or why.
