attempts.paper_title: Active Touch and Self-Motion Encoding by Merkel Cell-Associated Afferents
attempts.entry_title: Merkel and other whisker afferents during active touch and whisking (Severson et al. 2017)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Severson, Xu, Van de Loo, Bai, Ginty and O'Connor (2017) on dandiset 000226, which holds 56 trigeminal afferent recordings with high-speed whisker video and 4 EMG sessions. It checks the recordings against the paper's Table S1, the spike rates during non-whisking, whisking in air and touch, the classes of afferents, direction selectivity, the statistical and viscoelastic models of touch responses, phase tuning during whisking in air, the nasolabialis motor units and the curvature noise. The cutting conditions of the progressive cutting experiment, the intrinsic protractor EMG and the optogenetic tagging data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Severson et al. (2017) from dandiset 000226

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's recordings can be matched one to one to the recordings of Table S1, and the matched records agree on mouse, sex, mouse line and date.
outcomes.notes: All 60 files match a distinct Table S1 recording, 58 by recording id (the NWB identifier without "KS" and leading zeros) and 2 (KS0125_ and KS0128_, matched to 125B and 128D) by number and mouse. All 60 agree on mouse, sex, mouse line and date. Groups - 33 touch, 13 progressive cutting, 5 cut-whisker, 4 EMG, 3 excluded touch, 2 whisking-only. No Table S1 recording lacks a file. The transcription of Table S1 agrees with the table parsed from the supplement on all 60 rows and every column used.
deviations: The criterion's rule of removing "KS0" was applied as removing "KS" and leading zeros, so that the EMG files KS0007A to KS0011A match 7A to 11A.

outcomes.statement: The initial dataset of 33 touch afferents comprises 54,647,500 video frames with simultaneous single-unit recordings, and the paper analyses 65,257,500 frames (2,175 min) in total.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Quantification and Statistical Analysis
outcomes.notes: The 33 touch recordings hold 54,660,000 frames (paper 54,647,500, 5 trials more). The 53 analysed afferents hold 65,710,000 frames, 2,190 min (paper 65,257,500 and 2,175 min, 181 trials more). The other readings are also within 10% - 68,455,000 (53 afferents and EMG), 68,005,000 (56 afferents), 70,750,000 (all files).

outcomes.statement: Identified Merkel afferents account for 823 minutes of the initial dataset and 846 minutes (25,365,000 frames) overall, against 999 minutes for unidentified afferents in the initial dataset.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Quantification and Statistical Analysis
outcomes.notes: Merkel touch recordings 823.8 min (paper 823), unidentified touch recordings 998.2 min (paper 999), the 17 analysed Merkel afferents 846.4 min (paper 846). All 20 identified Merkel afferents hold 922.9 min, also within tolerance. Merkel identity is from Table S1; the minutes are from the dandiset's trials, and they agree with the paper's.

outcomes.statement: During non-whisking periods most afferents spiked at low rates (0.0 plus or minus 0.2 Hz, median and IQR, n = 33).
outcomes.notes: Median non-whisking rate 0.03 Hz, IQR 0.20 Hz, over the 33 touch afferents (paper 0.0 and 0.2). Range 0.00 to 34.39 Hz; 221B fires at 34.4 Hz without whisking.

outcomes.statement: All afferents responded with increased spike rates during whisker-pole contact (48.0 plus or minus 96.3 Hz, median and IQR, n = 33).
outcomes.notes: Median contact rate 47.9 Hz, IQR 94.8 Hz (paper 48.0 and 96.3), range 3.6 to 239.2 Hz. All 33 afferents are touch-sensitive by the Glossary rule, with bootstrap CIs over trials and with Poisson CIs. The median is also within 10% of the paper's value, so the outcome does not rest on the wide tolerance.
deviations: The Methods do not say what the bootstrap resamples; trials were resampled (1,000 times).

outcomes.statement: A subset of 13 of the 33 touch afferents (WT*) spiked especially strongly during whisking in air (19.1 plus or minus 58.2 Hz, median and IQR), and the other afferents divide into those sensitive to whisking and touch (WT) and to touch only (T).
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 2C; Glossary; Table S1
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b), spikes during whisking in air, 13 afferents are WT*, the same set as Table S1's (5 Merkel, 7 other SA, 1 RA), with a median whisking-in-air rate of 19.0 Hz and IQR 57.4 Hz (paper 19.1 and 58.2). Classes agree with Table S1 for 31 of 33; 223B and 243B are WT in Table S1 and T here (whisking-in-air rates 0.23 and 0.38 Hz, CIs overlapping the non-whisking rate). Under reading (a), all spikes, 15 are WT* (median 7.1 Hz) and 29 of 33 agree; 227A and 145B (1.05 and 1.26 Hz) have more than 1,000 spikes in all but 393 and 233 during whisking in air. With Poisson CIs, 15 are WT* and 29 of 33 agree.
deviations: The Glossary's "at least 1,000 spikes" can be read as spikes in the recording (a) or during whisking in air (b); only (b) matches the paper's count and Table S1's classes.

outcomes.statement: Merkel and SA afferents responded to contact in a dramatically direction-selective manner, far more strongly to contacts in either the protraction or the retraction direction.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 3A, E, H, I
outcomes.notes: 17 of 26 Merkel and SA afferents (65%) have a direction index of 0.5 or more (criterion 80%); 21 of 26 have 0.33 or more and 11 of 26 have 0.67 or more. Median index 0.65 over Merkel and SA, 0.59 over the 14 Merkel afferents, 0.23 over the 7 RA afferents, none of which reaches 0.5. 18 of 26 prefer protraction contacts. Contacts are classified by the sign of their mean M0; in 77% to 93% of contacts per recording that sign matches the whisker velocity at onset.
deviations: The paper shows direction selectivity in examples and tuning surfaces without a measure or threshold; the index and the 0.5 threshold were chosen before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: A full statistical model of ten mechanical and kinematic variables strongly predicted ongoing spike rate during touch (r = 0.71 plus or minus 0.16, mean and SD, n = 33).
outcomes.notes: Mean r 0.708, SD 0.141 (paper 0.71 and 0.16), median 0.726, range 0.363 to 0.919, 33 afferents. With lambda 100 the mean is 0.687. All 1,617 spline fits converged. Fits used a median of 60,000 frames per recording (at least 47,342) of a median 288,418 clean contact frames.
deviations: Penalized cubic B-splines (10 per variable, lambda 1) fitted as a binomial model with two trials per 2 ms frame replace mgcv GAMs on 1 ms bins with UBRE smoothing.
At most 60,000 randomly chosen contact frames per recording.

outcomes.statement: Models fitted to moment or its rate of change alone explained spiking relatively poorly (r = 0.45 plus or minus 0.19 and 0.42 plus or minus 0.21).
outcomes.notes: M0 alone mean r 0.441 (SD 0.178; paper 0.45), M0' alone 0.415 (SD 0.217; paper 0.42). With lambda 100, 0.415 and 0.398.
deviations: Spline models in place of mgcv GAMs, as for fig3d-gam-full.

outcomes.statement: M0 and its rate of change together explained spiking (r = 0.63 plus or minus 0.20) better than any other pair of variables, and better than a model of M0, Fax and Flat (r = 0.48 plus or minus 0.19).
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 3D; Figure S2C
outcomes.notes: M0 and M0' mean r 0.622 (paper 0.63); M0, Fax and Flat 0.475 (paper 0.48), lower than M0 and M0' in 31 of 33 (Wilcoxon p = 4.8e-08). Of the 45 pairs, M0 and omega (velocity) has the highest mean r, 0.633, and M0 and M0' is second; per afferent M0 and M0' is higher than M0 and omega in 19 of 33 (median difference 0.003). Flat and omega (0.620), Flat and M0' (0.606) and M0 and Flat' (0.605) follow. The values are within tolerance, but M0 and M0' is not the single best pair. The rank holds in two variants - with lambda 100 M0 and M0' is second (0.589 against 0.600 for M0 and omega, higher in 17 of 33), and fitted on a random half of the frames and evaluated on the other half it is second (0.620 against 0.630, higher in 20 of 33).
deviations: Spline models in place of mgcv GAMs; the ranking of close pairs may depend on the smoothing method.

outcomes.statement: A simple viscoelastic model of moment and its rate of change predicted spike rates of Merkel and SA afferents during touch at levels comparable to the statistical model based on M0 and its rate of change (25 of 26 afferents fitted).
outcomes.source: Results, third section; Figure 4C; STAR Methods, Viscoelastic model
outcomes.notes: Over 25 Merkel and SA afferents (Table S1's fitted set), mean r 0.656 for the viscoelastic model against 0.686 for the spline model of M0 and M0' on the same frames, difference -0.030 (95% bootstrap CI -0.061 to -0.006); viscoelastic higher in 10 of 25; Merkel afferents alone -0.034. The optimizer reported success for all 25, but 6 of 25 fits end with a parameter at a bound (eps_lim in 4, E in 1, eta in 2), so some fits may be local optima, which would only lower the viscoelastic r. These values differ slightly from the previous run (-0.029, 9 of 25, 7 at a bound) with the same code, data and locked packages; the cause was not established. With three other sets of random starts the mean difference is -0.037, -0.040 and -0.017, so the outcome holds, but single recordings change by up to 0.555 in r. Different parameter sets give nearly the same prediction, so the fitted parameter values are not interpreted.
deviations: Fitted with L-BFGS-B from 8 starts, with the rate of change of moment scaled by its 80th percentile inside the fit; the Methods used fmincon. During development an unscaled version found worse optima for the same model, so the result depends on the optimizer.
Fitted and evaluated on the same at most 60,000 contact frames as the spline models, which also exclude frames that are outliers on the other nine variables.

outcomes.statement: All 15 WT* afferents (13 touch WT* and 2 whisking-only) were dramatically modulated by whisk phase, with rates at non-preferred and preferred phases of 2.1 plus or minus 3.4 and 51.2 plus or minus 105.7 Hz (median and IQR).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 5A to C; Figure S3D
outcomes.notes: Over the 15 WT* afferents, non-preferred phase median 2.43 Hz, IQR 3.16 (paper 2.1 and 3.4); preferred phase median 51.1 Hz, IQR 96.6 (paper 51.2 and 105.7). All 15 fire at least 9.5 times more at the preferred than the non-preferred phase. Both medians are within the claim's tolerances (the paper's IQRs). Against a 10% band, which is not the criterion, the non-preferred median (16% above the paper's) would be outside and the preferred inside.

outcomes.statement: Across the population of WT* afferents, preferred phase spanned the whisk cycle.
outcomes.notes: Preferred phases occupy all four quarter cycles (7, 4, 1 and 3 of 15), but the Rayleigh test finds a preferred direction (R = 0.448, p = 0.047, just below 0.05). The outcome sits at the threshold and depends on the estimator of preferred phase, which the criterion fixes as the bin of highest rate of 30 - with the circular mean of the tuning curve p = 0.062 (which would be reproduced), with the highest of 20 or 60 bins, computed on the outlier-free frames kept for figs6-kinematic-gam, p = 0.023 and 0.046; all four quarters are occupied under every estimator. At the preferred phase the mean whisker velocity is negative for 11 of 15. Whether this agrees with the paper's slight abundance in retraction (Figure 7G, on 28 afferents) is not established, since the stored phase is negated and the paper's phase convention for the figure is not known.
deviations: The paper gives no test for spanning the whisk cycle; the quarter-cycle and Rayleigh criterion was chosen before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: The preferred phase of each WT* afferent was largely invariant across whisk cycles of different amplitudes, frequencies and setpoints.
outcomes.notes: Median absolute circular difference between the preferred phases of the two halves 0.37 rad (amplitude), 0.59 (frequency), 0.48 (setpoint), against pi/4 = 0.785. 4, 6 and 5 of 15 afferents differ by more than pi/4.
deviations: The paper shows invariance with tuning surfaces only; the median split and the pi/4 threshold were chosen before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: Statistical models fitted to whisker position, velocity, acceleration and jerk during whisking in air predicted phase tuning curves nearly perfectly (r = 0.97 plus or minus 0.04, n = 28), while single kinematic variables performed poorly.
outcomes.source: Results, fifth section; Figure S6A, B
outcomes.notes: On the 15 WT* afferents, the full model's mean r between predicted and observed phase tuning curves is 0.975, SD 0.013 (paper 0.97 and 0.04, on 28). Single-variable models give 0.524 (jerk) to 0.724 (acceleration); velocity and acceleration together give 0.960. No fit failed to converge.
deviations: Tested on 15 of the paper's 28 afferents; the intact condition of the 13 progressive cutting recordings cannot be separated.
Spline models in place of mgcv GAMs, fitted on 60,000 frames and evaluated on up to 400,000 whisking-in-air frames per afferent.

outcomes.statement: Preferred phases of all 28 WT* afferents spanned the whisk cycle, with a slight abundance in the retraction phase.
outcomes.notes: Needs the intact condition of the 13 progressive cutting recordings, whose trials are all labelled intact (see fig6-cut-eliminated). The 15 other WT* afferents are tested in fig5e-phase-span.

outcomes.statement: Progressive whisker cutting eliminated spiking during whisking in air in 6 of 13 afferents (from 50.1 plus or minus 42.3 Hz intact to 0.9 plus or minus 0.7 Hz after the final cut, mean and SD).
outcomes.notes: Every trial of the 13 progressive cutting recordings has cuttingGroup "intact" and each file has one MOI value, so the intact, sham and cut conditions cannot be told apart. The whisking-in-air rate falls over most sessions (last fifth below half the first in 10 of 13, below 10% in 5 of 13), so the files appear to hold the cut conditions under the intact label. Splitting by trial order would be a guess.

outcomes.statement: In 7 of 13 afferents self-motion responses remained after cutting (86.1 plus or minus 71.5 Hz intact against 70.3 plus or minus 58.5 Hz after the final cut).
outcomes.source: Results, fifth section; Figure 6C to E
outcomes.notes: As fig6-cut-eliminated.

outcomes.statement: Cutting shortened the whisker to near its base (final length 0.37 plus or minus 0.43 mm, mean and SD, n = 13).
outcomes.notes: The remaining whisker length after each cut is not in the dandiset; the trial table's MOI has one value per file, the same for all trials.

outcomes.statement: After whisker trimming, phase tuning curves of the 7 afferents that kept spiking were correlated with intrinsic protractor or nasolabialis EMG (r = 0.66 plus or minus 0.27).
outcomes.notes: Needs the intrinsic protractor EMG, which is not in the EMG files 7A, 8A and 9A (they hold tracked whisker series only, with no spike times and nothing in acquisition), and the cut condition of each trial (metadata insufficient, see fig6-cut-eliminated). The EMG is given as the main reason because no labelling of the trials would supply it.

outcomes.statement: The spike rate lost after cutting was correlated with positive acceleration, negative acceleration or jerk (r = 0.71 plus or minus 0.19, n = 13).
outcomes.notes: Needs the intact and fully cut conditions of the 13 progressive cutting recordings, which the trial tables do not distinguish (see fig6-cut-eliminated).

outcomes.statement: In 5 afferents recorded with the whisker already cut near its base, phase tuning was strongly correlated with intrinsic protractor or nasolabialis EMG (r = 0.76 plus or minus 0.06).
outcomes.notes: The 5 cut-whisker recordings and the nasolabialis motor units (11A) are in the dandiset, but the best match is chosen between the intrinsic protractor and the nasolabialis curves, and the intrinsic protractor EMG is not in the dandiset. The nasolabialis curve alone gives no useful bound - 4 of the 5 afferents are anticorrelated with it (mean r -0.277, SD 0.559), and only 305A correlates (0.695). As a stand-in that is not the criterion, the better of each afferent's correlations with its own positive and negative velocity curves has mean 0.753 (0.680 to 0.848), with positive velocity, which the paper relates to the intrinsic protractor, the better for 4 of 5.

outcomes.statement: Motor unit activity of m. nasolabialis was phase modulated and correlated with negative whisker velocity (r = 0.93) and anti-correlated with positive velocity (r = -0.75) within whisk cycles.
outcomes.notes: The spike times of 11A, taken as motor unit spikes, give r = 0.924 with negative velocity (paper 0.93) and -0.716 with positive velocity (paper -0.75) across 30 phase bins of 23.3 min of whisking; the rate ranges 0.7 to 37.6 Hz and peaks where velocity is negative. The raw EMG is not in the file.
deviations: The file does not say that its spike times are motor units of m. nasolabialis; this is taken from Table S1.

outcomes.statement: Intrinsic protractor EMG was correlated with positive whisker velocity within whisk cycles (r = 0.94, 0.97 and 0.96 in three mice).
outcomes.notes: Files 7A, 8A and 9A hold the tracked whisker series of the EMG sessions (position, velocity, Mi, dMi and others) but no EMG signal, no spike times and nothing in acquisition, analysis or stimulus. The archive's variableMeasured for them lists only BehavioralTimeSeries and ProcessingModule, and their size per trial (0.31 MB) equals that of 11A and of the progressive cutting files. The undescribed Mi (N*m) and dMi (N*m/s) do not follow positive velocity by phase - r -0.026 to 0.002 for Mi and -0.570 to -0.534 for dMi in 7A, 8A and 9A, close to the medians in every group of afferent files (-0.026 to -0.014 and -0.536 to -0.485) - so neither is the intrinsic protractor EMG.

outcomes.statement: The noise level of curvature estimates, curvature change during whisking in air as a percentage of that during contact, was 7.8 plus or minus 5.0% (mean and SD) across 33 sessions.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Video analysis, whisker baseline curvature; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: Mean 10.01%, SD 6.97, range 4.23 to 39.89 over the 33 touch recordings (paper 7.8 and 5.0). The mean is within the paper's stated spread but 28% above its mean value, outside a 10% band; 243B (39.89%) and 265A (28.49%) are high. Both readings of contact frames give the same values.
deviations: The Methods give no rule for frames with a missing distance to the pole; these are treated as far from the pole.

outcomes.statement: Identified Merkel afferents spiked at short latency (4.9 plus or minus 1.3 ms) and low jitter (SD of first-spike latency 0.91 plus or minus 0.29 ms) after brief light pulses.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Optogenetic identification; Figure S1C, D
outcomes.notes: The light pulse times and the optogenetic stimulation trials are not in the dandiset; no file has a member in stimulus, acquisition or analysis, or an optogenetic neurodata type.

outcomes.statement: In TrkC-CreER;Rosa-Ai9 mice, 99.2% of classified labelled afferent endings in whisker follicles were Merkel cell-associated (1,045 of 1,053).
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Histology quantification; Figure S1B
outcomes.notes: The histology (confocal stacks and their scoring) is not in the dandiset, and was not found in another public archive.

outcomes.statement: Automatic contact classification agreed with manual curation for 99.5 plus or minus 0.2% of frames, with a false positive rate of 0.3 plus or minus 0.1%.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Video analysis, contact detection
outcomes.notes: The files hold the final contact classification only, not the manually curated frames the classifier was tested against.

findings.statement: The files do not say which experiment each recording belongs to (touch, progressive cutting, cut-whisker, whisking-only, EMG), the afferent type (RA or SA), which afferents were identified as Merkel afferents by optogenetic tagging, or the whisking and touch class. All of these are in the paper's Table S1, whose recording ids match the NWB identifiers.
The paper excludes three touch recordings (227C, 214A, 271A) from all analyses except Figure S1. The dandiset holds them without saying so.

In the 13 progressive cutting recordings every trial has cuttingGroup "intact" and the trial table's MOI has one value per file, although the whisking-in-air rate falls over most of these sessions (last fifth below half the first in 10 of 13). The cutting conditions (intact, sham, cut 1 to 3) and the moment of inertia after each cut are missing, which blocks Figure 6 and parts of Figure 7.

The EMG files of the intrinsic protractor recordings (7A, 8A, 9A) hold the tracked whisker series but no EMG signal; the nasolabialis file (11A) holds spike times but not the EMG. The optogenetic tagging data, the histology, the whisker geometry and the manually curated contact frames are not in the dandiset.

Velocity, acceleration and jerk are stated in degree/s, degree/s^2 and degree/s^3, and dM0, dFaxial and dFlateral in N*m/s and N/s, but the values are per millisecond; each is close to half the change of its variable per 2 ms frame (median ratios 0.467 to 0.502 over files).

The stored whisk phase is the negative of the Hilbert phase of the band-passed whisker position; its sine is anticorrelated (median -0.9999 over files) and its cosine correlated (median 0.9999) with those of the Hilbert phase, and position peaks at phase 0 in all 60 files. So phases from -pi to 0 are retraction, the reverse of the convention the paper cites. Neither the files nor the paper describe the convention.

Every series has the description "no description". distanceToPoleCenter has unit "unknown"; its median in frames with contact = 1 is between -0.08 and 0.09 in every file but one (209A, a cut-whisker recording with almost no contact), which fits the Methods' distance from whisker to pole in mm, not a distance to the pole's centre. Series not used here (Mi, dMi, Fnorm, thetaAtContact, follicleCoordsX and Y) are not explained; Mi and dMi have units N*m and N*m/s and values below 3e-8 in absolute size, in every file including the EMG files.
Trial stop_time is 6.998 s after start_time in every trial of every file, while each trial's series hold 2,500 frames at 500 Hz (5 s), as the Methods describe.
The spike times of file sub-KSm31 (KS0277A) are not sorted.
Two identifiers, KS0125_ and KS0128_, lack the unit letter of their Table S1 recordings (125B and 128D). All session start times are 12:00, so only the dates carry information.

Some series hold extreme values, likely tracking errors, such as whisker position from -985 to 596 degrees, whisk frequency from -250 to 250 Hz and M0 down to -0.52 N m. The Glossary's percentile outlier removal excludes them, but they are not flagged in the files.

Two recordings made with the whisker cut before recording (199B and 209A) hold distance-to-pole series and frames with contact = 1 (5,014 and 32); in 209A the distance at those frames is 5.6 to 6.5. The files do not say whether a pole was presented in these sessions or what these frames are.
The paper's MATLAB and R analysis code is available only on request; no public repository was found, so the GAM and viscoelastic fits had to be reimplemented.

attempts.paper_title: Preprint for: Rule-based modulation of a sensorimotor transformation across cortical areas
attempts.entry_title: Rule-based modulation of a sensorimotor transformation across cortical areas (Chang et al. 2023)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Chang, Finkel, Xu and O'Connor (bioRxiv 2023, version 2) on dandiset 000232, which holds silicon-probe recordings from S1, S2, MM, ALM and AMM of mice performing a cross-modal sensory selection task, and the behaviour of optogenetic inhibition sessions in that task and in a tactile detection task. It covers behavioural performance, single-neuron rule and stimulus discrimination, population decoding of the rule, neural trajectories and subspaces, coding dimensions, rule transitions and the effects of optogenetic inhibition.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Chang et al. (2023) from dandiset 000232

outcomes.statement: Single units were recorded with 64-channel probes in S1 (6 mice, 10 sessions, 177 neurons), S2 (5 mice, 8 sessions, 162 neurons), MM (7 mice, 9 sessions, 140 neurons) and ALM (8 mice, 13 sessions, 256 neurons), one area per session, and in AMM (110 neurons).
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 1E and 1G; Figure S1K
outcomes.notes: Sessions, mice and units per area match exactly; S1 10, 6, 177; S2 8, 5, 162; MM 9, 7, 140; ALM 13, 8, 256; AMM 110 units in 9 sessions from 7 mice. The units are those left after the paper's quality filter.

outcomes.statement: The optogenetic experiments in the cross-modal task comprise S1/S2 (4 mice, 10 sessions), MM (4, 11), ALM (4, 10), sham (7, 28), AMM (7, 21) and PPC (7, 21); in the tactile detection task sham (5, 9), S1/S2 (3, 3), MM (3, 5), ALM (3, 4), AMM (3, 4) and PPC (3, 4).
outcomes.notes: All 24 counts of sessions and mice per optogenetic condition match the Figure 6 legend. The code's performance check, ported here, passes 27 of the 28 cross-modal sham sessions and all other cross-modal sessions.

outcomes.statement: Performance was about 75% correct under both rules (respond-to-touch 74 plus or minus 1%, respond-to-light 75 plus or minus 1%, mean and SEM over 12 mice), with no difference between them (paired t-test, p = 0.56).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), trials as deposited, gives 73.6 plus or minus 0.8% (touch) and 74.8 plus or minus 1.5% (light) over 12 mice, paired t-test p = 0.561, matching the reported 74, 75 and p = 0.56. Reading (b), without the last 20 trials, gives 72.8 and 74.2% (p = 0.558), with the touch value outside tolerance.
deviations: The Methods remove the last 20 trials of each session and the code does not; the files may already lack them. Both readings are shown and reading (a) matches.

outcomes.statement: The fractions of trial outcomes were similar under the two rules (touch against light; hit 36 against 35%, correct rejection 38 against 40%, miss 13 against 14%, false alarm 13 against 12%).
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) all eight fractions are within the paper's SEM (touch against light; hit 35.6 and 35.2, correct rejection 38.1 and 39.6, miss 13.0 and 13.6, false alarm 13.3 and 11.6%). Reading (b) puts 6 of 8 within. Gaps between rows, which mark removed trials, separate 4.5% of consecutive rows within the last 20 rows of a session against 12.7% earlier; this is consistent with the last rows being the end of the session but does not show it.

outcomes.statement: 18 to 33% of neurons discriminate tactile hits from tactile correct rejections in the first 150 ms after the stimulus (S1 28.8%, S2 17.9%, MM 32.9%, ALM 23.4%), and most of these respond more in tactile hits (AUC above 0.5).
outcomes.notes: S1 30.5, S2 16.7 and ALM 23.0% are within tolerance; MM is 36.4% against 32.9 plus or minus 3.29, and above the stated range widened by 10%. Over four other seeds MM gives 35.0 to 36.4%, S1 28.2 to 30.5, S2 17.9 to 19.1 and ALM 21.9 to 25.0%. MM is within tolerance in 3 of the 5 seeds, and the five-seed means (S1 29.7, S2 18.1, MM 35.6, ALM 23.1%) are all within tolerance, so the partial outcome depends on the bootstrap draw; it is judged on the main seed. 165 of 191 selective neurons (86.4%) have mean AUC above 0.5, as the claim states.
deviations: The bootstrap resamples are shared by all units and bins of a session; the code draws them separately. Each unit's interval depends only on its own resamples.

outcomes.statement: Before the stimulus (-100 to 0 ms), fewer than 5% of neurons in S1 and S2 discriminate the rule, while about 10 to 20% do in MM and ALM (S1 4.5%, S2 2.5%, MM 21.4%, ALM 10.2%).
outcomes.notes: S2 2.5, MM 20.0 and ALM 9.8% are within tolerance; S1 is 5.6% (10 neurons) against 4.5% (8 neurons). Over the main seed and four others S1 gives 3.4 to 5.6% and is within tolerance in none (9 neurons, 5.1%, is just above it); ALM is within tolerance in 2 of 5. The five-seed means (S1 5.0, S2 2.8, MM 20.7, ALM 9.9%) are all within tolerance. The outcome is judged on the main seed. MM and ALM each exceed S1 and S2, as the claim states.

outcomes.statement: As a negative control, almost no neuron discriminates tactile from visual trials before the stimulus (S1 0%, S2 0%, MM 0%, ALM 0.8%).
outcomes.notes: 0% in S1, S2 and MM and 0.8% (2 neurons) in ALM, as in the paper.

outcomes.statement: After the stimulus (0 to 100 ms), more than 35% of neurons in S1 and S2 and about 15% in MM and ALM discriminate tactile from visual trials (S1 37.3%, S2 35.2%, MM 15%, ALM 14.1%).
outcomes.notes: All four within tolerance of 37.3, 35.2, 15 and 14.1%.

outcomes.statement: Among neurons with significant rule discrimination before the stimulus, the pre-stimulus rule preference predicts the rule modulation of the early touch response (0 to 50 ms); Pearson r = 0.93 in MM (30 neurons) and 0.83 in ALM (26 neurons), both p < 0.001 (S1 r = 0.69, 8 neurons, p = 0.056; S2 r = 0.91, 4 neurons, p = 0.093).
outcomes.notes: MM r = 0.958 over 28 neurons and ALM r = 0.841 over 25 neurons, both p < 0.001 (paper 30 and 26 neurons). S1 r = 0.681 (10 neurons, p = 0.030) and S2 r = 0.902 (4 neurons, p = 0.0985), against the paper's 0.69 (8 neurons, p = 0.056) and 0.91 (4, p = 0.093).

outcomes.statement: The rule can be decoded from pre-stimulus population activity (-100 to 0 ms) in each area; median LDA accuracy over sessions, true against shuffled, S1 0.61 against 0.5, S2 0.62 against 0.53, MM 0.7 against 0.52, ALM 0.68 against 0.55.
outcomes.notes: Shuffled medians are 0.564, 0.532, 0.526 and 0.535; 37 of 40 sessions exceed their shuffled value. The S1 sessions differ from shuffled at Wilcoxon p = 0.055, the others at p below 0.01. The shuffled medians (0.526 to 0.564) are about equal to the larger block's share of correct trials (medians 0.529 to 0.556 by area).
deviations: The Methods name LDA; the code's diagonal LDA is used. The Methods' soft normalization and the code's z-score give the same diagonal LDA predictions.

outcomes.statement: Rule decoding is robust in the motor areas, whose bootstrap 95% CIs of mean accuracy do not overlap those of shuffled data (MM 0.60 to 0.73 against 0.48 to 0.53; ALM 0.56 to 0.66 against 0.49 to 0.54), and limited in the sensory areas, whose true CIs are above 0.5 but overlap the shuffled ones (S1 0.52 to 0.61 against 0.49 to 0.55; S2 0.53 to 0.63 against 0.49 to 0.54).
outcomes.notes: Bootstrap 95% CIs, true against shuffled; MM 0.601 to 0.731 against 0.472 to 0.523; ALM 0.560 to 0.655 against 0.495 to 0.544 (no overlap); S1 0.530 to 0.614 against 0.493 to 0.545; S2 0.528 to 0.619 against 0.488 to 0.539 (overlap). These are within 0.012 of the paper's bounds.
deviations: 200 resamples per area; the code's header sets 100 and its saved file names say 1000.

outcomes.statement: Population activity discriminates tactile from visual trials after the stimulus (0 to 100 ms) but not before it (-100 to 0 ms).
outcomes.source: Results, third section; Figure 3D and 3E; Figure S3C and S3D
outcomes.notes: Before the stimulus true means 0.495 to 0.509 with CIs overlapping shuffled in all areas; after it 0.642 (MM) to 0.805 (S2), no overlap in any area.

outcomes.statement: Support vector machines and random forests decode the rule from pre-stimulus activity about as well as LDA (median accuracy true against shuffled; SVM S1 0.6 against 0.53, S2 0.61 against 0.51, MM 0.71 against 0.51, ALM 0.65 against 0.52; random forests S1 0.59 against 0.52, S2 0.6 against 0.52, MM 0.65 against 0.49, ALM 0.7 against 0.5).
outcomes.source: Results, third section; Figure S3A and S3B
outcomes.notes: All eight within 10% and above their shuffled medians. With the code's z-score the SVM medians are 0.575, 0.603, 0.701 and 0.642.
deviations: scikit-learn's SVC and random forest stand in for MATLAB fitcsvm and TreeBagger with their defaults.

outcomes.statement: Sessions with a larger pre-stimulus distance between tactile hit and correct rejection trajectories (top 50% of 40 sessions) show a larger distance after the stimulus than the bottom 50% (permutation test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: Top 20 sessions 1.171 against bottom 20 0.966 mean post-stimulus distance, permutation p = 0.004. With the code's normalization (range without the offset 5) p = 0.001. Pre- and post-stimulus mean distances correlate over sessions (Spearman 0.54, p = 0.0004).
deviations: The code's windows are offset by one 10 ms bin from the stated ones; the stated windows are used.

outcomes.statement: In all four areas the subspace overlap of tactile correct rejections with tactile hits (0 to 150 ms) is lower than that of held-out tactile hits (tCR minus control tHit; S1 -0.23, 8 sessions, p = 0.0016; S2 -0.23, 7 sessions, p = 0.0086; MM -0.36, 5 sessions, p < 0.001; ALM -0.35, 11 sessions, p < 0.001; paired t-test).
outcomes.notes: Negative in all four areas with p = 0.0007, 0.025, 0.003 and below 0.0001 (8, 7, 5 and 12 sessions), but only S2 is within 10% of the paper. MM and ALM are larger in magnitude than the reported -0.36 and -0.35; the code's single-split procedure repeated 200 times gives 95% ranges of -0.497 to -0.376 (MM) and -0.473 to -0.359 (ALM), which exclude the reported values.
deviations: Sessions with at least 10 units (Methods), 12 ALM sessions; the code keeps more than 10, 11 ALM sessions, as the paper reports. Both are shown and give the same result.
Overlaps average 100 random equal splits with offset 5 throughout; the code uses one split drawn separately for each neuron and offsets 5 and 0.01, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Across sessions, the tCR subspace overlap before the stimulus (-100 to 0 ms) correlates with that after it (Pearson r = 0.68, p < 0.001, 31 sessions).
outcomes.notes: r = 0.688 over 32 sessions (p = 1.3e-05); 0.686 over the code's 31 sessions; the code's single-split procedure gives 0.573 to 0.734 over 200 runs.

outcomes.statement: Stimulus coding dimensions are aligned between the two rules in S1, S2 and MM but not in ALM, while choice coding dimensions (lick against no lick) are not aligned in any area (dot product magnitudes, true against shuffled, with 95% CIs).
outcomes.source: Results, sixth section; Figure S4E and S4F
outcomes.notes: Seven of eight judgements match. The MM stimulus CD is not aligned (0.366, CI 0.218 to 0.521, shuffled 0.150 to 0.441), where the paper reports 0.48 against 0.24 with non-overlapping CIs; with the code's sessions of more than 10 units it is 0.295 and also not aligned. S1, S2 and ALM values are close to the paper's (0.557, 0.620, 0.348 against 0.5, 0.62, 0.33).
deviations: All sessions are used, as the paper's session counts state; the code keeps sessions with more than 10 units, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Choice coding dimensions computed from right against left lick trials are still not well aligned between the two rules (true against shuffled; S1 0.39 against 0.2, S2 0.32 against 0.2, MM 0.35 against 0.18, ALM 0.28 against 0.21).
outcomes.notes: All four below 0.5; S1, MM and ALM within 0.1 of the paper, S2 0.422 against 0.32. All four CIs overlap the shuffled ones. Over the main seed and four others the S2 mean is 0.420 to 0.425, within 0.1 of the paper in 1 of 5 (0.420); the outcome is judged on the main seed.
deviations: The criterion's "needed condition" first read as each of the four rare categories left 1 of 10 S1 sessions, none in S2 and MM and 1 of 13 in ALM, so it could not decide; following the code's nanmean over stimuli, right- and left-lick trials are pooled over stimuli (at least 2 each, all 40 sessions). The first reading is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Mice switched before or immediately after the cue on the 9th trial; there were 88 switches into respond-to-touch blocks and 91 into respond-to-light blocks.
outcomes.notes: Non-first blocks with a hit, as the criterion and the code's GetFirstHitInfo define them, number 63 (touch) and 75 (light), against 88 and 91. Both counts fail, so two of the three conditions fail and the outcome is not reproduced (round 1 recorded partially reproduced, which the criterion does not allow). The third condition holds; first hits at or before the trial after the cue are 57.1% (touch) and 65.2% (light) of blocks with a cue row, counted in rows of the file, and 55.4% and 62.1% in trial numbers estimated from the gaps between rows. All blocks, including the first of each session, number exactly 88 and 91, and blocks with a hit including first blocks 87 and 91. The code's GetFirstHitInfo returns one entry per block, NaN for first blocks and blocks without a hit, so a count of its entries gives the number of blocks.
deviations: The code numbers trials by the behavioural system, including trials the files lack; first hits are placed relative to the cue row in the files, and as a variant in trial numbers estimated from the gaps between rows (xm.estimated_trial_numbers).

outcomes.statement: Over a rule transition, the fraction of trials classified as respond-to-touch from pre-stimulus activity changes progressively in MM and ALM (Kendall's tau, mean and 95% CI; touch to light MM -0.39 [-0.67, -0.11], ALM -0.29 [-0.54, -0.04]; light to touch MM 0.37 [0.07, 0.63], ALM 0.27 [0.03, 0.49]).
outcomes.notes: Touch to light MM -0.401 [-0.667, -0.111], ALM -0.302 [-0.538, -0.051]; light to touch MM 0.382 [0.074, 0.630], ALM 0.268 [0.026, 0.513]; all within 0.04 of the paper's values and bounds.
deviations: LDA with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage stands in for the code's optimized LDA; 500 resamples (code 1000).

outcomes.statement: Classification of trials in S1 and S2 shows no clear trend across block transitions (Kendall's tau touch to light S1 -0.16 [-0.43, 0.1], S2 -0.15 [-0.54, 0.21]; light to touch S1 0.21 [-0.07, 0.5], S2 0.25 [-0.17, 0.63]).
outcomes.notes: S1 -0.163 [-0.433, 0.117] and 0.219 [-0.067, 0.500]; S2 -0.140 [-0.500, 0.250] and 0.259 [-0.105, 0.620]; all include 0. The 10-fold estimates without resampling are as large in S1 and S2 as in MM and ALM (S2 to touch 0.583, MM 0.519), so the absence rests on wide CIs from 10 and 8 sessions.

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting MM or ALM before the stimulus reduces tactile detection sensitivity in respond-to-touch blocks, while inhibiting S1/S2, AMM or the sham does not (95% CI of the change; S1/S2 [-0.47, 0.08], MM [-0.65, -0.12], ALM [-0.68, -0.02], sham [-0.12, 0.13], AMM [-0.19, 0.06]).
outcomes.notes: MM -0.390 (CI -0.658 to -0.123) is below 0; ALM -0.373 has a CI of -0.707 to 0.005 when false-alarm trials are also resampled (Methods). S1/S2, sham and AMM include 0. With the code's resampling, which keeps the observed false-alarm rate, ALM is -0.682 to -0.018 and every CI is within 0.03 of the paper's, which would make the claim reproduced. The outcome is judged on the main seed; the ALM upper bound is at the edge of 0. Over ten other seeds it averages -0.001 (SD 0.003, range -0.006 to 0.001) and is below 0 in 7 of 10; with the code's resampling it is below 0 in all ten (mean -0.018). No other Methods-resampling bound of the optogenetic CIs checked over seeds changes side; the figs6b ALM interval with the code's resampling does (upper bound 0.002 on the main draw, below 0 in 9 of 10 other seeds), and the fig6ij laser-only calls keep their side in all ten seeds.
deviations: Hit and false-alarm trials are both resampled; the code resamples hits only, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The loss of tactile sensitivity with pre-stimulus inhibition is mainly a fall in the tactile hit rate (95% CI of the change; S1/S2 [-0.31, 0.01], MM [-0.49, -0.15], ALM [-0.46, -0.07]).
outcomes.notes: MM -0.318 (-0.492 to -0.152), ALM -0.227 (-0.463 to -0.007), S1/S2 -0.147 (-0.303 to 0.010). The ALM upper bound is close to 0. Over ten other seeds it is below 0 in all ten (mean -0.004, SD 0.002). The code's resampling is the same procedure here, as there is no false-alarm group; its draw gives 0.002 and is below 0 in 9 of 10 other seeds.

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting S1/S2, MM or ALM from the stimulus onset reduces tactile sensitivity (95% CI S1/S2 [-0.67, -0.08], MM [-0.6, -0.34], ALM [-0.55, -0.27]).

Visual detection sensitivity in respond-to-light blocks falls with pre-stimulus inhibition of MM [-0.6, -0.18] and AMM [-0.35, -0.08] but not of ALM [-0.5, 0.04] or S1/S2 [-0.27, 0.05]; with inhibition from the stimulus onset it falls for MM, ALM and AMM but not for S1/S2 [-0.44, 0.04].
outcomes.source: Results, eighth section; Figure S7G and S7H

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting PPC before or after the stimulus onset reduces both tactile and visual detection sensitivity (tactile pre [-0.4, -0.06], post [-0.43, -0.04]; visual pre [-0.31, -0.05], post [-0.54, -0.07]).
outcomes.source: Results, eighth section; Figure 6C and 6D; Figure S7G and S7H
outcomes.notes: Tactile pre -0.408 to -0.052, post -0.466 to -0.009; visual pre -0.333 to -0.031, post -0.555 to -0.070. The tactile post upper bound is below 0 in all ten other seeds (mean -0.011, SD 0.003).

outcomes.statement: In a simple tactile detection task without rule switching, inhibiting S1/S2, MM or ALM after the stimulus onset reduces sensitivity, but inhibiting them before it does not (pre S1/S2 [-0.34, 0.18], MM [-0.23, 0.06], ALM [-0.28, 0.07]; post S1/S2 [-0.59, -0.31], MM [-0.59, -0.25], ALM [-0.45, -0.1]); AMM and PPC have no effect in either window.
outcomes.notes: Pre-stimulus CIs include 0 for S1/S2, MM and ALM; post-stimulus S1/S2 -0.643 to -0.251, MM -0.628 to -0.233, ALM -0.471 to -0.065. AMM and PPC include 0 in both windows.

outcomes.statement: Lick probability on laser-only trials does not change during S1/S2, MM or ALM inhibition in either task, so the behavioural effects are not due to an inability to lick (cross-modal S1/S2 [-0.18, 0.24], MM [-0.31, 0.03], ALM [-0.24, 0.16]; detection S1/S2 [-0.13, 0.31], MM [-0.06, 0.45], ALM [-0.18, 0.34]).
outcomes.notes: 11 of 12 CIs include 0. On short laser-only trials of the detection task, MM inhibition raises the right-lick probability from 0.333 in the inter-trial window to 0.553 in the response window (change 0.258, CI 0.045 to 0.483; 141 trials, 5 sessions, 3 mice); over ten other seeds the lower bound is 0.040 to 0.053, and the other eleven CIs include 0 in every seed. All cross-modal CIs and all long- laser CIs include 0; the paper gives one CI per area and task (MM detection -0.06 to 0.45), without saying which laser duration. The windows are the code's (GetBehavInfo, GetBehavInfo_tDetection). In the cross-modal task, licks on short laser-only trials are scored 0 to 2 s after the laser offset, in the detection task -0.8 to 1.2 s from it, which covers the laser. The paper's cross-modal CIs match the long-laser rows (MM -0.312 to 0.030 against -0.31 to 0.03), so the criterion's twelve CIs test more than the paper reports. Its detection CIs match neither the short, the long nor the pooled rows (the code's "all laser trials"; pooled MM 0.020 to 0.274 also excludes 0). A rise in licking does not bear on the paper's point that inhibition does not prevent licking.
deviations: The paper reports one CI per area and task; short and long laser-only trials were tested apart, as the code computes them.

outcomes.statement: The probe locations were reconstructed histologically and lie in S1, S2, MM and ALM.
outcomes.notes: The files give the recorded area only as a label; electrode x, y and z are NaN, electrode locations are "unknown", and no histology images or reconstructed coordinates are in the dandiset or the code repository.

findings.statement: The ephys files hold only the trials and units the paper analysed. No trial has a lick between -1 and 0.1 s of the stimulus (the Methods remove about 25%; gaps of 8 to 64 per session remain in the trial times), and the units are those passing the quality filter and the 50 Hz cut (unit counts per area equal the paper's). The dandiset does not say that trials or units were removed.

Units carry only spike times and observation intervals; there are no quality metrics, waveforms, channel or depth, and unit ids run from 0, so units the paper names by cluster number (for example unit 127 of YT084, 2020-02-01) cannot be identified.
Electrode x, y and z are NaN in all 49 ephys files and electrode locations "unknown"; the probe locations of Figure 1E (histology) are not in the dandiset.

The trials table columns have no descriptions. `response` (1 right lick, 2 left, 0 none, 3 on trials without a stimulus), `blockType` ("Whisker", "Visual", and "Change" for the cue trial), the opto trial types and the TTT to VVN indicator columns are explained only by the paper's code.

In the 130 behaviour files `start_time` equals the stimulus onset (or laser time on laser-only trials), so trial intervals overlap and do not delimit trials; licks before the stimulus are stored in the trial's lists.
In the tactile detection files, trials without a whisker stimulus are labelled "Stim_Vis" and "Stim_Vis_NoCue" with a visual stimulus type, though no visual onset is given.
Two laser trials start 1.6 and 2.7 s before the reference time and one lasts 9.5 s, outside the stated 0.8 s pre-stimulus and 2 s post-stimulus inhibition; the code counts them as pre-stimulus.

Figure 5B gives 88 and 91 block switches; the 40 recording sessions hold exactly 88 touch and 91 light blocks when the first block of each session is counted, and 63 and 75 non-first blocks with a hit, so the reported numbers appear to count blocks, not switches. The code's GetFirstHitInfo returns one entry per block, NaN for first blocks and blocks without a hit, which a count of entries would give.

The Methods describe soft normalization (x - mean) / (range + 5) for population analyses; the code's trajectory distance divides by the range alone, its subspace overlap uses offset 5 for the reference and 0.01 for compared data, the coding dimensions use 0.01, and decoding uses a z-score. The Methods exclude sessions with fewer than ten units from the subspace analysis; the code requires more than ten.
The code's hierarchical bootstrap of optogenetic sensitivity draws resampled false-alarm trials but computes the false-alarm rate from the original trials, so only hits are resampled.
The coding-dimension code keeps sessions with more than ten units (S1 8, S2 7, MM 5, ALM 11), while Figure S4 reports 10, 8, 9 and 13 sessions.

The shared clock of spike times and trial times could not be established by the stimulus-decoding check for three sessions, YT084 2020-02-02 and 2020-02-03 (AMM, 2 and 5 units) and YT086 2020-03-20 (MM, 5 units, accuracy 0.63 before and 0.65 after the onset). They are kept.
The cross-modal sham session set includes one session (of 28) that fails the code's own performance check as ported here; it is kept, as deposited.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file. The attempt record was not among its materials. It checked the archive's file list and metadata for the blocked claim.

disagreements.reason: Under the criterion (non-first blocks with a hit) the counts are touch 63 and light 75, against 88 and 91. Both counts fail; the before-or-at-cue+1 condition holds (0.57, 0.65). The all-block counts are exactly 88 and 91, and the paper says "total number of block switches", so the criterion's definition is probably not the paper's. Problem 2, that the count of blocks with a hit including first blocks is never printed, and that `rel` is counted in file rows, so `rel <= 1` can cover trials several positions after the cue, which biases the fraction upward.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The full executed notebook of the second run (89 cells), the helper module, the claims file and the attempt record. Report in transcripts/000232/verifier-2-report.md. Points not tied to one claim were also answered. The introduction said 141 optogenetic behaviour sessions where the dandiset holds 130; corrected. The README said the run takes about 15 minutes, a quarter of it streaming, where streaming took 131 s of 14.7 min; it now gives the new run, 162 s of 8.7 min. The summary's "no other optogenetic call changes" and "with other seeds" were reworded (see fig6c, figs6b, fig6ij and fig1h). The clock part of round-1 problem B11 (three sessions, among them YT086 2020-03-20 in MM, where the stimulus-decoding check does not establish a shared clock), which was recorded only in the notebook, is now a finding. The re-run gives the same numbers as the second run in every cell that existed before.

attempts.paper_title: Cortical processing of flexible and context-dependent sensorimotor sequences
attempts.entry_title: Cortical processing of flexible sensorimotor sequences (Xu et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Xu, Dong, Chen, Delgado, Hughes, Zhang and O'Connor (2022) on dandiset 000239, which holds the trial tables, tongue tracking and sorted spikes of mice performing a sequence licking task. It decodes tongue kinematics, sequence identity and sequence time from S1TJ, M1TJ, ALM and S1BF populations, classifies backtracking and zigzag sequence context, and checks the behavioural measures and unit counts. The optogenetic and control experiments cannot be tested, as the files do not say which region was inhibited or which condition each session was.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Xu et al. (2022) from dandiset 000239

outcomes.statement: Silicon probe recordings gave 1537 single units and 303 multi-units from 57 recording sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, "Sequence tiling of single-unit responses"; Extended Data Fig. 4a-d
outcomes.notes: The 57 files described as ephys ALM, M1TJ, S1TJ, S1BF, M1B, S1L and ZZ hold 1917 units, within 10% of the paper's 1840. With an ISI violation rate (2.5 ms) of at most 1% and a contamination of at most 15%, 1578 are single units (1537 in the paper, within tolerance) and 339 multi-units (303, outside 272.7 to 333.3). Other thresholds give 1490 to 1732 single units; three variants put the multi-units inside the tolerance, the contamination criterion alone at 15% (331), the RPV criterion alone at 0.5% (309) and both criteria with a 20% contamination threshold (295). Other estimates of the contamination at 15% give 341 multi-units (0.5 ms censored period) and 478 (spikes inside the trial span only, T the whole span). On synthetic units the estimate is 0.163 for a true contamination of 0.15 and 0.233 for 0.20, so 85% of units at 0.15 are called multi-units. Multi-units range from 0 to 21 per session. The 22 "ephys others" sessions (742 units) and 14 opto efficiency recordings (414 units) are not among the 57.
deviations: The contamination estimate (Hill et al. 2011) uses a censored period of 0 and the mean rate over 1 s bins of the trial span holding a spike, with all of a unit's spikes in the count; the Methods give none of these.
Units recorded outside the target structure were excluded in the paper; the files do not say which these are, so all units are counted.

outcomes.statement: The population analyses of Figure 3 use 8 S1TJ, 9 M1TJ, 13 ALM and 5 S1BF sessions.
outcomes.notes: Counted from the session descriptions, the only place the files name the recorded area. The sessions come from 4, 4, 8 and 3 mice, and every one holds units and at least 13 selected standard trials per direction.

outcomes.statement: Regressions used the simultaneously recorded units of each session, 32 plus or minus 13 units (mean and SD).
outcomes.notes: Reading (b), all 57 recording sessions, gives 33.6 and 13.0 units, both within tolerance. Reading (a), the 35 Figure 3 sessions the claim refers to, gives a mean of 32.0 and an SD of 14.4, just outside 11.7 to 14.3. Single units alone give 26.4 and 13.2. Unit counts do not depend on a random seed, so the SD of reading (a) is 14.4 under every seed.
deviations: The reading that matches, all 57 sessions, is wider than the sessions the Results describe.

outcomes.statement: Figure 3a averages 2684 trials of standard and backtracking sequences.
outcomes.notes: The Methods' trial selection gives 2169 standard and 717 backtracking trials over the 35 sessions; together 2886 (reading a), within 10% of 2684. Standard trials alone are 2169. The count is a third of the candidates (at least 10) and does not depend on the search. The greedy search finds the best subset in 43 of 70 exhaustive checks on 16 candidates (at most 8.4% above the best mean distance); a swap search improves on it by at most 4.9% on the full sets, sharing a median of 97% of the trials.
deviations: The subset of most similar trials is found by a greedy search; the Methods do not say how it was searched.

outcomes.statement: Tongue length L is decoded from population activity best in S1TJ and M1TJ and poorly in ALM and S1BF (R2 0.56, 0.42, 0.11 and 0.04).
outcomes.notes: Mean R2 by area (S1TJ, M1TJ, ALM, S1BF) are each within the SD the figure prints, and S1TJ and M1TJ exceed ALM and S1BF. With folds that keep each trial in one fold, 0.551, 0.392, 0.087 and 0.016, same order. Decoding L with spikes shifted by 25 to 100 ms lowers R2 in S1TJ.
deviations: The inter-lick-interval standardisation of the Methods is not applied before the fits.

Fits use scikit-learn's elastic net path (l1 ratio 0.1, 30 penalties, standardised predictors, one-SE rule), not MATLAB's lasso; samples are assigned to folds at random, as MATLAB does by default. Random folds let the autocorrelation within a trial into the test folds; R2 values are higher than with folds that keep trials together, the orderings the same.
The fitting window is -0.5 to 0.5 s from the middle touch, read from the Methods' remark that 0.5 to 0.8 s of the decoding was new data; the paper does not state it.
The expected values were read from the figure image, as the text does not give them.

outcomes.statement: Tongue velocity L' is decoded best in S1TJ and M1TJ and poorly in ALM and S1BF (R2 0.35, 0.32, 0.07 and 0.01).
outcomes.notes: All four means within tolerance of 0.35, 0.32, 0.07 and 0.01, and the order holds with either fold scheme. L' is the derivative of L where the tongue is out.
deviations: As for fig3c-length.

outcomes.statement: Tongue angle theta is encoded comparably in S1TJ, M1TJ and ALM, but not in S1BF (R2 0.59, 0.57, 0.54 and 0.12).
outcomes.notes: All four means within tolerance of 0.59, 0.57, 0.54 and 0.12. S1TJ, M1TJ and ALM differ by 0.049 and S1BF is below each. With trial folds the spread is 0.059. theta is the angle of the tongue base-to-tip vector, used where L exceeds 1 mm.
deviations: As for fig3c-length. The sign of theta (left or right) cannot be fixed from the files; R2 does not depend on it.

outcomes.statement: Sequence identity I is encoded most strongly in ALM, then progressively less in M1TJ, S1TJ and S1BF (R2 0.67, 0.42, 0.23 and 0.14).
outcomes.notes: Means (S1TJ, M1TJ, ALM, S1BF) within tolerance of 0.23, 0.42, 0.67 and 0.14, in the order ALM > M1TJ > S1TJ > S1BF. With trial folds 0.188, 0.323, 0.657 and 0.049, same order.
deviations: As for fig3c-length.

outcomes.statement: Relative sequence time tau is encoded most strongly in ALM, then progressively less in M1TJ, S1TJ and S1BF (R2 0.60, 0.45, 0.17 and 0.08).
outcomes.notes: Means within tolerance of 0.17, 0.45, 0.60 and 0.08, in the stated order; with trial folds 0.145, 0.381, 0.601 and 0.063, same order.
deviations: As for fig3c-length. tau is the time from the middle touch without lick standardisation.

outcomes.statement: Any pair of the five behavioural variables (L, L', theta, I, tau) is uncorrelated.
outcomes.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding"; Extended Data Fig. 5b
outcomes.notes: Mean absolute correlations of the ten pairs range from 0.000 (I-tau, zero by the balanced design) to 0.118 (theta-I); the largest single-session value is 0.368 (L-theta).
deviations: The bound of 0.3 is a choice; the paper gives no threshold.

outcomes.statement: Across regions, the summed variance explained by the five coding axes reached about half that of the top five principal components.
outcomes.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding"; Extended Data Fig. 5e
outcomes.notes: The median ratio over 35 sessions is 0.454 (mean 0.490, IQR 0.387 to 0.544), inside 0.45 to 0.55 but close to its lower bound; per area medians are 0.433 to 0.476. One coding axis of 175 had all weights zero. With seeds 3, 11, 12 and 13 the median is 0.453 to 0.455, inside the range each time.
deviations: VE is computed on -0.5 to 0.8 s from the middle touch of the selected standard trials; the paper says "during sequence execution".

outcomes.statement: The five coding axes were largely orthogonal to each other.
outcomes.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding"; Extended Data Fig. 5f
outcomes.notes: Nine pairs have a mean absolute cosine of 0.114 to 0.225; L' and theta have 0.302, just above the bound of 0.3 the criterion fixed. Random directions in the same sessions give 0.154. With seeds 3, 11, 12 and 13, L' and theta give 0.302 to 0.320 and are the only pair at or above 0.3 each time.
deviations: The bound of 0.3 is a choice; the paper says "largely orthogonal".

outcomes.statement: After canonical correlation, ALM trajectories in the top three PCs correlate best with the theta, I, tau coding subspace (group 2), more than with L, L', theta (group 1) or all five variables with five PCs (group 3); in S1TJ and M1TJ the correlation is high only when the coding subspace includes L and L'.
outcomes.notes: Mean canonical correlation, groups 1, 2, 3; ALM 0.607, 0.900, 0.743; S1TJ 0.746, 0.589, 0.735; M1TJ 0.712, 0.662, 0.809. All five comparisons hold by exact sign-flip tests (ALM p = 0.0002 twice; S1TJ p = 0.023 and 0.008; M1TJ p = 0.020). The figure marks p < 0.001, which an exact paired permutation cannot reach with 8 or 9 sessions; the criterion uses 0.05.
deviations: Decoded variables come from the fits of fig3c-length, without lick standardisation.

outcomes.statement: ALM and M1TJ activity predicts whether the port backtracked from the initial missed lick on; S1TJ shows only an insignificant trend and S1BF no prediction.
outcomes.source: Figure 3f; Results, "Sequence branching signals in ALM, M1TJ"
outcomes.notes: Sessions with backtracking in both directions are 6 ALM (as in the paper), 9 M1TJ, 8 S1TJ and 5 S1BF. Mean accuracy in 0.2 to 0.4 s after the trigger is 0.740 (ALM), 0.734 (M1TJ), 0.595 (S1TJ) and 0.556 (S1BF), against null 95th percentiles of 0.526, 0.523, 0.516 and 0.515; before 0.1 s all are 0.487 to 0.519. ALM and M1TJ decode as stated; S1TJ and S1BF also exceed the null, which the paper reports as an insignificant trend and no prediction. In this window the classes differ in behaviour (1.854 against 0.113 missed licks, ed2e-missed-licks), which S1TJ and S1BF activity may reflect.
deviations: The paper's null and confidence intervals come from a hierarchical bootstrap; here the null is 20 label shuffles per session, averaged over sessions.
Trials are balanced across directions by random subsampling.
The PCA before the SVM is fitted on all trials of a session, without labels, before the cross-validation.

outcomes.statement: In the zigzag task, ALM population activity predicts the sequence identity (context) during subsequences with the same licking movements, across 6 sessions from 3 mice.
outcomes.notes: The 6 ZZ sessions come from 3 mice with 18 to 79 perfectly executed trials per sequence. Mean accuracies of the four comparisons are 0.785 to 0.858 against null 95th percentiles of 0.510 to 0.518; the lowest session is 0.651. By mouse 0.730 to 0.916. The files do not name the recorded area of the ZZ sessions; the paper says ALM.
deviations: Subsequences are aligned on touches (the seventh touch against the third or eleventh), not on the cross-correlogram of tongue angle, and the extra selection of trials closest to the median angle is not applied.
The null mean over bins uses every fifth 5 ms bin.

outcomes.statement: During the inter-trial interval, ALM populations encode the upcoming target position more strongly than the other regions.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 7e,f; Results, "ALM encodes upcoming sequences"
outcomes.notes: Mean R2 of the upcoming direction in the second before the cue is 0.271 (ALM), 0.097 (M1TJ), 0.075 (S1TJ) and 0.051 (S1BF); ALM is higher than each (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0025, 0.0007, 0.0014). With trial folds 0.159 against 0.022 to 0.034 (p = 0.023 to 0.047). Per ALM mouse 0.055 to 0.642. The 13 ALM sessions come from 8 mice; with one value per mouse, p = 0.012 to 0.024.
deviations: The paper's ITI window and trial set are not fully stated; the second before the cue of every standard trial is used.

outcomes.statement: None of the regions, including ALM, encoded time or distance to the trial start during the inter-trial interval.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 7h; Results, "ALM encodes upcoming sequences"
outcomes.notes: Mean R2 of the time to the cue is 0.008 to 0.034 by region (largest session 0.091, ALM), below 0.1 everywhere; 0.004 to 0.018 with trial folds.
deviations: The paper gives no test; the bound of 0.1 was fixed in the criterion.
Only the last second before the cue is used, where the paper may have used more of the interval.

outcomes.statement: Extended Data Fig. 4m counts 324 ALM, 233 M1TJ and 119 S1TJ neurons.
outcomes.notes: Single units with a maximal PETH rate of at least 10 spikes/s are 351 (ALM) and 223 (M1TJ), within 10% of 324 and 233, and 155 (S1TJ) against 119. With multi-units, 387, 261 and 251. At 5 and 15 spikes/s the single-unit counts are 387, 259, 164 and 321, 200, 140.
deviations: PETHs are not computed on standardised inter-lick intervals.
The unit classification is that of ephys-unit-counts, with its open choices.

outcomes.statement: More ALM neurons are tuned to sequence initiation than neurons of the other regions.
outcomes.source: Results, "Sequence tiling of single-unit responses"; Extended Data Fig. 4l
outcomes.notes: 91 of 351 active ALM neurons (25.9%) peak in the initiation window, against 48 of 223 in M1TJ (21.5%, Fisher one-sided p = 0.14) and 20 of 155 in S1TJ (12.9%, p = 0.0006). S1BF, outside the criterion, has 17 of 55 (30.9%), above ALM, against the statement's "the other regions". The windows differ in length (0.5, 2 and 1.2 s); per second of window ALM (0.519) is still above M1TJ (0.430) and S1TJ (0.258).
deviations: The paper shows histograms of peak times without a test; the test was chosen in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: S1TJ and M1TJ contain more neurons modulated by individual licks than ALM.
outcomes.source: Results, "Sequence tiling of single-unit responses"; Extended Data Fig. 4n,o
outcomes.notes: Median r_avg is 0.201 (S1TJ), 0.156 (M1TJ) and 0.093 (ALM); one-sided Mann-Whitney against ALM p = 2.5e-36 and 4.1e-24.
deviations: Without lick standardisation the rhythm of trial-averaged PETHs is blurred away from the middle touch, which lowers r in every region.

outcomes.statement: ALM contains neurons that fire during sequence execution and decrease firing abruptly when the tongue first contacts water, although licking continues.
outcomes.source: Results, "Reward modulation in ALM"; Extended Data Fig. 6a
outcomes.notes: Of 351 active ALM single units, 188 decrease and 92 increase from 0.5 s before to 0.5 s after the first water touch (p < 0.01 each; binomial p = 5e-09). S1TJ 50 against 51, S1BF 16 against 15, M1TJ 96 against 74 (p = 0.054).
deviations: The paper shows example neurons and decoded tau; the test over units was chosen in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: Expert mice completed the 7 port positions in about a second.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Extended Data Fig. 1h
outcomes.notes: Over 25438 standard trials of 17 mice (the paper's number), the median over mice from the first port-moving touch to the first touch at the last position is 0.992 s (0.890 to 1.138 s by mouse); from the cue, 1.324 s. Recording sessions alone give 1.004 s.
deviations: The paper does not list the sessions of Extended Data Fig. 1h; recording sessions (except zigzag) and the opto sessions' trials without light are used.

outcomes.statement: Over training, 15 mice reduced their sequence initiation time and increased their sequence speed.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 1l; Results, first section
outcomes.notes: 15 mice have learning files. Median over mice of the initiation time falls from 2.573 s (first 100 standard trials) to 0.291 s (last 100), Wilcoxon p = 0.00043, and the sequence speed rises from 4.902 to 6.038 positions/s, p = 0.0043; 14 of 15 mice improve in both. MX181003 does not; its file of 2018-10-02 was left out as a duplicate, so its other learning files may also be mislabelled. Without MX181003, 14 of 14 improve (p = 0.00012 each).

outcomes.statement: Mice reached proficiency in standard sequences after about 1500 trials of training.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Extended Data Fig. 1l-n
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) the median over mice of the trial at which sequence speed reaches 90% of its final value is 200 (150 and 250 at 80% and 95%); under reading (b), initiation time within 110% of final, 1100. Both are outside 1350 to 1650. One mouse (MX200101) reaches neither. The paper does not define proficiency, and the learning files may not start at the first day of training. Every mouse's first file holds standard sequences in both directions and almost nothing else (2 other trials in MX170903, 1 in MX180803 and 1 in MX181002), and in 3 of 15 mice (MX170903, MX180201, MX181003) the median initiation time of the first 100 standard trials is already under 1 s; if earlier training is missing, both counts are too low. In the median mouse the speed reaches 90% of its final value within 200 trials, so the result under reading (a) also reflects how proficiency was defined. MX200101 has no standard trials among its last 500 learning trials, so it has no final value.
deviations: Proficiency was defined in the criterion, as the paper gives no definition.

outcomes.statement: Backtracking analyses used 7458 standard and 2695 backtracking sequences from 47 sessions of the 9 mice trained on backtracking.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 2c,e legends; Methods, "Behavioural training"
outcomes.notes: Reading (c) gives 55 sessions of 9 mice with 10365 standard and 3839 backtracking trials; only the number of mice matches. Readings (a) and (b) give 74 and 59 sessions. A variant outside the criterion leaves out the 8 sessions whose touches are mostly a few ms long (5th percentile 3 to 7 ms, against 14 ms or more in the others), which fits the Methods' 8 sessions "where only touch onsets were correctly registered"; it gives 47 sessions, the paper's number, of 8 mice, with 8891 and 3207 trials. On these 47 sessions, removing the first and last trial and trials not finished within the video (the Methods' exclusions) leaves 8627 and 3104; both above tolerance. Adding initiation under 1 s, the Figure 3 trial selection and not an exclusion the Methods give for Extended Data Fig. 2, leaves 8058 and 2894, both within tolerance. This chain was built after seeing the results and does not decide the outcome; it has 8 mice where the paper has 9.
deviations: The paper's own trial exclusions (first and last trial, unfinished videos) are not applied in the readings of the criterion; they are shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: After the port backtracked, mice took on average 1 to 2 missed licks before relocating it.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Extended Data Fig. 2e
outcomes.notes: In 29 Figure 3 sessions with backtracking (8 mice), backtracking trials have a mean of 1.854 missed licks in the fourth interval, against 0.113 in standard trials (Mann-Whitney p printed as 0). By mouse 0.97 to 5.39. A touch tolerance of 0 or 25 ms in place of 12.5 ms gives the same mean on the same trials.
deviations: Sessions are the Figure 3 sessions with backtracking, not the paper's 47.

outcomes.statement: After the first lick that touched water, mice continued with about 5 consummatory licks.
outcomes.source: Results, "Reward modulation in ALM"; Extended Data Fig. 6b
outcomes.notes: After the first lick touching water, the bout continues for a median of 6 video licks (mean 6.38, 6864 trials), or 4 touches (mean 3.87); counting the first water lick, 7. None is within 4.5 to 5.5. The video ended during the bout in 88 trials, which are left out. By mouse, 4 to 10 video licks and 2 to 7 touches. Under (a) the most common count is 5 (20.2% of trials; 19.6% at 6, 12.8% at 4). With the bout threshold of (b) taken from video lick intervals (238 ms, against 243 ms from touches) the median is still 4 touches.
deviations: The paper does not say whether licks or touches are counted or where the bout ends; the bout rule (1.5 times the median interval) is the Methods' rule for lick bouts.

outcomes.statement: Expert mice usually initiated sequences from the correct side without exploring the other side.
outcomes.source: Results, "ALM encodes upcoming sequences"; Extended Data Fig. 7b
outcomes.notes: In all 11 mice of the Figure 3 sessions, 0.562 to 0.923 of standard trials start with no lick on the other side of the midline before the first touch (0.647 to 0.980 with a 5 degree margin); pooled 0.714. The paper shows 8 mice.
deviations: The side of the port is taken from the angle of the lick that made the first touch, as the files do not say which side each position is on.

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting S1TJ increased the across-trial variability of lick angle, SD(theta_shoot), without reducing the lateral reach |theta_shoot|, and did not shorten licks.
outcomes.notes: The 35 opto sessions at 4 mW (described "2s 5V") are 5 per mouse for 7 mice, one per region presumably, but no file names the inhibited region; trial tables mark only light times, and the opto1 and opto2 series give the LED drive. The 25 sessions at 2 mW are the same. Checked in all 74 opto files, in the trial columns (opto takes 0, 1, 2 or NaN, without a description), the session description (cut short in the files themselves), general (only experimenter, institution, lab and subject), acquisition (empty), stimulus (empty presentation and templates groups), and the attributes of the opto1 and opto2 series (unit "categorical", no description).

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting ALM/M1TJ reduced the ability to direct licks to the sides and decreased lick length; inhibiting M1B only slightly increased angle variability; inhibiting S1BF or S1Tr changed nothing.
outcomes.notes: As fig2b-s1tj-angle-variability; the inhibited region of each session is not stated.

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting ALM/M1TJ at sequence initiation strongly suppressed licking (licks largely absent in 4 of 7 mice), and less strongly at mid-sequence.
outcomes.notes: As fig2b-s1tj-angle-variability.

outcomes.statement: Inhibiting S1TJ or M1B at water consumption impaired the stopping of ongoing licking.
outcomes.notes: As fig2b-s1tj-angle-variability.

outcomes.statement: With half the illumination power (2 mW) the effects were consistent with, though weaker than, those at 4 mW, and the termination deficit of S1TJ and M1B inhibition was similarly strong.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 3l,m; Results, "Optogenetic inhibition screen"
outcomes.notes: The 25 sessions at 2 mW ("2s 2.5V", 5 mice) do not name the inhibited region either.

outcomes.statement: At 4 mW, light within 1 mm reduced the spike rate of putative pyramidal cells by 91%, at about 1.5 mm by 61% and at about 3 mm by 19%; FS neurons within 1 mm increased by 739%.
outcomes.notes: The 14 efficiency recordings (4 mice, 414 units) hold spike times and light trials, but no spike waveforms, which the paper uses to separate putative pyramidal and FS cells, and no distance of the fibre from the recording site. The distance is also missing from the metadata (metadata_insufficient).

outcomes.statement: Hearing loss with earplugs did not increase missed licks during sequences.
outcomes.notes: The 10 earplug sessions are two per mouse for 5 mice, as the Methods describe, but nothing in the files says which session had earplugs and which was the sham. Without the labels, the paper's test (paired one-tailed bootstrap of missed licks over mice) finds an effect under 4 of the 32 possible assignments, so the absence cannot be shown label-free. In all 5 mice the earlier session has the longer time to first touch (by 0.40 to 1.49 s), as the paper reports for earplugs; under that inferred assignment missed licks differ by +0.032 per trial (p = 0.36), no effect, as the claim says. The inferred labels do not decide the outcome.

outcomes.statement: Masking odours with an air flow did not change missed licks.
outcomes.notes: The 6 air sessions (6 mice) switch the air flow after the 100th trial, on first in two mice and off first in four; the files do not say which. Over the 15 possible choices of the two on-first mice, the paper's test finds an effect in one (smallest p = 0.018), so the absence cannot be shown label-free.

outcomes.statement: Numbing the tongue with lidocaine increased missed licks, so mice require tactile feedback from the tongue.
outcomes.notes: The 11 numbing sessions (6 mice, one with a single session) do not say which session was lidocaine and which saline. In all 5 mice with two sessions the earlier session has more missed licks in its first 30 min (0.99 to 2.74 against 0.23 to 1.07 per trial), significant in 4; the direction of the claim needs the labels.

outcomes.statement: The maximal force of a lick was on average about 4 mN.
outcomes.source: Methods, "Two-axis optical force sensors"; Extended Data Fig. 1f
outcomes.notes: The force sensor series (tubeH, tubeV) are in volts; the calibration to mN of Extended Data Fig. 1d is not in the files; their conversion is 1 and offset 0, and the paper gives no slope.

outcomes.statement: Clustering the PETHs of all neurons by NNMF was most consistent with 13 clusters.
outcomes.source: Methods, "PETH and NNMF clustering"; Extended Data Fig. 4j,k
outcomes.notes: The consistency measure needs cluster labels matched across bootstrap iterations, and the Methods do not say how; the paper's code could not be found.

findings.statement: The opto sessions do not name the inhibited region; 35 sessions at 4 mW and 25 at 2 mW, five per mouse, carry only the light times and LED drive. Figure 2 and Extended Data Fig. 3j-m cannot be tested.
The control sessions do not mark the condition; which earplug session had earplugs, which half of each air session had the air flow on, and which numbing session was lidocaine are not stated.

The recorded area and the kind of session are given only by the session description (the name of the lab's data folder); there is no electrodes table, unit location, depth or quality label, and the area of the zigzag (ZZ) and "ephys others" sessions is not given.
Spike waveforms are not included, so units cannot be classified as putative pyramidal or FS cells (Extended Data Fig. 3c-f), and the fibre distance of the efficiency recordings is not given.

1446 spike times in 35 files are duplicated within a unit, away from trial boundaries (median 2.9 s). The Methods say these Phy duplicates were removed before analysis; the deposited spike times keep them.

One training recording is deposited twice; the MX181003 learning file of 2018-10-02 15:30:57 repeats all 4028 touches of the MX181002 file with the same start time and then continues, so it is unclear which mouse it belongs to.
In the 574 learning files start_time and stop_time count from 0 while cue, touch, port and water times are on another clock (around 10^6 s), so trial intervals and events do not line up.
The seqId column of the learning files holds the text of an unconverted MATLAB categorical object, not a sequence identity.

Force sensor and lick port series are in volts without a calibration, tongue landmarks are in pixels without a scale (the Methods give 32 um per pixel), and every trial column is described as "no description".

The Methods leave out 8 sessions whose touch offsets were not registered; the files do not mark them. Eight sessions with backtracking have touches of a few ms (5th percentile 3 to 7 ms), and leaving them out gives the paper's 47 sessions.
The session description is cut short ("... se") in the files themselves, so the full name of the lab's data folder, the only place the area and kind of session are given, is lost.
The trial column opto (values 0, 1 and 2) and the opto1 and opto2 series (unit "categorical") have no description, and no file has optogenetics metadata (light source, site, power).
The paper says its MATLAB analysis code is available at GitHub but gives no address, and no repository was found under the authors' accounts.
