attempts.paper_title: Offline ensemble co-reactivation links memories across days
attempts.entry_title: Offline ensemble co-reactivation in the EEG/EMG experiment (Zaki et al. 2024)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Zaki et al. (2024) that can be tested on dandiset 000718, which holds two of the nine mice of the paper's calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment (one high-shock, one low-shock) with their encoding and recall sessions, the first offline recording after encoding, and cell registration for the high-shock mouse. It checks the deposited freezing against the paper's per-mouse values, compares freezing between the two mice, tests offline population bursts and their skew against shuffled activity and against movement, and compares overlap-neutral with overlap-aversive co-bursting in wake. The one-hour offline, behaviour-only, inhibitory tagging and no-shock experiments are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Zaki et al. (2024) from dandiset 000718

outcomes.statement: The two deposited mice are the mice of the same names in the paper's per-mouse source data, with the same shock group, and the freezing computed from the dandiset's freezing intervals agrees with the per-mouse freezing the paper reports for them.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 9b and 9c; source-data repository denisecailab/RetrospectiveMemoryLinkingData_2024
outcomes.notes: Both mice are matched by name (subject_id Ca_EEG2-1 and Ca_EEG3-4, the Mouse column of the source data), with the same shock amplitude in the files as the source data's group (1.5 and 0.25 mA). All four freezing values are within 10% under both readings; reading (a), given as measured, gives 64.09, 8.82, 17.40 and 15.06% against 63.87, 8.46, 16.90 and 14.60%, and reading (b) gives 63.45, 8.46, 16.91 and 14.61%. The recall session descriptions name the contexts (Recall1 shock, Recall2 novel, Recall3 neutral), as the source data assign them for Ca_EEG3-4. On which side a difference comes from, the dandiset's freezing intervals give the paper's per-mouse values to within 5% (reading a) and 1% (reading b), so the dandiset agrees with what the paper reports for these mice.
deviations: Only four per-mouse values can be compared, as the dandiset lacks the neutral and novel recall sessions of Ca_EEG2-1 and the other seven mice.

outcomes.statement: In the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment, high-shock mice froze more during aversive recall than low-shock mice (t7 = 8.99, p = 0.020).
outcomes.notes: Recall1 freezing is 64.09% for the high-shock mouse and 8.82% for the low-shock mouse (difference 55.27 percentage points). The 30 s bins differ by Mann-Whitney (U = 100, p = 0.00018); 15 s and 60 s bins give p = 8.9e-07 and 0.0079. The paper's t-test (t7 = 8.99, p = 0.020) over 5 and 4 mice cannot be run with one mouse per group, so its statistic is not tested. The bins are consecutive parts of one session per mouse and not independent, so the p-values overstate the evidence.
deviations: One mouse per group (the paper has 5 high-shock and 4 low-shock mice); the test is within sessions, over 30 s bins, chosen here.

outcomes.statement: During offline periods, hippocampal population bursts occur more often than expected from shuffled neuronal activity, so CA1 neurons fire in a more coordinated way than chance.
outcomes.source: Results, section "Neutral ensemble recruited into population bursts"; Extended Data Figure 3l and 3m
outcomes.notes: The analysis ran. Under the criterion's procedure (surrogates z-scored and thresholded at z = 2 as the data) the true burst rate is below the surrogate mean in all three offline recordings (5.30, 6.40 and 8.71 per min against 8.48 to 10.94; true over surrogate mean 0.63 to 0.80), which would be not reproduced. The paper's chance level for this test (source data for Extended Data Figure 3m, another cohort) is 3.38 to 4.39 surrogate bursts per min against 4.51 to 4.92 true, surrogate over true 0.72 to 0.96; this procedure gives 1.26 to 1.60, far from it, so the procedures differ and the claim is blocked as the protocol requires. The Methods do not say how bursts are counted in a surrogate. Variants disagree; merging events closer than 1 s leaves the true rate below the surrogates (4.40 to 7.31 against 6.56 to 8.52 per min), and thresholding surrogates at the true trace's own mean + 2 SD puts the true rate far above them (5.30 to 8.71 against at most 0.50 per min). At z = 2.5 the true rate is above the surrogate mean in 2 of 3 recordings and above the 95th percentile in none. On synthetic data with 6 coordinated events per minute, the criterion's test gives 5.6 true bursts per min against a surrogate mean of 34.98, and with independent cells 34.8 against 37.36, so it cannot detect coordination; the fixed-threshold variant separates the two (5.6 against 0.00, 34.8 against 38.37), but its chance level in the data (surrogate means at most 0.10 per min) is far below the paper's.
deviations: Run on the three 10 min offline recordings of the EEG/EMG experiment at 15 Hz; the paper shows the test for the one-hour recordings at 30 Hz of the single-experience cohort (Extended Data Figure 3), which is not deposited.
Burst events taken as maximal runs of frames above threshold, as the Methods do not define an event further.

outcomes.statement: The mean population activity during offline periods is more right-skewed than in shuffled data, showing brief burst-like activations that need coordinated activity of groups of neurons.
outcomes.notes: The population trace's skewness is 1.65, 1.34 and 1.72 in the three offline recordings, above all 1000 circular-shift surrogates in each (surrogate means 0.60, 0.40 and 0.37, 95th percentiles 0.72, 0.51 and 0.48). Both arms are lower than in the paper's source data for Extended Data Figure 3o (another cohort, 1 h at 30 Hz); the true skews are below the paper's lowest (1.76 to 3.65) and two of three surrogate means are below its lowest shuffled value (0.47 to 1.91), so the chance level is not shown to match the paper's. The outcome rests on the true skew exceeding every surrogate. On synthetic data the test separates coordinated activity (skew 8.54 against a surrogate 95th percentile of 0.94) from independent cells (0.98 against 1.09).
deviations: Run on the EEG/EMG experiment's three 10 min offline recordings; the paper shows the test for another cohort (Extended Data Figure 3o), which is not deposited.

outcomes.statement: Offline population bursts coincide with the mouse briefly slowing down about 1 s before the burst and resuming its movement about 1 to 2 s later.
outcomes.source: Figure 2d and 2e; Extended Data Figure 6e; Results, section "Co-reactivation occurs more during wake"
outcomes.notes: Telemetry movement in the second before a burst is not lower than 3 to 5 s before it in any of the three recordings under either reading of time zero (peak, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.76, 0.89, 0.39; onset, p = 0.88, 0.94, 0.41); 30 to 60% of bursts have lower movement before them. Movement 1 to 2 s after the peak is lower than in the second before it in two of three recordings (0.155 against 0.225, and 0.129 against 0.257). The telemetry activity signal is a coarse proxy whose relation to calcium activity is weak (movement decoded at r = 0.06 to 0.24 at zero shift; Spearman r with the population trace 0.07 to 0.32 in 1 s bins). The files describe it as motion of the probe relative to the receiver and a proxy for locomotion; its mean magnitude is 4 to 15 times higher in wake than in quiet wake epochs. The test is not calibrated, giving p = 0.016 at 300 random times in Ca_EEG2-1 (0.9999 and 0.92 in the others). The outcome says this proxy does not show the pause, and is weak evidence that the pause is absent.
deviations: Movement is the magnitude of the HD-X02 telemetry activity signal; the paper tracked locomotion with a webcam, whose video is not deposited.
Tested on the EEG/EMG experiment's offline recordings; the paper shows the effect for the single-experience cohort (Figure 2d and 2e) and the inhibitory tagging cohort (Extended Data Figure 6e).

outcomes.statement: After a strong (high-shock) aversive experience, during wake in the offline period the overlap ensemble co-bursts more with the neutral ensemble than with the aversive ensemble (t4 = 4.94, P = 0.016).
outcomes.notes: In Ca_EEG2-1's first offline recording after aversive encoding, under reading (a), wake and quiet wake together (all 87 bursts), OxN is below OxA (26.4 against 35.6% inclusive, 8.0 against 17.2% exclusive; 7 against 15 discordant bursts, McNemar p = 0.13). Reading (a) is the one the Methods imply. Their scoring (6 s epochs, two-state Gaussian mixture on EMG) applied to this mouse's log EMG RMS over the 12 h offline period puts 94.1% of quiet-wake frames and 98.5% of wake frames in wake (97.9% of quiet wake when fitted on the first 6 h), and all 87 bursts in wake. Under reading (b), wake alone, OxN exceeds OxA (32.0 against 28.0% of 25 bursts; 8.0 against 4.0%) on 2 against 1 discordant bursts (McNemar p = 1.0). Under the Methods' wake the order holds at thresholds 1.5 (34.9 against 41.1%) and 2.5 (21.7 against 30.0%), and no difference reaches p < 0.05. Outside bursts both are at most 1.02% of 0.5 s windows. The neutral, aversive and overlap ensembles each have more of their cells in bursts than the remaining cells (median differences 0.005 to 0.010, Wilcoxon p = 0.041 to 0.0003). The paper's statistic (t4 = 4.94, P = 0.016, across five mice) cannot be tested. The evidence against the paper is weak; one 10 min recording of 24 for one mouse of five, with ensemble traces z-scored within it, so levels are not comparable with the paper's source data for this mouse over all 24 recordings (10.37% OxN against 8.39% OxA in wake). Counted inclusively, co-participation here (26 to 36%) is 2.5 to 4 times those values; with the third ensemble excluded (8.0 and 17.2%) it is on their scale, with OxN the lower.
deviations: One high-shock mouse of five, and its first offline recording of 24 (10 min of 4 h).
The Methods z-score the ensemble traces over all 24 offline recordings concatenated; here only one is deposited, so they are z-scored within it.

The criterion fixed four readings (quiet wake in or out of wake; co-participation with or without the third ensemble) and would count the claim under any of them. After the first verification the outcome is judged on wake including quiet wake, as the Methods' own EMG scoring puts quiet wake in wake; under wake alone OxN exceeds OxA without a significant difference, which the criterion would have called partially reproduced.
The EMG feature of the Methods' scoring (log RMS per 6 s epoch) is chosen here, after the data were seen; the Methods do not name one. Without the log the mixture does not separate sleep from wake.
Bursts are assigned the sleep state of their peak frame, a choice made here.

outcomes.statement: Fear spreads from an aversive context to a neutral context experienced 2 days before (retrospective linking) but not to one experienced 2 days after (prospective), with no difference in aversive recall between the groups.
outcomes.notes: Behaviour-only experiment; its mice are not in the dandiset. The paper's source-data repository holds the per-mouse freezing plotted in Figure 1, but not the recordings they come from; these claims were not tested on figure values.

outcomes.statement: High-shock mice froze more than low-shock mice in the aversive context, and froze more in the neutral than in the novel context, while low-shock mice did not.
outcomes.notes: The one-hour imaging cohort of Figure 1d to 1f is not in the dandiset. Its EEG-cohort counterpart is tested in ed9b-aversive-freezing-high-vs-low.

outcomes.statement: In high-shock mice, aversive recall freezing correlates with the strength of retrospective memory linking (R2 = 0.45, P = 0.016), but not in low-shock mice.
outcomes.notes: Needs the one-hour imaging cohort's freezing in three contexts; not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Chemogenetic inhibition of the hippocampus in the 12 h after aversive encoding prevents retrospective memory linking and leaves the aversive memory intact.
outcomes.notes: The chemogenetic inhibition experiment is behaviour only and not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: A cocaine experience also drives retrospective memory linking to a neutral context experienced 2 days before.
outcomes.notes: The cocaine experiment is behaviour only and not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Cells active during aversive encoding are reactivated offline and preferentially during aversive recall.
outcomes.notes: The single-experience imaging cohort is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: During offline 2 the neutral ensemble is less active than the aversive and overlap ensembles in low-shock mice but no differently active in high-shock mice.
outcomes.notes: The one-hour offline cohort is not in the dandiset. The deposited high-shock offline recording gives one mouse of the EEG cohort, for which the paper does not report this analysis.

outcomes.statement: During offline 1 a greater percentage of the neutral ensemble participates in bursts than of the remaining ensemble, in both shock groups.
outcomes.notes: One-hour offline cohort not deposited. In the EEG cohort, the offline-day-1 recording of Ca_EEG3-4 is deposited without registration, and Ca_EEG2-1 has none.

outcomes.statement: During offline 2 the neutral ensemble preferentially participates in bursts relative to the remaining ensemble in high-shock mice (t7 = 4.88) but not in low-shock mice.
outcomes.notes: One-hour offline cohort not deposited. The notebook shows, as context only, that in Ca_EEG2-1's offline recording the neutral ensemble has more of its cells in bursts than the remaining cells (median difference 0.005, p = 0.041).

outcomes.statement: During burst periods the overlap ensemble participates independently in more bursts than the aversive and neutral ensembles, with no difference between shock groups.
outcomes.notes: One-hour offline cohort not deposited.

outcomes.statement: In the one-hour offline experiment, high-shock mice show more overlap-neutral than overlap-aversive co-bursting during bursts (t7 = 4.95), low-shock mice do not, and there is no such difference outside bursts.
outcomes.source: Figure 4e and 4f; Extended Data Figure 4k to 4o
outcomes.notes: One-hour offline cohort not deposited. The same analysis on the EEG cohort is tested in fig5c-wake-overlap-neutral-coburst.

outcomes.statement: The overlap ensemble is enriched in putative inhibitory neurons identified by chemotagging.
outcomes.notes: The inhibitory tagging (Gad2-cre, CNO) experiment is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Without a shock, overlap-neutral co-bursting does not exceed overlap-aversive co-bursting and no memory linking occurs.
outcomes.notes: The no-shock cohort is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Neural activity during neutral and aversive encoding is highly discriminable, with no difference between low- and high-shock mice.
outcomes.notes: The one-hour offline cohort of Extended Data Figure 7 is not in the dandiset. Ca_EEG2-1's neutral and aversive encoding are registered, but the paper does not report this analysis for the EEG cohort.

outcomes.statement: In the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment, high-shock mice froze more in the neutral than in the novel context (t4 = 4.02, p = 0.03), while low-shock mice did not.
outcomes.notes: The neutral and novel recall sessions of the only deposited high-shock mouse (Ca_EEG2-1) are not in the dandiset, and the paper's paired test needs several mice per group. The low-shock mouse's values (neutral 17.40%, novel 15.06%) are shown under source-data-link.

outcomes.statement: During NREM and REM sleep, overlap-neutral and overlap-aversive co-bursting do not differ in either shock group.
outcomes.notes: The three deposited offline recordings are each the first of 24 and hold only wake and quiet wake (no sws or rem interval); the later recordings, where sleep occurs, are not deposited.

outcomes.statement: In low-shock mice, overlap-neutral and overlap-aversive co-bursting during wake do not differ (t3 = 1.20, P = 0.32).
outcomes.notes: The only deposited low-shock mouse (Ca_EEG3-4) has no cell registration in the dandiset, so its ensembles cannot be formed. With one mouse the paper's paired t-test could not be run either.

outcomes.statement: Mice wearing a Miniscope sleep normally, the intermittent recording scheme captures the time spent in each state, and sleep structure is not changed by neutral or aversive encoding.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 9d to 9g and Extended Data Figure 10
outcomes.notes: Needs continuous EEG/EMG and sleep scores for nine mice and a control group. Only Ca_EEG2-1 has week telemetry, without sleep scores; the other mice and the scores are not deposited.

outcomes.statement: The overlap ensemble is reactivated more during neutral recall than during novel-context exposure in high-shock mice compared with low-shock mice (t12 = 3.2, P = 0.007).
outcomes.notes: One-hour offline cohort not deposited; in the EEG cohort Ca_EEG2-1 lacks neutral and novel recall and Ca_EEG3-4 lacks registration.

outcomes.statement: In high-shock mice the neutral encoding-to-recall population correlation is lower than in low-shock mice and lower than the aversive encoding-to-recall correlation.
outcomes.notes: As fig6a-overlap-reactivated-neutral-recall; the neutral recall session needed is missing for the registered mouse.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds two of the nine mice of the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment (Ca_EEG2-1, high shock; Ca_EEG3-4, low shock) and, of each offline period, only the first 10 min recording of the 24 the Methods describe. Ca_EEG2-1 has no offline-day-1 recording and no neutral or novel recall session. The mice of the one-hour imaging and offline experiments (Figures 1d to 1g, 2 to 4 and 6, Extended Data Figures 3, 4 and 7), the behaviour-only experiments, and the inhibitory tagging and no-shock experiments are not deposited. Twenty of the 26 claims cannot be tested for this reason.

Ca_EEG3-4 has no cell registration in the dandiset, so its ensembles cannot be formed. The Week file of Ca_EEG2-1 holds 19 registration tables for offline-day-2 recordings, of which only the first recording is deposited, and none for offline day 1.
The dandiset does not say why these two mice, and only the first offline recording of each period, were deposited, nor that the paper analysed more.

The session start times of the Ca_EEG2-1 behaviour sessions (NeutralExposure, FC, Recall1), and the Week epochs built from them, are about 1 h later than the telemetry and Miniscope clock. As deposited, OfflineDay2Session1 starts 47 min before the FC session it follows. The telemetry is absent (mouse out of its home cage) in windows that contain each of these epochs moved 1 h earlier, and the offline file's EEG sits exactly at its own epoch in the week recording.

The OnePhotonSeries timestamps of three files (Ca_EEG2-1 NeutralExposure, Ca_EEG3-4 OfflineDay1Session1, Ca_EEG3-4 Recall2) run at 16.7 ms and end at half the recording's length, while their frame counts fit 30 Hz over the full length given by the deconvolved timestamps.

The sleep states include `quiet wake`, which the paper neither uses nor maps to its wake, NREM and REM states, so it is not known which state the paper assigned these epochs to. The Methods' scoring, applied to the EMG of Ca_EEG2-1, puts 94% of them in wake. The three offline recordings hold no NREM (`sws`) or REM epochs.
The telemetry (EEG, EMG, activity) is sampled at 500 Hz in the offline files and the Week file; the Methods say the HD-X02 implants recorded at 100 Hz.

The session description of the offline recordings says that mouse behaviour and calcium were recorded for an hour with a webcam above the home cage. The deposited offline recordings last 10 min, hold telemetry and no video, and the Methods describe this experiment's offline recordings as 10 min in the telemetry home cage.

The fluorescence series carry placeholder descriptions ("description of deconvolved traces") and unit "n.a.", the FC session descriptions give the shock amplitude without a unit, and the Week file has an empty session description.

The analysis code repository the paper names (github.com/denisecailab/RetrospectiveMemoryLinkingAnalysis_2024) returns 404, so how bursts are counted, in the data and in shuffled surrogates, could not be checked; the surrogate burst rates here differ from the paper's chance level.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file. The attempt record was not among its materials, so it took its counts from the claims file and the notebook.

disagreements.reason: Not reproduced as the criterion is written, as the true burst rate is below the shuffled mean in all 3 recordings at z = 2. It did not count this as evidence against the paper, because z-scoring each surrogate again makes the test unable to detect coordination (in its synthetic data, 5.9 per min true against a null mean of 31.7 with planted coordination); the fixed-threshold variant behaves correctly but neither variant matches the paper's chance level. The criterion needs revising, or the claim should be treated as blocked with methods_underspecified. It asked for a positive control in the notebook.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the revised run, with its conclusions and summary, the helper module, the claims file, the README and the attempt record. It read the paper from Europe PMC (PMC11666460) and did not re-run the notebook. Other points it raised, not tied to one claim, were corrected in the text; cell 10 now gives the random-pair centroid distances as 169 to 196 px.

attempts.paper_title: Mapping the Neural Dynamics of Locomotion across the Drosophila Brain
attempts.entry_title: Brain-wide neural correlates of walking in Drosophila (Brezovec et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Brezovec, Berger, Druckmann and Clandinin (2022) on dandiset 000727, which holds whole-brain two-photon imaging and ball tracking of nine walking flies. It streams 12 planes of the authors' processed volumes in the Functional Drosophila Atlas for all flies, and tests the voxel correlations with forward and turning velocity, their symmetry, the principal components and the models that predict velocity from them, the demixing of velocity components, and the timing of neural activity relative to behaviour. Region-level results cannot be tested, as the dandiset has no neuropil labels.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Brezovec et al. (2022) from dandiset 000727

outcomes.statement: Nine flies were imaged for 30 minutes each at a volume rate of about 1.8 Hz, with 256 x 128 x 49 voxels of 2.6 x 2.6 x 5 um (about 1.6 million voxels per volume), giving 30,456 volumes in all, while the ball was tracked at 50 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 1A legend; STAR Methods, Two-Photon Imaging and Behavior Tracking
outcomes.notes: Nine flies, one session each, 3384 volumes per fly (30,456 in all) at 1.8797 Hz, 1,605,632 voxels of 2.61 x 2.61 x 5 um per raw volume, 30.0 minutes per session, FicTrac 90,000 frames at 50 Hz. The subject ids match the nine flies of the paper's code.

outcomes.statement: About 39% of the brain volume correlates with at least one of forward velocity, left and right angular velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread; Figure 2C; Figure S2
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), single voxels at p < 1e-4, gives 31.1% of the 191,119 in-brain voxels of the 12 planes, below 35.1 to 42.9% and above 19.5%. Reading (b), 6 x 6 blocks at p < 1e-8, gives 53.5% of the same in-brain voxels, above the band. With each fly's behaviour rolled in time, 0.0% pass under either reading. With behaviour sampled at the start of each volume in place of its midpoint, reading (a) gives 39.2%, so the value depends on the neural times, which the dandiset does not hold. The fraction is 0.0 to 7.5% in the outermost planes and 21.0 to 39.1% in the others. Within single flies 2.4 to 19.7% of voxels pass the threshold for 3384 points. Almost no voxel is negatively correlated (at most 0.01% per component).
deviations: Processed volumes in the Functional Drosophila Atlas, not the paper's mean brain; 12 of 91 planes.
Behaviour sampled at the midpoint of each volume, as the dandiset has no per-plane times; the paper used each plane's acquisition time.
Blocks of 6 x 6 voxels in place of the paper's Ward supervoxels for reading (b).
In-brain voxels are those inside the brain in all nine flies; with voxels inside in any fly the fraction is 20.3%.

outcomes.statement: Of the brain volume, about 15% correlates only with forward velocity, 20% with forward velocity and turning, and 4% only with turning; only about 10% of correlated voxels correlate with all three components, so 90% show a tuning preference.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread; Figure 2C
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), VF only 11.9% (expected 15), VF and turning 15.9% (20), turning only 3.2% (4), and 11.5% of correlated voxels correlated with all three (10). None is within its tolerance; the ranking holds and fewer than 20% of correlated voxels correlate with all three, so most show a tuning preference, as the statement says. Under reading (b) VF and turning is 39.4% and all three 32.2%. With behaviour at the start of each volume, reading (a) gives 11.6, 24.1, 3.5 and 25.7%.
deviations: As for fig2c-fraction-correlated.

outcomes.statement: Forward velocity correlations are mirror-symmetric across the midline, while left and right turning correlations are anti-symmetric, with more correlated voxels in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the turn.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread; Figure 2D, E
outcomes.notes: The VF map correlates with its mirror image at r = 0.823. The VL map correlates with the mirrored VR map at 0.672 and with its own mirror at 0.449. Voxels significant for VL are 2.38 times as many in image half A (x < 157) as in half B, and voxels significant for VR 3.2 times as many in half B. Per fly, the VF mirror correlation is 0.166 to 0.580, summed VL correlation is larger in half A in 8 of 9 flies, summed VR correlation larger in half B in 7 of 9, and both in 6 of 9; fly_098 and fly_105 have VR on the same side as VL and fly_099 has VL on the other side. Against the pooled maps of the other eight flies, no fly matches better mirrored for both VL and VR, as a left-right flip would give; 7 of 9 match better unflipped for both. fly_099's VL map matches the mirrored map slightly better (0.158 against 0.190), its VR map clearly does not (0.439 against 0.199). For fly_105 the check does not decide (VL 0.274 against 0.234, VR 0.212 against 0.214), so a flip of that fly is not excluded; it would lower the pooled asymmetry. The ipsilateral part of the statement is not tested; it holds if half A is the fly's left, which the dandiset does not state.
deviations: Mirror about the centre of the FDA's left-right axis (156.5), chosen from the symmetry of the brain mask; the 0.7 threshold for symmetry is a choice of this attempt, made after the prototype run had shown r = 0.82.

outcomes.statement: Behaviour-correlated voxels occupy most neuropils with non-uniform velocity preferences, strongly in the central complex, posterior slopes, vest, superior medial and lateral protocerebrum, higher visual, olfactory and auditory areas and the mushroom body; IPS, AOTU and VES hold turning-only voxels, MB and LAL forward-and-turning, SMP and SIP forward-only.
outcomes.source: Results, two paragraphs from "We next wondered"; Figure 2E-I
outcomes.notes: Needs the neuropil of each voxel. The dandiset holds no neuropil labels, atlas or mean brain for the FDA space of its processed volumes, nor the paper's own mean brain and its registered atlas. The FDA and its labels come from a later paper (BIFROST, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.8pk0p2nx1) that the preprint does not use, so they cannot be brought in under the protocol. Dryad holds no deposit of this paper's data.

outcomes.statement: Within neuropils, voxels of different velocity tuning are spatially organized, for example a forward and ipsilateral-turning column in PLP, left and right compartments in IPS, bands in LO, a dorsal-ventral split in LH, layers in FB, alternating turning in PB, glomeruli in NO and medial and lateral compartments in LAL.
outcomes.source: Results, Distinct topographic maps; Figure 3; Figure S3
outcomes.notes: Needs neuropil boundaries; see fig2e-region-fractions.

outcomes.statement: The first principal components of brain-wide activity are structured by behaviour; PC1 is low when the fly is stopped and high otherwise, PC2 increases with forward velocity and not with angular velocity, and PC3 carries the sign of angular velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive; Figure 4B-D
outcomes.notes: All three parts hold under both readings of the threshold. Reading (a); PC1's below-threshold correlation with VF is 0.202 against 0.065 (PC2) and -0.045 (PC3); above the threshold PC2 has the largest correlation with VF (0.272, PC1 0.162, PC3 0.086) and 0.091 and 0.087 with VL and VR; PC3's above-threshold correlations are 0.114 with VL and -0.259 with VR (p = 3.5e-14 and 5.6e-72). Within each fly over all time points, PC1 correlates positively with VF (0.22 to 0.57) and PC3 more with VL than VR, in 9 of 9 flies. PC1 explains 2.22% of block variance.
deviations: PCA of 5363 blocks from 12 planes, not of 98,000 supervoxels from 49 planes.

outcomes.statement: Linear models on the principal components predict forward, left and right velocity on held-out data with average R2 of about 0.3 using 100 PCs, performance improving over the first 100 PCs before declining.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive; Figure 4F, G
outcomes.notes: With 100 superfly PCs the median R2 over flies is 0.155 (VF), 0.196 (VL) and 0.212 (VR); the means are 0.038, 0.155 and 0.178. None is within 0.27 to 0.33; all medians are at least 0.15. Mean R2 rises to 100 PCs and declines after for each component, as stated. Three flies have negative VF R2 (-0.307, -0.306, -0.503). Variants; interleaved folds give medians 0.318, 0.252 and 0.271; alpha chosen within the training folds 0.134, 0.180, 0.212; each fly's own PCs 0.151, 0.210, 0.217. With behaviour rolled in time R2 is at most -0.002. With interleaved folds two of the three medians fall in the band (VF 0.318, VR 0.271; VL 0.252), so the folds, which the paper does not state, account for much of the gap; the outcome would stay partial.
deviations: Five contiguous folds within each fly, a choice; the code does not show its folds.
Alpha is chosen by the best held-out score, as the code does, which selects on the test folds.
The 1000 and 2000 PC models were not run (at most 500 PCs).
PCs of 5363 blocks from 12 planes.

outcomes.statement: Flies that moved less along a velocity component were poorly predicted (R2 near 0), while flies that explored it more were well predicted, with R2 up to 0.6.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive; Figure 4H
outcomes.notes: The Spearman correlation of a fly's mean amount of a component with its R2 is positive for all three components (VF 0.017, VL 0.383, VR 0.683, p = 0.042 for VR only); the pooled within-component rank correlation is 0.361 with p = 0.064. The largest R2 is 0.534 (fly_094, VF), just below 0.54 to 0.66, and the smallest -0.503. Partially reproduced under the clause that the correlation is positive for at least two components.
deviations: Rests on the R2 of fig4fg-ridge-r2, with its contiguous folds.

outcomes.statement: The model weights given to each PC are stereotyped across flies; PC1 is used for all components, PC2 mainly for forward velocity, and PC3 for left and right turning with opposite signs.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive; Figure 4I
outcomes.notes: Median correlation of the weights on PCs 1 to 20 between pairs of flies is 0.646 (VF), 0.732 (VL) and 0.761 (VR). PC3's weight is positive for VL and negative for VR in 9 of 9 flies, PC2's weight is largest for VF in 7 of 9, and PC1's weights have one sign for all three components in 9 of 9. With each fly's behaviour rolled in time (20 rolls), the median pair correlation is at most 0.151, PC3 has opposite signs in 3 to 8 of 9 flies and PC1 one sign in 0 to 6 of 9. Part (iv) follows in part from PC1's orientation, signed to correlate positively with VF, with which it also correlates positively with VL and VR (0.222 and 0.188).
deviations: Weights from a ridge fit to all of each fly's time points at the alpha chosen in fig4fg-ridge-r2, with each component scaled to unit s.d.

outcomes.statement: Demixing with linear models shows that forward velocity is uniquely encoded by a spatially organized subset of voxels, while locomotor state (walking or stopped) is not uniquely encoded anywhere, although the single-variable maps of forward velocity and locomotor state are very similar.
outcomes.source: Results, Demixing the unique contribution; Figure 5A
outcomes.notes: At the 0.01 threshold, 5 blocks (0.09%) encode walking state uniquely and 40 (0.75%) encode VF uniquely, 8 times as many, but fewer than the 5% the criterion requires. Unique contributions are small everywhere (largest 0.032 for VF, 0.012 for walking state) and the full model's median held-out R2 is 0.0019. The single-variable maps of VF and walking state correlate at 0.882 over blocks, as the statement says. At a threshold of 0.005 walking state is unique in 1.88% of blocks and VF in 2.24%; with the walking state the code intended, in 0.97% and 0.91%, so the VF advantage depends on the 0.01 threshold, which lies far above the median full-model R2, and on the definition of walking state. Within single flies walking state is unique in up to 8.35% of blocks (fly_094).
deviations: Ridge alpha 1 on behaviour scaled to unit s.d., folds as fifths of every fly, and the 0.01 threshold are choices; the Methods give none of them.
Walking state as the code computes it, which uses forward velocity alone.
Blocks in place of supervoxels.

outcomes.statement: The functional regions defined by the unique contributions of forward, left and right velocity are all correlated with velocity when the fly is below the movement threshold, a widespread increase in activity at the initiation of movement, while above the threshold each region correlates most with its own velocity component.
outcomes.source: Results, Demixing the unique contribution; Figure 5B, C; Figure S5B
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b) of the threshold all nine below-threshold correlations of the forward, left and right regions (40, 4 and 8 blocks) with the three components are positive with p < 0.05 (0.013 to 0.221), and above the threshold each region correlates most with its own component (0.377, 0.170, 0.266). Under reading (a) the left region with VR is -0.008 (p = 0.2), so only reading (b) satisfies the criterion. The Pearson p-values treat time points as independent; against 200 rolls of each fly's behaviour in time, which keep the autocorrelation, all nine are above chance under reading (b), the weakest (left region with VR, r = 0.013) with p = 0.025 against a null 95th percentile of 0.010. The left region holds only 4 blocks.
deviations: Regions are the few blocks with a unique contribution of at least 0.01 in fig5a-unique-variance.
The threshold readings are two interpretations of the 0.75 s.d. of Figure 4E.

outcomes.statement: When the fly turns, neural activity increases in specific regions of the ipsilateral hemisphere and decreases in the same regions of the contralateral hemisphere.
outcomes.source: Results, Demixing the unique contribution; Figure 5F
outcomes.notes: Turning raises activity mostly on one side, opposite for the two directions (82% of the top 10% of blocks in half A for left turns, 25% for right turns), but the mirror blocks rise as well; their median change against slow walking is +0.0064 for left turns and +0.0022 for right turns, and 36% and 42% of them fall. The same holds with turning thresholds of 50 and 150 deg/s, and in 8 of 9 flies for left turns and 9 of 9 for right turns. With the change predicted by the demixing model of fig5a-unique-variance, as the paper derives Figure 5F, the mirror blocks rise as well (medians 0.0254 and 0.0111; 6.5% and 18.8% fall), as do the model's VL and VR coefficients of the mirror blocks (median 0.0064). The ipsilateral increase holds; the contralateral decrease does not.
deviations: The bounds for slow walking (1 to 3 mm/s, below 30 deg/s) and turning (beyond 100 deg/s) are choices; the paper does not state its own.
Neural activity and behaviour at the same volume time, without a lag.
The main test compares mean activity in turns and slow walking; the paper uses the demixing model, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The time of peak cross-correlation between supervoxel activity and forward velocity ranges from about 300 ms before the change in behaviour, the earliest, to more than 1 s after it.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior; Figure 6A-E
outcomes.notes: Reading (b); the 99th percentile of VF lead over the 2145 top blocks is 0.32 s, within 0.27 to 0.33 s, and the 1st percentile a lag of 1.23 s. Reading (a) gives an earliest lead of 0.44 s (outside tolerance) and a latest lag of 1.44 s. VL and VR give 99th percentiles of 0.30 and 0.22 s and 1st percentiles of lags of 1.24 and 1.22 s. With volume-start times the VF 99th percentile is 0.58 s. The median VF lead changes steadily with FDA plane from 0.36 s (plane 17) to -0.30 s (plane 80), a spread of 0.66 s against a volume period of 0.532 s, the pattern unknown plane acquisition times would produce; the dandiset gives neither the times nor the order of the planes. With each plane's median removed the 99th percentile is 0.50 s and the 1st -1.02 s, so the match within 0.03 s is not robust to the neural times; the lag of more than 1 s holds in both (1st percentile at least 0.84 s of lag in every plane from 38 to 80, more than 1 s in planes 59 to 73). Only the lag of more than 1 s is robust; the earliest lead cannot be tested with the timing the dandiset gives, and the outcome follows the criterion fixed in advance. Fitted per fly, the 99th percentile is 0.36 to 4.55 s.
deviations: Neural times at the volume midpoint, an error of up to 0.27 s per block.
Notch filter Q = 2 is a choice; the code's notch coefficients are not in the repository.
Top 40% by peak value of the deconvolved filter.

outcomes.statement: Supervoxels whose peak correlation lags behaviour have broader temporal kernels, while those that anticipate behaviour have narrow kernels.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior; Figure 6H
outcomes.notes: Over the 2145 top VF blocks, lag and FWHM correlate at r = 0.672 (p = 2.2e-281, Spearman 0.703); mean FWHM is 1.38 s for blocks leading by up to 0.5 s and 2.62 s for blocks lagging by more than 1 s. VL and VR give r = 0.442 and 0.449; volume-start times 0.673. The plane means of lag and FWHM correlate at 0.979 over 10 planes, so plane accounts for part of the relation; with plane means removed r = 0.623 (p = 6.3e-231), and within single planes r is positive in all 10 planes with at least 10 blocks (0.222 to 0.751), with p < 0.05 in 8.
deviations: As for fig6-peak-time-range; FWHM measured from 0, around the peak.

outcomes.statement: Across nearly all brain regions, the peak correlation with angular velocity comes first in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the turn, then in the contralateral one.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship, paragraph on angular velocity; Figure 6F, G
outcomes.notes: For VL, over 868 mirror pairs, the block in half A leads its partner by a median 0.16 s and is earlier in 67% of pairs; for VR, over 849 pairs, the block in half B leads by 0.14 s and is earlier in 72%; both Wilcoxon p-values print as 0. The median difference is 0.26 to 0.33 s in planes 17 to 38 for VL and 0.19 to 0.29 s in planes 17 to 59 for VR, and -0.03 to 0.03 s in planes 73 and 80. Both blocks of a pair lie in one FDA plane; whether the two halves of a plane were acquired at the same time is not known.
deviations: The ipsilateral half is the image half with more significant correlations for that turn, from fig2-symmetry, since the dandiset does not say which half is left.

outcomes.statement: Peak correlations follow a sequence across regions; for forward velocity the antennal lobe and lateral horn first, then mushroom body, GNG and saddle, the central complex spanning onset, and the optic lobes lagging by up to more than a second; for angular velocity IPS, GOR and VES lead and the central complex and optic lobes lag.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior; Figure 6E-G
outcomes.notes: Needs the neuropil of each supervoxel; see fig2e-region-fractions. The timing would also need the per-plane acquisition times and the paper's z-depth maps, which are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Within brain regions, peak correlation times form spatial gradients, for example a dorsal before ventral order in LH for forward velocity and ipsilateral before contralateral order in LAL, MB-ML and PLP for angular velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Individual brain regions display spatiotemporally structured patterns; Figure 7; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: Needs neuropil boundaries (see fig2e-region-fractions) and per-plane acquisition times, neither of which is in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Correlations computed from the tdTomato structural channel show no behaviour-related signal, so motion artefacts are undetectably small.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds the tdTomato channel only raw, without motion correction or registration. Repeating the paper's per-volume ANTs SyN motion correction for 30,456 volumes, and the warps to a common space, is also out of reach here (not_runnable). A check on the raw, uncorrected channels (raw planes 18 and 30, high-pass filtered as the code does, within each fly) does not decide the outcome; the median share of voxels correlated with VF, VL or VR at p < 1e-4 is 0.23% for tdTomato and 0.60% for GCaMP6f, tdTomato exceeds GCaMP6f in 5 of 18 fly-planes, and it reaches 3.53% in fly_089, against 0.83% for GCaMP6f.

outcomes.statement: Behaviour prediction peaks at 2000 supervoxels per plane, among 1 to 10,000.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Agglomerative Clustering Supervoxel Creation; Figure S4A
outcomes.notes: Needs Ward clustering of every plane of the nine flies pooled at seven cluster numbers, so every voxel of all 91 planes. The 12 planes streamed here are 22.1 GB compressed and took 306 s in the latest run (214 s in the run before), including about 40 s for metadata; all 91 planes are several times that, which leaves no room within the 30 minute limit for the clustering itself. The files total 610 GB. A partial sweep on the 12 streamed planes was not attempted. It would need each plane's voxel time series held in memory (about 27,000 in-brain voxels x 30,456 points, some 3 GB per plane) for Ward clustering at seven sizes, followed by the PCA and ridge models at each size, while the streaming here keeps only block means and per-voxel sums.

findings.statement: The processed volumes are registered into the Functional Drosophila Atlas, but the dandiset holds no neuropil labels, atlas or template for that space, nor the paper's own mean brain and registered atlas. None of the paper's region-level results (Figures 2E to I, 3, 6E to G, 7) can be tested.

The processed series is in the Functional Drosophila Atlas, a space from a later paper of the lab, while the preprint analyses its data in its own mean brain. The dandiset does not say how the FDA series relates to the preprint's analysis space or which preprocessing it shares.

The per-plane acquisition times of the Bruker recordings are not in the files, which give only a volume rate. The paper aligns behaviour to each plane's time. Sampling behaviour at the start in place of the middle of each volume changes the correlated share of the brain from 31.1% to 39.2% and the 99th percentile of forward-velocity lead from 0.32 to 0.58 s.
The supervoxel labels, the z-depth maps used to give each supervoxel its acquisition time, and the motion-corrected tdTomato channel used as the paper's motion control are not deposited.
The processed series has grid spacing 1, 1, 1 in unit "unknown", so its voxel size is not given, and nothing states which half of the volume is the fly's left.

Imaging and FicTrac both start at 0 s; the conversion code set FicTrac timestamps to a uniform 50 Hz from 0 because synchronisation data were missing, and the dandiset does not say so. The data are consistent with a shared start (brain-wide activity follows walking speed by 0.4 to 0.8 s in every fly), to within a few hundred milliseconds.

Every FicTrac SpatialSeries has unit "meters" and conversion 0.0045 (the ball radius), while most hold angles in radians, as their descriptions say (heading, orientations, positions in radians, speed in radians per frame). SpatialSeriesRotationDeltaError, described as an error in radians, has medians of 6067 to 10,435.

The paper's code computes the walking state with np.sqrt(a, b), where b is taken as the output array, so the state reduces to absolute forward velocity over its s.d. above 0.2; the line was written to combine forward and rotational velocity. The two versions mark 47.2% and 57.3% of time points as walking.

The Methods cite Figure 3F and 3G for the PCA model sweep and the per-fly PCs, which are in Figure 4F and 4G. The Results describe Figure 3G as the Nodulus, while the Figure 3 legend calls panel G the Ellipsoid Body.

The preprint says the microscopy and behavioural data were deposited at Dryad and the code at GitHub, with DOIs in a key resources table that the preprint does not include. No Dryad record of these data was found, and the dandiset links neither the analysis code nor Dryad. The analysis code was found as ClandininLab/brezovec_volition_2023, whose README gives a different title.

attempts.paper_title: Neural activity during a simple reaching task in macaques is counter to gating and rebound in basal ganglia-thalamic communication
attempts.entry_title: GPi and VLa activity during reaching in macaques (Schwab et al. 2020)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Schwab, Kase, Zimnik, Rosenbaum, Codianni, Rubin and Turner (2020) on the pre-MPTP recordings of dandiset 000947, single units from the internal globus pallidus and the ventrolateral anterior thalamus of two monkeys performing a reaching task. It compares rates, spike widths, peri-movement responses and their latencies, spike and rate correlations of simultaneously recorded pairs, and the effect of GPi bursts and pauses on VLa activity, and links the dandiset's units to the paper's own unit list.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Schwab et al. (2020) from dandiset 000947

outcomes.statement: The units the paper analysed can be found in the dandiset, and the dandiset's spike times and trials reproduce the per-unit peri-movement activity the paper's code stored.
outcomes.source: Data Availability; Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnvxm, Gaia_Analy.mat and Isis_Analy.mat
outcomes.notes: Records are matched by file, channel id and sort letter. 364 of the 394 records the paper's code keeps (92.4%) are found in every file they span (Isis GPi 104 of 104, Gaia GPi 95 of 105, Gaia VLa 60 of 66, Isis VLa 105 of 119). For 724 matched unit-directions the SDF from the dandiset correlates with the stored SDF at a median r of 0.9992, above 0.9 for 94.6%. Valid trial counts equal the paper's for 62.6%. Detection agrees on the presence of an increase for 90.9% and of a decrease for 80.7% of unit-directions. 25 matched units the paper calls VLa are labelled "Thalamus" in the dandiset, and 97 records span 2 to 5 files. On the side of the outside data, the paper's list gives 209 GPi and 185 VLa units, as Table 1 does.
deviations: Trial exclusion follows the Methods (6 median absolute differences from the mean); the paper's stored trial counts differ for 37% of unit-directions, by a median of 0.

outcomes.statement: 209 single units met the criteria to be included as GPi neurons (105 in NHP G, 104 in NHP I) and 185 as VLa neurons (66 and 119).
outcomes.notes: The dandiset rule gives 268 GPi units (Gaia 137, Isis 131) and 279 VLa units (78 and 201), against 209 and 185 (218 in the text). Counting the same channel and sort letter on one day once gives 132 and 186; the paper's records found in the dandiset are 199 and 165. That merge joins some units the paper kept apart (47 of the 117 merged units spanning several files hold more than one of the paper's records). 518 of the 547 units are in files the paper used. Taking the rate over the length of the raw recording instead of the span of the spike train would leave out 2 more GPi units. The dandiset holds more units than the paper analysed and does not say which were kept or which units in consecutive files are one neuron.
deviations: Units are selected by the dandiset's location labels and the Methods' rate and trial criteria; the paper's anatomical criteria (within 0.5 mm of an M1-responsive site, the VLa border) cannot be applied from the files.
Each file's unit is counted once; the paper pools a neuron recorded over consecutive files.

outcomes.statement: The resting firing rate of GPi neurons (mean 70.1 spikes/s) is significantly higher than that of VLa neurons (13.5 spikes/s), and the rates are consistent between the two animals.
outcomes.notes: Mean rest rate over unit-directions 75.65 spikes/s in GPi (531) and 12.78 in VLa (552), GPi higher with rank sum p = 1.2e-171. The animals differ slightly in GPi (73.17 and 78.25, p = 0.041), where the paper reports no difference; not in VLa (p = 0.53). With one record per presumed neuron the animals do not differ in GPi (74.23 and 74.21, p = 0.69). With the paper's records 64.26 and 13.53, with one record per presumed neuron 74.22 and 12.77.
deviations: Unit selection by the dandiset rule (see table1-unit-counts).

outcomes.statement: Action potentials of GPi neurons are shorter than those of VLa neurons (trough to peak 0.24 against 0.50 ms; rank sum p = 1e-33).
outcomes.notes: Mean trough-to-peak width 0.247 ms in GPi and 0.509 ms in VLa, 532 of 547 units measured, rank sum p = 2.9e-37. One width is 0 and 9 reach the end of the 1.2 ms window; without them the means are 0.249 and 0.499 ms (p = 1.9e-35). No file gives one channel id to two electrodes, so each unit's channel names one electrode.
deviations: Widths come from the dandiset's 200 Hz high-pass filtered traces (the paper filtered at 300 Hz) and from the spikes in one stored chunk (about 3.2 s, median 273 spikes) per file and series.

outcomes.statement: The firing rate of most units ramps during the start-position hold period (97% of GPi and 98% of VLa units with a significant linear trend); slopes are distributed symmetrically around zero, without a difference between GPi and VLa (rank sum p = 0.29).
outcomes.notes: 98.5% of GPi and 98.6% of VLa units have a significant control-period slope (97.0% and 97.5% at alpha 0.01), and 49.9% of significant slopes are positive. GPi and VLa slopes differ (mean -0.598 against 0.233 spikes/s2, rank sum p = 0.042), where the paper finds no difference (p = 0.29); they also differ with one record per presumed neuron (p = 0.013) and with one mean slope per presumed neuron (p = 0.033). With the paper's records the fractions are 99.5% and 98.8% and the slopes do not differ (p = 0.187), which would meet the criterion, so the outcome depends on the selection of units. With every trial aligned to a random time, the same slope test finds a significant slope in 98.4% of GPi and 99.0% of VLa units, so the fractions do not show ramps beyond what noise in a smoothed function gives; the paper's code uses the same test.
deviations: The criterion did not define a partial outcome; the outcome is partial because the first part (ramps are common) holds and the second (no difference between areas) does not.

outcomes.statement: Nearly all units change their discharge around movement for at least one direction (GPi 99%, 206 of 209; VLa 88.1%, 163 of 185 in Table 1, 94% in the text).
outcomes.notes: 264 of 268 GPi (98.5%) and 272 of 279 VLa units (97.5%) respond in at least one direction. VLa matches the text's 94% but not Table 1's 88.1%; the criterion accepts either reading. With alpha 0.0001 the fractions with an increase alone are 81.0% and 77.4%. With every trial aligned to a random time 62.3% of GPi and 70.8% of VLa units are responsive, so the data are well above chance; with one record per presumed neuron the fractions are 100.0% and 98.4%.
deviations: The paper gives 88.1% (Table 1) and 94% (text) for VLa; both readings were listed and only the text's matches.

outcomes.statement: Monophasic increases are the most common form of response in both GPi and VLa (48.7% and 65.3% of responses), and increases make up most detected changes (61.5% and 68.8%, biphasic responses counted twice), more than decreases (chi-squared p = 1.2e-17).
outcomes.notes: Monophasic increase is the most common form in GPi (46.9%) and VLa (50.9%), and increases are 58.8% and 60.2% of changes (746 of 1254 overall, binomial p = 1.9e-11). The GPi values are within tolerance; the VLa values are below 65.3% and 68.8% by more than 10%, also with the paper's records (54.1% and 61.4%), with one record per presumed neuron (50.1% and 60.3%) and at alpha 0.0001 (51.9% and 60.1%). With random alignment the detector finds a decrease in 25.2% (GPi) and 33.7% (VLa) of unit-directions and an increase in 14.8% and 16.2%, so chance detections add mostly decreases.
deviations: Detrending of the control period and the ISI function are implemented here from the Methods; the paper's own implementation of these steps is not in its deposit.

outcomes.statement: Monophasic changes are more common in VLa than in GPi (88.9% against 66.7% of responses; chi-squared p = 2.8e-12), and polyphasic responses more common in GPi.
outcomes.notes: Monophasic responses are 71.0% in GPi and 76.7% in VLa, chi-squared p = 0.051, and VLa is outside tolerance. With the paper's records 69.0% and 81.2% (p = 0.00036), both within tolerance, so the outcome depends on the selection of units. With one record per presumed neuron 62.6% and 74.5% (p = 0.0023), VLa outside tolerance.
deviations: Unit selection by the dandiset rule (see table1-unit-counts).

outcomes.statement: The mean integrated change in firing over the peri-movement epoch is positive in both GPi and VLa (3.89 and 1.75 spikes), significantly different from zero.
outcomes.notes: The mean integrated change is positive in GPi (3.07 spikes, signed rank p = 1.1e-10) and VLa (1.50 spikes, p = 3.7e-18), both more than 10% below 3.89 and 1.75. With the paper's records 3.42 and 1.97, with one record per presumed neuron 2.13 and 1.34.
deviations: Table 1 gives the unit as spikes x 10^3; the code's computation gives spikes, the reading used.

outcomes.statement: Peri-movement changes begin later in GPi than in VLa (median onsets -47 and -90 ms; rank sum p = 2.4e-5).
outcomes.notes: Median onsets of all changes are -48 ms in GPi (641) and -67 ms in VLa (613); GPi is later by 19 ms without significance (rank sum p = 0.079, one-sided p = 0.04), and the VLa median is outside tolerance. In Gaia the medians are equal (-48.5 and -48 ms). With one record per presumed neuron -73 and -72 ms (p = 0.95), with one value per presumed neuron -47 and -53 ms (p = 0.44). With the paper's records -49 and -85 ms (p = 0.004), which meets the criterion, so the outcome depends on the selection of units. At alpha 0.0001 -42.5 and -63 ms (p = 0.052).
deviations: Unit selection by the dandiset rule (see table1-unit-counts).

outcomes.statement: GPi decreases lag behind VLa increases (median onsets -27 and -88 ms; rank sum p = 4.9e-4), against the gating prediction.
outcomes.notes: GPi decreases begin at a median of -29.5 ms (264) and VLa increases at -84 ms (369), rank sum p = 0.00021. The GPi median is 0.2 ms inside its tolerance (-29.7 to -24.3 ms). Gaia 0 against -95 ms (p = 0.0014), Isis -44 against -81 ms (p = 0.055). The lag also holds with the paper's records (-36 against -85 ms, p = 0.00069), with one record per presumed neuron (-46.5 against -92 ms, p = 0.011), with one value per presumed neuron (-1.5 against -71.2 ms, p = 0.00074) and at alpha 0.0001 (-30 against -81.5 ms, p = 0.00054), but in all four the GPi median is outside its tolerance. With the paper's records the outcome would be partially reproduced, so it depends on the selection of units, and the match of the medians is fragile.

outcomes.statement: VLa decreases precede GPi increases (median onsets -108 and -62 ms; rank sum p = 0.01).
outcomes.notes: VLa decreases begin at a median of -19 ms (244) and GPi increases at -69 ms (377); VLa does not lead (rank sum p = 0.17). In Gaia VLa decreases come later (12.5 against -75 ms, p = 0.0028). With the paper's records VLa leads by 13 ms without significance (-86 against -73 ms, p = 0.2). The paper itself gives -62 ms for GPi increases here and -76 ms in Table 1. With one record per presumed neuron VLa decreases come later (-8 against -92 ms, p = 0.0082), and with one value per presumed neuron too (20.5 against -45 ms, p = 0.021). With random alignment the detector finds a decrease in 33.7% of VLa unit-directions (44.2% in the data), with a median onset of -8 ms, so many VLa decreases here may be chance detections, which would pull their median late. At alpha 0.0001 the medians are -21.5 (VLa) and -57.5 ms (GPi), p = 0.3, and chance still gives a decrease in 30.8% of VLa unit-directions (42.0% in the data), so the stricter threshold does not remove the chance decreases.
deviations: The ISI-based detection finds more decreases than the paper's on the same units (330 against 286 on the linked units), which weighs on this comparison.

outcomes.statement: Comparing every GPi response with every VLa response, 96% of comparisons conflict with gating (178,846 of 187,154); only 4% have a GPi onset 0 to 50 ms before the VLa onset with the opposite sign.
outcomes.notes: 95.4% of 392,933 comparisons conflict with gating (95.6% with the paper's records, 95.1% with one record per presumed neuron). With onsets shuffled across unit-directions the fraction is 95.1% (95.0 to 95.2), so the number does not distinguish the data from random onsets; it follows the gating window (98.0% for 0 to 20 ms, 86.6% for 0 to 200 ms).

outcomes.statement: A majority of GPi neurons (109 of 206) and some VLa neurons (56 of 179) respond significantly more strongly to one movement direction.
outcomes.notes: 122 of 264 responsive GPi units (46.2%) and 66 of 272 VLa units (24.3%) are directional, chi-squared p = 1.7e-07; both fractions are more than 10% below 52.9% and 31.3%. With the paper's records 48.2% and 26.8%, with one record per presumed neuron 53.8% and 21.9% (p = 9.8e-09).

outcomes.statement: Short-time-scale spike-to-spike correlations between simultaneously recorded GPi and VLa units are rare (3.5% of 427 pairs over whole recordings, 2.2% of 183 at rest, 5.2% of 172 during movement) and their peaks are not larger than those of jittered controls (p = 0.975, 0.675 and 0.998).
outcomes.notes: By the KS permutation test the peak CCFs exceed those of jittered controls over whole recordings (338 pairs, p = 0.003) and during movement (306 pairs, p = 0.045), not at rest (298 pairs, p = 0.705). Significant pairs are 5.6%, 3.4% and 6.5%, none above 5% by a binomial test, and mostly positive (15 of 19 whole, 15 of 20 movement). The shift is small (median peak 0.042 against a control median of 0.038). The part of the statement that correlations are rare holds; the part that peaks are not larger than controls does not. Keeping only pairs with an approximate c0 of at most 0.3 leaves 332, 121 and 172 pairs (paper 427, 183 and 172) with KS p = 0.003, 0.333 and 0.025; one file per pair of presumed neurons gives 0.003, 0.627 and 0.037. The significant peaks fall at lags spread over 0 to 10 ms, and GPi and VLa spikes share a sample as often as independent trains would (11,376 against 11,435 expected), so shared artefacts do not explain the excess. Spike times are at the sample resolution (24414.0625 Hz) in every file. With the paper's records, paired when a GPi and a VLa record share a file (329, 298 and 301 pairs), the peaks exceed the controls over whole recordings (p = 0.005) and at rest (p = 0.033), not during movement (p = 0.203), so the outcome would be the same. Neither pair set matches the paper's 427 whole-recording pairs (338 on the dandiset rule, 329 on the paper's records); this attempt did not find out how the paper counted its pairs.
deviations: The paper's exclusion of pairs with a minimum detectable correlation c0 above 0.3 is not applied in the main test, which the criterion fixed before the analysis; the paper's simulation is not in its deposit. It is shown as a variant, with c0 approximated by a simulation on the CCF counts (independent Poisson counts at the pair's expected count, plus an injected peak).
Only VLa spikes are jittered; the Methods do not say which train.

outcomes.statement: Trial-to-trial noise correlations between GPi and VLa are rare (5.4% of 332 pairs at rest, 7.2% of 372 during movement), not different from shuffled controls (p = 0.07 and 0.388), and equally often positive and negative.
outcomes.notes: Absolute noise correlations exceed trial-shuffled controls at rest and during movement (KS permutation p < 0.001 in both). 10.1% and 10.8% of pair-targets (17.5% and 18.6% of pairs) are significant against 5.4% and 7.2% in the paper. Signs are balanced (38 and 29 at rest, p = 0.33; 39 and 33 during movement, p = 0.56), as the paper reports. Spike counts drift with trial time in many units (VLa 36.1% and 38.3% of pair-targets, Spearman p < 0.05), but with counts linearly detrended the excess remains (9.3% and 9.7% significant, KS p < 0.001), and so it does against each pair-target's own shuffles (10.8% and 14.2%), with one file per pair of presumed neurons (KS p < 0.001) and with the paper's records (9.1% and 7.4% significant, KS p < 0.001 in both).
deviations: The paper's test statistic for noise correlations is not printed in its code; the KS permutation test on absolute correlations was fixed in the criterion before the analysis.
Significance uses the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles of the shuffles pooled over pairs, as the paper's code does per time point.

outcomes.statement: At rest, GPi burst onsets, burst offsets and pause onsets are each followed by a small, slow decrease of the population VLa firing rate.
outcomes.notes: The population VLa rate does not fall below the control band within 300 ms of GPi burst onsets (150 pairs, lowest point 2.5% below baseline), burst offsets (150, 1.9%) or pause onsets (110, 1.9%). Bursts here last 67.1 ms on average and pauses 145.3 ms, against 24 and 195 ms in the paper, and 50.7% of pairs show a change after burst onsets against 11.6% in the paper. The same per-pair test on the shifted controls gives 47.5%, 47.8% and 47.0%, so the test as the Methods describe it is at chance here, and the paper's per-pair test must differ. Computed as Fig5_S14.m does (each pair in percent of its baseline, band shifted over 0 to 800 ms), the population rate does not fall below the band either (lowest 98.1%, 98.4% and 96.9%). The Methods' rule on noisy baselines leaves out more than half of the pairs with at least 5 events (157 of 307 for burst onsets and offsets, 143 of 253 for pause onsets). With the paper's records (131, 132 and 86 pairs kept) the rate does not fall below the band either. Because the burst detector and the per-pair test differ from the paper's, this outcome says little about the paper's finding.
deviations: Burst and pause detection is a reimplementation of the Legendy and Salcman surprise method; the paper's implementation is not in its deposit (Fig5_S14.m plots stored averages and builds the control band; it holds no burst detector and no per-pair test).

A first run used log10 in the surprise and gave bursts far longer than the paper's; the natural log, as in the Methods' formula in the paper's MATLAB, was then used. The notebook shows the durations with log10 (bursts 254.0 ms, pauses 237.0 ms) as a variant.
The control shifts all events of a pair by one random offset of 2 to 20 s and uses VLa rate in rest samples only; the paper does not describe its control for Fig 5.

outcomes.statement: Reaction times do not differ between the animals or reach directions; movement durations are longer for reaches to the right target, and NHP G moves more slowly than NHP I.
outcomes.notes: In the 165 files that hold the units analysed, reaction times differ neither between the animals (F = 0.02, p = 0.89) nor between directions (F = 0.69, p = 0.41), and movement durations are longer to the right target (Gaia 0.273 against 0.216 s, Isis 0.195 against 0.174 s; p = 5.8e-38) and longer in Gaia (p = 7.3e-56). Over all 250 pre-MPTP files with trials reaction times differ between the animals (F = 15.19, p = 0.00011); over the files of the paper's records they do not (F = 3.79, p = 0.053). The paper also reports a significant animal by direction interaction for reaction times (p = 0.002), which is not part of the claim; here p = 0.12.
deviations: The first version used all 250 pre-MPTP files with trials, including files with motor cortex, SMA or VLp units only, and gave a reaction-time difference between the animals. After round 1 the test was restricted to the 165 files with units of the dandiset rule, the files of the paper's data as the dandiset identifies them; the outcome changed from partially reproduced to reproduced. All files and the files of the paper's records are shown as variants.
Movement durations exist for 20 of the 91 Gaia files used.

The observations are file and direction medians (330 for RT); the paper's ANOVA has 452 error degrees of freedom and does not say what its observations are. No file set here gives 452 (326 on the files with units, 496 on all files, 320 on the files of the paper's records), and the reaction-time animal effect depends on the files used.

outcomes.statement: Agonist EMG activity begins well before movement onset, at similar times in both animals (-123 and -135 ms).
outcomes.notes: The EMG is not in the dandiset; it is in the paper's Dryad deposit (S3_EMGdata files). The Methods do not say how the onset of the EMG change was determined, and FigS3.m only plots the trial-averaged EMG with reaction times, so the onsets cannot be recomputed by the paper's method.
outcomes.where: Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnvxm (S3_EMGdata_NHP_G.mat, S3_EMGdata_NHP_I.mat), mirrored on Zenodo record 4000719

outcomes.statement: Thalamic neurons inhibited by GPi stimulation lie dorsal and anterior to neurons excited by SCP stimulation, with a narrow border between VLa and VLp.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Fig 1; S1 Fig
outcomes.notes: The stimulation mapping (responses to GPi, SCP and motor cortex stimulation along electrode tracks) is not in the dandiset, which holds task recordings only, nor in the Dryad deposit. The files give electrode coordinates and location labels, which do not test the claim. As a proxy the notebook compares electrodes labelled VLa and VLp. VLa electrodes lie anterior of VLp ones in both animals (p = 6.4e-10 and 5.5e-58) and, by the coordinates as described (ventral positive), ventral of them (p = 1.8e-11 and 2e-27), where the claim places VLa dorsal. The files do not say how the labels were assigned.

outcomes.statement: In a model thalamocortical cell with N converging GPi inputs, post-spike inhibition grows with GPi synchrony c and shrinks with convergence N, approximately as ((N - 1)/N)c + 1/N.
outcomes.notes: A simulation that uses no recorded data. The Dryad deposit holds its output (Data_Fig6.mat) and a plotting script, but not the model thalamocortical cell or the generator of correlated GPi spike trains; reimplementing the model of the paper's reference 103 in XPPAUT was not attempted.
outcomes.where: Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnvxm (Data_Fig6.mat, simulation output), mirrored on Zenodo record 4000719

findings.statement: The dandiset holds more GPi and VLa units than the paper analysed (268 GPi and 279 VLa units under its own labels and the Methods' rate criteria, against 209 and 185) and does not say which units the paper kept. The paper's unit list is only in its Dryad deposit.
No identifier links a neuron recorded over consecutive files. 97 of the paper's 394 units span 2 to 5 files, and the dandiset stores them as separate units.

Location labels are inconsistent. GPi and VLa are written GPI and VLA in some files, 54 Gaia thalamic units are labelled only "Thalamus" (25 of them are VLa units in the paper), and 33 Isis units have an empty location and no channel id.

30 of the 394 units the paper analysed are not among the curated units. 21 of 254 pre-MPTP files have no curated units. 13 of them hold sorted clusters in processing/ecephys/units (124 in all, 16 in G-140813-2), whose only columns are spike times, unit name and location, so there is no channel or sort letter to match them; 8 have no such table.
In all 254 pre-MPTP files the session_start_time is two days after the date in the session_id.

Sort labels are letters in some files and numbers in others, and the unit quality column is missing from some files and holds free text (for example "B -> C") in others, without a description of its values.

Error trials are flagged only in files with an error_onset_time column (127 of 253 files with trials), and movement ends are missing from 87 files, all of them Gaia (32 of 119 Gaia files have them), so the Methods' trial exclusion can be applied only in part.
One pre-MPTP file (I-160616-4) has no trials table, though it has 5 curated units and raw data, and one spike train is stored twice in I-170518-2, as two M1-S units on channels 40 and 43.
The pre-MPTP NWB files name the paper only by its bioRxiv preprint (doi:10.1101/546598); the dandiset metadata names the published paper.
The EMG of S3 Fig and the stimulation mapping of Fig 1 are not in the dandiset; the EMG is in the paper's Dryad deposit and the mapping is not public.

The electrode table's coordinates relative to the anterior commissure (acx_y, acx_z) put the electrodes labelled VLa ventral of those labelled VLp, if z is ventral positive as the column description says, where the paper places VLa dorsal of VLp. The files do not say how the VLa and VLp labels were assigned, so it cannot be told whether the description of the z axis or the labels differ from the paper.

The Results give 218 VLa units and 94% responsive VLa units where Table 1 gives 185 and 88.1%; the text gives median onsets of -62 ms for GPi increases and -108 ms for VLa decreases (Fig 3C) where Table 1 gives -76 and -95.5 ms.
