The full executed notebook of the first revision, with its conclusions and summary, the attempt record, the README, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier checked every conclusion sentence against the printed outputs and said which of its round-1 points were resolved.

attempts.paper_title: Targeted micro-fiber arrays for measuring and manipulating localized multi-scale neural dynamics over large, deep brain volumes during behavior
attempts.entry_title: Striatal dopamine release patterns and targeted stimulation through micro-fiber arrays (Vu et al. 2024)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Vu, Brown, Wen et al. (2024) on dandiset 001084, which holds multi-fiber photometry from mice with arrays of 30 to 103 fibers across the striatum. It re-runs the paper's GLM of dopamine release to light and tone in 280 fibers of 7 mice (amplitude maps, latencies and their spatial gradients), the isosbestic controls, the D1 calcium correlations, the chronic reward responses, and the spread of release evoked by single-fiber stimulation with its controls. The freely moving, histology and jaw movement data of Figures 3, 7 and S1 are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Vu et al. (2024) from dandiset 001084

outcomes.statement: In a D1-cre mouse expressing GCaMP7f in D1 spiny projection neurons, fluorescence under 470 nm excitation shows Ca2+ transients across fibers that are absent under 405 nm (isosbestic) excitation.
outcomes.notes: Mouse 842, session 2022-11-23, 61 included fibers. The SD of DF/F under 470 nm exceeds that under 405 nm in 61 of 61 fibers (median ratio 3.01, range 1.56 to 19.41). Frames above 5 times the median 405 nm SD make up a median 6.7% of each 470 nm trace (range 0.13% to 35.9%) and a median 0.0% of each 405 nm trace (at most 1.2%; 11 of 61 have none). The session of 2022-11-18 gives a median ratio of 2.84.
deviations: The paper shows example traces; the SD ratio and its thresholds were chosen here before the analysis.
Figure 1C describes a 93-fiber array; the mouse its code reads (842) has 82 fibers per channel, 61 included.

outcomes.statement: Pairwise correlations of D1 SPN Ca2+ signals are generally low but variable, and drop off significantly with the distance between fiber tips.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure S2D; code SuppFig02/DEF/surface_brain_dist.m
outcomes.notes: Over 1830 pairs of the 61 included fibers (470 nm, 2022-11-23), the median pairwise correlation is 0.163 (IQR -0.025 to 0.361, range -0.678 to 0.904), and correlations fall with tip distance (r = -0.190, p = 2.8e-16; mean 0.293 in the closest quarter of pairs against 0.133 in the farthest). The session of 2022-11-18 gives r = -0.238. The p-value treats pairs as independent, as the paper's code does.
deviations: The code's set of fibers (goodROIs.mat) is not published; the included fibers are used.
The threshold of 0.3 for "generally low" was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: After accounting for distance in the brain, signal correlations do not depend on the distance between fibers on the bundle surface, so nearby fibers in the bundle do not cross-talk.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure S2E-F; code SuppFig02/DEF/surface_brain_dist.m
outcomes.notes: In the code's linear model of pairwise correlation on Euclidean, AP, ML and DV tip distances and bundle-surface distance (ROI centroids), the surface coefficient is -3.4e-05 per pixel (95% CI -2.7e-04 to 2.0e-04, p = 0.77), while Euclidean tip distance has -0.278 (p < 1e-5). The other session gives p = 0.41. Pairs adjacent on the bundle correlate at 0.222 against 0.156 for others, which the model attributes to their tips also being closer (tip and surface distances correlate at r = 0.437).
deviations: Surface distance is in pixels of the bundle image; the code converts it to mm, which does not change the p-value.

outcomes.statement: Dopamine release to unpredicted water reward is reliable and of comparable amplitude over at least 12 weeks after implantation (median over 44 fibers, normalized to week 5).
outcomes.source: Figure 1D; Results, second section; code Fig01/D
outcomes.notes: In the 17 sessions with rewards and 25 rewards or fewer (2021-08-19 to 2021-09-13), the median over the 44 fibers of the weekly peak reward response, relative to week 5, is 0.903, 0.932 and 1.196 in weeks 6 to 8, within the band of 0.7 to 1.3. These sessions end at week 8; from 2021-09-10 the sessions have 44 to 70 rewards, of which the paper keeps only those of one task phase, which the files do not record, so weeks 9 to 12 cannot be tested. With all rewards of all sessions the median falls to 0.767 in week 8, 0.609 in week 10 and 0.392 in week 13, as expected if predicted rewards are included; this variant does not test the claim.
deviations: Weeks are counted from the first session, labelled week 5, because the files give no implantation date; the paper's code puts the first session on day 35, which gives the same weeks.
Only weeks 5 to 8 can be tested.

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's DF/F traces, fibers and stimulus times are those behind the paper's salient-stimulus analysis, so that its per-fiber responses can be linked to the paper's.
outcomes.source: Figure 4E-F; the paper's intermediate file glm_spline_results.mat (Zenodo, Fig04)
outcomes.notes: Fibers matched by order within each mouse. The raw triggered averages from the dandiset equal the published cue1_roi_mu for light in all 7 mice and cue2_roi_mu for tone in the 6 mice other than DL18 (largest difference 0.0). The GLM spline estimates correlate with the published ones at r = 0.9957 for light and 0.9922 for tone over all fibers, and significance agrees for 93.6% of fiber and stimulus pairs (lowest DL18 tone 0.684, where 44 tones are used in place of 14; DL29 light 0.822). DL18's 14 published tone trials match 14 distinct tones of the file (r at least 0.952, best competitor at most 0.693), whose raw average equals the published one. Refitted with these 14 tones, DL18's tone spline estimates correlate with the published ones at r = 0.9977 and significance agrees for 0.947 of its fibers; with them, agreement over all pairs is 94.5% and the pooled tone r is 0.9974. Per mouse, r is below 0.99 for DL29 light (0.979) and DL27 and DL29 tone (0.989, 0.986).
deviations: The GLM is a re-implementation in Python; filtering and lag selection differ in detail (see the salient-stimulus claims), which explains the significance disagreements.

outcomes.statement: The light evokes transient increases in dopamine release across many striatal locations.
outcomes.notes: 240 of 280 fibers (86%) have a significant increase to light and 38 a significant decrease; by the signed largest value 237 are increases and 11 decreases. Each mouse has increases in most fibers (34 of 51 in DL21 to 50 of 53 in DL20). The chance rate of a significant increase per fiber, from 200 null refits per mouse, is 0.024 (about 7 of 280 fibers), and 0.043 for an increase or a decrease.
deviations: The paper gives p < 1e-6 for its test (3 consecutive frames outside the 99% band), which is 0.01 cubed and assumes independent frames. With the same test, three given consecutive frames are all outside the band at a rate of 0.0037 in the null refits, and the per-fiber chance rate is 0.024. The protocol blocks a claim when the chance rate of a selection is far from the paper's, as a sign that the procedures differ; here the procedure is shown to be the paper's (raw averages identical, significance agreeing with the published calls for 93.6 to 94.5% of pairs, fig4-link-published-results), so the gap is in how the paper states the rate, and the outcome is kept. 240 increases against about 7 expected by chance.

The low-pass filter of overall velocity is a zero-phase Butterworth filter in place of MATLAB's lowpass; locomotion lags come from a cross-correlation that shifts negative lags, where the paper's code does not (its version correlates at r = 0.997 with the light values used).
DL18's tone regressors include all 44 tones (the files do not give tone frequency).

outcomes.statement: Light-evoked dopamine increases follow an amplitude gradient from the anterior striatum into the posterior tail, where increases are less prevalent and smaller.
outcomes.source: Figure 4E; Figure S4A; Results, fourth section
outcomes.notes: The light value is larger anteriorly (Spearman rho(AP, value) = 0.168, p = 0.0047) and smaller in the tail (median 0.0055 against 0.0117 DF/F, p = 0.0013), but increases are as prevalent there (83% of 35 tail fibers against 86% elsewhere, p = 0.38). The result is the same with the tail at -0.8 or -1.3 mm and with the code's lags (rho = 0.162). Per mouse the gradient is positive in DL18, DL20 and DL27 (rho 0.45 to 0.69) and negative in DL23 (-0.43), DL29 and DL30. With AP and the light value ranked within each mouse and a permutation test within mice, so that differences between mice cannot drive it, the correlation is r = 0.152 (p = 0.013); (a) holds this way too.
deviations: The tail boundary (AP at most -1.0 mm) was fixed here; the paper gives none.

outcomes.statement: The tone evokes the strongest dopamine increases at sites in the posterior tail, while anterior to the tail it evokes primarily decreases.
outcomes.source: Figure 4D, 4F; Figure S4C; Results, fourth section
outcomes.notes: Tail fibers have larger tone values than anterior fibers (median 0.0092 against -0.0026 DF/F, p = 5.5e-13), all 10 of the largest values are in the tail, and 32 of 35 tail fibers have a significant increase (none a decrease). Anterior to the tail 103 significant responses are decreases and 60 increases (binomial p = 0.00047). The amplitude comparison and the anterior excess of decreases hold at every tail boundary, with the code's lags, and with DL18 restricted to its 14 tones of 12 kHz identified from the paper's results (108 against 60). At the -1.3 mm boundary only 5 of the 10 largest values are in the tail, so part (a) of the criterion, which needs 6, fails at that variant boundary. The anterior decrease dominates in DL21 (36 against 3) and DL23 (17 against 6) but not in DL18, DL20, DL27 or DL30.
deviations: DL18 uses all 44 tones in the main analysis.

outcomes.statement: Tone-evoked decreases are slightly more prevalent in the anterior lateral and ventral striatum, with many sites showing both increases to the light and decreases to the tone.
outcomes.notes: Of 245 anterior fibers, the 103 with a significant tone decrease are more ventral than the others (median DV 3.66 against 3.30 mm, p = 0.0031) but not more lateral (median ML 2.07 against 1.97 mm, p = 0.43); the same at the other tail boundaries. They are also more anterior (p = 1e-06). 79 anterior fibers (32%) have both a significant light increase and a significant tone decrease, so "many sites" holds by the 20% reading.

outcomes.statement: The modality-specific release patterns are consistent within and across mice.
outcomes.notes: The tone correlation with AP is negative in all 7 mice (rho -0.44 to -0.70, each p < 0.03). The light correlation is positive in 4 of 7 mice (significant in DL18, DL20 and DL27) and negative in DL23 (rho -0.43, p = 0.026), DL29 and DL30, below the 5 required.
deviations: The supplementary legend of Figure S4 was not available; the test per mouse was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: Locomotor changes to the stimuli are variable and bi-directional, while the dopamine release patterns to light and tone are consistent, so the patterns are stimulus and not movement driven.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section (Figure S4); Methods; code SuppFig04/EFGH/sal_stim_bubbles_loco.m
outcomes.notes: Locomotion after the stimuli varies between mice and presentations (acceleration and deceleration splits from 0 and 21 in DL29 light to 21 and 23 in DL18 tone; mean velocity change of either sign for both stimuli). The fiber maps of the two splits correlate (light r = 0.873 over 235 fibers, tone r = 0.784 over 229). The tone pattern holds after acceleration (tail median 0.0073, anterior -0.0031 DF/F) but not after deceleration, where the anterior median is positive (0.0042; tail 0.0098). The test uses raw DF/F, as the paper's code for Figure S4E-H (sal_stim_bubbles_loco.m) does, with no baseline and without the GLM's locomotion regressors. With each split's mean over the 1 s before onset subtracted (a variant, which does not decide the outcome), the maps correlate at r = 0.755 (light) and 0.823 (tone) and the tone pattern holds in both splits (anterior median -0.0043 after acceleration and -0.0024 after deceleration, tail 0.0069 and 0.0101), so the failure under the code's measure follows from the level before onset in the deceleration trials.
deviations: The supplementary legend was not available; the correlation threshold and the tone-pattern test were chosen here.

outcomes.statement: With isosbestic (415 nm) excitation, large fluorescence changes and spatial patterns to light and tone are not observed, ruling out a hemodynamic origin of the release patterns.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section (Figure S5E-H); code SuppFig05/EFGH
outcomes.notes: In DL31 and DL32 (96 fibers), 2 fibers respond significantly to light and 1 to tone at 415 nm, against 45 and 18 at 470 nm, and the AP correlations of the tone values at 470 nm (-0.49, -0.43) are absent at 415 nm (-0.19, 0.16). The median absolute value at 415 nm is 0.49 of that at 470 nm for light but 0.68 for tone, above the criterion's half; for tone most 470 nm fibers are not significant either, and both medians (0.0027 and 0.0018 DF/F) are near the noise level. With random onsets the median absolute value is 0.0025 at 470 nm and 0.0019 at 415 nm, so the tone median at 470 nm is only 0.0002 above this floor and the ratio cannot fall to half; for light the 470 nm median is 0.0017 above the floor and the 415 nm one 0.0001. With 13 spline functions (the Methods' number for the main GLM) in place of the code's 9 at 18 Hz, the ratios are 0.55 (light) and 0.70 (tone), with 36 and 15 significant fibers at 470 nm against 1 and 0 at 415 nm.
deviations: The spline basis has 9 functions at 18 Hz, as the paper's code (run_sal_stim_glm_470_415.m, knots every 3 frames) has; the Methods give 13 for the GLM at 30 Hz. The 13-function basis is shown as a variant.

Events are placed by behaviour sample index for both channels, because the stored regular frame rate drifts from the frame timestamps by up to half a second; the clock check for these two sessions is weak (decoding 0.90 and 0.80 with true onsets against 0.40 to 0.65 with shifted ones, 20 presentations each).
The 470 and 405 nm sessions of Figure S5A-D are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Latencies to half-maximum are shorter for dopamine increases to light than to tone, and shorter for increases than decreases to tone (light increase 221.6 ms, SD 42.5; tone increase 305.4 ms, SD 100.0; tone decrease 428.3 ms, SD 197.1).
outcomes.notes: Counted from the onset frame as the Methods define latency, the means are 187.5 ms (240 light increases), 271.7 ms (94 tone increases) and 393.2 ms (108 tone decreases); the order holds and the tone decrease is within tolerance, the other two are below it. Counted as the paper's code counts (its 1-based index divided by the frame rate, one frame later), they are 220.8, 305.0 and 426.5 ms, within 2 ms of the paper's values, with SDs of 38.1, 98.7 and 196.5 ms against 42.5, 100.0 and 197.1. One tone increase has no half-maximum crossing before its peak.
deviations: Latency follows the Methods (from the onset frame); the code's count, one frame later, is shown as a variant and matches the paper.
Tone onsets are shifted by 11 frames, the speaker delay in the paper's code, which the Methods do not mention.

outcomes.statement: Dopamine release latencies to light follow an anterior-posterior gradient, with faster increases in the anterior striatum, consistent with wave-like dynamics.
outcomes.source: Figure 5C, E, G; Results, fifth section; code Fig05/general_functions
outcomes.notes: Over 240 fibers with a light latency (median 18 presentations each), relative latency is shorter anteriorly (Spearman rho(AP, latency) = -0.285, p = 7e-06); it also increases laterally (rho = 0.263, p = 3.8e-05) and not with depth (p = 0.93). Ranked within each mouse and tested by permuting within mice, which removes differences between mice and the dependence of relative latency on the number of fibers in a mouse, the gradient remains (r = -0.223, p = 0.0014).
deviations: Relative latencies do not depend on the code's one-frame offset, which cancels in the difference.

outcomes.statement: Dopamine release latencies to tone follow a different gradient, faster in the posterior striatum than in the anterior striatum.
outcomes.source: Figure 5D, F, H; Figure S6A-B; Results, fifth section
outcomes.notes: Over 196 fibers with a tone latency (earlier of increase and decrease), relative latency is shorter posteriorly (rho(AP, latency) = 0.254, p = 0.00033; tail median 308 ms against 368 ms anterior). Increases alone (rho = -0.07, p = 0.5) and decreases alone (rho = -0.21, p = 0.028) do not show it, so the gradient comes from the tail's fast increases and the slower anterior decreases, as the paper says of Figure S6A-B. Ranked within each mouse and tested by permuting within mice, the gradient remains (r = 0.214, p = 0.003).

outcomes.statement: The spatial latency gradients are also present in individual mice.
outcomes.notes: The tone gradient is positive in 6 of 7 mice (significant in DL20 and DL23); the light gradient is negative in 4 of 7 (significant in DL18 and DL27), zero in DL21 and positive in DL23 and DL29.
deviations: The supplementary legend was not available; the count of mice was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: In the mouse with ChR2 in dopamine axons and rDAm3.0 in the striatum, 24 recording locations lie within or on the border of the striatum; 18 of the 24 stimulated locations evoke a significant response at another location, and 22 of the 24 recording locations respond to at least one stimulation.
outcomes.source: Methods, "DA release to optogenetic stimulation"; Figure 6G legend
outcomes.notes: In Opto2, 22 fibers are flagged included and 20 of them respond to at least one stimulation, both within tolerance; 14 of the 19 stimulated included fibers evoke a significant response at another included fiber, below 18; as a fraction (0.74) this is close to the paper's 18 of 24 (0.75), but the denominators differ because fewer included fibers were stimulated in the files. Counting only responses to another fiber's stimulation, so that a stimulated fiber's own photoswitching does not count, still gives 20 responding locations. Adding the two fibers labelled Caudoputamen but not flagged (16 and 34) gives the paper's 24 locations and 22 responding ones, and 16 of 21 stimulated fibers with a response elsewhere; the files have 29 single-fiber sessions, of which 21 stimulate a striatal fiber, so 24 stimulated locations cannot be reached. With the code's further exclusions of fibers 8, 9 and 21 the counts are 19, 14 of 19 and 18. Session 2023-03-20f, with the laser artefact on 13 fibers, is left out.
deviations: Stimulation epochs and the stimulated fiber are found from the DF/F alone (artefact above 0.4), without the code's check against the trigger line, which the files do not hold.
The bootstrap counts responses of either sign as significant, as the code does.

outcomes.statement: Stimulating dopamine axons through one fiber evokes release at neighbouring non-stimulated sites that drops off sharply with distance in all three dimensions.
outcomes.notes: Over 266 pairs of 14 stimulated and 20 recording fibers (378 pairs, 18 by 21, in the paper), the fit is a = 0.0147 DF/F and b = -1.096 per mm (95% bootstrap interval over stimulation sites -1.325 to -0.890), and the response falls with absolute distance along ML, AP and DV (Spearman rho -0.30, -0.27, -0.39, all p < 1e-5). The binned mean falls from 0.0079 DF/F at 0.54 mm to 0.0013 to 0.0017 beyond 2 mm.
deviations: Fewer stimulation and recording sites than the paper, from the inclusion of fig6-inclusion-counts.

outcomes.statement: Evoked release drops off less with distance dorsal to the stimulated fiber than ventral to it, consistent with dorsally extending dopamine axon branches.
outcomes.notes: The decay rate is -0.971 per mm for 156 dorsal pairs and -1.403 for 109 ventral pairs, in the claimed order, but the 95% bootstrap interval of the difference (-0.094 to 0.969) includes 0.
deviations: The paper shows binned means; the comparison of fitted decay rates was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: In control mice expressing tdTomato in place of rDAm3.0, single-fiber stimulation evokes no significant fluorescence increase at non-stimulated sites (0 of 48 sites, 26 stimulations in 2 mice), so the release is not a hemodynamic effect.
outcomes.notes: No included non-stimulated fiber has a significant increase after stimulation in 304 fiber and session pairs of Opto4 (13 sessions) or 203 of Opto9 (12 sessions); median responses are -0.0002 and 0.0003 DF/F, and one Opto9 pair has a significant decrease. The same test finds increases in 142 of 619 pairs (20 distinct fibers) in Opto2. The files hold 25 tdTomato stimulations against the paper's 26.
deviations: In these mice the laser artefact spreads to many fibers, and the stimulated fiber is taken as the one with the largest artefact, which can be wrong; the true stimulated fiber is then among the fibers tested, which makes the test stricter.

outcomes.statement: In mice expressing rDAm3.0 without opsin, light through one fiber raises fluorescence at the stimulated site by photoswitching, but at no other site (0 of 22 non-stimulated sites for 3 stimulations).
outcomes.source: Results, seventh section; Figure 6E, Figure S7A
outcomes.notes: In each of UG21's 3 sessions the stimulated fiber (12, 18 and 24, the numbers of the paper's code folders) has a significant increase after the laser (0.0118 to 0.0144 DF/F), and none of the 21 other included fibers responds significantly in either direction.
deviations: The paper included these sites only if they responded to reward; UG21 has no reward events in the files, so that step is not applied.
The files give UG21's indicator as tdTomato; it is treated as the paper's rDAm3.0 mouse without opsin from its sessions, fiber counts and stimulated fibers (see findings).

outcomes.statement: Neuronal density is not reduced under 50 um fiber tips or between neighbouring fibers relative to unimplanted tissue.
outcomes.notes: Not attempted. The histology is not in the dandiset; the paper deposited the NeuN and DAPI images and its density results on Zenodo (SuppFig01.zip, about 180 MB of TIFF images). Testing it needs the neuron detection of the paper's MATLAB code on those images.
outcomes.where: Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.10272874 (SuppFig01.zip, NeuN and DAPI images and densities)

outcomes.statement: The magnitude and type of targeting errors (fiber tip relative to its intended target) vary across mice and fibers.
outcomes.notes: The fiber table of every file holds the localized tips (stereotactic and Allen coordinates), the location label and the included flag, and no planned target (data check). The paper's code (SuppFig03/B/analysis_code/planned_v_actual.m) reads the planned targets from per-mouse calibration files (calibPath), which are in none of the archives of the Zenodo record; SuppFig03.zip holds the CT fiber tables (MATLAB table objects) and the code only. Changed after verification round 1 from blocked by other with the data taken to be on Zenodo.

outcomes.statement: Fiber arrays imaged with a miniscope in freely moving mice show robust D1 SPN Ca2+ signals during locomotion, and dopamine transients associated with the approach to food rewards.
outcomes.notes: Not attempted. The miniscope recordings in freely moving mice are not in the dandiset; Zenodo holds two videos (3.3 GB) and the example DF/F traces with scored times (Fig03.zip).

outcomes.statement: Stimulating D1 SPNs through a group of ventral striatum fibers, but not dorsal ones, increases jaw movement, an effect absent in a control mouse (interaction p = 7.4e-7; ventral p = 0.0002, dorsal p = 0.45).
outcomes.notes: Not attempted. None of the D1-cre mice of Figure 7 (OptoD1_6, 7, 8 and 10 in the paper's code) is in the dandiset. Their DeepLabCut outputs, DF/F and stimulation files are on Zenodo (Fig07.zip, 2.1 GB, about 24 sessions for this panel).
outcomes.where: Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.10272874 (Fig07.zip, DeepLabCut outputs and stimulation files)

outcomes.statement: Of the eight ventral fibers stimulated singly in each mouse, only one per mouse has a significant effect on jaw movement (3 mice), located in the posterior medial striatum.
outcomes.source: Figure 7E-F, Figure S7B; Results, eighth section
outcomes.notes: Not attempted, as fig7d-ventral-not-dorsal-jaw (Fig07.zip and SuppFig07.zip on Zenodo).

findings.statement: The optogenetic sessions (Opto2, Opto4, Opto9, UG21) hold no stimulation times and no record of which fiber was stimulated; the trigger line the paper's code uses is not in the files. Both can be recovered only from the laser artefact in the DF/F, which is unambiguous in Opto2 and UG21 but spreads over many fibers in the tdTomato mice.

The event table gives tone presentations without their frequency. DL18 has 44 tones, of which the paper analysed the 14 at 12 kHz; the frequency is stored only in a MATLAB object of the behaviour file on Zenodo. The tone start times are the trigger times, 11 frames before the sound according to the paper's code, which the dandiset does not say.

DL15's sessions from 2021-09-10 (44 to 70 rewards) were run in a ViRMEn task; the paper keeps only rewards of one task phase, but the task variables are not in the files, so unpredicted rewards cannot be separated and Figure 1D can be tested only to week 8.

The FiberPhotometryTable column `included` is described as "whether this fiber has been successfully implanted", but it marks fibers within the striatum (the paper's in_striatum); in Opto2 two fibers labelled Caudoputamen are not included, and with them the counts match the paper's "within or on the border of the striatum" (24 locations).

UG21's indicator is given as tdTomato. Its 3 sessions, 22 included fibers and stimulated fibers 12, 18 and 24 match the paper's rDAm3.0 mouse without opsin (Figure S7A), so the indicator is consistent with being a mislabel; the files cannot show which indicator was expressed.

In DL31 and DL32 (18 Hz, interleaved 470 and 415 nm) the fiber photometry series store a regular rate, but the frame timestamps of the behaviour drift from it by up to 0.43 and 0.54 s over the session, so times computed from the stored rate are wrong by up to half a second.

The data of Figures 2, 3, 7, S1 and S5A-D are not in the dandiset (the CT scans, the freely moving recordings, the D1-cre jaw experiments, histology and the 470 and 405 nm sessions of the salient-stimulus mice); they are on Zenodo. Opto9 has 12 sessions, so one of the paper's 26 tdTomato stimulations is missing.

The planned fiber targets behind Figure S3 are neither in the dandiset, whose fiber table gives only the localized tips, nor on Zenodo, where the code reads them from calibration files that were not deposited.

The paper gives p < 1e-6 for its test of a significant response (3 consecutive frames outside the 99% band of the null), the value for independent frames. With the same test the chance rate of a significant increase is 0.024 per fiber and stimulus, and three given consecutive frames are all outside the band at a rate of 0.0037.

The paper's latency code (sal_stim_lat_plots.m) divides the 1-based index of the half-maximum frame by the frame rate, so its latencies are one frame (33 ms) longer than the Methods' definition. With that count the dandiset gives the paper's means within 2 ms.

In the paper's cross-correlation of DF/F with locomotion (sal_stim_iti_acc_cc.m), negative lags are not shifted; they correlate the two signals at zero lag over a truncated range. The Methods describe a cross-correlation over +-500 ms.
The Figure 1C legend describes 23 example fibers of a 93-fiber array; the paper's code for the figure plots 33 fibers of mouse 842, whose recording has 82 fibers.

The archive's summary gives the approach as "cell population imaging" and lists only NWB container types as variables measured; the files hold multi-fiber photometry, treadmill velocity and behavioural events.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)

The verifier tested the helper functions on synthetic inputs and checked the archive's asset list for the blocked claims. Its report had no attempt record and gave its own outcome for each claim; all 26 outcomes agree with the record, and for the five blocked claims it gave data_missing as the reason.

The verifier agreed with all 26 outcomes, found the round-1 reasons stated faithfully, and listed six sentences the outputs do not support; README line 46 said the notebook takes about 14 minutes where cell 85 printed 16.4 min. The re-run took 12.2 min, and the README now says 12 to 16 minutes.

attempts.paper_title: Encoding of female mating dynamics by a hypothalamic line attractor
attempts.entry_title: A hypothalamic line attractor for female mating (Liu, Nair et al. 2024)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Liu, Nair et al. (2024) on dandiset 001097, which holds miniscope imaging of VMHvl alpha-cells in female mice during mating, with annotations of male and female behaviour. It tests the behavioural dynamics of mating, single-cell tuning, GLM fits and persistence, and, with the authors' deposited rSLDS weights for two mice, how the receptive-day integration dimension and its cells behave across the oestrus cycle. Claims that need new rSLDS fits are blocked, as the model cannot be built or fit within the registry's environment and time limit.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Liu, Nair et al. (2024) from dandiset 001097

outcomes.statement: During mating the probability of accepting behaviours (lordosis, wiggle) increases gradually over the interaction, while resistance behaviours (dart, top up, kick, turn) first increase and then slowly decrease.
outcomes.source: Figure 1b, Extended Data Figure 1a, Results "Dynamics of female behaviours in mating"
outcomes.notes: Over the first 600 s after male entry the mean probability of accepting behaviour rises (Spearman 0.74, p = 3e-6, 69 annotated trials; 0.59, p = 6e-4, 58 receptive trials), from 0.11 in the first third of the 20-s bins to 0.19 in the last. Resistance peaks in the third bin (0.14) and falls to 0.07 in the last third. Later bins hold fewer trials (69 down to 11); with the same 63 trials in each of the first 15 bins the rise remains (Spearman 0.63, p = 0.012, 0.080 to 0.151). Within single mice the accepting correlation is positive in 12 of 23, and within single trials in 33 of 58 (median 0.01, sign test p = 0.36), so the rise is a property of the pooled trials.
deviations: 69 distinct annotated trials from 23 mice, where the paper has 74 from 28; the paper's trials are not identified.
Time is counted from male entry and the curves are cut at 600 s; the paper's figure does not state either.

outcomes.statement: Females spend 83.9% of their mating behaviour time in male-responsive behaviours (accepting, resistance, staying) and 16.1% in self-initiated ones (approach, sniff, check genital area).
outcomes.notes: Male-responsive behaviours take 84.1% of female mating time on average over the 69 annotated trials (83.5% pooled; 82.9% over receptive trials), against 83.9%. Per mouse the receptive-trial average runs from 65% to 94%.
deviations: 69 distinct annotated trials from 23 mice, where the paper has 74 from 28.

outcomes.statement: Males spend 11.3 times more time in self-initiated mating behaviours (sniff, mount, intromission) than females do in theirs (approach, sniff, check genital area).
outcomes.notes: The mean per-trial ratio of male to female self-initiated time is 11.75 over the 69 annotated trials, within the tolerance of 11.3. Only this one of the six readings matches; the ratio of summed times is 7.5 (7.1 on receptive trials), the median per-trial ratio 9.2 (8.2), and the mean ratio over receptive trials 9.3. Every reading is well above 1.
deviations: 69 distinct annotated trials from 23 mice, where the paper has 74 from 28.
The paper does not say how the ratio is averaged; six readings were set out before the analysis and the match rests on one of them.

outcomes.statement: Male copulation (mounting and intromission) comes in bouts separated by interbout intervals with a mean of 13.7 s (1,685 bouts and 1,611 intervals in 74 trials).
outcomes.notes: Merging mount and intromission annotations less than 0.1 s apart, the mean interbout interval is 14.0 s over the 69 annotated trials (1,540 bouts, 1,471 intervals), 14.9 s over receptive trials and 14.6 s over all 88 distinct sessions, against 13.7 s. Merging gaps up to 1 s gives 15.5 to 16.3 s and not merging gives 9.8 to 10.8 s.
deviations: The rule for joining annotations into bouts is not stated; three were set out before the analysis.
69 distinct annotated trials from 23 mice, where the paper has 74 from 28.

outcomes.statement: Females show social behaviours (accepting, resistance and appetitive) for 62% of the duration of each male copulation bout and continue them for 23% of each interbout interval.
outcomes.notes: Over the 69 annotated trials females show social behaviour for 63.3% of each copulation bout and 21.8% of each interbout interval on average, against 62% and 23%. This is the only one of the four readings that matches; over receptive trials the interval value is 17.4%, outside the tolerance, and pooled over time the values are 74% and 11%. Leaving out m930's oestrogen days 3 and 4, the two closest to its receptive session, gives 21.7% to 21.9% for the interval value, still within tolerance.
deviations: 69 distinct annotated trials from 23 mice, where the paper has 74 from 28.
Social behaviour follows the Methods' grouping, which leaves out staying.

outcomes.statement: Only a small percentage of VMHvl alpha-cells (approximately 2 to 13%) are tuned to any one mating behaviour by choice probability; most show mixed selectivity.
outcomes.source: Figure 2c, Extended Data Figure 2a,b, Methods "Choice probability"
outcomes.notes: In the 15 receptive sessions (1,335 cells), 6.9% (approach) to 37.4% (dart) of cells are tuned to a behaviour, median 22.0% over the 11 behaviours with enough bins, against about 2 to 13%. Eight of the 11 exceed 15%. The shuffle test alone passes 21% to 75% of cells. Comparing pairs of behaviours, as the Methods describe, tunes 15.4% to 57.6% over 20 pairs (median 39.3%), with none within 1 to 15%.
deviations: Each behaviour is compared with every other 1-s bin of the interaction. The Methods compare two behaviours without saying which pairs Figure 2c uses, and only this comparison was set out before the analysis. Pairs of behaviours are shown as a variant, added after the first round of verification.
A bin belongs to a behaviour when the behaviour covers at least half of it; the shuffle permutes bin labels. Neither is stated in the paper.

outcomes.statement: A linear model of each neuron's activity from behaviour explains little of its variance, with mean cross-validated R2 of 0.08 from female behaviours, 0.14 from male behaviours and 0.15 from both.
outcomes.notes: The outcome is the one both verification rounds agreed with. After the second round the author proposed partially_reproduced, from a penalty selection added then; that change has not been verified (protocol pilot-4, "Hand over for verification"). With tenfold contiguous cross-validation and the ridge penalty chosen per cell by fivefold cross-validation within each training set, the mean cvR2 over 1,335 cells is -0.041 from female behaviours, -0.005 from male behaviours and -0.004 from both (mouse means -0.026, 0.014 and 0.016), against 0.08, 0.14 and 0.15. The ordering holds, both against male by a margin of 0.0003 over cells and 0.0014 over mouse means, and all three are below 0.25, so the partial rule is met by a thin margin. With the penalty chosen on the last fifth of each training set, the design used in the first two rounds, the means are -0.077, -0.013 and -0.057 (mouse means -0.050, 0.008 and -0.017) and both scores below male, so the ordering failure that gave not_reproduced came from that selection. A model with only an intercept scores -0.086 under the same folds, so the negative values come from the fold design; with the cross-validated penalty the gain over it is 0.045, 0.081 and 0.082 (mouse means 0.054, 0.095 and 0.096), below the paper's values. With the last-fifth penalty, R2 within single folds is dominated by the same offsets (medians -0.61 to -0.71, intercept -0.70). With frames assigned to folds at random, a variant not named in the criterion, the means are 0.229, 0.207 and 0.322, with neighbouring frames in both training and test sets; the value from both behaviours is then above 0.25. The test is weak, since no design here separates behaviour from the slow drift of the traces.
deviations: Lags in 1-s steps over 0 to 10 s, not every frame, to keep the run short.

Contiguous folds, the ridge penalty chosen per cell by fivefold contiguous cross-validation within each training set, and R2 on pooled held-out predictions; the Methods state none of these. The cross-validated penalty selection was added after the second round of verification; the outcome would change with it, and that change is proposed, not verified.
Fit over the interaction (male entry to end of annotation) on z-scored, unsmoothed traces.

proposed.reason: With the ridge penalty chosen by fivefold cross-validation within each training set, a selection added after the second round, the ordering of the criterion holds (both above male by 0.0003 over cells) and all three values are below 0.25, which meets the partial rule.

outcomes.statement: Adding the activity of the other simultaneously imaged neurons as regressors raises the mean cross-validated R2 to 0.46.
outcomes.notes: Adding the instantaneous activity of the other cells gives a mean cvR2 of 0.477 over cells (0.458 over mouse means) with the cross-validated penalty, and 0.450 (0.434) with the last-fifth penalty, against 0.46. With the last-fifth penalty 73 of 1,335 cells remain below zero and the gain over the intercept-only baseline is 0.536 (0.563 with the cross-validated penalty). With random folds it is 0.814. It shares the fold design questioned for fig2e-glm-behaviour-explains-little.
deviations: As for fig2e-glm-behaviour-explains-little. Coupling uses the other cells at the same time point; the Methods do not say whether coupling filters had lags.

outcomes.statement: About 30% of cells have an autocorrelation half-width (ACHW) longer than 25 s, and the mean ACHW is 20 s, longer than the mean interbout interval.
outcomes.notes: Over the whole recording, smoothed as in the authors' code, 20.0% of 1,335 cells have an ACHW above 25 s and the mean is 15.5 s, against 30% and 20 s. The first-crossing rule gives the same, and the other readings give 10 to 17% and 9.9 to 13.1 s. Per mouse the fraction runs from 0 to 0.48, and four mice reach 0.28 or more; the lower panel of Figure 2i has n = 4 mice, which are not identified. Ending the window at the last annotation, a variant that drops the unannotated imaging at the end of 7 sessions, gives 15.5 to 19.7% and 12.7 to 15.0 s. The mean ACHW is still longer than the mean interbout interval (14.0 s), as the paper says.
deviations: The ACHW follows the authors' code (the lag closest to 0.5, up to 50 s), where the Methods say the lag where the function reaches 0.5; both are shown.

outcomes.statement: The ACHW of the same cells is shorter when the male is behind a perforated pencil cup (14.3 s) than during free interaction (19.6 s), 470 neurons from 5 mice.
outcomes.notes: No annotation marks the pencil-cup period. In 17 sessions imaging continues for up to 7 minutes after the last annotation, which may be that period, but the files do not say so. An exploratory look, not judged, at the 7 receptive sessions with at least 3 minutes of it (544 cells, where the paper has 470 from 5 mice) finds a shorter mean ACHW in the tail than over the interaction (4.0 to 11.5 s against 7.3 to 17.9 s), but against a stretch of the interaction of the same length the tail is longer in 5 of 7 sessions, so the difference comes from the window length.

outcomes.statement: An rSLDS fit to each receptive mating trial explains 64.08% (SD 6.8) of the variance of the neural trajectories, n = 15 mice.
outcomes.notes: Needs rSLDS fits. The ssm package is a Cython extension installed from GitHub that does not build in the registry's locked environment (it needs numpy at build time), and with the authors' settings one 10,000-frame session takes about 7.5 minutes to fit (10 of 150 iterations took 30 s in a separate environment), so the fits the blocked claims need would take hours against the 30-minute limit. A single linear dynamical system was tried as a stand-in and fitted rotations with two equal time constants in 14 of 15 receptive sessions, so it cannot separate an integration dimension and was not used. The Methods also leave the forward simulation interval open, and the authors' code computes this variance explained differently (a full free-running simulation). Neither timing nor stand-in is run in the notebook, so they cannot be checked from its outputs; the build failure alone blocks the fits here.

outcomes.statement: The rSLDS reveals one integration dimension with a long time constant (110.7 +- 13.6 s) compared with the next (24.5 +- 5.1 s), forming an approximate line attractor; n = 15 mice, P = 6.5e-5.
outcomes.notes: Needs rSLDS fits to the 15 receptive sessions, which are in the dandiset; see fig3a-rslds-fit for why they cannot be run here. The Methods also find the integration dimension by partial least squares onto a ramp (Extended Data Figure 3d,e). That gives a direction but no time constants, so it cannot test this claim, and using it for the ramp and persistence claims would assume the ramp they test; it is not used.

outcomes.statement: A single-state linear dynamical system driven by male sniff, mount and intromission predicts activity in the integration dimension with cvR2 of 0.88 +- 0.02 and an intrinsic time constant above 200 s.
outcomes.notes: Needs the integration dimension from rSLDS fits; see fig3a-rslds-fit.

outcomes.statement: Of neurons contributing to the integration dimension, 56% correlate with an ideal ramp with r2 above 0.5, but they peak at different times.
outcomes.notes: Needs the integration dimension from rSLDS fits; see fig3a-rslds-fit. The Methods do not define the ideal ramp either. An exploratory look, not judged, in the two natural-cycle mice with deposited weights, with a ramp chosen here (0 before male entry, rising linearly to the end of the annotation), finds r2 above 0.5 in 0 of 44 weighted cells in m541 and 1 of 14 in mouse 543, against 56%; these are not the paper's 15 receptive sessions.

outcomes.statement: Transient optogenetic inhibition of VMHvl pushes population activity off the line attractor, after which it relaxes back to the attractor, as the flow field fit to unperturbed data predicts; n = 3 mice.
outcomes.notes: The sessions with 10-s optogenetic inhibition of VMHvl are not in the dandiset; no label marks such an inhibition. The eight male-inhibition sessions have one or two inhibition epochs of 106 to 351 s, the male manipulation of Figure 4c,d. The authors' code repository carries one such session (sub-M1188) as example data, outside the archive.

outcomes.statement: Activity in the integration dimension during copulation interbout intervals is as high as in the preceding bout, so a decoder cannot tell bouts from intervals (0.52 against a shuffle of 0.49, n = 4 mice, P = 0.2).
outcomes.notes: Needs the integration dimension from rSLDS fits; see fig3a-rslds-fit. The four mice of the figure are not identified.

outcomes.statement: When male mating is stopped for minutes by optogenetic activation of the male's VMH, activity in the female's integration dimension stays elevated; n = 4 mice.
outcomes.notes: The male-inhibition sessions are in the dandiset (8 mice, where the figure has 4), but the claim needs the integration dimension from rSLDS fits; see fig3a-rslds-fit.

outcomes.statement: Activity in the integration dimension peaks just before ejaculation and drops immediately after; n = 4 mice.
outcomes.notes: Twelve sessions annotate an ejaculation, but the claim needs the integration dimension from rSLDS fits; see fig3a-rslds-fit.

outcomes.statement: Over the natural oestrus cycle, rSLDS models fit on receptive days have a line attractor and those fit on unreceptive days do not (line-attractor score 1.9 +- 0.2 against 0.05 +- 0.02, n = 4 mice, P = 0.02).
outcomes.notes: Needs rSLDS fits on each day; see fig3a-rslds-fit. The files also do not say which day of a natural-cycle series was receptive, and the female's behaviour is not annotated on those days; the receptive day can be found only by matching a day to the mouse's separately deposited receptive session. The matching rule (same count of male annotations, offsets within 0.5 s) finds it for 4 of the 7 mice (543, m541, m542, m551); m438 day 1 has the same frame count and interaction length as m438's receptive session but different male annotations (60 against 76), and m610 and m764 have no receptive session.

outcomes.statement: Projected onto the integration dimension found on the receptive day, activity on unreceptive days does not ramp and stays low during male mounting (normalised value 0.09 on unreceptive against 0.69 on receptive days, n = 4 mice).
outcomes.notes: With the authors' weights, the normalised integration value during mounting in m541 is 0.61 on the receptive day against 0.23 and 0.19 on the unreceptive days (paper 0.69 against 0.09; the unreceptive values here are about twice the paper's). In mouse 543 it is 0.61 against 0.64 and 0.63, not higher. The ramp part of the claim holds in both mice; the projection rises by 2.5 and 2.1 receptive-day SDs on the receptive day and by -0.4 to 0.5 on unreceptive days. The outcome depends on which factor is taken as the integration factor. On the other factor the receptive day is higher in both mice (m541 factor 1, 0.62 against 0.48 and 0.49; 543 factor 2, 0.66 against 0.54 and 0.51), which would meet the criterion in both, though on 543's factor 2 the unreceptive days also ramp (1.07 and 1.03 SDs).
deviations: Two mice, where the paper has four; the weights of only two are deposited, and the file labelled m542 holds mouse 543's cells.

The authors' weights are applied to the stored traces of each day; the paper's projection procedure and normalisation are not described, and min-max over the three days is used. The cell order was checked after the first round of verification; 171 of 176 cells (m541) and 71 of 72 (543) best match the session cell of the same index. The per-mouse files' own traces were processed differently (same-index median correlation 0.86 and 0.80), but the projections from them and from the stored traces correlate at 0.94 to 0.96.

The integration factor is not labelled in the files; it is chosen by the longer ACHW of its receptive-day projection. Both factors reach the code's 50-s cap in m541, so the tie was broken with lags up to 300 s, a step not set out in the criterion. The outcome changes with the factor chosen.
The receptive day is the one matching the mouse's deposited receptive session.

outcomes.statement: Cells weighted on the integration dimension have shorter ACHW on unreceptive than on receptive days (16.1 +- 0.8 s against 25.2 +- 1.5 s, P < 0.001), while cells that do not contribute to it do not change.
outcomes.notes: In both mice weighted cells have longer ACHWs on the receptive day, 28.4 against 17.2 s in m541 (44 cells, KS p = 2e-5) and 26.7 against 9.1 s in 543 (14 cells, KS p = 2e-4), against 25.2 and 16.1 s in the paper. Other cells do not differ in m541 (KS p = 0.23) but do in 543 (12.8 against 10.8 s, KS p = 0.005). The top 25% of weights give the same pattern; with the top 10% the 8 weighted cells of 543 no longer differ (p = 0.13). The change is not specific to the integration factor; in m541 the 44 cells above one SD on the other factor, 23 of them shared, lengthen as much (30.8 against 17.5 s, KS p = 7e-6). In 543 the 20 cells of the other factor, 7 shared, do not differ at p 0.05 (21.0 against 12.9 s, p = 0.07).
deviations: Two mice where the paper has four, with the factor and receptive day chosen as for ed6e-projection-unreceptive-days.

outcomes.statement: Attractor dynamics disappear after ovariectomy and return after hormone priming.
outcomes.notes: The ovariectomy series of three mice is in the dandiset, but the claim needs rSLDS fits on each day; see fig3a-rslds-fit. The deposited weights of m541 cover 176 cells, its ovariectomy days 184, so they cannot be applied.

outcomes.statement: In oestrogen-injected females, the area under the curve of the integration dimension correlates with the percentage of time spent in accepting behaviours (r2 = 0.62, P < 0.0001, n = 50 trials), and not with resistance or appetitive behaviours.
outcomes.notes: The oestrogen-injected cohort is in the dandiset (42 trials where the paper has 50), but the claim needs an rSLDS fit per trial; see fig3a-rslds-fit.

outcomes.statement: In the same trials, the area under the curve of the population mean of all neurons does not correlate with the percentage of time spent in accepting behaviours.
outcomes.notes: Over 42 trials from 6 mice the area under the population mean does not correlate with the percentage of time in accepting behaviour under any of three readings (r2 0.015, 0.003 and 0.027; p 0.45, 0.73 and 0.30). Within mice the Spearman correlations run from -0.67 to 0.52. Without the two sessions that fail the clock check (m928 day 2, m940 day 7), r2 is 0.011, 0.005 and 0.025 over 40 trials.
deviations: 42 trials where the paper has 50.
The window of the area under the curve is not stated; three readings were set out before the analysis.

findings.statement: No rSLDS fits or latent factors are deposited apart from the per-cell weights of two mice, though the dandiset's description says it contains low-dimensional latent factors from dynamical models. The per-mouse files hold under analysis only a table of two weight columns, and under processing one trace series and the annotations; there are no latent time series or dynamics matrices. The paper's central line-attractor results can only be checked by refitting.
The sessions with optogenetic inhibition of VMHvl during imaging (Figure 3h-k, Extended Data Figure 5) are not in the dandiset.

The per-mouse file sub-m542/sub-m542_behavior.nwb is labelled m542 but its neural data are those of mouse 543 (72 cells and 10,527 frames, matching 543's receptive day cell by cell with a median correlation of 0.80); m542's own sessions have 129 cells.
One mouse is labelled 543 in its natural-cycle files and m543 in its receptive session.

The same recording is filed under two experiments five times. m764's natural-cycle day 1 has the same traces and annotations as its primed ovariectomy session; m776's primed session has the same traces as its male-inhibition session, with different annotations; and day 3 of the ovariectomy series of m438, m541 and m551 has the same traces as the mouse's primed session, with annotations that differ in m541 and m551 and an interaction of 290.7 against 274.6 s in m438.

The traces in the two per-mouse files, which carry the rSLDS weights, were processed differently from the session files of the same recordings (same-index median correlation 0.86 and 0.80, rising with smoothing of the session traces), and the files do not say how. The cell order matches the session files.

Which natural-cycle days were receptive is not recorded, and the female's behaviour is not annotated on most of those days, so the paper's definition of a receptive day cannot be applied. The receptive session of each mouse is deposited separately, without a link to the day it repeats.

The dandiset holds more animals or fewer trials than several analyses use, without saying which were used; 7 natural-cycle mice where Figure 5c has 4, 8 male-inhibition mice where Figure 4d has 4, 42 oestrogen-injected trials where Figure 5k has 50, and 69 annotated trials from 23 mice where Figure 1 has 74 from 28.

In 17 sessions imaging continues for up to 7 minutes after the last annotation, which may be the pencil-cup period of the Methods, but nothing marks it. The labels other and eat, and the two names for the male-inhibition epoch (laser_on and mating_inhibition), are not described.

Every session file describes a two-photon microscope with 920-nm excitation, where the paper used a one-photon miniscope; the raw traces are labelled lumens but are arbitrary units with negative values; the traces described as z-scored are not z-scored per file (per-cell means -1.6 to 2.4); experimenter, lab, institution and session start time are placeholders; image masks are 1 by 1 pixel; and the file names say ecephys for imaging data. The per-mouse files describe their session as a resident-intruder assay.
The linked code holds demonstration notebooks, not the code for the paper's figures, so the GLM, choice-probability, decoder and projection procedures cannot be checked against it.

attempts.paper_title: Conserved neural dynamics and computations across species in olfaction
attempts.entry_title: ON and OFF odor responses in the mouse olfactory bulb and locust antennal lobe (Ling et al. 2023)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Ling, Moss, Smith, Deng, Kroeger, Reimer, Raman and Arenkiel (bioRxiv 2023, v2 2024) on dandiset 001170, which holds two-photon imaging of olfactory bulb glomeruli in awake mice, seven sessions from four mice under the paper's block protocol and five random-order sessions. It compares glomerular ON and OFF responses, contrast enhancement between sequential odors, and odor classification after offset, and tests the locust findings on the recordings the paper deposited on Figshare.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Ling et al. (2023) from dandiset 001170

outcomes.statement: The mouse block-protocol data (four odors, 5 s pulses, 55 s between trials, blocks of ten, 15 min between blocks) come from seven imaging sessions in four mice, with a median of 215 glomeruli per imaging session.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 2H and 4B legends; Methods, Odor delivery to mice
outcomes.notes: The trials tables give seven block-protocol sessions from mice 134, 141, 148 and 149. The median ROI count over these is 210 (reading a); over all twelve sessions it is 296 (reading b). The ROI counts of sub-141 ses-8 (198), sub-149 ses-1 (219) and sub-148 ses-3 (318) equal the glomerulus counts the Methods give for Figures 2F and 4C, 6D and 7. The published version's Table 1 gives the same seven counts in four mice, but puts the 318 session with the 219 session (mouse 4), where the dandiset puts it with the 286 session (sub-148).
deviations: Sessions are matched to the paper's figures by ROI count; no identifier links them.

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's raw fluorescence of the 198-glomerulus session is the data the paper deposited for its Figure 2D to 2F and 4C (Figshare data1_mouse_glom198.mat), up to the normalisation, with glomeruli in the same order.
outcomes.source: Methods, Time-bin-by-time-bin correlation analysis (n = 198 glomeruli for Fig. 2F); the paper's Figshare record
outcomes.notes: Matched by ROI count (sub-141 ses-8, the only 198-ROI session) and ROI order. With the code's frame-counted windows the median within-trial r between the dandiset's raw F and the deposited array is 0.968 (5th percentile 0.834, 0.947 to 0.994 by block), and every deposited glomerulus correlates best with the dandiset ROI of the same index. With windows placed in seconds the median r is 0.307, as the code counts 16 frames per second in a session imaged at 15.5 Hz. The deposited values are close to F z-scored within each trial window (r = 0.927). No other claim depends on this one.

outcomes.statement: In the mouse OB the angle between glomerular ON and OFF response vectors is greater than 90 degrees for each odor (mean 121.8 +/- 2.98 SEM, 4 odors, 7 sessions), so ON and OFF responses are inverted relative to each other.
outcomes.notes: With the code's procedure (median subtraction, vectors centred over the 160 frames) the median ON-OFF angle exceeds 90 degrees in all 28 session-odor pairs (101.7 to 153.9) and in each odor's mean (111.0 to 140.0), but the mean is 127.9 (SEM 3.2), outside 121.8 +/- 2.98. After centring the mean ON vector is exactly opposite the mean OFF vector (cosine -1 in every case), and without centring the mean angle is 71.8 with 2 of 28 above 90. The same centred procedure gives 101.1 between the two halves of the ON window (28 of 28 above 90), 101.6 between the halves of OFF and 129.7 between the 2 s before onset and ON, and on synthetic frames around patterns 2.4 to 13.0 degrees apart it gives 91.6 to 115.6; so the angles above 90 follow the criterion but do not show that ON and OFF are inverted. Without the median subtraction the mean is 124.2 and with per-trial z-scored traces 119.5, both within tolerance; with F z-scored on the 2 s before onset 125.8 and with frame-counted windows 126.1. By mouse the means are 136.3 (134), 136.3 (141), 116.0 (148) and 117.9 (149).
deviations: dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before onset; the paper's deposited arrays are close to per-trial z-scores. The z-scored result is shown as a variant.
Windows placed in seconds on a 16 Hz grid; the code counts frames at a nominal 16 per second.

outcomes.statement: Time-averaged glomerular ON and OFF responses to the same odor are anticorrelated; glomeruli active during the odor tend to be suppressed after it and the reverse.
outcomes.source: Results, first and second sections; Figure 2D, 2F and 4C
outcomes.notes: The time-averaged ON and OFF vectors are positively correlated in all 28 session-odor pairs (median r 0.481, Wilcoxon p = 7.5e-09), for every odor (0.391 to 0.535) and every mouse (0.245 to 0.596). The median subtraction does not change r, by construction. With F z-scored on the 2 s before onset the median r is 0.526 and with frame-counted windows 0.446 (0 of 28 below 0 in both). With per-trial z-scored traces the median r is 0.068 (12 of 28 below 0, p = 0.33); on synthetic glomeruli with excitation only, that normalisation gives r = -0.90 between ON and 10 to 15 s after offset, against 0.30 with the pre-onset z-score. The angles of fig2h exceed 90 degrees only after centring, which makes the mean ON and OFF vectors opposite by construction.
deviations: dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before onset, not the paper's (undocumented) normalisation.

outcomes.statement: In the mouse OB the ON response to a reference odor is closer in angle to the ON responses of the other odors than to any OFF response, including its own, and this holds for every odor of the panel.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 4B and S4B
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) holds for acetophenone only (ON-ON 105.7, ON-OFF 127.5 degrees, paired p = 0.018). Methyl salicylate and eugenol show no difference (p = 0.76 and 0.83), and allyl sulfide goes the other way (ON-ON 112.1, ON-OFF 59.6, p = 0.00035). Reading (b) holds in none of the seven sessions for any reference odor. Full-dimensional vectors give the same pattern. The session-mean ON-ON angles are 85.6 to 123.1 degrees, against a median of 44.7 for the acetophenone reference in the published version (Figure 2G), so the paper's procedure probably differs from the one used here.
deviations: The mouse code for this figure is not in the Figshare record (it loads precomputed angles); the locust code's procedure (top three PCs, mean vectors) was used.

outcomes.statement: Hierarchical clustering of glomerular responses cleanly separates ON responses from OFF responses.
outcomes.notes: In 0 of 7 sessions, the 198-glomerulus session included, does the two-cluster cut put the four ON vectors apart from the four OFF vectors, with dF/F or with z-scored traces.
deviations: The paper shows one representative session without naming it; the 198-glomerulus session is taken as it, and all seven are reported.

outcomes.statement: Methyl salicylate presented 1 s after another odor evokes a response less correlated with that odor's solitary response than the solitary methyl salicylate response is (history dependent contrast enhancement; one-tailed t-test p < 0.01, 3 sessions from 2 mice).
outcomes.notes: Over 21 session-odor pairs the solitary r (0.229) and the sequential r (0.219) do not differ (difference 0.009, positive in 10 of 21, one-tailed paired p = 0.39); per session p = 0.40, per first odor p = 0.33 to 0.51. On the three sessions the published version's Table 1 names (sub-148 ses-2, sub-148 ses-3, sub-149 ses-1) the solitary r is 0.133 and the sequential r 0.064 (p = 0.082). With F z-scored on the 2 s before the pair's onset there is no difference (0.251 against 0.258, p = 0.58). With per-trial z-scored traces the solitary r is 0.289 and the sequential r 0.118 (p = 5.6e-07; 0.0025 on the three sessions), as the claim states, but that normalisation can produce negative correlations with later activity by itself (fig2f).
deviations: All seven block sessions are used, as the preprint does not identify its three sessions from two mice; the three the published version names are shown as a variant.
dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before the pair's first onset.

outcomes.statement: Acetophenone presented 1 s after another odor evokes a response less correlated with that odor's solitary response than solitary acetophenone (one-tailed t-test p < 0.05, 4 sessions from 2 mice).
outcomes.notes: No sequential pair in the dandiset ends in acetophenone; in all seven block sessions the second odor is always methyl salicylate (ace, als or eug first). The Figshare code builds only (X)msc sequences too, so the (X)ace data of Figure 6E (right) and S6 were not found in public form. The published version's Table 1 assigns this panel to the 73-, 210-, 153- and 198-glomerulus sessions, which in the dandiset hold only (X)msc pairs; in those sessions the first odor's response in the pairs correlates 0.94 to 0.99 with solitary acetophenone when the first odor is labelled acetophenone, and the second odor's response 0.76 to 0.95 with solitary methyl salicylate, consistent with the dandiset's labels.

outcomes.statement: After odor offset the glomerular population activity stays negatively correlated with the odor-evoked ON response for several tens of seconds, although overall activity returns to baseline quickly.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 7B, 7D and S7C
outcomes.notes: The median r with the ON vector over the 28 pairs is 0.481 at 0 to 5 s after offset, 0.312 to 0.328 from 5 to 20 s and 0.094 at 45 to 50 s, above 0 in every bin (p <= 0.014), while the mean dF/F falls from 0.071 to 0.005. With F0 from before each block r is positive in every bin (0.304 to 0.600); for the first block of sub-134 and sub-141 that baseline is only 14 to 24 s. With F z-scored on the 2 s before onset r is positive in every bin (0.152 to 0.527), and with frame-counted windows too (0.152 to 0.446). With per-trial z-scored traces r is negative from 5 s on (-0.344 to -0.480, 26 to 28 of 28), as the claim states, but on synthetic glomeruli with excitation only that normalisation gives negative values of the same sign and larger size (-0.90 and -0.93). Mice 148 and 149 keep r near 0.2 to 0.4 for the whole 50 s.
deviations: Correlation of the ON vector with 5-s bins, a summary of the paper's frame-by-frame matrix.
dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before onset.

outcomes.statement: Glomerular activity averaged over the 50 s after each odor offset classifies the preceding odor with high accuracy (k-NN, k = 20).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 7G and 7H; Methods, Classification analysis of average ITI periods
outcomes.notes: In sub-148 ses-3 (318 glomeruli) accuracy is 45%, above the null's 99th percentile (37.5%, null mean 16.7%) but below 50%; by odor 0.9, 0.0, 0.3 and 0.6. The code's choice (cosine on the top three PCs) gives 12.5%. Across the seven sessions accuracy is 22.5% to 47.5%, above the null's 99th percentile in three. The null mean of this leave-one-out vote (16.7% to 17.4%) is below the nominal 25%, as with k = 20 only 9 of the 39 other trials share the own odor; the paper gives no chance value for this panel. With k at or below the class size accuracy is 90.0% (k = 5) and 82.5% (k = 9) in sub-148 ses-3 and 80.0% to 100% in every session (null 99th percentiles 42.5% to 45.0%). All trials of one odor lie in one block, so neither k separates the odor from slow differences between blocks (fig7j).
deviations: k = 20 from the legend; the Methods' k = 50 exceeds the 39 other vectors.
dF/F with F0 the session median of each ROI.

outcomes.statement: A time-bin k-NN classifier identifies the preceding odor from glomerular activity throughout the 55 s inter-trial interval; accuracy stays high for its whole duration and falls to chance with shuffled labels.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 7J and S8C
outcomes.notes: In sub-148 ses-3 accuracy is 88.5% in the first 10 s after offset and 71.9% to 75.6% from 10 to 50 s, above 50% and the null's 99th percentile (32.5% to 35.9%); the other sessions give 72.2% to 99.4% in every segment. The statement's reading as odor memory is not supported by the outputs. The trial-label null does not keep the block structure, and as each odor has one block no label permutation that keeps whole blocks can serve as a null. On pseudo-trials within the 15 min after each block, where no odor is given, the same classifier names the preceding block at 69.6% to 96.9% (sub-148 ses-3 69.6% to 71.2%), nearly as high as in the ITIs (the pseudo-trial maximum is below the ITI minimum in 4 of 7 sessions), so slow differences between blocks are enough for most of this accuracy.
deviations: dF/F with F0 the session median of each ROI.
The shuffled-label control is a permutation of whole-trial labels with the neighbours kept.

outcomes.statement: During the 15 min between blocks odor-specific information is no longer present; classification of 1-min bins of the inter-block interval by the preceding odor is near chance (34.8%).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure S7D and S7E, Figure 7K
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' k = 50 on 60 one-minute bins the rate is 0.0% to 13.3% (mean 3.8%) in the four sessions with complete IBIs, and this procedure's permutation null averages 10.8%, not the 25% chance of four odors, so the paper's 34.8% cannot come from it. With k = 20 the IBI bins are classified by the preceding block at 73.3% to 95.0% in those four sessions and 35.0% to 66.7% in the other three (permutation p <= 0.02), and with k at or below the 14 other bins of the own IBI at 69.4% to 98.3% (k = 10) and 90.0% to 98.3% (k = 5) in all seven (null means 21.8% to 25.5%, p < 0.001). These rates contradict the claim, but each odor has one IBI per session, so no validation can hold out a block, and slow drift between neighbouring minutes could give them.
deviations: The 318-glomerulus session has only three complete IBIs (54 bins), so k = 50 was run on the four sessions that have four.

outcomes.statement: When eleven odors are presented in random order (1 s pulses, 19 s apart), odor information after offset is variable across odors and on average declines to chance after several seconds.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure S8D and S8E
outcomes.notes: In all five random-order sessions accuracy in the first 2 s after offset is above the null (24.4% to 56.8% against 99th percentiles of 10.6% to 12.3%, chance 9.1%), with large differences between odors. In the last 5 s it is 9.6% to 15.3%, still above the null's 95th percentile in four of five sessions (not in sub-134 ses-6). The published version's Table 1 lists random-order sessions with 175, 340, 323, 306, 286, 204, 250 and 280 glomeruli; only sub-126 ses-1 (323) and sub-134 ses-6 (306) have one of these counts. In those two early accuracy is 24.4% and 29.0%, and late accuracy is above the null's 95th percentile in sub-126 ses-1 (9.6% against 9.0%) and not in sub-134 ses-6 (9.9% against 10.0%).
deviations: The paper's random-order session (286 glomeruli, mouse 129 in the Figshare code) is not in the dandiset; five sessions with the same paradigm, four of them from mice not in the block sessions, were used.
In three of these sessions odors have different concentration values; the first 10 presentations of each odor were used regardless.

outcomes.statement: Photoionization detector recordings at the nostril show odor concentration rising and decaying quickly at onset and offset, for every odor.
outcomes.source: Figure S2; Methods, Odor delivery to mice
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds no photoionization detector recordings (acquisition holds the movies, treadmill and in one file respiration). No PID file is in the Figshare record's file list.

outcomes.statement: In the locust antennal lobe the median angle between PN population ON and OFF response vectors exceeds 90 degrees for every one of 11 odors (mean 106.7 +/- 0.84 SEM).
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 1F and 1G, S1
outcomes.notes: All 11 odors give a median ON-OFF angle above 90 degrees (99.2 to 108.7); the mean is 104.9 (SEM 0.87), 1.8 degrees below 106.7 +/- 0.84. Without centring the mean is 58.5; with each PN's pre-odor mean subtracted and no centring it is 91.9, with 9 of 11 above 90. The centring alone gives angles above 90 degrees; the two halves of the ON window are 96.0 apart on average (11 of 11 above 90).
deviations: Data from the Figshare record of the published version; the preprint's data may differ.

outcomes.statement: In the locust the ON response to a reference odor is closer to other odors' ON responses than to OFF responses for most reference odors, significantly for 5 of 11.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 3B and S4A
outcomes.notes: Four reference odors have ON angles significantly smaller than OFF angles (hex, hxa, phn, vny), and 9 of 11 have smaller ON angles on average. Ammonia differs significantly the other way (ON 107.3, OFF 52.5 degrees, p = 0.0033). The 11 ON angles include the reference's own 0 degrees, as the criterion states; without it the count is still 4, and ON is smaller on average for 8 of 11. Benzaldehyde (p = 0.052) and octanoic acid (p = 0.059) are near the threshold.

outcomes.statement: In the locust, PN responses to geraniol presented 0.5 s after another odor are less correlated with that odor's solitary response than solitary geraniol is (one-tailed t-test p < 0.05, 5 odor pairs).
outcomes.notes: Solitary first odors correlate with solitary geraniol at 0.486 on average and with geraniol after them at 0.227, lower for all five (one-tailed paired p = 0.0055). With hexanol as the second odor the difference is smaller (0.407 against 0.321, p = 0.13).

outcomes.statement: In the locust, PN activity averaged over the 20 s after odor offset classifies the preceding odor (k-NN on angular distance), so ITI activity is odor specific.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 7E and 7F; Methods, Classification analysis of average ITI periods
outcomes.notes: The 20-s ITI averages classify all 70 trials correctly (null 99th percentile 25.7%, chance 14.3%); the code's choice (k = 4, cosine on three PCs) gives 97.1%. The published version's Table 1 gives this dataset a solitary block structure; the Figshare file holds only the 40 s around each trial, so no control for slow differences between blocks can be built, and the accuracy cannot be attributed to the odor alone.

outcomes.statement: In the locust a time-bin k-NN classifier's accuracy decays across the 20 s after offset to about 40% averaged over odors, but for most odors does not fall to chance.
outcomes.notes: Accuracy decays from 78.7% in the first 2 s after offset to 29.0% averaged over odors in the last 5 s, below 40 +/- 4; every one of the 7 odors stays above its null's 99th percentile in the last 5 s (16.0% to 54.0% against 14.0% to 27.6%). Averaged over the whole 0 to 21 s the accuracy is 39.6%, a reading of "about 40%" the criterion did not list. As for fig7f, the files allow no control for the block structure.
deviations: The paper's ~40% is read from its text; the last 5 s of the ITI was taken as the end.

findings.statement: The fluorescence traces are raw F (unit "n.a.") with no description of how they were extracted or of the normalisation the paper applied. The paper's deposited arrays are close to F z-scored within each 57-s trial window. With that normalisation the contrast enhancement and negative correlations between the ON response and activity from 5 s after offset appear in these data, and they do not with dF/F relative to the 2 s before each odor or with F z-scored on those 2 s. The time-averaged ON and OFF vectors are not anticorrelated with any of these (median r 0.068 with the whole-window z-score, 12 of 28 below 0). On synthetic glomeruli with excitation only, the whole-window z-score gives such anticorrelations by itself.

The trials table has one row per second of valve opening, without a description; odor presentations, blocks and sequential pairs have to be rebuilt from timing. Five block sessions fill the gaps with "Empty" rows and two do not. The concentration column has no unit, gives 0.0 to two odorants (2-ethylphenol, anisaldehyde) in three random-order sessions, and 0.1 to the Empty rows of sub-141 ses-5.

In sub-134 ses-22, sub-141 ses-5 and sub-141 ses-8 the raw TwoPhotonSeries holds half the frames of the fluorescence traces (91000 against 182000 in sub-134 ses-22) at twice the frame interval; the conversion notes give 182000 frames for sub-134 ses-22.

No sequential pair ends in acetophenone (Figure 6E right, S6) and no PID recordings are included (Figure S2). The published version's Table 1 assigns the acetophenone panel to the 73-, 210-, 153- and 198-glomerulus sessions, which in the dandiset hold only pairs ending in methyl salicylate. The random-order session of Figure S8D and S8E (286 glomeruli) is not in the dandiset, and of the eight random-order sessions that Table 1 lists (175, 340, 323, 306, 286, 204, 250 and 280 glomeruli) only two (323 and 306) match a dandiset session by ROI count.

The dandiset holds the paper's seven block-protocol sessions from four mice and five random-order sessions from five mice (four not in the block sessions) with odor-specific concentrations, apparently from a second study (the conference paper it also names, whose authors are the dandiset's contributors). Neither the metadata nor the description says which sessions belong to which paper, and the description is that of the second study.

No identifier links the paper's datasets to the dandiset's sessions. They match by ROI count (198, 219, 318), but the session names in the paper's Figshare code (for example m149_3_1, m129_1_2) do not all exist in the dandiset (it has no mouse 129 and only session 1 of mouse 149).

The dandiset and the published version's Table 1 disagree on which mouse one session belongs to. The dandiset puts the 318-ROI session under sub-148 with the 286-ROI session; Table 1 puts the 318-glomerulus session under mouse 4 with the 219-glomerulus session (sub-149 here). Which is right cannot be told from the data.

The random-order odorant names differ from the paper's; the files have 2-ethylphenol and anisaldehyde where the Methods list 2-ethylpyrizine (2ep) and isoamyl acetate (asa). Names are spelled differently across sessions ("Anisole" and "anisole"), and "2-methypyrazine" is misspelled.
The genotype (Thy1-GCaMP6f) and the ages are not stated, and every session starts at 00:00, so the time of day is missing. In sub-124 ses-3 the last trial ends 8.9 s after the last imaging frame.

The paper's code counts windows in frames at a nominal 16 per second, while the sessions are imaged at 13.7 to 17.8 Hz, so a nominal 57-s window of 912 frames lasts 51.2 to 66.4 s; in sub-141 ses-8 (15.5 Hz) the deposited trial windows match the dandiset only when counted in frames (r 0.968) and not in seconds (r 0.307).

The Methods give k = 50 for the ITI-average classifier of Figure 7H, which has 40 vectors, while the legend gives k = 20 and the code uses k = 20 on three PCs. For the IBI classifier (60 vectors, k = 50) the procedure's own null is 10.8%, not the 25% chance of four odors.
The Figure 5E legend states a one-tailed t-test; Script_Fig4.m uses MATLAB's ttest, which is two-tailed (p = 0.011 against 0.0055 one-tailed here).

The verifier had no attempt record and took its counts from the claims file. bioRxiv refused the preprint download, so it read the v2 abstract and the published version (iScience, PMC13066794); the preprint's Fig 4B ON-ON value and Table S1 were not checked. It gave its own outcome for each claim; 18 of 19 agree with the record.

disagreements.reason: The k = 50 rate is 3.8%, far below 34.8 +/- 3.48 and below chance, because the k = 50 classifier is degenerate; on random data with 4 x 15 vectors it gives 10.7%, so the <= 38.3% criterion is met by construction (problem 1). The only usable classifier (k = 20) gives 73 to 95% with permutation p = 0 in the four complete sessions, which contradicts "no longer present", though adjacent 1-minute bins of the same IBI serve as each other's neighbours, so slow drift alone could explain it.
