It agrees with 19 of 19 outcomes.

attempts.paper_title: Dual color mesoscopic imaging reveals spatiotemporally heterogeneous coordination of cholinergic and neocortical activity
attempts.entry_title: Cholinergic and calcium dynamics across behavioural states (Lohani, Moberly et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Lohani, Moberly et al. (2022) on dandiset 001172, which holds dual-colour mesoscopic imaging of ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b with face video, pupil and wheel data from 4 of the paper's 6 mice. It tests the regression of both signals on behaviour, transients at face movement and locomotion onsets, amplitudes in sustained states, and the state dependence of correlations between areas and between the two signals, using the Allen parcel masks of the paper's code. ECoG, pharmacology, control mice and cholinergic axon imaging are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Lohani, Moberly et al. (2022) from dandiset 001172

outcomes.statement: The paper's Allen parcel masks, from its code, can be laid on the dandiset's ΔF/F pixels, so that the areas the paper names can be found in the data.
outcomes.source: Methods, Preprocessing of imaging data and Post-processing analysis; parcells_updated121519.mat and brainMask.mat in the paper's code at commit c337686
outcomes.notes: Per session (pixels non-zero in either ΔF/F movie) the non-zero pixels equal the code's brainMask.mat rotated by 180 degrees in all 9 sessions (agreement 1.0; best other orientation 0.98). Per movie, 25 of the 26 movies of the 13 sessions (the 9 state sessions and the 4 visual stimulus sessions) agree at 1.0; the calcium movie of grabAM08 11232019 spont agrees at 0.996, as 263 pixels inside the mask, all in the right AUD parcel, are zero in every frame and none outside is non-zero. With 100% contrast gratings in one visual stimulus session per mouse (47 to 49 trials), the largest calcium response of the 46 parcels is in a left visual parcel in all 4 mice and left VISp exceeds right VISp in all 4 (0.108 to 0.216 against -0.024 to 0.065 percent ΔF/F), but left VISp ranks 1, 1, 3 and 2, so first in 2 of 4 mice where the criterion asks 3 for reproduced. The dependent claims are tested; the partial result bears on parcel borders, not on which areas are where.
deviations: The criterion's "pixels with non-zero ΔF/F in the blue and green movies" can be read per movie or per session; the per-session reading was chosen after seeing that one movie fails the 99.9% bar under the per-movie reading. Under the per-movie reading the mask part fails on that movie and the claim would be not reproduced by the letter of the criterion. The failing pixels are all in the right AUD parcel, which the left-hemisphere analyses do not use.

outcomes.statement: The variance of ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b signals explained by a ridge regression on FaceMap PCs 1 to 25, locomotion speed and pupil area differs across cortical areas (Friedman's ANOVA p < 0.001 for both, n = 6 mice).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state; Figure 2a,b
outcomes.notes: Friedman across the 23 left parcels with 4 mice, ACh chi2 = 67.98, p = 1.4e-06, calcium chi2 = 63.51, p = 6.7e-06. Full-model R2 ranges 0.030 to 0.397 (ACh) and 0.084 to 0.387 (calcium). Spontaneous sessions alone give p = 6e-07 and 0.005. With |speed| as the wheel predictor p = 1.3e-06 and 7.7e-06. For the three mice that match rows of the paper's own R2 file (grabAM05, grabAM07, grabAM08), mean full-model R2 is 0.182, 0.126 and 0.140 (ACh) and 0.207, 0.216 and 0.227 (calcium) against the file's 0.166, 0.126 and 0.142 and 0.193, 0.229 and 0.254.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice; spontaneous and air-puff sessions (9) averaged per mouse, as the Methods do not say which sessions were used.
The ridge regression code is not public; the penalty is chosen per parcel by marginal likelihood over a grid of 91 values, as ridgeMML does by optimisation.

The wheel predictor is the files' WheelSpeed, which is signed, as the Methods ("a differential of distance") and the code's wheel_changepoints.m (db1SpeedMpS) define speed. The first revision had switched to |speed|; the second revision returned to the signed series, and |speed| is a variant.
Predictors are scaled with the training folds' statistics; the first run z-scored them over the whole session.

outcomes.statement: The coupling of behaviour to fluorescence has anterior-posterior gradients that are inverted between the signals, with ACh most strongly linked to behaviour in frontal areas and calcium in posterior areas.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state; Figure 2b
outcomes.notes: Spearman of mean R2 with anterior-posterior rank (1 = MOs) gives ACh rho = -0.761 (p = 2.5e-05) and calcium rho = 0.555 (p = 0.0059). Per mouse ACh rho -0.44 to -0.87; calcium 0.57 to 0.70 in three mice and -0.01 in grabAM05. Spontaneous sessions alone give -0.897 and 0.655. With |speed| -0.758 and 0.558.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: For ACh3.0, facial movement (FaceMap PC1) predicts activity better than locomotion or pupil, in single-variable models (Friedman p = 0.006, face against locomotion and against pupil p = 0.031) and as unique contribution (Friedman p = 0.003).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state; Figure 2c
outcomes.notes: Single-variable R2 averaged over left parcels, face PC1 0.081, wheel 0.026, pupil 0.009; face highest in all 4 mice, Friedman p = 0.018 (exact p = 0.0046). Unique contributions face 0.081, pupil 0.016, wheel 0.004, face largest in all 4 mice, Friedman p = 0.039 (exact p = 0.042). The same holds with |speed|. Signed-rank tests give p = 0.125, the smallest possible with 4 mice, so the paper's p = 0.031 cannot be reached.
deviations: The paper's post hoc signed-rank tests are replaced by the direction in every mouse.
Unique contribution of face is from shuffling PC1 only; the Methods do not say which face PCs were shuffled.

outcomes.statement: For jRCaMP1b, facial movement (FaceMap PC1) is the most robust predictor of activity (single-variable Friedman p = 0.006; face against locomotion and pupil p = 0.031).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state; Figure 2c
outcomes.notes: Changed to reproduced in the third verification round, from the partially_reproduced of the first revision, which rested on |speed| as the wheel predictor. With the signed speed of the Methods and the code, now the main analysis, single-variable R2 is face PC1 0.112, wheel 0.084, pupil 0.010, face best in all 4 mice by 0.016 to 0.053 over wheel speed, Friedman p = 0.018 (exact p = 0.0046). Unique contributions face 0.058, pupil 0.025, wheel 0.014, face largest in all 4 mice (in grabAM05 by 0.002 over pupil), Friedman p = 0.039. With |speed| wheel speed is higher in grabAM06 (0.147 against 0.142), face is best in 3 of 4 mice and the claim would be partial. In the paper's own per-mouse values (Fig2RawData.mat) face PC1 is the best single variable in all 6 mice, and in grabAM05 (row 1, matched by full-model R2 across parcels, Spearman 0.94 to 0.98) the wheel R2 is 0.0246 for calcium against 0.0253 here with signed speed and 0.0483 with |speed|. The paper found face against pupil not significant for the unique contribution here (p = 0.063).
deviations: As for fig2c-face-best-predictor-ach.
The regression code is not public; signed speed follows the Methods and wheel_changepoints.m.

outcomes.statement: Facial movement onset without locomotion is associated with significant whole-cortex transients in ACh (0.64 ± 0.09 ΔF/F, p = 0.001) and calcium (0.69 ± 0.15 ΔF/F, p = 0.006).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on state transitions; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: ACh 0.728 ± 0.119 percent ΔF/F (paper 0.55 to 0.73), calcium 0.920 ± 0.131 (paper 0.54 to 0.84), positive in all 4 mice, one-sample t-test p = 0.0089 and 0.0060. 12 to 31 onsets per mouse. The ACh mean is inside tolerance by 0.002. The same peak at random times in sustained quiescence (200 draws) has per mouse means 0.049 to 0.088 (ACh) and 0.113 to 0.177 (calcium); every mouse's transient is above the null's 95th percentile. Keeping the quiescent period after the last locomotion epoch (which the code's onset function drops) gives 0.728 and 0.871.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice; face onsets from the code's procedure, which the Methods describe only in part.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion onset is associated with transient increases in ACh (0.68 ± 0.17 ΔF/F, p = 0.010) and calcium (1.50 ± 0.11 ΔF/F, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on state transitions; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: ACh 0.761 ± 0.272 percent ΔF/F (paper 0.51 to 0.85, p = 0.068 here), calcium 1.985 ± 0.489 (paper 1.39 to 1.61, p = 0.027), positive in all 4 mice; grabAM08 has the largest values (ACh 1.555, calcium 3.436). 17 to 39 onsets per mouse. Null peaks at random quiescent times have per mouse means 0.044 to 0.082 (ACh) and 0.111 to 0.212 (calcium); every mouse's transient is above the null's 95th percentile.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: ACh transients vary across cortical areas (p < 0.001) but do not differ between locomotion and facial motion onsets (p = 0.734, two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on state transitions; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA (4 mice), onset type F = 0.03, p = 0.88; area F = 9.39, p < 0.0001. Whole-cortex locomotion minus face per mouse -0.285 to 0.625 (three negative, one positive), mean 0.034 percent ΔF/F. An absence result with 3 denominator degrees of freedom, which carries little weight.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Calcium transients vary across cortical areas (p < 0.001) and states (p = 0.005), with locomotion onset associated with the largest signal.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on state transitions; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: Locomotion transient above face transient in all 4 mice (by 0.447 to 2.245, mean 1.065 percent ΔF/F), onset type F = 6.94, p = 0.078; area F = 31.6, p < 0.0001.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice; the ANOVA has 3 denominator degrees of freedom for onset type.

outcomes.statement: Transient magnitudes show a significant anterior-posterior gradient for ACh but not for calcium.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on state transitions; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: ACh rho = -0.605 (p = 0.0022) at face onset and -0.752 (p = 3.5e-05) at locomotion onset, larger anteriorly; calcium rho = 0.014 (p = 0.95) and 0.106 (p = 0.63).
deviations: The paper does not say which onsets the gradient refers to; both are tested.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial movement and locomotion are associated with progressively increasing 30 to 100 Hz ECoG power.
outcomes.notes: The files hold no ECoG; the conversion code reads the Spike2 LFP channel but does not write it. The paper offers its data on request only.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial motion elevates whole-cortex ACh (low face -0.13 ± 0.04, high face 0.18 ± 0.08 ΔF/F; low against high p = 0.046, post hoc LSD), with a main effect of state (p = 0.015).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on sustained states; Figure 3c
outcomes.notes: With 3 mice (grabAM07 has no sustained high face epoch), low face -0.129 ± 0.031 and high face 0.158 ± 0.047 percent ΔF/F, both inside the paper's ranges; high above low in all 3 mice (0.138 to 0.384), LSD p = 0.027; state effect F = 11.1, p = 0.023. Matched epochs per mouse 10, 2 and 13 (71.7, 14.6 and 93.7 s per state). Without grabAM06, high exceeds low in both other mice but LSD p = 0.207.
deviations: 3 of the paper's 6 mice; grabAM06 contributes 2 epochs per state.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion does not further increase whole-cortex ACh beyond high facial motion (locomotion 0.16 ± 0.06 ΔF/F; locomotion against high face p = 0.717).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on sustained states; Figure 3c
outcomes.notes: Locomotion minus high face LSD t = 1.09, p = 0.34. The locomotion mean, 0.250 percent ΔF/F, is above the paper's 0.10 to 0.22, and exceeds high face in all 3 mice (by 0.027 to 0.179), so the data point against the claim; the outcome rests on an absence test with 3 mice, which carries little weight.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial movement and locomotion both increase whole-cortex calcium (low face -0.02 ± 0.02, high face 0.17 ± 0.04, locomotion 0.63 ± 0.19 ΔF/F; low against high p = 0.020, locomotion against high p = 0.044), with a main effect of state (p = 0.005).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on sustained states; Figure 3c
outcomes.notes: Low face -0.002, high face 0.164 (inside the paper's ranges), locomotion 1.106 percent ΔF/F (paper 0.44 to 0.82). High above low in all 3 mice (0.124 to 0.222) but LSD p = 0.24; locomotion above high in all 3 (0.656 to 1.2), LSD p = 0.001; state effect F = 48.3, p = 0.0016. Without grabAM06 high minus low has p = 0.266 and locomotion minus high p = 0.019.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Differences across sustained states have significant anterior-posterior gradients, for ACh comparing high and low facial movement, with larger increases in anterior areas, and for calcium comparing locomotion and high facial movement.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on sustained states; Discussion; Figure S7
outcomes.notes: ACh high minus low face rho = -0.801, p = 4.3e-06 (larger anteriorly); calcium locomotion minus high face rho = 0.329, p = 0.125. Without grabAM06 (2 epochs per state) ACh rho = -0.874 (p = 5.3e-08) and calcium rho = 0.437 (p = 0.037), so the calcium half would be met with 2 mice; the criterion fixes the 3 mice.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: During high facial motion ACh3.0 amplitude is higher in frontal-motor areas than in visual areas (paired t-test, p < 0.05).
outcomes.notes: High face ACh, frontal-motor 0.166 to 0.427 against visual 0.032 to 0.108 percent ΔF/F, higher in all 3 mice, paired t = 4.34, p = 0.049. Without grabAM06 (2 epochs per state) the difference holds in both other mice but p = 0.247.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice; p is just below 0.05.

outcomes.statement: The muscarinic blocker scopolamine decreases cortical activity in motor but not visual areas, and the nicotinic blocker mecamylamine has no significant effect.
outcomes.notes: No drug or vehicle sessions are in the dandiset (its sessions are spontaneous, air-puff and visual stimulus); the paper offers its data on request only.

outcomes.statement: Increased facial movement is associated with significant increases in between-area correlations of ACh in anterior somatosensory and motor areas.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture; Figure 4a
outcomes.notes: High minus low face, 64 of 253 pairs increase significantly (BY q = 0.01) and none decreases; 39 of 45 motor-somatosensory pairs (0.867) against 25 of 208 other pairs (0.120). Mean change in z per mouse 0.095, 0.314 and 0.362. At q = 0.05, 98 increases.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice; the permutation test permutes epochs within mice, so its power comes from epochs (25 per state in all) more than mice.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion is associated with a reduction in between-area correlations of ACh that is significant across the cortex.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture; Figure 4a
outcomes.notes: Locomotion minus high face, 243 of 253 pairs (0.960) decrease significantly, none increases, all six area groups involved; mean r 0.539 against 0.791; per mouse mean change in z -0.337 to -0.648.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Increased facial movement is associated with broad, significant increases in between-area calcium correlations.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture; Figure 4b
outcomes.notes: High minus low face, 161 of 253 pairs (0.636) increase significantly, none decreases, all six area groups involved; per mouse mean change in z 0.227 to 0.567.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion occurs with modest decreases in calcium correlations that are significant primarily across posterior cortical areas.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture; Figure 4b
outcomes.notes: Locomotion minus high face, 100 pairs decrease significantly and none increases; 55 of 66 posterior pairs (0.833) against 45 of 187 other pairs (0.241). Per mouse mean change in z -0.183 to -0.513.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice; posterior is defined here as ranks 12 to 23 of the Methods' order.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial movement is associated with a significant increase in the correlation between ACh and calcium signals broadly across the cortex.
outcomes.notes: ACh-calcium coupling increases in all 23 left parcels (z 0.173 to 0.737) and significantly in 10 (none decreases), short of the 12 the criterion asks; 22 have uncorrected p < 0.05 and 20 pass BY at q = 0.05. Mean r 0.573 against 0.185; per mouse mean change 0.182 to 0.694.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Sustained locomotion is associated with a significant reduction in the correlation between ACh and calcium that is restricted to the frontal cortex.
outcomes.notes: No parcel decreases significantly at q = 0.01 (2 at q = 0.05). Coupling is lower with locomotion in all 23 parcels (z -0.370 to -0.037) and in each mouse (-0.138 to -0.269); the largest decreases are in PTLp and SSp-tr (p = 0.0007 and 0.0006), and MOs and MOp have p = 0.072 and 0.076. The decrease is broad here, not restricted to frontal cortex.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice, with 25 matched epochs per state in all.

outcomes.statement: The spatial regression on 395 nm signals removes stimulus-evoked and behaviour-related negative hemodynamic transients better than pixel-wise regression, shown in GFP and mCherry control mice and in ACh3.0 mice.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Methods, Validation of hemodynamics correction; Figures S3, S4
outcomes.notes: The comparisons rest on GFP, mCherry and backscatter data from control mice, which are not in the dandiset. The ACh3.0 part (visual stimulus negativity in V1 before and after correction) would need the uncorrected blue ΔF/F, which is not in the files. It could in principle be recomputed from the raw blue and violet movies of the visual stimulus sessions (about 50 GB each), but that needs a reimplementation of the spatial regression and the atlas areas in native space, because the code's registration transforms are not in the files; this attempt did not do it. A check on one session (data check) shows the archived blue ΔF/F shares almost no fluctuation with the violet ΔF/F (r = 0.070) where the raw movies share much (r = 0.576), consistent with a correction having been applied.

outcomes.statement: ACh3.0 specifically reports cholinergic signalling, ex vivo (carbachol, blocked by scopolamine) and in vivo (basal forebrain stimulation).
outcomes.notes: The slice imaging with carbachol and scopolamine and the basal forebrain stimulation sessions are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The relationship between behavioural state and cholinergic signalling is also seen with mesoscopic imaging of GCaMP6s in cholinergic axons.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on sustained states; Figure S8
outcomes.notes: No ChAT-Cre Ai162 (GCaMP6s) mice are in the dandiset.

findings.statement: The ΔF/F series (DFFOnePhotonSeriesBlue, Green and Violet) are given the starting time of the first LED pulse, the time of raw frame 0, but their frame 0 is raw frame 499, as the detrending drops the first frames. Their times are 49.9 s early in every session; both the raw movies and the alignment of calcium with wheel speed show it.

The FaceMap, pupil, eye and video timestamps are spaced 111 ms (9 Hz) where the camera pulses are 100 ms apart, span about 10% longer than the session, and end with two values equal to the first camera pulse. With these timestamps face movement and wheel speed are misaligned by 23 to 60 s; with frame i at camera pulse i, as the paper's code does, they align.

RoiResponseSeriesParcellated holds the calcium (green excitation) ΔF/F averaged over its ROIs, but its segmentation is linked to the ACh imaging plane. Its image masks are transposed relative to the ΔF/F images, and its starting time is that of the first green pulse, 64.9 s before its first frame (150 frames after the ΔF/F's first frame).

The ΔF/F descriptions mention detrending only; the blue and green ΔF/F are also hemodynamically corrected and registered to the Allen atlas, rotated by 180 degrees, as the paper's code shows (the data are consistent with the correction, in one session checked). The Allen parcels the paper analyses are not in the files; they come from the paper's code. The parcellation in the files is a different, functional one with 89 to 107 ROIs per session and no area names.
In the VisualStimulus tables the columns from stimulus_size on are shifted by one; stimulus_size holds the duration (2) and the first screen coordinate holds the size (20 degrees).
The air-puff session grabAM07 11262019 has no Airpuff table, so its puff times are unknown.

No air puff in the Airpuff tables is followed by a locomotion onset within 5 s (29 puffs), which fits the paper's code keeping only puffs without running. The tables then hold a selection of the puffs given, which the files do not say.

WheelSpeed and pupil_area have the unit "unknown"; the paper's code treats wheel speed as m/s, and its range fits that. WheelSpeed is signed (minimum -0.07 to -0.14 per session), which its description does not say.

In the calcium ΔF/F of grabAM08 11232019 spont, 263 pixels inside the brain mask, all in the right AUD parcel, are zero in every frame; in the other 25 ΔF/F movies every pixel of the mask is non-zero.
The VisualStimulus tables give screen coordinates but not where the monitor stood relative to the mouse, so the hemisphere expected to respond cannot be read from the files.

The dandiset holds 4 of the 6 ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b mice of the paper's code (grabAM05 to grabAM08, not grabAM09 and grabAM10), and no ECoG, drug sessions, control mice or ChAT-GCaMP6s mice. Five of the paper's findings cannot be tested.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper (PMC10661869). The verifier had no attempt record and took its counts from the claims file. It gave its own outcome for each claim; all 26 agree with the record as it then stood.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the first revision, with its conclusions and summary, the helper module, the claims file, the attempt record and the paper (PMC10661869). The verifier agreed with 25 of the 26 outcomes and did not accept the reason for fig2c-face-best-predictor-calcium. It also asked for corrections to the robustness text without grabAM06, the runtime and some minor statements.

disagreements.reason: The arithmetic is not disputed; with |speed| wheel beats face in grabAM06 (0.147 vs 0.142), so the result is partial. The reason for switching to |speed| is disputed. The Methods define speed as "a differential of distance" after unwrapping, which keeps its sign; the paper's code computes it signed (wheel_changepoints.m line 50, db1SpeedMpS) and takes abs only for the threshold on mean epoch speed (line 135); the file's WheelSpeed is very likely that same series. The code repository contains Figure2Regression/Fig2RawData.mat, the paper's own per-mouse R2 (6 x 52); for calcium its single-variable face R2 is above wheel in all 6 mice; if its rows 1 to 4 are grabAM05 to grabAM08 (not established), its wheel R2 for mouse 1 is 0.0246 (calcium) and 0.0014 (ACh), against 0.0253 and 0.0017 here with signed speed and 0.0483 and 0.0031 with |speed|; the other mice are mixed. On this evidence signed speed is the better-supported reading, and under it the claim is reproduced. The outcome should either go back to reproduced with |speed| as the variant, or stay partial with a reason that matches the sources. Compare the per-mouse values with Fig2RawData.mat after confirming its row-to-mouse mapping; this would also give the first external check of the ridgeMML port.

attempts.paper_title: Neural circuits underlying divergent visuomotor strategies of zebrafish and Danionella cerebrum
attempts.entry_title: Optomotor swimming of zebrafish and Danionella cerebrum (Fouke et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the freely swimming findings of Fouke, He, Loring and Naumann (2025) on dandiset 001453, which holds the tracking data of 25 zebrafish and 12 Danionella cerebrum larvae during the optomotor protocol. It compares swimming speed, turning and angular acceleration between species and stimuli, the response to monocular stimuli, and how steady the swimming is. The imaging and head-fixed tail tracking of the paper's Figures 2 to 4 are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Fouke et al. (2025) from dandiset 001453

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's stimulus codes can be linked to the stimuli the paper names, using the paper's analysis code and the protocol file of its stimulus software, and the values computed through that link agree with those the paper's code printed.
outcomes.source: Data and Code Availability; the paper's Fig1-S1.ipynb at GitLab commit 33a5c29
outcomes.notes: Codes are matched by their integer value. All 21 codes are in the dandiset, including every code the analysis uses. Through the link, 17 of 18 species and stimulus speed medians are within 10% of the values printed by Fig1-S1.ipynb (DC static is 10.52 against 11.9 mm/s), and the angular velocities differ from the printed ones by a median of 0.02 deg/s. The fish counts (25 ZF, 12 DC) match the code's lists; fish cannot be matched one by one, as no identifier links the dandiset's subjects to the code's folders. The static window is the code's (first 35 s of the code-20 block, measured from 3 s), and no fish median is exactly 0, so the code's exclusion of zero medians changes nothing. On codes 9 and 11 the ZF medians are 0.02 and 1.59 deg/s. Over 3 to 35 s DC turn more to the right for code 11 than for code 9 (median difference 5.82 deg/s, 10 of 12 fish, Wilcoxon p = 0.0093), and ZF go the same way without significance (1.66 deg/s, 16 of 25 fish, p = 0.141). If fish turn with lateral motion as they do with medial motion, code 11 is lateral right, as the protocol file has it; the data do not show that they do, so the assignment is not settled.
deviations: The code's filter on a `vel` column is not applied to DC trials, as the DC files have no such series; this is the remaining difference that may explain the one DC static value outside 10%.
The timing of the DC stimulus labels could not be confirmed from the turning response (the contrast is 4.6 deg/s with true labels and 0.1 with shifted ones); the DC labels are taken as they are.

outcomes.statement: Danionella cerebrum (DC) swim at a higher median velocity than zebrafish (ZF) across the visual stimuli.
outcomes.notes: Over all 21 codes, the median over fish and code values is 94.0 pixels/s for DC and 55.2 for ZF; species effect F = 78.4, p = 6.3e-18. The ANOVA treats each fish and code value as independent; with one value per fish, DC 87.4 against ZF 52.9 pixels/s, Mann-Whitney p = 0.02. With positions resampled to 30 Hz, 95.2 against 53.8 (p = 1.3e-08). DC are faster within each frame-rate group.
deviations: Tested over all stimulus codes without their names; the paper's figure uses nine whole-field stimuli.
The comparison assumes one spatial scale for all rigs, which the files do not state.

outcomes.statement: Across the whole-field stimuli DC have a higher median velocity than ZF (9.8 against 6.4 mm/s), with a significant main effect of species in a two-way ANOVA.
outcomes.notes: All four readings put both values within tolerance; (a) median of stimulus medians DC 10.02 and ZF 6.39 mm/s, (b) median of fish and stimulus values 9.87 and 6.41 (given as measured), (c) median of fish medians 9.36 and 6.33, (d) median of trials 9.88 and 6.28. Species effect F = 20.8, p = 7.5e-06. With 30 Hz positions DC 9.43 to 10.15 and ZF 6.07 to 6.30 (p = 0.0011). Without the trial rejection (4487 trials in place of 4458) readings (a) to (c) are unchanged and (d) gives DC 9.85 and ZF 6.30 (p = 6.7e-06).
deviations: The paper does not say how the overall median is taken; four readings are shown, and all match.
25 ZF, where the paper states 26.
Speeds rely on the code's scale of 10 pixels per mm, which the dandiset does not state.

outcomes.statement: ZF modulate their velocity with the direction of motion; forward motion increases their median velocity (static 5.0 mm/s, forward 8.8 mm/s).
outcomes.notes: ZF static 4.84 mm/s over 18 fish and forward 8.78 mm/s over 25 fish. Of 18 fish with both, 14 are faster to forward motion (median difference 3.67 mm/s, Wilcoxon p = 0.0077). The static value is 8.31 mm/s in the 5 fish from 167 to 171 Hz files and 4.50 in the 13 from 32 to 35 Hz files. Static is the start of the blank block after all motion trials (4 hours in the protocol, 0.2 to 787.3 min in the files), one period per fish, and 7 ZF have none.
deviations: 25 ZF, where the paper states 26.

outcomes.statement: DC lack the direction-dependent velocity modulation seen in ZF.
outcomes.notes: By the paper's test (Tukey's HSD over the 18 species and stimulus groups) 3 of 36 DC pairs differ, all static against a motion direction (backward left, backward right, forward left; adjusted p 0.030 to 0.049). The DC static values come from 9 fish and include one at 106.5 mm/s and two near 0. Among the eight directions no DC pair differs (smallest adjusted p 0.999), DC per-stimulus medians span 8.81 to 10.52 mm/s (ratio 1.19, ZF 2.03), and a one-way ANOVA across the nine DC stimuli gives p = 0.479 (ZF p = 0.00082). With values above 100 mm/s left out, no DC pair differs. The same Tukey test finds no ZF pair over the 18 groups (smallest p 0.835). The printed output of Fig1-S1.ipynb finds the same three DC pairs significant (adjusted p 0.0236, 0.0373 and 0.0397), so the paper's own test disagrees with the claim and this result matches the paper's computation. The DC-sub-2 static value of 106.5 mm/s is one trial measured over a 14.6 s motion phase in a 100 mm dish, likely a tracking artefact. It passes the code's speed check because the check covers 0 to 35 s (21.9 mm/s from the stored `dist`, 92.5 from positions); computing the check from positions, or leaving out zero medians as the code does, gives the same 3 pairs. The outcome is a property of the paper's test on this data, not evidence that DC modulate their speed with stimulus direction.
deviations: The DC static block is the code's window, but the code's filter on DC `vel` cannot be applied (DC static 10.52 against the code's printed 11.9 mm/s).

outcomes.statement: DC swim at a significantly higher velocity than ZF for oblique stimuli.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b), motion at 90 degrees or more, DC are significantly faster than ZF for right (p = 0.0002) and backward right (p = 0.0047), 2 of 4; under reading (a), the intercardinal directions, for 1 of 4 (backward right). Backward motion also differs (p = 0.0002).
deviations: The legend's "oblique" can be read two ways; the claim is reproduced under one of them (b) and not under the other (a).

outcomes.statement: Both species follow the direction of optic flow, turning right (positive angular velocity) to rightward motion and left to leftward motion.
outcomes.notes: ZF turn with the motion; the rightward minus leftward difference is positive in 23 of 25 fish (median 29.51 deg/s, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 9.8e-07). DC do not by this test; 7 of 12 positive, median 0.88 deg/s, p = 0.151, and the DC median for left motion is +0.25 deg/s, the same sign as the paper's code printed (+0.3). DC turn right to right motion (8.67 deg/s).
deviations: The paper gives no test for following the direction; the per-fish rightward minus leftward difference and its test were chosen here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: Across directional stimuli ZF have higher angular acceleration than DC, and the distributions of the two species differ for every stimulus.
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 1H (Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction)
outcomes.notes: With angular acceleration as the Methods define it, DC are higher than ZF for all nine stimuli (medians 143 to 191 against 55.4 to 66.4 deg/s2, Kruskal-Wallis p below 0.05/9 for each), the reverse of the claim. Per-fish medians, and the files at 128 to 171 Hz alone (ZF 84.9, DC 178.6 deg/s2, p = 6.3e-05), give the same. The quantity Fig1-S1.ipynb computes gives ZF higher with p below 0.05/9 for 7 of 9 stimuli; it divides the heading change per frame by the file's mean frame interval, which in DC files is a median 8.73 times the frame interval (ZF 1.37), as DC files hold only trial frames. Part of the DC values may be tracking noise. In the 3 s stationary phase the DC median is 205 deg/s2, higher than the 171 during motion (per fish median ratio 1.24, p = 0.016), but ZF are also higher at rest (66.9 and 60.8, ratio 1.07, p = 0.00012), so this does not separate the species. In frames where the fish is still (below 1 mm/s) DC are higher than ZF (per-fish medians 72.4 and 34.9 deg/s2, Mann-Whitney p = 0.00014), and DC are higher in every speed band (at 5 mm/s or more, 207 and 85.8). The outputs cannot say whether the higher values in moving DC are noise or turning during continuous swimming. With the heading from the unwrapped `f0_theta` DC are higher still (218 to 278 against ZF 61.8 to 77.3 deg/s2, 0 of 9). The reversal should not be read as evidence against the paper.
deviations: Follows the Methods' definition (degrees per second squared) on heading resampled to 30 Hz; the code's quantity, which disagrees with the Methods, is shown as a variant.
Heading is taken from the cumulative sum of `f0_vtheta`, as the code does; in DC files it does not match `f0_theta`.

outcomes.statement: DC generally respond less than ZF to monocular stimuli, suggesting that they need more visual motion input to drive the optomotor response.
outcomes.notes: Species effect F = 23.3, p = 2.5e-06. DC turn less toward the stimulus than ZF for medial stimuli (3.26 against 13.48 deg/s, p = 0.0003) and binocular ones (2.87 against 21.87, p = 0.0002). For lateral stimuli DC are below ZF only nominally (-1.07 against -0.13 deg/s, p = 0.96); neither species turns toward lateral motion. With the protocol file's assignment of codes 9 and 11, the lateral medians change sign and DC are no longer below ZF there, which would make the claim partially reproduced. The DC turning to codes 9 and 11 leans toward the protocol file's assignment (see stimulus-code-link), so the lateral part is fragile.
deviations: Codes 9 and 11 are assigned as the figure code has them; the stimulus software's conversion has them the other way, and the data do not settle it.

outcomes.statement: ZF swim in discrete bouts separated by glides, while DC swim continuously at a relatively constant velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure 1C and Figure S1D
outcomes.notes: The median-to-mean ratio of instantaneous speed is 0.306 in ZF (25 fish, 0.244 to 0.580) and 0.908 in DC (12 fish, 11 above 0.74, one at 0.140), Mann-Whitney p = 5.4e-05. It holds in files at 128 to 171 Hz alone (0.298 against 0.898, p = 0.0028) and in forward trials alone.
deviations: The paper shows this with representative traces and a bout analysis whose bout files are not in the dandiset; the measure was chosen here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: In representative trials ZF bouts reach a peak velocity of 44.7 mm/s with a median of 1.8 mm/s, DC swim at a median of 13.7 mm/s to forward motion; to oblique motion ZF show a median angular velocity of 12.0 degrees/s and median peak angular acceleration of 174 degrees/s2, and DC an average peak of 103 degrees/s2 to rightward motion.
outcomes.source: Results, first and second sections; Figure 1C, 1E and 1F
outcomes.notes: The numbers come from single representative fish and trials. Fig1-S1.ipynb selects them by the index of a data folder and a trial number (for example DC folder 29, trial 79), and the dandiset gives no mapping from those folders to its subjects, nor the original file names.

outcomes.statement: Both species have spatially intermixed, direction-selective neurons enriched in the pretectum and anterior hindbrain, and share the major functional response types.
outcomes.notes: The two-photon imaging data are not in the dandiset, which holds only freely swimming tracking. The GitLab repository the paper names for "all behavioral and imaging data" holds notebooks only, and no other dandiset of this lab or paper was found on the archive.

outcomes.statement: The average direction selectivity index is similar in ZF and DC (0.62 against 0.66, p > 0.05, Student's t-test, 5 fish each).
outcomes.notes: Imaging data not in the dandiset, nor found elsewhere (see fig2d-shared-architecture).

outcomes.statement: ZF tend to have a higher proportion of motion-responsive neurons than DC (0.13 against 0.06, p = 0.059).
outcomes.notes: Imaging data not in the dandiset, nor found elsewhere (see fig2d-shared-architecture).

outcomes.statement: DC have a higher proportion of purely monocular neurons than ZF (0.37 against 0.16, p < 0.05).
outcomes.notes: Imaging data not in the dandiset, nor found elsewhere (see fig2d-shared-architecture).

outcomes.statement: The binocularity index ratio is higher in ZF than in DC (0.72 against 0.24, p = 0.010).
outcomes.notes: Imaging data not in the dandiset, nor found elsewhere (see fig2d-shared-architecture).

outcomes.statement: Head-fixed DC perform longer swims than ZF (median 0.75 s against 0.29 s, p < 0.0001).
outcomes.notes: The head-fixed tail tracking recorded during imaging is not in the dandiset, nor in the paper's GitLab repository.

outcomes.statement: Head-fixed ZF show larger directional tail angles than DC to turn-inducing stimuli, and shorten their swims for oblique stimuli while DC do not.
outcomes.notes: The head-fixed tail tracking is not in the dandiset, nor in the paper's GitLab repository.

outcomes.statement: Swim-onset-associated neurons in DC have a longer active (ON) phase than in ZF, while non-motor-associated neurons have similar ON durations.
outcomes.notes: Needs the imaging and the head-fixed tail tracking, neither of which is in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Motor-associated neurons in the putative ventromedial spinal projection neurons of both species encode turn direction in a lateralized way, correlating more with ipsilateral turns.
outcomes.notes: Needs the imaging, the tail tracking and the registration to the mapzebrain atlas, none of which is in the dandiset.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only the freely swimming tracking of Figure 1 and Figure S1. The two-photon imaging and the head-fixed tail tracking behind Figures 2 to 4 are not in it, and the GitLab repository the paper names for all behavioural and imaging data holds analysis notebooks only. Nine of the paper's main findings cannot be tested.

The stimulus codes 0 to 20 have no names or description in the files or the dandiset metadata. They can be named only from the paper's analysis notebook and the protocol file of its stimulus software.

The paper's analysis notebook labels code 9 as lateral right and 11 as lateral left, while its conversion of the stimulus software's names gives the reverse (it carries a remap that swaps them). The data do not settle which is right; zebrafish barely turn to either, and Danionella turn more to the right for code 11, which fits the stimulus software's assignment only if the fish turn with lateral motion.

Subject ids 0 to 11 are each used for one zebrafish and one Danionella cerebrum, so subject_id does not identify an animal. The archive's summary counts 25 subjects and lists only Danio rerio; the files hold 37 fish of two species.

f0_vtheta is stated in radians/s but holds the heading change per frame in radians, and f0_vx and f0_vy are stated in pixels/s but are per frame. In most Danionella files the sum of f0_vtheta over a trial does not match the change of f0_theta (median ratios 0.09 to 0.89).

18 of 25 zebrafish files and 1 of 12 Danionella files are sampled at 32 to 35 Hz, where the Methods state tracking at more than 150 Hz. Their timestamp intervals are regular (28.8 to 30.8 ms) and their trials last the protocol's 35 s, so these are the acquisition rates. Some measures differ with frame rate, such as the zebrafish static speed (8.31 against 4.50 mm/s).

No spatial scale is given; positions are in pixels. They are consistent with the 10 pixels per mm in the paper's code, except one Danionella file (sub-5) whose positions reach 1490 pixels against about 1120 in the others.

Zebrafish and Danionella files were exported differently. Zebrafish files keep untracked frames and frames between trials; Danionella files hold only tracked trial frames and add a `dist` series. The paper's code filters Danionella frames on a `vel` column that is not in the files.

The paper's code computes the angular acceleration of Figure 1H as the heading change per frame divided by the file's mean frame interval, an angular velocity. In Danionella files the mean interval includes the gaps between trials (a median 8.73 times the frame interval), which scales their values down. With the Methods' definition Danionella have the higher angular acceleration.

Figure 1H and its legend state a Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction; the code runs two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and its loop selects the stimulus with a variable left from an earlier loop, so the nine tests compare the same stimulus.

The Results state that Danionella lack the direction-dependent speed modulation of zebrafish, but the Tukey test printed by Fig1-S1.ipynb for Figure 1D finds three Danionella pairs significant (static against backward left, backward right and forward left, adjusted p 0.024 to 0.040), as this attempt does.

The `dist` series of the Danionella files does not agree with the positions; over the first 35 s of a trial its sum is a median 1.11 times the path length of the smoothed positions, with a 5th to 95th percentile of 0.31 to 3.79. The paper's speed check uses it, though computing the check from positions passes the same trials.
The Figure 1D legend gives 26 zebrafish; the paper's code lists 25, its ANOVA degrees of freedom fit 25, and the dandiset holds 25.
The dandiset holds the 25 zebrafish and 12 Danionella the code keeps after exclusion (its comments give 28 and 40 recorded). The dandiset does not say that the excluded fish were left out or why.

attempts.paper_title: Parkinson’s Disease-vulnerable and -resilient dopamine neurons display opposite responses to excitatory input
attempts.entry_title: Responses of SNr GABA and SNc dopamine neuron subtypes to STN and PPN input (Hadjas et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the mouse fiber photometry findings of Hadjas et al. (2025) on dandiset 001528, which holds recordings from 120 mice during optogenetic stimulation of STN or PPN inputs to the substantia nigra. It compares responses of SNr GABA neurons, SNc pan-DA neurons, striatal dopamine release in TS and DLS, DA terminals, and Vglut2+ and Anxa1+ DA neurons across train durations and frequencies, using the lab's dF/F stored in the files. The human tissue counts of Figure 1 are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Hadjas et al. (2025) from dandiset 001528

outcomes.statement: The number of mice per experimental group is as given in the figure legends; SNr GABA neurons STN 7 and PPN 8 (Figure 2); SNc pan-DA neurons STN 11 and PPN 9 (Figure 3); GRAB-DA in TS and DLS, STN 6 and 7, PPN 9 and 9 (Figure 4); DA terminals in TS and DLS with STN stimulation, 9 and 9 (Figure S3); Vglut2+ DA neurons STN 10 and PPN 10, Anxa1+ terminals in DLS STN 8 and PPN 10 (Figure 5); Anxa1+ cell bodies in SNc STN 5 and PPN 4 (Figure S4).
outcomes.source: Legends of Figures 2 to 5, S3 and S4
outcomes.notes: 10 of 16 counts match. SNr GABA, pan-DA and GRAB-DA groups match exactly, as do DA terminals in TS and Vglut2 with PPN. DA terminals in DLS have 8 mice (paper 9) and Vglut2 with STN 9 (paper 10). The Anxa1 groups have DLS recordings for 5 (STN) and 4 (PPN) mice against the paper's 8 and 10, and SNc recordings for 8 and 10 against 5 and 4. All four Anxa1 counts would match if the nine recordings without a site suffix were DLS recordings; their signals resemble the SNc recordings, and the paper's cell-body statistics are matched by the dual mice's SNc recordings alone, so the DLS recordings of those nine mice appear to be missing. For Vglut2 STN the paper's own Wilcoxon statistics fit 9 mice (W = 41, 43, -5 give exact p = 0.0117, 0.0078, 0.82 with n = 9, the paper's values, and 0.037, 0.027, 0.85 with n = 10), so the legend's 10 is likely an error; counted that way 11 of 16 match, still below 12.
deviations: Counted from the durations protocol; the frequencies protocol gives the same counts.

outcomes.statement: Optogenetic stimulation of STN or PPN inputs increases SNr GABA neuron activity (paired t-test on the 1 s train, STN t = 3.8, p = 0.008; PPN t = 9.2, p < 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Results, second section; Figure 2B and 2E with insets
outcomes.notes: 1 s 40 Hz trains, mean during the train against the 1 s before onset. STN mean 18.89 % dF/F, paired t = 3.86, p = 0.0083, n = 7 (paper t = 3.8, p = 0.008); PPN 6.45 %, t = 9.19, p = 3.7e-05, n = 8 (paper t = 9.2). The 0.25 and 4 s trains also give significant increases (p 1.4e-05 to 0.0066).
deviations: The response window (mean during the train) and pre-stimulus window (same length, before onset) are choices; the paper does not state them.
All seven STN mice have 10 trials per condition, where the Methods state 5.

outcomes.statement: The SNr GABA response scales with stimulation frequency from 5 to 40 Hz (Friedman test on 1 s trains, STN F = 21.0, p = 0.0001; PPN F = 18.2, p = 0.0004).
outcomes.notes: 1 s trains of the frequencies protocol. STN means rise from 4.07 to 32.66 % between 5 and 40 Hz, Friedman 21.00, p = 0.00011, 7 of 7 mice higher at 40 than 5 Hz; PPN 1.57 to 6.10 %, Friedman 18.15, p = 0.00041, 8 of 8 (paper 21.0 and 18.2). A repeated-measures ANOVA variant gives p = 0.014 and 0.0001.
deviations: The conversion code names the STN 1 s block of these mice as 10 mW, while the files and the Methods give 5 mW; the analysis takes the files as they are.

outcomes.statement: A 250 ms 40 Hz train of STN inputs elicits a net increase in SNc pan-DA neuron activity that peaks after stimulus offset (latency to peak 0.50 +/- 0.03 s, mean +/- SEM).
outcomes.notes: With the window fixed in the criterion (peak from onset to 2.25 s) the mean latency is 0.786 s, SEM 0.204, n = 11, outside 0.50 +/- 0.03 s, because two mice peak at 2.03 and 2.24 s. Ten of 11 mice peak after offset and the net response over 0 to 1.25 s is positive (2.89 %, t = 3.28, p = 0.0083). With a window ending at 1.25 s, a variant, the mean latency is 0.492 s, SEM 0.033, the paper's value. The two late-peaking mice (C4217, B8612) have small responses, an early local maximum at 0.41 and 0.62 s, and a slow rise that continues past the window (maximum over 0 to 5 s at 2.97 and 2.78 s), which looks like a late rebound or drift.
deviations: The paper does not give the window in which the peak is sought; the criterion fixed 0 to 2.25 s, and the variant 0 to 1.25 s matches the paper.

outcomes.statement: For SNc pan-DA neurons the STN-evoked response varies with train duration; with 1 and 4 s trains an initial increase is followed by inhibition (Friedman test, F = 13.0, p = 0.005).
outcomes.notes: Means during 0.25, 1 and 4 s trains are 0.52, 0.97 and -3.13 %, n = 11. Reading (a), Friedman over three durations, 13.64, p = 0.0011; reading (b), with the pre-stimulus window as a fourth group, 12.93, p = 0.0048, matching the paper's F = 13.0, p = 0.005; reading (c), area under the curve, p = 0.06. In 4 s trains the first 0.5 s (0.71 %) is above the last 1 s (-5.05 %) in all 11 mice, paired t = 4.81, p = 0.00071.
deviations: The paper's F and p fit four groups while three durations were tested; readings (a) and (b) match, and (b) gives the paper's value.

outcomes.statement: The amplitude of the SNc pan-DA response during STN stimulation does not scale with frequency (Friedman test, F = 4.2, p = 0.24).
outcomes.notes: 1 s trains, Friedman 4.20, p = 0.24, n = 11 (paper F = 4.2, p = 0.24); 40 minus 5 Hz 0.21 % dF/F. Variants with 0.25 s (p = 0.31) and 4 s trains (p = 0.18, 5 mice with all four frequencies) also find no effect.
deviations: The paper does not say which train duration Figure 3D shows; the 1 s train was fixed in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: PPN stimulation also evokes SNc pan-DA responses that vary with train duration (Friedman test, F = 11.5, p = 0.009).
outcomes.notes: Means during 0.25, 1 and 4 s PPN trains are -0.60, 1.03 and 0.70 %, n = 9. Friedman p = 0.26, 0.25 and 0.46 under readings (a) to (c), where the paper reports F = 11.5, p = 0.009. Without the three PPN recordings whose clock could not be shown from the response (C3164, C5007, C5008), n = 6, readings (a) and (b) give p = 0.11 and 0.14.
deviations: The paper's measure for this comparison is not stated; the mean during the train (and the area under the curve) were used, as for the STN comparison, which matches the paper there.

outcomes.statement: The SNc pan-DA response to PPN stimulation does not vary with frequency (repeated-measures one-way ANOVA, F2,15 = 1.35, p = 0.28).
outcomes.notes: 1 s trains, repeated-measures ANOVA F = 1.35 on Greenhouse-Geisser corrected df 1.85 and 14.8, p = 0.29, n = 9 (paper F2,15 = 1.35, p = 0.28); 40 minus 5 Hz 1.30 %. Variants with 0.25 and 4 s trains give p = 0.83 and 0.32.
deviations: The 1 s train was fixed in the criterion, as the paper does not name the duration.

outcomes.statement: STN or PPN stimulation evokes opposite DA release in TS (increase) and DLS (decrease) (two-way ANOVA, striatal site, STN F1,11 = 40.9, PPN F1,16 = 36.4, p < 0.0001; site by time interaction of the same size).
outcomes.notes: GRAB-DA, 1 s 40 Hz trains. STN, TS 12.45 % (6 of 6 above 0), DLS -8.91 % (7 of 7 below 0), site by time interaction F(1, 11) = 40.9, p = 5.1e-05; PPN, TS 11.39 % (9 of 9), DLS -5.75 % (9 of 9), F(1, 16) = 36.4, p = 1.7e-05, the paper's values. The 0.25 and 4 s trains give the same pattern.

outcomes.statement: In TS, the DA increase evoked by either input scales with frequency, for all train durations (STN, repeated-measures ANOVA, 0.25 s F2,8 = 7.5, 1 s F2,7 = 13.6, 4 s F2,9 = 16.9; PPN, Friedman, F = 20.0, 24.0, 23.2).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 4D and 4G; Figure S3C, S3D, S3I and S3J
outcomes.notes: All six tests hold, with the 40 Hz mean above the 5 Hz mean. STN repeated-measures ANOVA F = 7.62, 13.76, 17.31 for 0.25, 1 and 4 s (p = 0.019, 0.0044, 0.0011; paper 7.5, 13.6, 16.9); PPN Friedman 19.80, 24.33, 23.27 (p at most 0.0002; paper 20.0, 24.0, 23.2).

outcomes.statement: In DLS, the DA inhibition scales with frequency and is most prominent at higher frequencies (STN, repeated-measures ANOVA, 0.25 s F = 7.5, 1 s F = 12.8, 4 s F = 46.8; PPN, 0.25 s Friedman F = 12.3, 1 s and 4 s repeated-measures ANOVA F = 12.8 and 10.2).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 4E and 4H; Figure S3E, S3F, S3K and S3L
outcomes.notes: All six tests hold, with the 40 Hz mean below the 5 Hz mean (p below 0.0001 to 0.013). STN 0.25 and 4 s F = 7.89 and 47.23 (paper 7.5, 46.8); PPN 0.25 s Friedman 11.53 (paper 12.3), PPN 1 and 4 s F = 12.98 and 15.92 (paper 12.8, 10.2). STN 1 s gives F = 26.17 where the paper gives F1,11 = 12.8, p = 0.0005, the same F and df it gives for PPN 1 s.

outcomes.statement: Low-frequency (5 Hz) stimulation of either STN or PPN increases DLS dopamine.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure 4E and 4H; Figure S3F and S3L
outcomes.notes: 1 s trains at 5 Hz (Figure 4E and 4H), mean GRAB-DA in DLS during the train, STN 1.51 % (4 of 7 above 0, p = 0.22), PPN 1.40 % (6 of 9, p = 0.13). The sentence also cites Figure S3F and S3L, the 4 s DLS panels; for 4 s trains, a variant, STN 5.41 % (7 of 7, p = 0.00062) and PPN 2.01 % (6 of 9, p = 0.07), one input of two, which would be partially reproduced under that reading. The 1 s after offset is positive in all six conditions (0.96 to 6.76 %).
deviations: The paper does not state the window or test for this observation; the mean during 1 s trains (Figure 4E and 4H) against 0 was fixed in the criterion. The sentence cites both the 1 s panels and the 4 s panels (Figure S3F and S3L), and its account of summation over pulses fits longer trains; under the 4 s reading the effect holds for STN only.

outcomes.statement: In DLS the DA inhibition is followed by a post-stimulus rebound above baseline.
outcomes.notes: After 1 s 40 Hz trains, PPN 4.53 % (8 of 9 above 0, p = 0.017), STN 0.87 % (5 of 7, p = 0.29). After 0.25 and 4 s trains the rebound is significant for both inputs (p 0.0039 to 0.015).
deviations: The rebound window (1 s after offset) and test are choices; the paper gives no statistic.

outcomes.statement: Calcium in DA terminals in TS and DLS shows opposite responses to STN stimulation, as the GRAB-DA recordings do.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth section; Figure S3N and S3O
outcomes.notes: DA terminal GCaMP, 1 s trains, TS 8.96 % (9 of 9 above 0), DLS -4.41 % (7 of 8 below 0), site by time interaction F(1, 15) = 26.2, p = 0.00013. The DLS terminals rebound after offset (6.73 %, 8 of 8 above 0).
deviations: 8 DLS mice, where the paper has 9.

outcomes.statement: Stimulation of STN or PPN inputs increases the activity of Vglut2+ DA neurons in SNc (STN, Wilcoxon, 0.25 s W = 41, p = 0.012, 1 s W = 43, p = 0.008, 4 s W = -5, p = 0.82; PPN, paired t-test, 0.25 s t = 2.9, p = 0.02, 1 s t = 3.4, p = 0.008, 4 s t = 3.0, p = 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, fifth section; Figure 5B, 5C, 5G and 5H; Figure S4A and S4D
outcomes.notes: STN Wilcoxon W = 43 and 43 for 0.25 and 1 s (p = 0.0078 each, n = 9; paper 41 and 43); PPN paired t = 2.89 and 3.42 (p = 0.018 and 0.0076, n = 10; paper 2.9 and 3.4). For 4 s trains STN W = -5, p = 0.82 as in the paper, and PPN t = 2.56, p = 0.031 (paper 3.0, p = 0.01).
deviations: 9 STN mice, where the legend gives 10; the paper's W and p values are the exact values for 9 mice.

outcomes.statement: The Vglut2+ DA neuron increase scales with frequency for short STN trains and for all PPN durations (Friedman, STN 0.25 s F = 15.5, p = 0.001, 1 s F = 5.9, p = 0.11, 4 s F = 7.0, p = 0.07; PPN F = 18.8, 24.8, 20.2, p <= 0.0003).
outcomes.notes: STN 0.25 s Friedman 13.53, p = 0.0036; PPN 0.25, 1 and 4 s 11.23, 17.91, 16.20 (p = 0.011, 0.0005, 0.0010), all with the 40 Hz mean above the 5 Hz mean. STN 1 and 4 s are not significant (p = 0.43 and 0.16), as in the paper (0.11 and 0.07).
deviations: The PPN tests use the 7 of 10 mice that have all four frequencies; C3412, C3798 and C4707 have no 5 Hz trains in the dandiset. The paper's PPN 1 s Friedman statistic of 24.8 needs at least 9 mice (the maximum is 3n), so the paper had 5 Hz trains that are not deposited.

outcomes.statement: In DLS terminals of SNc Anxa1+ neurons, STN and PPN stimulation produce inhibition (STN, 0.25 s t = 6.4, p = 0.0004, 1 s W = -36, p = 0.005, 4 s W = -36, p = 0.008; PPN, 0.25 s t = 3.9, p = 0.004, 1 s W = -55, p = 0.002, 4 s t = 3.8, p = 0.004).
outcomes.source: Results, fifth section; Figure 5L, 5M, 5Q and 5R; Figure S4B and S4E
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds Anxa1 DLS recordings for 5 (STN) and 4 (PPN) mice where the paper has 8 and 10. At these numbers the Wilcoxon tests the paper uses for three of the six conditions cannot reach p < 0.05 (smallest p 0.0625 and 0.125), so reproduced (6 of 6) cannot be reached with the deposited mice. The three t-tests can reach it, so partially reproduced (3 to 5 of 6) was reachable and was not reached; 2 of 6 tests are significant (STN 0.25 s t = -6.14, p = 0.0036; PPN 0.25 s t = -3.46, p = 0.041; PPN 4 s p = 0.13). No STN mouse goes up in any condition, and one PPN mouse in 4 s trains. With the nine recordings without a site suffix added to DLS, a variant, all 6 tests are significant. Its STN 4 s W = -36 (p = 0.0078) is the paper's, but the other two W (-34 and -51 against -36 and -55) and the t values (2.65, 2.47, 2.98 against 6.4, 3.9, 3.8) differ, while the cell-body statistics match closely with the dual mice (p to two digits, t within 0.08). The paper's statistics fix its n; W = -36 and -55 equal -n(n+1)/2 for n = 8 and 10, and t = 6.4 with p = 0.0004 needs 7 df (4 df give p = 0.0031). The DLS recordings of nine of the paper's mice are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The Anxa1+ terminal inhibition scales with frequency (STN, 0.25 s F = 18.0, 1 s F = 15.5, 4 s F = 15.3; PPN, 0.25 s F = 11.5, 1 s F2,15 = 11.0, 4 s F2,18 = 7.2).
outcomes.notes: With the dandiset's DLS recordings (5 STN, 4 PPN mice) 5 of 6 tests hold (p 0.0043 to 0.026, 40 Hz below 5 Hz); PPN 4 s does not (F = 1.95, p = 0.24). With the unsuffixed recordings added, 3 of 6 hold. The paper's F2,15 and F2,18 for PPN 1 and 4 s imply about 8.5 and 10 mice (6.8 to 13.3 with the dfs rounded), against 4 here, so the samples are smaller than the paper's for the reason given under fig5-anxa1-dls-inhibited.
deviations: 5 and 4 mice, where the paper has 8 and 10 (see fig5-anxa1-dls-inhibited).

outcomes.statement: Anxa1+ terminals in DLS show a transient increase in activity at stimulus offset, for both inputs.
outcomes.notes: After 1 s trains, STN 1.02 % (5 of 5 above 0, p = 0.0044), PPN 0.57 % (3 of 4, p = 0.14). The 0.25 and 4 s trains give the same picture (STN p = 0.036 and 0.026, PPN p = 0.20 and 0.11).
deviations: 5 and 4 mice, where the paper has 8 and 10.
The rebound window (1 s after offset) and test are choices; the paper gives no statistic.

outcomes.statement: Anxa1+ SNc cell bodies show stimulation-induced inhibition (paired t-test, STN 0.25 s t = 3.1, 1 s t = 4.0, 4 s t = 7.2, n = 5; PPN t = 4.8, 8.4, 3.3, n = 4) followed by post-stimulus rebound activation.
outcomes.source: Results, fifth section; Figure S4C and S4F
outcomes.notes: With all SNc-labelled recordings (8 STN, 10 PPN mice) 5 of 6 tests show a significant decrease (p 0.0003 to 0.014); STN 0.25 s does not (t = -1.56, p = 0.16). Restricted to the mice with both a DLS and an SNc file (5 and 4, the paper's n), a variant, all 6 are significant with the paper's statistics (t = 3.13, 3.98, 7.26, 4.72, 8.35, 3.33 against 3.1, 4.0, 7.2, 4.8, 8.4, 3.3). The statement's post-stimulus rebound is not seen in the cell bodies after 1 s trains (STN -0.08 %, PPN 0.03 %, p = 0.65 and 0.80; dual mice p = 0.53 and 0.16).
deviations: The dandiset labels 8 and 10 mice as SNc where the paper analysed 5 and 4; the outcome uses the dandiset's labels as fixed in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: Excitatory inputs from STN and PPN activate PD-resilient Vglut2+ DA neurons but inhibit PD-vulnerable Anxa1+ DA neurons.
outcomes.source: Title; Abstract; Results, fifth section; Figure 5
outcomes.notes: 1 s 40 Hz trains. STN, Vglut2 6.54 % against Anxa1 DLS -1.73 % (Welch t = 3.56, p = 0.0066); PPN 9.35 % against -1.48 % (t = 3.90, p = 0.0032). It holds with the unsuffixed Anxa1 recordings added to DLS (p = 0.0097 and 0.005) and against the Anxa1 SNc recordings (p = 0.017 and 0.0065).
deviations: Anxa1 DLS recordings of 5 and 4 mice, where the paper has 8 and 10.

outcomes.statement: In human SNc, TH+ neurons (Mann-Whitney U = 2.0, p = 0.002) and TH+/ANXA1+ neurons (U = 1.0, p < 0.0001) are fewer in PD cases (n = 7) than in controls (n = 12).
outcomes.notes: The human RNAscope counts are not in the dandiset, which holds mouse photometry only. The preprint has no data availability statement, and the dandiset metadata and the conversion repository link no other deposit.

outcomes.statement: Among remaining DA neurons in PD, ANXA1+ neurons are de-enriched to 10 +/- 7% of control, ALDH1A1+ to 41 +/- 12%, while CALB1+ neurons trend toward enrichment (301 +/- 103%).
outcomes.notes: Human tissue counts are not in the dandiset nor in any deposit the paper or the dandiset names (see fig1de-th-anxa1-reduced).

outcomes.statement: TH+/CALB1+ neuron counts are not significantly changed in PD (U = 19.5, p = 0.08) while TH+/ALDH1A1+ counts are reduced (U = 1.0, p < 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure S1B to S1F
outcomes.notes: Human tissue counts are not in the dandiset nor in any deposit the paper or the dandiset names (see fig1de-th-anxa1-reduced).

outcomes.statement: Immunofluorescence confirms fewer TH+ and TH+/ALDH1A1+ neurons and a lower fraction of TH+ neurons expressing ALDH1A1 in PD (n = 11) than in controls (n = 15), and counts agree with RNAscope in four cases processed both ways.
outcomes.source: Results, first section; Figure S1G to S1J
outcomes.notes: Human immunofluorescence counts are not in the dandiset nor in any deposit the paper or the dandiset names (see fig1de-th-anxa1-reduced).

findings.statement: For the Anxa1 mice the dandiset holds DLS terminal recordings for 5 (STN) and 4 (PPN) mice where the paper analyses 8 and 10. Nine mice (C5903, C5906, C5992, C6900, C6902, C7244, C7245, C7248, C7249) have only recordings labelled SNc, without a site suffix in the file name. Their signals resemble SNc recordings, and the paper's cell-body statistics are reproduced closely by the other nine mice's SNc recordings (p to two digits, t within 0.08), so the DLS recordings of these nine mice appear not to be deposited, and the nine SNc recordings were not used in the paper.
The dandiset includes Anxa1 SNc recordings from nine mice that the paper's cell-body analysis (n = 5 and 4) leaves out, and it does not say which recordings the paper used.
The human RNAscope and immunofluorescence counts of Figure 1 and Figure S1 and the histology of Figure S2 are not in the dandiset, and the preprint has no data availability statement.
DA terminals in DLS have 8 mice where Figure S3 gives 9.

The Figure 5 legend gives 10 mice for Vglut2+ neurons with STN stimulation, while the paper's Wilcoxon statistics (W = 41, 43, -5 with p = 0.012, 0.008, 0.82) are the exact values for 9 mice; the dandiset holds 9.
Three Vglut2 PPN mice (C3412, C3798, C4707) have no 5 Hz trains in their frequencies sessions, while the paper's Friedman statistic for PPN 1 s (24.8) needs at least 9 mice with all four frequencies.
Subject C4608 (SNr GABA, PPN) has no 4 s trains in its frequencies session; the conversion notes say they were recorded in a separate session, which is not in the dandiset.

The dF/F series are stated in a.u. but hold percent (100 times (Gc - fit) / fit); a recomputation from the stored signals agrees with a median correlation of 0.9999 (durations) and 0.9988 (frequencies).
Every session start time carries the offset -00:01, the local mean time of London that pytz gives when a time zone is attached with replace; the true offset is lost.
The session description of the frequencies protocol gives an interval of 10 s between trains; the epochs and the Methods give 20 s.
Thirteen mice (SNr GABA and pan-DA, ids starting with B) have 10 trials per condition where the Methods state 5, and 30 mice have 16 s trains that the paper does not mention.
The conversion code names the 1 s block of the STN to SNr GABA frequencies sessions s1s10mW, suggesting 10 mW, while the epoch tables and the Methods give 5 mW.

The conversion repository's Python re-implementation of the dF/F forces the robust fit through the origin, saying the MATLAB version does so, while its own description of the MATLAB scripts includes an intercept.

The files describe the modulation inconsistently. The excitation source descriptions give 465 nm modulated at 210 Hz and 405 nm at 330 Hz, as the Methods do, while the processed series descriptions give the calcium signal as demodulated at 330 Hz and the isosbestic signal at 210 Hz, as the conversion repository's description of the MATLAB scripts does. This attempt did not check which is right against the raw signal.

The file names and session ids of nine Anxa1 mice carry no recording site, and every Anxa1 file lists both an SNc and a DLS fiber in its fiber photometry table, so the site rests on the name of the dF/F series alone.
Eight subject ids are written in lower case (c3015, c3016, c4379, c4708, c4709, c4977, c4978, c5113) while the others are upper case.

The Results give F1,11 = 12.8 for the DLS frequency effect with 1 s trains for both STN (p = 0.0005) and PPN (p = 0.002); F(1, 11) = 12.8 gives p = 0.0043, and the data give F = 26.2 for STN. Two Friedman entries for Anxa1 terminals also do not fit their p-values (F = 11.5 with p = 0.0002, F = 15.5 with p = 0.015; with 3 df these give 0.0093 and 0.0014). F1,11 is also not possible for a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA in 7 or 9 mice. The Figure 5 legend says the Anxa1 STN frequency panels (N, O) show no significant effect of frequency, while the Results report significant effects for all three STN durations.
The lab's MATLAB analysis scripts are not public; the preprint names custom MATLAB code and has no code availability statement. The conversion repository describes them.
The dandiset has no published version; this attempt used the draft as modified on 2026-09-01T15:27:47Z.
