attempts.paper_title: Decoding movie content from neuronal population activity in the human medial temporal lobe
attempts.entry_title: Single units of the human medial temporal lobe during a full-length movie (Gerken, Darcher et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Gerken, Darcher et al. (eLife reviewed preprint 106758, 2025) on dandiset 001616 (SUMMER), which holds 2286 units from 29 patients watching "500 Days of Summer" with 53 frame-wise annotations. It counts units responsive to the onsets of movie features, runs the cluster permutation test by region, and decodes characters, location and cuts with the paper's logistic regression, pooled, per patient, per region and on subsets of units. The paper's LSTM is not run.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Gerken, Darcher et al. (2025) from dandiset 001616
Top-ranked units for decoding Summer (Figure 7)
Responsive units by the dataset code's ZETA test, camera and scene cuts (variant)
Responsive units by the dataset code's ZETA test, character, person and location labels (variant)

outcomes.statement: The data are 2286 single and multi-units from 29 patients (17 female), 30 to 137 units per patient, in the amygdala (580), hippocampus (794), entorhinal cortex (440), parahippocampal cortex (373) and piriform cortex (99).
outcomes.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1d; Patient-wise decoding performance
outcomes.notes: 29 patients, 2286 units and 17 female patients, as stated, with 30 to 137 units per patient. With AH, MH and PH grouped as hippocampus (the dataset's code), the regions hold A 559 (paper 580), H 846 (794), EC 493 (440), PHC 293 (373) and PIC 68 (99), and 27 units lie in FF, LG and PRC. A and H are within 10%; EC, PHC and PIC are not. Every unit's region matches that of its electrode.
deviations: Regions are read from the dandiset's `brain_region` and grouped as in the dataset's code; the paper gives no mapping.

outcomes.statement: Over half of the parahippocampal neurons responded to camera cuts (193 of 373, 51.74%).
outcomes.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons; Figure 2b; Table S1
outcomes.notes: The Methods' test counts 222 of 293 PHC units (75.77%) responsive at alpha 0.001 and 228 (77.82%) at 0.01 (paper 193 of 373, 51.74%). The same test counts 72.35% of PHC units and 68.4% of all units responsive at random event times (69.2% in the per-label check with 884 random times), and all synthetic Poisson units at 2 Hz with 884 random events, so its false-positive rate is far from its alpha and the procedure differs from the paper's. The test compares integer counts in 100 ms bins with the baseline mean per 100 ms across hundreds of trials, which a signed-rank test finds different even without a response. The dataset code's ZETA test (responsive_zeta_cuts.ipynb, all units) is not anticonservative (none of 400 units at random times at alpha 0.001, 1.0% at 0.01) and finds 35 of 293 PHC units (11.95%) at 0.001 and 67 (22.87%) at 0.01, below the paper's fraction; neither test as run here gives the paper's count.
deviations: The responsive-unit test follows the Methods as fixed in the claims file (baseline count over -1000 to 0 ms divided by 10, 19 overlapping 100 ms bins, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, Simes); the Methods do not say more.
The ZETA variant uses 100 resamplings in place of the code's 1000, for time; for PHC units and scene cuts, 1000 resamplings change the counts by 1 and 2 units.
The fraction is compared, as the dandiset's PHC holds 293 units against the paper's 373.

outcomes.statement: Camera cuts evoked responses in a large share of neurons in every region (amygdala 46.90%, entorhinal cortex 45.68%, hippocampus 38.92%).
outcomes.source: Table S1; Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig2b-phc-camera-cuts. The miscalibrated test counts A 73.70%, EC 73.63%, H 64.54% and PHC 75.77% at alpha 0.001 (paper 46.90, 45.68, 38.92, 51.74%), and 62 to 73% of each region at random times. The ZETA test of the dataset's code counts A 3.22%, EC 0.61%, H 1.30% and PHC 11.95% (responsive_zeta_cuts.ipynb).
deviations: The responsive-unit test follows the Methods as fixed in the claims file (baseline count over -1000 to 0 ms divided by 10, 19 overlapping 100 ms bins, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, Simes); the Methods do not say more.

outcomes.statement: Few parahippocampal neurons responded to scene cuts (25 of 373, 6.70%), but the modulation was consistent across the responsive neurons (cluster permutation test, p = 0.018).
outcomes.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons; Figure 2b; Table S1
outcomes.notes: The Methods' test counts 138 of 293 PHC units (47.10%) at alpha 0.001 and 180 (61.43%) at 0.01 (paper 6.70%); with as many random times as there are scene cut onsets it counts 48.25% of all units, so it is miscalibrated. With this split the largest cluster has p = 0.055 with the Methods' z-scoring and p = 0.020 with the code's per-trial z-scoring at alpha 0.001, and there is no cluster at 0.01. The ZETA test finds 12 of 293 (4.10%) at 0.001 and 29 (9.90%) at 0.01, either side of the tolerance of 4.16 to 9.24%; with 1000 resamplings 11 and 31 (responsive_zeta_cuts.ipynb).
deviations: The responsive-unit test follows the Methods as fixed in the claims file (baseline count over -1000 to 0 ms divided by 10, 19 overlapping 100 ms bins, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, Simes); the Methods do not say more.
Cluster p is the fraction of 1000 label permutations whose largest cluster is at least the observed largest cluster; the Methods compare each cluster with the permuted histogram.

outcomes.statement: Only a few neurons responded to the onset of semantic features (Summer 46, Tom 216, Persons 6 and Outdoor 4 of 2286 neurons), in contrast to camera cuts (1025).
outcomes.source: Abstract; Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons; Table S1
outcomes.notes: The test counts 1013 units responsive to Summer and 1174 to Tom at alpha 0.001 (paper 46 and 216), and 9.93 to 51.36% of units for each semantic label. At random times, as many as each label's onsets, it counts about as many (Summer 44.05% against 44.31% at the real onsets, Tom 50.26% against 51.36%), so the counts are dominated by false positives. The code's onset rule (no minimum duration) changes them little (1019 and 1191). The ZETA test of the dataset's code, conservative at random times, counts 11 for Summer and 13 for Tom (responsive_zeta_labels.ipynb), and 79 for camera cuts (paper 1025).
deviations: The responsive-unit test follows the Methods as fixed in the claims file (baseline count over -1000 to 0 ms divided by 10, 19 overlapping 100 ms bins, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, Simes); the Methods do not say more.
Onsets for labels with a duration also last at least 1 s (Results); the code does not require this, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: No neuron responded to the onset of indoor scenes.
outcomes.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons; Table S1
outcomes.notes: The test counts 299 units responsive to Indoor onsets at alpha 0.001 and 810 at 0.01, and 439 for McKenzie and 227 for Summer Presence at 0.001, where Table S1 has 0; with 44 random times in place of the Indoor onsets it counts 11.46% of units. An absence cannot be judged with this test. The paper's test as written is the one run here; the alpha of 0.001 is that of the Results paragraph making the claim. The ZETA test of the dataset's code, which is not the paper's test, counts 2 Indoor units at 0.001 (responsive_zeta_labels.ipynb).
deviations: The responsive-unit test follows the Methods as fixed in the claims file (baseline count over -1000 to 0 ms divided by 10, 19 overlapping 100 ms bins, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, Simes); the Methods do not say more.

outcomes.statement: By the cluster permutation test, parahippocampal neurons responded to the largest set of features (Summer, Persons, Camera Cuts, Scene Cuts, Outdoor), compared with the hippocampus (Tom, Camera Cuts, Outdoor), the amygdala (Camera Cuts) and the entorhinal cortex (none).
outcomes.notes: The responsive and non-responsive split comes from the miscalibrated test. With it, 11 of 32 cells agree with the paper at alpha 0.001 and 12 at 0.01; camera cuts give no cluster in any region (p = 1.000), and at 0.001 PHC has 6 significant labels against 7 in H.
deviations: The responsive-unit test follows the Methods as fixed in the claims file (baseline count over -1000 to 0 ms divided by 10, 19 overlapping 100 ms bins, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, Simes); the Methods do not say more.

outcomes.statement: Thresholding the activity of single neurons does not reliably predict whether Summer is on screen; most neurons perform near chance, below the population decoder.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding from neuronal activity; Figure 3b; Methods, Single-neuron decoding performance
outcomes.notes: Median unit kappa for Summer 0.0076 over 2286 units; 89.8% below 0.05; best unit 0.276 (patient 7, amygdala); no unit reaches 0.31 or the pooled logistic regression (0.301).
deviations: The threshold and its direction are searched over 50 quantiles of each unit's window counts on the validation set; the Methods say only that the best threshold was chosen on the validation set.

outcomes.statement: A logistic regression on spike counts decodes characters and location about as well as the LSTM; pooled over patients it reaches kappa 0.28 for Summer and 0.31 for Indoor/Outdoor.
outcomes.source: Results, Choice of architecture and Patient-wise decoding performance; Figure 3c; Figure 4a
outcomes.notes: Pooled logistic regression, mean over 5 folds, Summer 0.301 (SEM 0.056), Indoor/Outdoor 0.359 (SEM 0.049), both within tolerance of 0.28 and 0.31; Tom 0.218, McKenzie 0.324 and Persons 0.410 reach the LSTM values less their SEM. Test-label shuffles give p = 0.001 in every fold for Summer, McKenzie, Persons and Indoor/Outdoor; one Tom fold has kappa 0.002 (p = 0.45). Over the C grid the test kappa ranges from 0.266 to 0.311 (Summer) and from 0.349 to 0.393 (Indoor/Outdoor). With Summer labels shifted by 300 s the kappa is 0.015.
deviations: Class weights balanced in place of oversampling the minority class.
C chosen on the validation kappa from 0.001, 0.003, 0.01 and 0.03; the Methods do not give the range.
The fold layout is that of the dataset's code with the 1.6 s window added to the 32 s gap, which gives the paper's sample counts (30822, 7194, 7194 against 30800, 7200, 7200).
The 0.28 for Summer is the pooled value of Figure 4; the paper does not state the Figure 3c logistic regression values in numbers.

outcomes.statement: For scene and camera cuts the logistic regression performs below the LSTM, by 0.1 and 0.07, that is about kappa 0.10 and 0.11.
outcomes.source: Results, Choice of architecture; Figure 3c; Table S2
outcomes.notes: Scene Cuts 0.0771 (SEM 0.027) and Camera Cuts 0.0961 (SEM 0.020), within tolerance of 0.10 and 0.11 (Camera Cuts by 0.001 above the lower bound of 0.095) and below the LSTM's 0.20 and 0.18. Camera Cuts are above chance in every fold (p = 0.001); one Scene Cuts fold is not (kappa -0.008, p = 0.89).
deviations: Scene cut labels are extended to 520 ms after the cut, as the Methods state for camera cuts.
The expected values are derived from the stated drops (0.1, 0.07) and the LSTM values of Table S2.

outcomes.statement: Without temporal gaps between training, validation and test samples, decoding of Summer is almost perfect (kappa 0.99), and it falls to 0.31 as the gap grows to 32 s.
outcomes.source: Results, Avoiding spurious decoding performance; Figure 3e; Figure S9
outcomes.notes: Summer with a random split 0.948 (5 draws, 0.942 to 0.953); with gaps of 4, 8, 16 and 32 s 0.555, 0.524, 0.451 and 0.301. The LSTM values held in the dataset's code are 0.987, 0.584, 0.539, 0.429 and 0.309.
deviations: Logistic regression in place of the LSTM.
Gaps other than 32 s use the dataset's code table of repeated parts per gap.

outcomes.statement: Decoding from a single patient's neurons is lower than from the pooled population; no patient matches the pooled performance, for Summer, Scene Cuts or Indoor/Outdoor.
outcomes.notes: No patient reaches the pooled kappa. Summer best patient 7 at 0.268 against 0.301 (median 0.060); Scene Cuts patient 20 at 0.043 against 0.077 (median 0.010); Indoor/Outdoor patient 2 at 0.256 against 0.359 (median 0.099). By the test-label shuffle 5, 5 and 12 patients are above chance (p = 0.001) in all five folds for the three labels.

outcomes.statement: For Summer, patients 7, 10, 15 and 22 exceed kappa 0.2; for Indoor/Outdoor, patients 2, 13, 20 and 25 exceed 0.2.
outcomes.source: Results, Patient-wise decoding performance; Figure 4b and 4d
outcomes.notes: 7 of 8 named pairs exceed 0.2; Summer patients 7 (0.268), 10 (0.227), 22 (0.241), and 15 at 0.197, each above chance in all five folds; Indoor/Outdoor patients 2 (0.256), 13 (0.210), 20 (0.217), 25 (0.201). For Scene Cuts three of the paper's patients (20, 19, 2) are among the four best here, and patient 10 is fifth.
deviations: Assumes the dandiset's subject ids are the paper's patient numbers; neither gives a mapping, and the Figure 4 legend gives no unit counts per patient to compare. The agreement of the named patients supports this.

outcomes.statement: Decoding from single regions depends on the feature; the amygdala is best and the hippocampus worst for Summer, and the parahippocampal cortex is best and the amygdala worst for Indoor/Outdoor.
outcomes.source: Results, Parahippocampal cortex drives decoding; Amygdala drives decoding; Figure 5
outcomes.notes: Summer A 0.291, EC 0.149, PHC 0.096, H 0.068, so A highest and H lowest hold. Indoor/Outdoor PHC 0.357, H 0.302, A 0.122, EC 0.117, so PHC highest holds; A is not lowest, though A and EC differ by less than their SEMs (0.041, 0.052). 3 of 4 orderings hold. Six region folds have test-shuffle p above 0.05 (A Indoor/Outdoor, EC Summer, EC Indoor/Outdoor and PHC Summer once each, H Summer twice).
deviations: Logistic regression in place of the LSTM.
Regions as stored in the dandiset, which hold different units from the paper's (PHC 293 against 373).

outcomes.statement: Face labels decode slightly better than character labels (Summer 0.33, Tom 0.27), and Summer Presence (0.27) is decoded best from the amygdala (0.26).
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in character's visual appearances; Figure 5b and 5c
outcomes.notes: One of three conditions holds. Summer Presence is decoded best from the amygdala (0.292; PHC 0.132, EC 0.110, H 0.103; pooled 0.234). Face labels decode worse than the character labels, Summer Faces 0.217 against Summer 0.301 and Tom Faces 0.167 against Tom 0.218 (paper LSTM 0.33 against 0.31 and 0.27 against 0.23). Every fold of the three labels is above chance (p = 0.001). The face labels keep as negatives the frames the Methods exclude, which may lower their kappa; the dandiset does not mark those frames, so this cannot be checked.
deviations: Logistic regression in place of the LSTM; the criterion was written after the first verification round, before these labels were decoded.
Face labels keep the frames the Methods exclude (a face neither shown nor clearly absent) as negatives.

outcomes.statement: Responsive neurons drive decoding of camera cuts but not of Summer; without them, Summer is decoded about as well as from all neurons while camera cuts drop the most, and responsive neurons alone decode camera cuts about as well as all neurons but Summer less well.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding with non-responsive versus responsive neurons; Figure 6
outcomes.notes: Depends on the responsive sets of the miscalibrated test (1013 units for Summer, 1616 for Camera Cuts at alpha 0.001). With them three of four conditions hold; Summer 0.294 without responsive units, 0.256 with them only (condition b needs below 0.251), 0.301 complete; Camera Cuts 0.115 with responsive units only, 0.013 without, 0.096 complete. Size-matched non-responsive sets give 0.262 to 0.300 for Summer; none can be drawn for Camera Cuts (670 non-responsive units). 548 of those 670 spike in fewer than a third of the pseudo-trials and get p = 1 untested; the 122 that spike give 0.034, a drop of 0.062, against 0.060 for the 730 active non-responsive units of Summer.
deviations: Logistic regression in place of the LSTM, over all regions together.

outcomes.statement: Across the five rankings of neurons by logistic regression weights for Summer, the top 500 neurons share 78 neurons, against about 1 expected by chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Top-ranked neurons; Figure 7b; Methods, Intersection of top-performing neurons
outcomes.notes: 95 units are common to the top 500 of the five rankings, against 78 (tolerance 70.2 to 85.8) and a chance level of 1.14 by the paper's formula (1.12 simulated), 83 times chance. No unit in a top 500 was tied at zero; ties by unit index give the same 95. Chance values for 100, 350, 750 and 1000 (0.00, 0.19, 8.69, 36.6) match the paper's (0, 0, 9, 37), so the chance computation agrees; observed overlaps are 20, 65, 156 and 252.
deviations: The four sub-splits of a test fold take each of the other four folds once as validation; the Methods say only that they alternate training and validation data.
The Methods average the absolute coefficients 'across the five splits' within a set of four models; the mean over the four models is used.

outcomes.statement: Decoding Summer from the 500 top-ranked neurons gives the peak performance (kappa 0.38), above that of the full population.
outcomes.source: Results, Training on pre-selections of top-ranked neurons; Figure 7a
outcomes.notes: With the logistic regression and nested averaging over the 20 sub-splits, the top 500 units give kappa 0.375 against 0.357 for all 2286 units, a difference of 0.018, less than the SEMs (0.026, 0.029). The peak is at 229 units (0.394), with 150 units at 0.389 and the top 23 at 0.341. Every fit is above chance (p = 0.001). The paper's LSTM peaks at 0.38 with 500 units.
deviations: Logistic regression in place of the LSTM; the criterion was written after the first verification round, before any fit on top-ranked units.
Sizes of 23, 114, 150, 229, 500, 750, 1000, 1500 and 2286 units; the paper does not list its sizes besides 500 and 150.

outcomes.statement: An LSTM decodes every label above chance from the pooled population, with kappa 0.36 for Persons, 0.31 for Indoor/Outdoor, 0.31 for Summer, 0.32 for McKenzie, 0.23 for Tom, 0.20 for Scene Cuts and 0.18 for Camera Cuts.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding from neuronal activity; Figure 3c; Table S2
outcomes.notes: The LSTM's code is not in the paper's materials, the dataset's GitHub repository (commit 59fc242) or its Zenodo archive, which hold a two-layer linear baseline; the Methods choose layers, hidden sizes, batch size, learning rate, weight decay and dropout per label without stating them. Training 700 epochs per label and fold on a CPU would also exceed the time limit; this was not tried. The logistic regression results are under fig3c-logreg-characters-location and fig3c-logreg-cuts-lower.

outcomes.statement: Shuffling the order of time bins in the test data lowers the LSTM's performance, most for visual transitions.
outcomes.notes: Needs the trained LSTM; see fig3c-lstm-decoding. The logistic regression on window sums does not see the order of the 20 bins, so it cannot stand in.

findings.statement: The units' `brain_region` gives A 559, hippocampus 846 (AH 418, MH 16, PH 412), EC 493, PHC 293 and PIC 68 units, and 27 in FF, LG and PRC, where the paper reports A 580, H 794, EC 440, PHC 373 and PIC 99 for the same 2286 units. Neither the dandiset nor the paper maps one assignment to the other, so the paper's region analyses cannot be repeated on the paper's regions.
Spike times in the units table are in milliseconds (its description says so), where NWB requires seconds; the watchlogs' recording times are also in milliseconds.
The start and stop columns of `annotations_patient_aligned` are described as seconds but hold milliseconds of the recording clock, as the table's own description says.

The face labels (summer-faces, tom-faces and others) hold only 0 and 1. The Methods define face labels with frames excluded when a face is neither shown nor clearly absent; those frames cannot be identified.

Published version 0.260519.1133 holds 57 files, the 29 of the later version and 28 older copies (`ses-1_behavior+ecephys`) with the same units and spike times, one per patient except patient 3. Version 0.260702.0824 holds each recording once.

The dataset's code identifies responsive units with the ZETA test (zetapy; alpha 0.01 in its notebook), where the Methods describe a bin-wise Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Simes correction. With ZETA, 79 units respond to camera cuts at alpha 0.001 (Table S1 1025), 11 to Summer (46) and 13 to Tom (216), and 11.95% of PHC units to camera cuts (51.74%).

The responsive-unit test as the Methods describe it (spike counts in 19 bins of 100 ms against the baseline count per 100 ms, signed-rank across pseudo-trials, Simes) counts 68% of units responsive at random event times on this data with 884 events, and 10 to 55% with as many as each label's onsets, so the procedure behind Figure 2 and Table S1 cannot be recovered from the text. The ZETA test of the dataset's code does not give the paper's counts either. The paper's LSTM code and its per-label hyperparameters are not published.
The threshold for responsive units is alpha 0.01 in the Methods and 0.001 in the Results, the Figure 2 legend and Table S1; the cluster test section splits units at p 0.01.
The Results give the 29 patients' ages as 22 to 63; the Methods give 19 to 62 for all 46 patients recorded. The dandiset's 29 patients are 19 to 62.
The dandiset has 958 camera cuts in the 83-minute film, one every 5.25 s; the supplement says one every 3 s.

The training code of the dataset's repository (ML_framework/nwb_loading/nwb_loading.py, get_unit_ids_for_patient_nwb) compares `brain_region` with the region group name in place of its subregions; no unit is labelled `H`, so asking for the hippocampus selects no unit.

Neither the dandiset nor the paper states that subject ids are the paper's patient numbers. Taking them as such, the patients the paper names in Figure 4 are among the best here (7 of 8 above kappa 0.2).

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper's full text. The verifier listed the version's assets, and tested wilcoxon_simes, split, kappa, ranking, threshold_unit and the L1 setting of fit_logreg on synthetic inputs.

disagreements.reason: LSTM claim. The summer-presence, summer-faces and tom-faces labels are in the files (0/1 only), so a logistic regression stand-in for the orderings could have been tested, as was done for fig5-region-decoding. Its list of problems marks this block as affecting a conclusion.

The Results compare the full-population value with the LSTM's 0.31, which suggests an LSTM, but the Methods describe the 20-split logistic regression. The 20 sub-split fits and rankings already exist, so a logistic regression stand-in on the top-k units was cheap to run. Its list of problems marks this block as affecting a conclusion, and it asked for kappa on the top-k units (k = 100 to 2286) with nested averaging over the 20 sub-splits.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The full executed notebooks of the revision (the main notebook, top_ranked_units.ipynb, responsive_zeta_cuts.ipynb and responsive_zeta_labels.ipynb) with their conclusions and summary, the helper module, the claims file, the README and this record.

attempts.paper_title: Primary motor cortex of the parkinsonian monkey: altered neuronal responses to muscle stretch
attempts.entry_title: M1 responses to muscle stretch in the parkinsonian monkey (Pasquereau and Turner 2013)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Pasquereau and Turner (2013) on dandiset 001636, which holds single-unit recordings from M1 of two monkeys before and after MPTP, with torque perturbations, joint angle and EMG. Only monkey V can be tested, as the monkey L files mark no perturbation. The notebook checks the cells, resting rates and antidromic latencies, detects torque responses, and compares the torque-evoked movements and triceps EMG before and after MPTP.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Pasquereau and Turner (2013) from dandiset 001636

outcomes.statement: In monkey V, 112 neurons were studied before MPTP and 159 after, of which 49 and 54 were PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs; three neurons in all were activated from both the peduncle and the putamen.
outcomes.source: Supplementary table (monkey V); Results, Database; Table 1
outcomes.notes: Monkey V units with at least 5 perturbations of each direction number 112 before and 159 after MPTP, with 49 and 54 PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs, exactly the supplementary table's counts. The files hold 3 units activated from both the peduncle and the putamen, all in monkey V and all among the cells studied. Dropping the two unit copies found in repeated files gives 53 post-MPTP PTNs.
deviations: The paper's location and isolation criteria cannot be applied; the units in the dandiset are taken as the selected units, which the matching counts support.

outcomes.statement: In monkey L, 57 of 115 neurons before MPTP and 35 of 73 after responded to torque perturbations of the wrist, and the monkey L responses enter all pooled results.
outcomes.notes: No monkey L (Leu) file marks a torque perturbation; torque_perturbation_type is "none" and the onset NaN in every Leu trial. The Leu torque command is NaN in all 98 pre-MPTP files with analog data, and 15 of 51 post-MPTP Leu files have no analog data. The joint moves by more than 2 deg in the hold window in 15% (pre) and 1% (post) of Leu trials, against 66 to 86% of monkey V perturbed trials. The 35 post-MPTP Leu files with a torque command show 91 to 413 command excursions per file, starting a median 0.31 to 0.84 s after the lateral target appears, during the active movement; one of their 2048 trials has an excursion starting in the hold window. In monkey V such an excursion starts in the hold window in 1811 and 3563 trials, against 1862 and 3649 labelled perturbations. The perturbations may exist in the lab's source files; they are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Before torque onset, the firing rate of M1 neurons was lower after MPTP, because PTN rates fell (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001) while CSN rates did not change (p = 0.5). In monkey V the rates were 12.6 and 8.9 spikes/s for all cells, 20.3 and 14.8 for PTNs, and 3.5 and 3.4 for CSNs, before and after MPTP.
outcomes.notes: All six monkey V means are within tolerance. PTN rates are lower after MPTP (Mann-Whitney p = 0.034), CSN rates do not differ (p = 0.73), and the M1 rate is lower (p = 0.0033, below the paper's 0.05/2). The statement's p < 0.001 for PTNs, from both monkeys, is not reached in monkey V alone.
deviations: Monkey V only.
The baseline is the mean SDF over the 500 ms before onset over all perturbation trials, a reading of the Methods.

outcomes.statement: Before MPTP, PTNs fired much faster than CSNs at rest (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: Pre-MPTP monkey V PTNs 18.03 spikes/s (n = 49), CSNs 3.42 (n = 31), Mann-Whitney p = 1.3e-11. The paper's pooled means differ between its text (16.3 and 3.6) and Table 1 (18.3 and 3.2).
deviations: Monkey V only.

outcomes.statement: PTN antidromic latencies did not change after MPTP (1.9 ms, p = 0.9), while CSN latencies were longer (5.1 against 6.1 ms, p < 0.05/3).
outcomes.notes: The four means are within tolerance and PTN latencies do not differ (p = 0.54). CSN latencies are longer after MPTP with p = 0.018, just above the paper's 0.05/3 = 0.0167, so one test fails. With every monkey L PTN and CSN unit added (their selection by perturbations cannot be made), p = 0.0071 for CSNs and 0.91 for PTNs, and the post-MPTP CSN mean (7.01 ms) is outside tolerance. 18 PTNs and CSNs studied have no antidromic latency.
deviations: Monkey V cells studied, against expected values that pool both monkeys.

outcomes.statement: The detection threshold, p < 0.01 divided by 5 independent comparisons, holds the chance of a false response over the 200 ms epoch near 0.01.
outcomes.notes: The analysis ran. At a pseudo onset 600 ms before the torque, a threshold crossing in the 200 ms epoch occurs in 0.22 of the 542 monkey V cell-directions with the main detection and 0.46 with the t-test variant; unperturbed trials taken at the usual torque time give 0.19 and 0.45. A response with onset in 20 to 60 ms occurs in 0.044 (pseudo onset) and 0.047 (unperturbed trials), against 0.37 at the true onset. The paper's threshold implies 0.01; the rates here are about 20 times higher, so the procedure differs from the paper's in a way the Methods do not settle (how the SDF values are compared with the baseline, and any minimum duration), and this claim and those that rest on the selection are blocked. Stationary Poisson spike trains at each cell-direction's baseline rate give 0.15 (main) and 0.49 (t-test), so most of the excess comes from the detection procedure, though about a third of the observed 0.22 is not explained by the Poisson trains, and the rate does not fall with baseline rate (0.17 to 0.27 by quartile) or number of trials (0.21 to 0.24). The pseudo-onset rate of responses is 0.12 of the true-onset rate. 14 cell-directions (10 CSN) have no baseline spike and cannot respond. A threshold calibrated to a pseudo-onset rate of 0.01 (t = 6.67 against 3.11) finds 30.4% and 32.7% of M1 cells torque-related. Whether the paper's procedure differs or its stated rate does not hold cannot be told from this analysis.
deviations: The detection compares the trial-averaged SDF with mean +/- t * SD of its baseline values, a reading of the Methods; a t-test across trials is shown as a variant.

A response's onset is its first crossing within 20 to 60 ms; the Methods define the onset as the first crossing, so a variant takes the first crossing anywhere in 0 to 200 ms (6 of 202 responses have an earlier crossing).

outcomes.statement: In monkey V, 84 of 112 M1 neurons (75%) were torque-related before MPTP and 108 of 159 (68%) after; for PTNs 27 of 49 (55%) and 37 of 54 (68%); for CSNs 14 of 31 (45%) and 10 of 48 (21%).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is (false-positive-rate). The analysis finds 61 of 112 and 75 of 159 monkey V cells torque-related (54.5% and 47.2%, paper 75% and 68%), PTNs 71.4% and 66.7%, CSNs 16.1% and 16.7%; only the post-MPTP PTN value is within tolerance. The t-test variant gives 39.3% and 59.7% for M1, the calibrated threshold 30.4% and 32.7%, and taking the first crossing anywhere in 0 to 200 ms as the onset 52.7% and 46.5%.

outcomes.statement: MPTP did not change the fraction of torque-related neurons, in M1, in PTNs or in CSNs (chi-square, p > 0.05/3).
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP; Figure 3A
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. With the main detection the paper's test finds no change in M1 (-7.3 points, p = 0.29), PTNs (-4.8 points, p = 0.76) or CSNs (+0.5 points, p = 1.0). The t-test variant finds increases in M1 (+20.5 points, p = 0.0014) and PTNs (+25.3 points, p = 0.016), both below 0.05/3.

outcomes.statement: PTNs responded to torque more often than CSNs (68% against 31% over both monkeys, chi-square 32.3, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, prevalence; Figure 3A
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. PTNs 71 of 103 (68.9%) against CSNs 13 of 79 (16.5%), chi-square 47.5, p = 5.6e-12; both fractions are outside tolerance (PTNs above 62.1 +/- 6.2, CSNs below 30.4 +/- 3.0). The t-test variant gives 60.2% and 32.9% (p = 0.00046).

outcomes.statement: About half of the torque-related cells (124 of 284, 44%) responded to only one direction of rotation.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. 70 of 136 torque-related cells (51.5%) respond to one direction only (59.0% pre, 45.3% post); the t-test variant gives 63.3%.

outcomes.statement: Most torque responses were increases in firing (86% of M1 responses before and 88% after MPTP; 70% and 75% for PTNs), and MPTP did not change the PTN balance (chi-square 0.1, p = 0.7).
outcomes.source: Table 1; Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Increases are 82.6% and 76.7% of M1 responses and 68.1% and 59.3% of PTN responses; the PTN balance does not change (chi-square 0.53, p = 0.47). The paper's Table 1 marks its CSN change p < 0.01, but its own counts (23 of 24 against 19 of 22) give p = 0.54 with the Yates-corrected chi-square test that reproduces its other values.

outcomes.statement: The magnitude of torque responses did not differ before and after MPTP, for M1 cells or for PTNs, by any of three measures (mean change, maximum change, area; Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Mann-Whitney, all p > 0.15).
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP; Figure 4A
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. With the main detection, responses are smaller after MPTP; 11 of the 12 tests (directions pooled) have p < 0.05, for example M1 maximum change 43.7 against 32.4 spikes/s (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 0.0017) and PTN mean change 23.4 against 15.4 (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0001).

outcomes.statement: In monkey V, the mean response magnitudes were 42.4 and 37.9 spikes/s for M1 flexion responses, 50.9 and 42.6 for M1 extension responses, 33.4 and 26.1 for PTN flexion and 38.8 and 29.3 for PTN extension responses, before and after MPTP.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Under reading (a), maximum change, the four pre-MPTP means are within tolerance and none of the post-MPTP ones; readings (b) and (c) match 1 and 0 of 8.

outcomes.statement: Response latencies were shorter after MPTP for M1 cells and for PTNs, for flexion and extension (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, all p < 0.05). In monkey V the means were 39.2 and 34.6 ms (M1 flexion), 40.4 and 33.4 ms (M1 extension), 43.9 and 35.5 ms (PTN flexion) and 44.4 and 36.7 ms (PTN extension), before and after MPTP.
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP; Figure 4B; supplementary table
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. With the main detection all four comparisons are shorter after MPTP (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 0.0086, 0.0048, 0.022, 0.0023) and all eight means are within tolerance; pooled, M1 responses 41.8 and 35.9 ms and PTN responses 45.0 and 37.8 ms (earliest per cell 40.9 and 34.7, 44.2 and 35.4). The t-test variant finds no significant shortening (p 0.27 to 0.87).

outcomes.statement: The latency shortening was not a history effect; latencies did not correlate with the days of training (monkey V Spearman |rho| = 0.02, p = 0.85).
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Over both states latency correlates with the recording day (Spearman rho = -0.26, p = 0.0022, n = 136), as post-MPTP sessions come later and have shorter latencies; within each state it does not (rho = 0.11, p = 0.42; rho = -0.15, p = 0.21).

outcomes.statement: Torque-evoked increases in PTN firing were briefer after MPTP; the FWHM fell from 73 to 50 ms over both monkeys (Mann-Whitney, p < 0.05 for each direction). In monkey V the PTN FWHM was 97 and 52 ms for flexion and 57 and 41 ms for extension, before and after MPTP.
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP; supplementary table
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. PTN increases are briefer after MPTP for flexion (p = 0.039) but not for extension (p = 0.39); over all PTN responses the means are 97.4 and 52.3 ms for flexion and 56.9 and 60.7 ms for extension.

outcomes.statement: Directional selectivity fell after MPTP; reciprocal and unidirectional responses became less common and bidirectional and non-directional ones more common (by about 10% of torque-related M1 cells; chi-square 22.2, p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Reciprocal and unidirectional cells fall from 59.0% to 52.0% of torque-related cells (-7.0 points), chi-square 6.26 (3 dof), p = 0.10. For PTNs they fall from 65.7% to 50.0% (p = 0.015). With categories set from the DSI value as the paper words them, 62.3% and 50.7% (p = 0.42). There is no reciprocal cell before MPTP; the smallest expected count is 2.2.
deviations: Categories are set from which directions respond and their signs, as fixed in the claims file; the paper words them by DSI value. The DSI value reading is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: In monkey V the mean DSI of torque-related cells was 0.72 and 0.66 for M1, 0.73 and 0.75 for PTNs and 0.81 and 0.83 for CSNs, before and after MPTP.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Three of six means are within tolerance (PTN pre and both CSN values).

outcomes.statement: The loss of selectivity was not due to resting rates, as pre-torque rates did not differ between directional categories (one-way ANOVA, F = 0.77, p = 0.46).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Baseline rates do not differ between the four categories (F = 0.58, p = 0.63) or three groups (F = 0.69, p = 0.50).

outcomes.statement: After MPTP, torque-induced displacements were slower and smaller; mean peak velocity fell by 16.2% and amplitude by 6.6% (ANOVA, F > 515 and F > 49).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP; Figure 1
outcomes.notes: Over 294 monkey V sessions (repeated files left out), torque-induced movements are faster and larger after MPTP; session-mean peak velocity +28.8% and amplitude +15.2% (flexion +30.3% and +12.0%), MPTP F = 103 and 26, p < 0.0001. The torque command's pulse is about four times larger in most post-MPTP sessions; in the sessions with the same command size (43 pre, 12 post) the increases are +101.9% and +113.4%. The mean of the session-mean peak velocities is 58.7 deg/s, and only one response comes from a session in the paper's 130 to 200 deg/s window of matched sessions; mean displacements (3.09 deg) are smaller than its 10 deg. The angle's scale agrees with the files' own kinematic columns (active movements measured here within 2% of derived_peak_velocity and derived_movement_amplitude), so the small movements are in the data. The torque command differs between the states, so the change cannot be attributed to MPTP.
deviations: Monkey V only; the paper's ANOVA has animal as a third factor.
The peak velocity and amplitude windows (0 to 200 and 0 to 300 ms) and the FIR length are choices; the Methods give the filter and velocity threshold only.
Perturbations with the joint moving before onset (490 of 5413) are kept.

outcomes.statement: The latency of torque-induced displacements did not change after MPTP (F < 0.2, p > 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP; Figure 1
outcomes.notes: Movement onset is earlier after MPTP (session means 9.8 and 3.2 ms for flexion, 11.0 and 6.0 ms for extension; MPTP F = 1032, p < 0.0001), with an MPTP by direction interaction (F = 19.1; the paper reports F > 94). In sessions with the same command size it does not differ (7.81 and 7.73 ms, p = 0.79). The zero-phase filter can move an onset earlier, and 219 of 5413 perturbations have a latency of 0 ms. With a causal 10 ms average of the unfiltered velocity the session means are 12.6 to 18.6 ms and still shorter after MPTP (F = 781); without the trials already moving before onset F = 1037 (filtered) and 743 (causal). At the middle command size the causal variant gives p = 0.25, and 0.026 without the trials moving before onset. The difference goes with the torque command, so it cannot be attributed to MPTP.
deviations: Monkey V only.
Zero-phase (forward and backward) filtering; the Methods do not say how the filter was applied.

outcomes.statement: The long-latency (m2, 41 to 80 ms) EMG response of the stretched triceps was larger after MPTP (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP; Figure 2
outcomes.notes: For flexion torques the m2 response is larger after MPTP in both triceps longus channels and the triceps lateralis (medians 3.0 against 164.2, 3.1 against 297.5 and 5.2 against 76.2 A/D units; Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 1.1e-58, 1.9e-50, 4.7e-15). The increase follows the torque command; median m2 is 0.61 at the smallest command size (pre only), 40.8 (pre) and 1.81 (post) at the middle, and 17.09 (pre, n = 5) and 194.6 (post) at the largest, so within a state it does not rise simply with command size, and in the middle-size sessions m2 is not larger after MPTP (triceps longus 1 median 46.7 against 1.3, p = 0.013, with 40 and 6 sessions). The outcome is the criterion's comparison; as the torque command is about four times larger in most post-MPTP sessions, the increase cannot be attributed to MPTP.
deviations: EMG in A/D units; the paper reports microvolts.

outcomes.statement: The total duration of EMG responses to torque increased after MPTP, from 57 +/- 6 to 79 +/- 3 ms (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP; Figure 2
outcomes.notes: Responses last longer after MPTP (24.5 against 50.4 ms, Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 1.8e-39, 283 and 281 channel-sessions), but both means are outside tolerance (57 +/- 6 and 79 +/- 3); thresholds of 1.5 and 3 SD give 16.4 against 48.5 and 17.3 against 49.5 ms. At the middle command size they do not differ (28.4 and 27.9 ms, p = 0.96). Before MPTP 63.6% of the durations are 10 ms or less (median 9 ms, against 59 ms after).
deviations: The response threshold (2 SD of the baseline) and the pooling of three triceps channels are choices; the Methods cite an earlier paper for the EMG analysis.

outcomes.statement: The latency of the earliest EMG responses did not change after MPTP (p > 0.05).
outcomes.notes: EMG responses start earlier after MPTP (40.8 against 24.0 ms, Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 5.5e-21), in the same direction at 1.5 and 3 SD. At the middle command size the onsets do not differ (28.8 and 45.6 ms, p = 0.18), the post-MPTP onset being the later one there.
deviations: The paper does not name its test here; the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test it uses for the other EMG measures is used.

outcomes.statement: The short-latency m1 component (15 to 40 ms) was poorly formed and generally much smaller than the m2 component.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP; Figure 2
outcomes.notes: After MPTP, m2 exceeds m1 in 96.5% of 282 channel-sessions, median m1 / m2 0.22 (0.23 over channel-sessions with m2 > 0). Before MPTP the median ratio is 0.10 (0.09 with m2 > 0) but m2 exceeds m1 in 73.5% of 310, below the criterion's 75%.

outcomes.statement: In sessions with equivalent torque-induced velocities (130 to 200 deg/s), MPTP did not change the magnitude of responses (Mann-Whitney, p = 0.19 for flexion and 0.46 for extension, with 24 and 33 flexion and 22 and 31 extension responses).
outcomes.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP; Supplementary Figure 1
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Also, only one response comes from a session whose mean peak velocity is between 130 and 200 deg/s (session means reach 145.3 deg/s), so the matched groups cannot be formed on this velocity scale.

outcomes.statement: Across sessions, the mean PTN response latency did not correlate with the peak velocity of the torque-induced movement (|rho| < 0.18) or with the m2 EMG response (|rho| < 0.26; Spearman, p > 0.05 with threshold 0.05/4).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as the selection is. Over 67 sessions mean PTN latency against mean peak velocity gives rho = -0.22, p = 0.080; against triceps longus 1 m2 (64 sessions) rho = -0.32, p = 0.011, below the paper's 0.0125. Within each state neither correlates (p 0.36 to 0.997).

outcomes.statement: Trial by trial, PTN response latencies did not correlate with the peak velocity or the m2 EMG response (Spearman |rho| < 0.34, p > 0.05).
outcomes.notes: The Methods define response onset on the trial-averaged SDF and give no single-trial latency, which the test needs. No analysis code is published.

findings.statement: The monkey L (Leu) files mark no torque perturbation; torque_perturbation_type is "none" in every Leu trial, the Leu torque command is NaN in every pre-MPTP file, and 15 of 51 post-MPTP Leu files have no analog data. The monkey L half of the paper (115 and 73 cells, and its EMG and kinematics) cannot be tested.

The analog streams (ElbowAngle, ElbowTorque, ElbowVelocity, EMG) are not on the clock of the trials table and spikes. The conversion lays each trial's analog samples end to end by sample count, while trials and spikes use the behavioural trial end, about 5 ms later per trial, so the stored analog clock falls behind by up to 365 ms within a session. Moving each analog segment to its trial's start puts the torque command step 4 to 7 ms after every labelled onset; on the stored clock it falls up to 108 ms before it.

The torque command's 50 ms pulse has three sizes (about 46, 91 and 183 units above rest). Most pre-MPTP monkey V sessions have the smallest (108 of 157) and most post-MPTP sessions the largest (129 of 141), and post-MPTP pulses are followed by an opposite swing. The paper describes one 0.1 Nm, 50 ms impulse; the command's scale is not given, so the change may be of the torque or of the command's recording. Movement and EMG results differ between command sizes.

The ElbowAngle reference_frame says positive is extension; active flexion movements and flexion torques raise the angle in both monkeys, so positive is flexion. The series are named Elbow for monkey L, whose task used the wrist.

Four monkey V files (v4527b, v4810b, v5604b, v5812) repeat a block of another file's trials. In two of them the same unit, with identical spikes in every repeated trial, is stored twice with different projection types (v4527 unit 2 not_tested and v4527b unit 2 a PTN; v5811 unit 2 a PTN and v5812 unit 2 no_response).

unit_also_in_session_id uses the prefixes V and L where session ids use Venus and Leu, and 35 of its 43 references name files that are not in the dandiset. Where the file is present, it holds a different unit (another unit number, spike count and often projection type), not the same neuron.

The dandiset description says MPTP was given systemically, that both monkeys made elbow movements and that Leu was recorded in 1993. The files and the paper say unilateral intracarotid MPTP, monkey L used the wrist, and Leu files date from August 1992.

The monkey L analog streams are sampled at 100 Hz; the paper says 200 Hz. The EMG is described as sample-hold integrated over 10 ms in the files and low-pass filtered at 100 Hz in the paper, and is stored in uncalibrated A/D units.

The torque onset comes 1.70 to 1.73 s after center_target_appearance_time in 90% of monkey V perturbations, where the Methods put it 1 to 2 s after center capture at random. Either the column marks another event or the torque was predictable from the target's appearance.

No analysis code is published. The response detection as described gives a false-positive rate near 0.2 over the 200 ms epoch, against the 0.01 its threshold implies, and stationary Poisson spike trains give 0.15, most of it, so the paper's exact procedure cannot be recovered, and single-trial latencies are not defined.

The pre-MPTP PTN and CSN resting rates are 16.3 and 3.6 spikes/s in the text and 18.3 and 3.2 in Table 1. Table 1 marks the CSN change in the fraction of excitatory responses p < 0.01, but its own counts (23 of 24 against 19 of 22) give p = 0.54 with the Yates-corrected chi-square test that reproduces its other chi-square values.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper's full text. The verifier streamed 7 monkey L files and ran synthetic checks of stretch.detect (stationary Poisson spike trains) and stretch.kinematics.

disagreements.reason: Cell 27: the any-crossing rate over 0 to 200 ms is 0.22 (main) and 0.46 (t-test variant). Unperturbed trials give 0.19, and stationary Poisson spike trains through detect give 0.13 to 0.20 (the verifier's test), so the excess comes from the threshold procedure, whose threshold is t times the SD over time of the trial-averaged SDF and is not a test of trial-to-trial variance. A single run cannot tell whether the paper's claim is wrong or its procedure differs. The Methods' literal reading, a 2-tailed t-test against the baseline, is closer to the t-test variant, which also fails (0.46). The response rate at the pseudo onset is 0.044 against 0.37 at the true onset, so about 12% of detected responses are expected to be false. It asked for example mean SDFs with their thresholds drawn, and the pseudo-onset false-positive rate split by baseline rate and by number of trials.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook with conclusions and summary, the attempt record, the README, the helper module, the claims file, the round-1 report and the paper's full text from Europe PMC. It checked the paper_inconsistency finding against the paper and found it supported. Other changes in reply are the README run time (the verifier saw 1.5 min printed by cell 104; this run printed 2.4 min) and the round-1 false-positive-rate reason, which now carries two points from its round-1 problem 1 that it found left out. It did not inspect the plotted figures.

attempts.paper_title: An anatomical hotspot for striatal dopamine-acetylcholine interactions during reward and movement
attempts.entry_title: Striatal dopamine-acetylcholine hotspot (Bouabid, Vu et al. 2026)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Bouabid, Vu et al. (2026) on dandiset 001692, which holds multi-fiber photometry of dopamine and acetylcholine across the striatum of 17 mice. It reproduces the spontaneous cross-correlations and their anterior dorsolateral hotspot, paired transients, reward, Pavlovian cue, locomotion and optogenetic stimulation analyses, and the control mice, and tests the ex vivo slice statistics of Figure 8 on the paper's source data on Zenodo.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Bouabid, Vu et al. (2026) from dandiset 001692

outcomes.statement: Across 174 sites in 5 mice, the dominant DA-ACh cross-correlation (the largest magnitude Pearson r within 1 s lags) during spontaneous behavior is negative at 132 sites, 127 of them with DA leading, and positive at 42 sites, 31 of them with ACh leading.
outcomes.notes: Of 174 sites, 133 have a dominant negative correlation (128 with DA leading) and 41 a dominant positive one (32 with ACh leading); 6 have their extreme at lag 0. All four counts are within 10% of the paper's. Every mouse has more negative than positive sites. Correlation over concatenated sessions gives 133, 128, 41 and 30.
deviations: One UG27 reward session (240313r) lacks the artifact-removed green series and is skipped, as the code skips empty series; it is not a spontaneous session, so this claim is unaffected.

outcomes.statement: The dominant correlations form a significant hotspot, identified by local Moran's I, in the anterior dorsolateral striatum (aDLS), where the strongest correlations are negative.
outcomes.notes: The hotspot procedure finds a significant hotspot of 1.01 mm3 with mean smoothed r -0.368 (hull mean -0.185). Its centroid (AP 0.63, ML 2.02, DV -3.14 mm) is anterior and dorsal of the median site (0.10, 2.04, -3.21 mm) but 0.02 mm medial of it, which fails the lateral part of the criterion fixed beforehand. With the 99th percentile of the null the hotspot has 518 voxels and its centroid is at ML 2.09 mm, lateral of the median. 28 sites from all five mice are inside. The location test against the median site is a coarse stand-in for the paper's maps, in which the hotspot lies in aDLS; the shortfall is small. Finding a hotspot is not evidence on its own, as the procedure finds one in 67 of 100 shuffles of the values across sites; none of these is as large (at most 482 voxels) or has a mean as low.
deviations: The hotspot procedure is simplified from the paper's code (linear in place of natural-neighbor interpolation, 100 um voxels in place of 50 um, the convex hull of the sites in place of the Allen striatum mask, 200 in place of 10000 shuffles).
The paper does not define the aDLS location in numbers; the criterion compares the centroid with the median site coordinates.

outcomes.statement: Sites inside the aDLS hotspot have more negative dominant correlations than sites outside (Wilcoxon rank-sum p = 1.67e-16).
outcomes.notes: The 28 sites inside have median dominant r -0.41 against -0.14 for the 146 outside, rank-sum p = 1.9e-13 (the paper 1.67e-16). The test is partly circular, as in the paper.
deviations: The hotspot is the simplified one of fig1f-adls-hotspot.

outcomes.statement: Dominant positive correlations lie in the posterior striatum.
outcomes.notes: Sites with a positive dominant r have median AP -0.40 mm (41 sites) against 0.24 mm for negative sites (133), one-sided rank-sum p = 4.3e-07. The direction holds in all five mice and is significant in UG27, UG29 and UG31.
deviations: The paper shows this on maps; the test of AP coordinates was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: The hotspot is consistent across mice; in each mouse, sites inside the group hotspot have more negative dominant correlations than sites outside.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 2d; Results, first section
outcomes.notes: All five mice have lower median r inside the group hotspot; p < 0.05 in UG27, UG28, UG30 and UG31, and p = 0.084 (exact p = 0.087) in UG29, which has 2 sites inside.
deviations: The per-mouse hotspots of Extended Data Figure 2b-c are not computed.

outcomes.statement: Mice expressing non-functional sensors (a mutant ACh sensor and tdTomato, n = 3) show only sparse, weak positive red-green correlations with no anatomical organization; no hotspot is found.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 1i-k; Results, first section
outcomes.notes: In AD4 to AD6 (ACh4.3mut and tdTomato) the hotspot procedure finds a hotspot with mean smoothed r +0.33 (551 voxels, centroid AP 0.68, ML 1.29, DV -4.14 mm), so by the paper's test the claim of no organization fails. The procedure also finds a hotspot in 73 of 100 shuffles of the control values across sites, but none of those reaches 551 voxels (31 have a mean of at least +0.33), so by the paper's own test the control correlations are organized in space. The correlations are mostly positive (68% of 124 sites, median 0.20), as stated, but not weak; the median absolute dominant r is 0.238 against 0.240 in the sensor mice, and 65% of control sites exceed 0.2 against 54%. One control site has no defined correlation (a constant red trace) and is dropped; 19 site-sessions have constant red traces. Keeping the reward periods gives median r 0.22. Two deviations could add correlated red-green signal and so bear on this outcome; the controls use the high-pass series without artifact removal (none is in their files), and only their 15 reward sessions, where the paper used all ITI data.
deviations: The 15 uncued reward sessions of the control mice are used, with 6 s after rewards and first licks left out; the paper used the ITI data of all their sessions, which the files' event tables would allow but which would take most of the time limit to stream.
The control files hold no artifact-removed series; the high-pass series is used.

outcomes.statement: For coincident transients of opposite polarity (ACh trough with DA peak, ACh peak with DA trough) the DA transient leads; for same-polarity pairs (peak with peak, trough with trough) the ACh transient leads.
outcomes.notes: Median directionality indices are -0.27 (ACh trough with DA peak), -0.30 (ACh peak with DA trough), +0.33 (peak with peak) and +0.12 (trough with trough) over 174 sites, each with Wilcoxon p below 1e-24, and each mouse has the same four signs.
deviations: Pairs are matched by the Methods' rule (each first transient takes its earliest partner, each partner used once), a simplification of the code's two-way matching.
The code keeps only sites flagged as having signal in both channels (`sig`); these flags are not in the files and all 174 included sites are used, as the paper reports 174.

outcomes.statement: Magnitudes of paired transients are negatively correlated at many sites for opposite-sign pairs (121 of 174 for ACh troughs with DA peaks, 81 of 174 for ACh peaks with DA troughs) and positively for same-sign pairs (97 of 174 peak-peak, 78 of 174 trough-trough), with no site significant in the other direction.
outcomes.notes: Significant sites of the stated sign are 114, 69, 97 and 78 against 121, 81, 97 and 78; the second is 3.9 below its tolerance. The counts move by several sites with the random draws (the first run gave 115, 70, 90 and 76). No site is significant in the opposite direction, as stated. All sites have at least 100 pairs. The code's computation (Pearson r over all pairs, p < 0.05) finds 142 to 149 sites per type, so the paper's counts fit the Methods' bootstrap.
deviations: 1000 in place of 10000 repetitions of the 100-pair bootstrap.

outcomes.statement: Magnitude correlations of opposite-sign pairs, but not same-sign pairs, are stronger inside the aDLS hotspot than outside (rank-sum p < 0.05 for opposite-sign pairs, p > 0.05 for same-sign pairs).
outcomes.notes: ACh troughs with DA peaks are more negative inside (median -0.33 against -0.23, p = 0.0001); ACh peaks with DA troughs do not differ (-0.19 against -0.16, p = 0.11). Same-sign pairs do not differ (p = 0.11 and 0.22), as stated.

outcomes.statement: The frequency of paired transients is highest in aDLS, in a region overlapping the correlation hotspot, for all four pair types (volume overlap test, p < 0.01 for each).
outcomes.notes: The occurrence hotspot of each pair type overlaps the correlation hotspot by 780 to 826 voxels against null medians of 88 to 111 (overlap p 0.005, 0.015, 0.005 and below 0.005; the paper 0.005, 0.005, 0.002 and below 0.001). Occurrence is higher inside than outside for each type (p < 0.001). With the chance occurrence subtracted (DA and ACh transients from different sessions of the same site, as in the Methods), every site keeps an excess for every type, the excess is higher inside (p < 0.001), and its hotspots overlap the correlation hotspot with p 0.030, 0.005, 0.015 and below 0.005.
deviations: 200 random volumes in the overlap test, so p cannot fall below 0.005.
The chance occurrence is the mean of 10 shuffles of sessions, in place of 10000.

outcomes.statement: DA and ACh transient rates are higher at sites inside the global correlation hotspot than outside.
outcomes.notes: All four transient types are more frequent inside the hotspot (for example DA peaks 0.226 against 0.176 per second of usable data), p of 0.0013 or less. Rates are now per second of data that is not NaN and not within 6 s after a reward; the first run divided by the whole session and gave the same result.

outcomes.statement: After unpredicted rewards, trial-by-trial DA peak magnitude correlates with ACh; dominant correlations are negative at 114 of 174 sites with DA leading (mean latency 177.9 +/- 96.7 ms) and positive at 58 of 174 with ACh leading (-41.2 +/- 218.9 ms).
outcomes.notes: 122 sites are dominant negative (mean latency 172.1 ms, 120 with DA leading) and 52 dominant positive (mean latency -59.8 ms, 37 with ACh leading). Three values are within tolerance; the positive count is 0.2 below its range (52.2 to 63.8). Negative sites outnumber positive ones in every mouse.
deviations: The latency tolerances are the standard errors implied by the paper's spreads.
One UG27 reward session (240313r) is skipped for lacking the artifact-removed green series.

outcomes.statement: Reward-evoked DA-ACh correlations are significantly more negative inside the global hotspot than outside.
outcomes.notes: Median r -0.52 inside against -0.31 outside, p = 7.3e-09; same sign in all five mice, significant in three.

outcomes.statement: Reward anti-correlations form an aDLS hotspot that significantly overlaps the hotspot of spontaneous correlations (volume overlap test, p = 0.008).
outcomes.notes: The reward hotspot has mean -0.53 (1022 voxels, centroid AP 0.54, ML 2.07, DV -3.26 mm) and shares 721 voxels with the spontaneous hotspot against a null median of 116, overlap p = 0.01 (the paper 0.008).
deviations: 200 random volumes in the overlap test.

outcomes.statement: After Pavlovian conditioning, the conditioned light cue evokes an ACh peak, then a DA peak, then an ACh dip at a majority of sites (49 of 75).
outcomes.notes: The sequence is found at 58 of 75 sites under both readings (code percentiles 55 and 52), above the tolerance of 44.1 to 53.9. The qualitative statement holds; a majority of sites shows the sequence overall and in each mouse (12 of 17, 19 of 24, 27 of 34). The criterion counted only a shortfall as partial; a count above the range is not reproduced by its wording.
deviations: The paper does not define how the sequence is identified; significant ACh peak, DA peak and ACh dip with ordered extremes in the mean trace was chosen here.
Learning sessions are identified from the events (every light cue rewarded); the last 3 per mouse are used, following the code's intent (see findings on the code).
Tone trials cannot be analysed (no tone events); the paper's figure uses light trials.

outcomes.statement: For conditioned light cues, ACh correlates with the trial-by-trial DA peak negatively at lagging times at 39 of 75 sites (ACh lagging, 202.28 +/- 128.4 ms) and positively at leading times at 26 of 75 (ACh leading, -79.1 +/- 224.0 ms).
outcomes.notes: All 75 sites have a significant cue DA peak, so the two readings agree. 41 sites are negative (mean latency 206.0 ms, 37 with ACh lagging) and 34 positive (-83.3 ms, 22 with ACh leading). The positive count is above its range (23.4 to 28.6); the paper's 39 plus 26 make 65, which fits neither reading here. The code's percentiles also give 75 sites, and the null draws from 68868 to 74196 candidate times per mouse, so neither explains the difference. The difference remains unexplained.
deviations: The denominator is ambiguous (75 sites or those with a significant DA peak); both readings are shown and agree here.

outcomes.statement: After cue-specific extinction (light cue rewarded on 20% of trials), cue-evoked DA dips correlate negatively with lagging ACh (DA dip then ACh late peak) at 41 of 74 sites, mean lag 117.9 +/- 176.2 ms.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), 38 of 61 sites with a significant DA dip are negative with mean lag 118.4 ms (the paper 41 of 74, 117.9 ms). Over all 75 sites, 47 negative with mean lag 114.7 ms. Only 28 of the 38 have ACh lagging, and AD2's negative sites have a mean lag of -79.4 ms. The code's polarity (DA peak) gives 44 sites with mean lag 137.6 ms.
deviations: The DA trough is used, as the legend and Methods state; the code correlates the DA peak in this step, shown as a variant.
The paper's denominator (74) and the legend's 48 sites in 5 mice do not match each other or the 75 sites in 3 mice of the files; two readings are shown.

outcomes.statement: Conditioned-cue DA-ACh correlations are more negative at sites inside the global aDLS hotspot than outside.
outcomes.notes: The 9 AD1 to AD3 sites inside the global hotspot have median r -0.31 against 0.02 for the 66 outside, p = 0.024 (exact p = 0.022). The cue hotspot's own overlap with the global hotspot is not significant (p = 0.175), unlike the paper's Figure 4e.
deviations: Sites of the Pavlovian cohort are placed in the global hotspot by their coordinates on the shared grid.

outcomes.statement: After extinction, DA dip to ACh correlations are more negative at sites inside the global aDLS hotspot than outside.
outcomes.notes: Among dip sites, median r -0.35 inside (8 sites) against -0.21 outside (53), p = 0.035 (exact p = 0.034); all sites p = 0.018. The extinction hotspot's overlap with the global one is not significant (p = 0.17).

outcomes.statement: At locomotion initiations, ACh rises and then falls at 131 of 174 sites; DA dips at 119 of 174 sites, rises at 73, and both rises and dips at 32.
outcomes.notes: DA dips at 129 sites and rises at 77 are within 10% (the paper 119 and 73); both at 46 is not (32). ACh rise then fall at 107 sites under reading (a) and a rise at 147 under reading (b), neither within 117.9 to 144.1. Code percentiles give 114 dips, 61 rises and 26 both. The code's bout of 2.2 s gives 132, 74 and 44. UG27 contributes 501 initiations against 92 to 149 for the others; its wheel velocity exceeds the threshold 49% of the time.
deviations: A zero-phase Butterworth filter replaces MATLAB's lowpass.
1000 bootstrap samples in place of 10000.
The Methods' bout of 2.27 s is used; the code's 2.2 s is a variant.

outcomes.statement: Initiation-related signals occur in sequence; DA dips first (median latency 111.11 ms), then ACh peaks (222.22 ms) and DA peaks (227.78 ms), then ACh dips (611.11 ms).
outcomes.notes: Medians are 111.1 ms (DA dips), 277.8 ms (ACh peaks), 277.8 ms (DA peaks) and 666.7 ms (ACh dips), in the stated order; the ACh peak and dip medians are exactly one sample later than the paper's, at the edge of the tolerance. The per-mouse order is irregular (DA peak medians from -388.9 to 527.8 ms).
deviations: The Methods do not say how latency is measured; the time of the extreme of the triggered average in -0.5 to 1 s was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: Initiation-related DA dips are concentrated in the aDLS and DA peaks in dorsomedial and posterior striatum; ACh dips are localized to the aDLS.
outcomes.notes: Dominant DA dips are more anterior than DA rises (median AP 0.36 against -0.48 mm, p < 0.0001) but more medial (ML 1.88 against 2.30 mm) and ventral; ACh-dip sites (148 of 174) are not more anterior or lateral than the 26 others (p = 0.33 and 0.25). All 28 hotspot sites have a dominant DA dip and an ACh dip. The paper describes maps; with ACh dips at 85% of sites a contrast between sites with and without dips may not capture where dips are strongest.
deviations: The paper shows the topography as smoothed maps; site-level coordinate tests were chosen here.

outcomes.statement: At sites with initiation-related DA dips (119 sites), trial-by-trial DA dip magnitudes correlate negatively with ACh with DA leading (mean latency 193.80 +/- 177.68 ms).
outcomes.notes: Of 129 sites with a DA dip (the paper 119), 98 are dominant negative (88 with ACh lagging), mean latency 188.8 ms under reading (a); 98.2 ms under reading (b). Most dip sites are negative in every mouse. The trough search now ignores NaNs; before the fix a trough within 2 samples of a NaN was missed. 2197 of 30341 site-trials have a NaN in the range searched, so at most that many were affected. Before the fix the result was 99 sites and 182.4 ms.
deviations: The latency tolerance is the standard error implied by the paper's spread.

outcomes.statement: Initiation DA dip to ACh correlations are concentrated in the aDLS and more negative inside the global hotspot than outside.
outcomes.notes: Median r -0.35 inside (28 sites) against -0.21 outside (101), p = 1.7e-05 (6.1e-08 before the fix of the trough search).

outcomes.statement: At locomotion invigorations, GLM-estimated DA peak magnitudes correlate negatively with ACh at lagging times, and these correlations are concentrated in the aDLS, more negative inside the global hotspot (131 sites with invigoration DA peaks).
outcomes.source: Results, sixth section; Figure 6e-h; Methods, generalized linear model
outcomes.notes: The GLM finds invigoration DA peaks at 160 sites (the paper 131); 105 are dominant negative (97 with ACh lagging, mean lag 179.4 ms); median r -0.34 inside (28) against -0.21 outside (132), p = 4.5e-05.
deviations: Ordinary least squares in numpy in place of MATLAB fitglm (normal family, identical model).

outcomes.statement: Optogenetic stimulation of midbrain DA neurons evokes significant DA release at 179 of 180 sites.
outcomes.source: Results, seventh section; Extended Data Figure 10b
outcomes.notes: 179 of 180 sites show a significant DA peak after ITI stimulation (178 with the code's percentiles); 115 ITI trains in total (20 per mouse, 15 in ADS6).

outcomes.statement: DA stimulation evokes significant ACh suppression at a subset of sites (116 of 180, 64%).
outcomes.notes: 147 of 180 sites (82%) show a significant ACh dip against 116 (64%); 128 (71%) with the code's percentiles. The 33 sites without a dip are mostly in ADS19 (17 of 27) and ADS16 (9 of 37).
deviations: 1000 bootstrap samples in place of 10000.

outcomes.statement: The stimulation cohort replicates the aDLS anti-correlation hotspot in spontaneous release outside stimulation periods; its dominant correlations are more negative inside the original hotspot, and its own hotspot overlaps the original.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 9a-d; Results, seventh section
outcomes.notes: The 9 cohort sites inside the original hotspot are more negative (median -0.42 against -0.30, p = 0.049, exact p = 0.048; OR exclusion p = 0.041). The cohort's own hotspot is negative (mean -0.44, 1536 voxels, centroid AP 0.71, ML 2.00, DV -3.45 mm) and shares 564 voxels with the original against a null median of 65, but overlap p = 0.085 with 200 random volumes. 167 of 180 cohort sites are dominant negative. The AND exclusion leaves out 6.5% of samples and the OR exclusion 32.7%. Of the samples within 3 s after a stimulation, AND keeps 42% and OR none. With OR the cohort hotspot is similar (mean -0.41, centroid AP 0.72, ML 2.08, DV -3.43 mm), with overlap p = 0.085.
deviations: The code's AND of the three exclusions is followed; OR is a variant.

outcomes.statement: Stimulation-evoked ACh dips are larger inside the cohort's correlation hotspot than outside, and their own hotspot overlaps it.
outcomes.notes: ACh minima are deeper inside the cohort hotspot (median -0.0179 against -0.0149 dF/F, 17 against 163 sites, p = 0.0005). The AND exclusion keeps 42% of the samples within 3 s after a stimulation, so its cohort hotspot is built partly from stimulation responses; with the hotspot of the OR exclusion, which leaves them out, the result holds (19 against 161 sites, median -0.0188 against -0.0149, p = 0.0003). Against the original hotspot p = 0.094; the ACh-minimum hotspot's overlap with the cohort hotspot has p = 0.065, so the claim's second part is not supported at p < 0.05; the criterion treats it as a variant. Inside sites are lower in all six mice, significantly in ADS19.

outcomes.statement: The D2 agonist quinpirole suppresses evoked ACh release in DLS and NAcC, more strongly in DLS; two-way ANOVA region effect F(1,40) = 105.9, region by stimulus interaction F(4,40) = 3.014, stimulus effect F(4,40) = 17.80.
outcomes.notes: Region F 105.87, interaction F 3.014 and stimulus F 17.80 match the paper; DLS mean 25.1 against NAcC 68.1. Type III sums of squares are used, as Prism computes them; Type II gives the same values here.

outcomes.statement: Cocaine reduces evoked ACh release more in DLS than in NAcC; two-way ANOVA stimulus by region interaction F(4,55) = 10.75, stimulus effect F(4,55) = 36.37, region effect F(1,55) = 199.9.
outcomes.notes: With Type III sums of squares, interaction F 10.75, stimulus F 36.37 and region F 199.86 match the paper (10.75, 36.37 and 199.9); DLS 32.8 against NAcC 74.1. The design is unbalanced (8 DLS and 5 NAcC slices). The first run used Type II sums of squares, which give stimulus F 47.68, and scored the claim partially reproduced.

outcomes.statement: The D2 antagonist L-741,626 attenuates the cocaine-induced suppression in both regions; D2R block effect F(1,55) = 231.9 in DLS and F(1,40) = 32.57 in NAcC.
outcomes.notes: Block F 231.87 (DLS) and 32.57 (NAcC) match; the antagonist raises ACh in both (32.8 to 78.6, 74.1 to 107.9). With Type III sums of squares the DLS stimulus F is 34.46, as in the legend (Type II 45.04).

outcomes.statement: Cocaine elevates evoked DA release to a similar degree in DLS and NAcC (two-way ANOVA, cocaine by region interaction F(8,36) = 0.20, p = 0.98).
outcomes.notes: The sheet Figure_8c_TP holds a voltammogram (voltage and current). Figure_8c_LP and _RP hold mean DA time courses (24 time points from 0.625 to 3.5 s) for three mice per region and two conditions. The legend's ANOVA has 8 degrees of freedom for cocaine and 36 residual, which fits neither a two-level cocaine factor nor the 24 time points, so the test cannot be repeated. Descriptively, the cocaine peak is 1.48 times the control peak on average in both regions (per mouse 1.31 to 1.77 in DLS, 1.10 to 2.09 in NAcC).

findings.statement: Every photometry series states a sampling rate of 9 Hz (starting_time rate 8.999 to 9.0). Each series has as many samples as the behavior series, which steps at 55.6 ms (18 Hz), and the Methods and code use 18 Hz; at the stated rate the recordings would last twice as long as their timestamps.

No field in the files states which experiment (spontaneous, unpredicted reward, Pavlovian learning or extinction, control, stimulation) a session belongs to, or which Pavlovian phase. Cohorts can be told only from subject names and indicators, and phases only by counting rewarded light cues (1.0, 0.8 or 0.2). The paper's Zenodo record has a table of this mapping outside the dandiset.

The Pavlovian files have light cue events but no tone cue events, although each session has 30 tone cues (the 68 rewards of a learning session are 30 light, 30 tone and 8 uncued). Tone trials cannot be analysed.
Session sub-UG27_ses-240313r lacks the high-pass, artifact-removed green series that all other UG sessions hold, so it cannot enter the analyses that use it.

The device description of ExcitationSource470 describes 470 nm and 405 nm (isosbestic) light alternated at 100 Hz, and that of ExcitationSource570 reads "405 nm"; the Methods alternate 470 and 570 nm at 36 Hz. The mutant sensor is named ACh4.3mut in the files where the Methods and Key Resources Table name ACh3.0-mut. The session description gives 9 uL rewards at 5 to 30 s, where the Methods give 5 uL at 10 to 30 s, and stores the micro sign mis-encoded.

The code keeps only sites with signal in both channels (a `sig` flag per site) for the transient analyses; the flags are not in the files. All 174 included sites gave the paper's count, so this did not change the result here.

In fig4_pav.m (commit 833fa3d) the loop over a phase's last three sessions loads exp_dirs{d} in place of task_dirs{d}, so it reads the mouse's first three recordings for every phase, and the extinction correlation is called with polarity 1 (the DA peak) although the legend and Methods describe the DA trough. The notebook follows the evident intent and the Methods.

The code departs from the Methods in several parameters; triggered-average significance uses the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles (Methods 2.5th and 97.5th), the minimum locomotion bout is 2.2 s (Methods 2.27 s), paired-transient magnitude correlations are Pearson r over all pairs (Methods a 100-pair bootstrap), and the stimulation cohort's exclusion of reward and stimulation periods combines the three conditions with AND, so a sample is dropped only when all three hold. hotspot_comparison.m places the second hotspot's random volumes with the first grid's dimensions.

For extinction, the Results give 41 of 74 sites and the Figure 4g legend 48 sites in 5 mice, while the Methods give 3 Pavlovian mice and the files hold 75 sites in 3 mice. For learned cues the Results give 39 of 75 negative and 26 of 75 positive sites, which sum to 65.
In the Figure 8 source data, the Figure 8b DLS group holds 6 slice labels from 4 mouse labels (slice_B_4 holds only stimulus 5) where the legend states 5 slices from 5 mice.
The ex vivo slice data of Figure 8 are not in the dandiset; their source data are in the paper's Zenodo record (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18202873).
