attempts.paper_title: Age-dependent alterations in the head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
attempts.entry_title: Head-direction coding in juvenile and adult Fmr1-/y rats (Moore et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Moore, Duszkiewicz, Asiminas, Dudchenko, Peyrache and Wood (bioRxiv 2025) on dandiset 001699, which holds silicon-probe recordings of the postsubiculum of 24 juvenile and adult Fmr1-/y and wild-type rats during open-field exploration and sleep. It recomputes the cell selection, head-direction tuning, its stability within and between sessions, decoder drift, and tuning to the Isomap angle of waking and REM population activity, and compares genotypes in each age group.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Moore et al. (2025) from dandiset 001699

outcomes.statement: 406 units were recorded from 7 juvenile WT rats and 372 from 5 juvenile Fmr1-/y rats; 543 units from 6 adult WT rats and 507 from 6 adult Fmr1-/y rats.
outcomes.notes: Counting all units of each recording once (reading a), juvenile WT 406 units in 7 rats, juvenile Fmr1-/y 372 in 5 and adult WT 543 in 6 match the paper exactly; adult Fmr1-/y has 440 units in 5 rats against 507 in 6, as H4825's file holds H4824's recording. Counting H4825's file as a recording of its own gives 528 units in 6 rats, within tolerance, but counts one recording twice. As putative excitatory units (reading b) no group matches (326, 249, 399, 289). With the archive's labels no group matches (juvenile WT 328 units in 5 rats, juvenile Fmr1-/y 221 in 4, adult WT 575 in 7). Version 2 of the paper gives 372 units in 6 adult Fmr1-/y rats and 406 in 6 adult WT rats, the juvenile numbers repeated.
deviations: H3026 is counted as a juvenile Fmr1-/y rat and H3029 as a juvenile WT rat, where the archive labels H3026 WT and gives H3029 a birth date that makes it an adult; this grouping is the one that matches the paper's counts, and it was chosen from those counts.
H4825's file is left out as a copy of H4824's recording.

outcomes.statement: Juvenile recordings held 8 to 83 putative excitatory units each, adult recordings 30 to 114.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), all units, juvenile recordings hold 8 to 83 units (paper 8 to 83) and adult recordings 55 to 114 (paper 30 to 114), so the juvenile pair and the adult maximum match and the adult minimum does not. Under reading (b), putative excitatory units by trough-to-peak duration, juvenile 5 to 50 and adult 30 to 81; under (c), cells of session 1, juvenile 5 to 49 and adult 30 to 80. The paper's adult minimum of 30 is the putative excitatory count of H4822, while its other three bounds are counts of all units, so the reported ranges mix two readings.
deviations: The paper calls these putative excitatory units; three of its four bounds match all units instead.

outcomes.statement: Juvenile Fmr1-/y and WT rats do not differ in the time spent inactive, the time spent in the centre of the arena, or the speed while active.
outcomes.source: Figure S1c (t-tests on animal averages, t(10) = 1.53, 1.07 and 1.53, P > 0.05)
outcomes.notes: t-tests on the means of 7 WT and 5 Fmr1-/y rats; time inactive (speed below 1 cm/s) 0.177 against 0.107, t(10) = -0.90, p = 0.39; time in the centre 0.084 against 0.180, t(10) = 1.86, p = 0.093; speed while active 4.88 against 5.74 cm/s, t(10) = 2.10, p = 0.063. With 2 cm/s thresholds and a larger centre, p = 0.25, 0.11 and 0.26. With the first day of each rat alone the active speed differs (t(10) = 2.45, p = 0.034), so the absence of a speed difference is fragile.
deviations: The paper does not define inactivity, the centre or the active period; the thresholds were fixed in the criterion and variants are shown.

Sessions are cut to their first 20 min, the paper's session length, where the claims file cuts only tracking blocks over 30 min, to 1300 s; the change was made after the first round of verification, and the claims file's definition is shown as a variant in the notebook.

outcomes.notes: REM Isomap HD information does not differ between genotypes (median 0.413 in Fmr1-/y against 0.332 in WT; LME p = 0.27; with the REM inside exploration left out p = 0.73; rat means p = 0.27).
deviations: Sessions are cut to their first 20 min, the paper's session length, where the claims file cuts only tracking blocks over 30 min, to 1300 s; the change was made after the first round of verification, and the claims file's definition is shown as a variant in the notebook.

outcomes.statement: In every rat the probe tracts passed through PoSub, confirmed histologically.
outcomes.source: Figure S1d, Figure S2d; Methods, Recording
outcomes.notes: Every one of the 36 files holds RGB histology images (acquisition/histology_images, for example H3001_D2 and H3001_D3), including the four whose asset names lack +image (H3001 on both days, H4822, H4823). No image annotates the probe tract or the postsubiculum, and the electrodes table gives a location string per channel but no histological confirmation. Judging whether a tract passes through PoSub from the images needs an anatomist; it was not attempted.

findings.statement: The paper's unit counts (406 units in 7 juvenile WT rats, 372 in 5 juvenile Fmr1-/y rats, 543 in 6 adult WT rats) and its range of 8 to 83 units per juvenile recording are matched exactly only if H3026, labelled WT, is a juvenile Fmr1-/y rat and H3029, whose date of birth makes it 97 days old, is a juvenile WT rat. With the archive's labels the juvenile groups have 5 WT and 4 Fmr1-/y rats, and the juvenile effects weaken (HD information p = 0.23, offsets p = 0.17).

The dates of birth of H3023 (2022-08-13) and H3026 (2022-09-13) are after their recordings in 2021, so the archive's asset metadata, which derive the age from the date of birth, give them negative ages (P-366D to P-344D). H3029 shares H4830's date of birth. No NWB file sets the subject's age.

The file of H4825 holds the recording of H4824 (identical waveforms, unit and spike counts, and spike times up to 1248 s), with its spike and tracking times shifted piece by piece onto H4825's epoch table and clipped at its end, where 131373 spikes share the last spike time and 12970 tracking frames repeat a timestamp. H4825's own recording is not in the dandiset, so the adult Fmr1-/y group has 5 rats and 440 units where the paper has 6 and 507.

The units table holds all curated units with only spike times, mean waveforms, electrode group and sampling rate; no cell type, contamination or depth. The paper excluded cells recorded in the part of PoSub already recorded on the previous day, and the files give no probe depth per day, so that selection cannot be repeated.

The epochs and processing/tasks tables do not mark the exploration sessions reliably. In H3001 200202 task epoch 1 is called wake but lasts 94 min without tracking; in H3026 211003 epoch 1 spans 112 min of waking and sleep; in H3023 210813-1 epoch 2 runs from the end of the first session into the second; H4823 has a single epoch and no sleep task. Every file's session description mentions a cue rotation, and most files hold a third tracked session (`wake_cue_rot`), which version 1 of the paper does not describe.
In H3015 210417 and H4823 221108 position is stated in centimetres but spans about 300 and 700 units, so it is in pixels, and head direction runs from -pi to pi where the other files use 0 to 2 pi.
One unit of H3023 210812 has spike times out of order. 22 of the 24 juvenile files have one to three tracking frames whose timestamp does not increase.
The dandiset's `about` field lists "Fmr1 protein, rat" as an anatomy term with the MeSH identifier of Fragile X Syndrome (D005600).

The paper's analysis code (Matlab and R, per its Methods) is not public; its Code Availability says it will be released at publication. The repository the dandiset links, woodcode (commit 61ee178), is the lab's general library and does not hold the paper's analysis. Version 1 does not describe the Bayesian decoder; version 2 does.

The Methods exclude units with contamination scores "below 0.5", which would remove nearly every unit (1727 of 1761 are below). The ranges of units per recording mix counts of all units (8 to 83, maximum 114) with a count of putative excitatory units (minimum 30), while the text calls them all putative excitatory. Version 2 gives the adult counts as 372 and 406 units in 6 rats each, the juvenile numbers repeated.

attempts.paper_title: Altered Use of Prior Expectations and Modified Neural Dynamics in a Mouse Model of Autism
attempts.entry_title: Prior use and cortical dynamics in a Nrxn1a mouse model (Davatolhagh et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Davatolhagh et al. (2025) that can be tested on dandiset 001712, which holds one widefield imaging and behaviour session of one mouse of unstated genotype in the IBL biased choice task. It tests the psychometric curve, reaction times, the use of the block prior, adaptation after block switches, lateralized visual responses and a linear encoding model of the imaging with task and movement predictors. The comparisons between knockout and wild-type mice cannot be tested.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Davatolhagh et al. (2025) from dandiset 001712
Encoding model with the video components of all three cameras (variant)

outcomes.statement: Mice of both genotypes show sigmoidal psychometric curves, with the proportion of rightward choices increasing as the stimulus contrast increases on the right.
outcomes.notes: P(right) rises at every step of signed contrast, from 0.112 at -100% to 1.000 at +100% (Spearman rho 1.000 over nine levels, span 0.887). The lapse-and-erf fit gives sigma 17.04% contrast (bootstrap 95% interval 13.98 to 20.47), bias -6.77% and left lapse 0.116. The claim covers both genotypes; this is one mouse of unknown genotype.
deviations: One session of one mouse, where the paper pools 10 sessions from each of 19 mice.
The criterion (Spearman rho and span) was set here; the paper shows the curves without a test.

outcomes.statement: Psychometric bias, slope and lapse rates do not differ between WT and KO mice (bias p = 0.94, slope p = 0.95, left lapse p = 0.16, right lapse p = 0.22).
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes. The dandiset holds one mouse (FD-28), and its genotype is not in the files or the dandiset metadata, nor in the public IBL database (openalyx subject FD_28 has an empty genotype list, from a query made by hand during the attempt and not part of the notebook). Openalyx holds other sessions of the cohort's FD and MFD mice, but is a live database without a pinned version and also has no genotypes.

outcomes.statement: Reaction time (time to first movement) is longer at lower contrasts in both genotypes.
outcomes.notes: Over 750 trials with a movement onset after the stimulus, the Spearman correlation of absolute contrast with reaction time is -0.053 (p = 0.15); the median at 0% (0.089 s) exceeds that at 100% (0.081 s), the second part of the criterion. Medians are 0.081 to 0.095 s at every contrast, and 161 trials have no movement onset after the stimulus (149 with an onset at or before it and 12 with no onset). With reaction times above 0.15 s only (226 trials) the correlation is -0.226 (p = 0.00062), so the relation appears among slower responses. Of the 899 onsets, 149 fall at or before the stimulus and 346 within 0.08 s after it, so many may mark movements begun before the stimulus could guide them. The response time (choice registration minus stimulus onset) is shorter at higher contrast over all 911 choice trials (rho -0.134, p = 5.2e-05; medians 0.326 s at 0% and 0.281 s at 100%), a variant that does not decide the outcome. The paper's text calls reaction time the time to first movement and does not say how that movement is detected or how earlier movements are treated.
deviations: One session of one mouse.
Trials with a movement onset at or before the stimulus onset are left out; the paper does not say how it treats them.

outcomes.statement: Reaction times do not differ between genotypes on correct (p = 0.234) or incorrect (p = 0.522) trials.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: WT and KO mice learn the task with similar trajectories, reaching asymptotic performance after about 20 sessions.
outcomes.notes: Needs the training sessions of both genotypes; the dandiset holds one biased-task session.

outcomes.statement: Mice use the block prior; rightward choices are more frequent in right-likely blocks than in left-likely blocks, most clearly when contrast is low, shifting the psychometric curve toward the likely side (shown for WT, and present but smaller in KO).
outcomes.notes: At 0% contrast P(right) is 0.831 (74 of 89) in right-likely blocks and 0.507 (37 of 73) in left-likely blocks, difference 0.325, one-sided Fisher p = 9.2e-06. The difference is 0.182 to 0.458 at every signed contrast except +100% (0.000), and the psychometric bias moves by 19.41% contrast between blocks. Whether the shift is smaller in KO than in WT is not testable here.
deviations: One session of one mouse; the test (Fisher exact at 0% contrast) was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: KO mice shift their choices less between biased blocks than WT mice, with a difference in psychometric bias and none in slope or lapses.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: After a block switch, mice adapt their choices toward the newly likely side, and the proportion of choices toward the block side rises from an initial value A to an asymptote B with a time constant tau.
outcomes.notes: Over 14 switches between biased blocks, choices toward the new block side are 0.543 in trials 0 to 4 and 0.827 in trials 20 to 39 (one-sided Fisher p = 2.7e-06). The fit gives A = 0.480, B = 1.000 (at its bound) and tau = 25.12 trials (SE 16.14), so tau is poorly determined. Resampling the switches gives 95% intervals of 0.279 to 0.643 for A, 0.836 to 1.000 for B and 6.41 to 38.37 trials for tau; B exceeds A in every draw and tau is 40 or more in 0.018 of them. A maximum-likelihood fit on single trials gives A = 0.479, B = 1.000, tau = 25.03. At contrasts of 12.5% or less, 0.452 against 0.820, tau 21.57.
deviations: The paper's parametric curve is not given; B - (B - A) exp(-t / tau) over trials 0 to 39, all contrasts, was chosen here.

outcomes.statement: KO mice adapt more slowly after a block switch (longer tau, p = 0.004) and have lower initial performance after the switch (p = 0.041) than WT littermates.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: Visual cortex (VISp) responds robustly to contralateral visual stimuli.
outcomes.notes: Under the criterion, the right-minus-left and left-minus-right peaks both fall at the left edge of the frame (columns 0 and 2, rows 0 and 539), on the same side of the estimated midline (column 316), with trial tests at p = 0.053 and 0.14. These corner pixels are darker in the mean image (534 and 926) than 95% of the frame (5th percentile 1538), outside the imaged brain; the spatial components cover the whole frame with no mask. In a variant restricted to bright pixels 20 or more from the edge, the right-minus-left peak lies left of the midline (column 199) and the left-minus-right peak right of it (column 481), p = 8.1e-15 and 1.6e-17; the variant does not decide the outcome. It does not show that the lateralization is visual. At these two pixels the side difference exceeds 3 standard errors from 0.128 s after the stimulus, while the median movement onset is 0.086 s. Only 27 trials (13 right, 14 left) have no movement before 0.4 s; on them the difference at the two pixels points the same way (p = 0.02 and 0.091), but a masked peak search on these trials alone puts the peaks on the reverse sides (columns 550 and 72, p = 0.0062 and 0.012), which is not explained here. The slow trials exclude only wheel movement. In the same window paw speed and camera motion energy rise on 0.90 to 0.96 of all trials at 25 or 100% contrast, and wheel velocity, the right paw in both side cameras and the left camera's motion energy differ between right and left stimulus trials (p = 0.0005 or less); on the 27 slow trials paw speed rises on 0.44 to 0.78 of trials and the right paw in the right camera still differs by side (p = 0.014). Neither VISp nor the hemispheres can be named without an atlas registration.
deviations: Tested in image coordinates, with a midline estimated from the mean image, as the dandiset has no atlas registration.
The peak search of the criterion did not exclude pixels outside the brain; the masked search is a variant.

outcomes.statement: KO mice show elevated dF/F across cortex in the ITI (most prominent in motor regions), stimulus and feedback periods compared with WT.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype. The atlas registration needed for regional measures is also missing.

outcomes.statement: KO mice show globally increased pairwise correlations between regional dF/F time series during the task.
outcomes.source: Figure 3D (legend labelled E); Results, third section
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes and the registration to Allen areas, neither of which is in the dandiset; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: KO mice show higher pixel-wise trial-to-trial variance across all cortical regions and task periods.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: The full linear encoding model explains more than half of single-trial cortical variance (cvR2 0.60 +/- 0.02 in KO and 0.54 +/- 0.02 in WT).
outcomes.notes: Full-model cvR2 is 0.471 pooled in pixel space (reading a), 0.422 as the mean over pixels (b) and 0.126 as the mean over components (c); minus the intercept-only model (the time-point columns alone), 0.123, 0.133 and 0.078. None is within 0.486 to 0.660; reading (a) is above 0.3, which the criterion counts as partial. Without the body camera's video components the pooled cvR2 is 0.414. Variants that do not decide the outcome are as follows. With the video components of the left and right cameras added, as in the paper (encoding_all_cameras.ipynb), cvR2 is 0.574 (a) and 0.525 (b), within the range, and 0.208 (c). With folds that keep each trial's frames together and each frame once per trial, it is 0.422, 0.363 and 0.047 with the body camera only, and 0.472, 0.405 and 0.046 with all three cameras, below the range. Over the masked pixels of the fig3b variant (pixels brighter than the median of the mean image and 20 or more from the edge) reading (b) is 0.434. The paper's Results give 0.60 and 0.54 as the full model's cvR2 and say it accounts for more than half of the variance, while its Figure 4C legend says the full model is shown with the trial time regressor subtracted out. Under that reading the values here are 0.123 and 0.133 (a, b) with the body camera and 0.226 and 0.236 with all three cameras, far below the range.
deviations: One session of one mouse of unknown genotype; the expected range spans the WT and KO means.

No video components from the left and right cameras in the design that decides the outcome (left out for runtime; the body camera's are included; a second notebook adds them as a variant), paw speeds from Lightning Pose where the paper uses DeepLabCut, ROI motion energies assumed to be the whisker pads and body.

The subjective prior is an action-kernel model fitted here; trial windows, the penalty selection (generalized cross-validation) and the readings of cvR2 were chosen here, as the paper's widefield model code is not public.

outcomes.statement: Movement predictors account for most of the explained variance; shuffling them reduces cvR2 by much more than shuffling task predictors (delta R2 for movement 0.40 +/- 0.02 in KO and 0.33 +/- 0.02 in WT; task shuffle beta -0.02).
outcomes.notes: Shuffling movement predictors lowers cvR2 by 0.104 (a), 0.119 (b) and 0.067 (c); shuffling task predictors by 0.017, 0.015 and 0.013. Movement dominates under every reading and in every fold (smallest movement drop 0.065, largest task drop 0.019), but the movement drop is below 0.297 to 0.440 under every reading. Without the body camera's video components the movement drop is 0.042 against 0.021 for task pooled, and 0.010 against 0.015 over components. Variants that do not decide the outcome are as follows. With folds by trial and each frame once per trial, the movement drop is 0.049, 0.060 and -0.005 against 0.017, 0.016 and 0.012 for task, so over components task exceeds movement, which the criterion would count as not reproduced. With all three cameras the movement drop is 0.216, 0.232 and 0.161 against 0.008, 0.008 and 0.007 for task, still below the range; with folds by trial, 0.109, 0.115 and 0.008 against 0.008, 0.008 and 0.000.
deviations: As for fig4c-full-cvr2; the missing side-camera video components likely lower the movement contribution.

outcomes.statement: KO mice lose more explained variance than WT when movement predictors are shuffled (Group x Movement beta = 0.071, p = 0.006; delta R2 KO 0.40 against WT 0.33, p = 0.032), with no group difference for task predictors; full-model cvR2 tends to be higher in KO (p = 0.076).
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: KO mice show elevated baseline motion energy relative to WT, with comparable stimulus-evoked movement dynamics after baseline correction.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

outcomes.statement: Individual movement variables explain more unique variance in KO than in WT mice, and task variables explain little unique variance in either group.
outcomes.notes: Needs mice of both genotypes; see fig1d-psychometric-params-genotype.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds one session of one mouse (sub-FD-28). The paper analyses 10 sessions from each of 11 wild-type and 8 Nrxn1a knockout mice. Eleven of the paper's findings, all comparisons between genotypes, cannot be tested.

The genotype of the mouse is not given in the NWB files, the dandiset metadata, or the public IBL database (subject FD_28 has an empty genotype list, from a query made by hand during the attempt). The subject description is the paper's general description of the cross. A comment in the conversion script lists the session under knockout sessions, but next to a note that the list is a placeholder.

Neither NWB file holds the cortical landmarks or the registration to the Allen atlas that the conversion code's documentation describes for the processed file (lab_meta_data localization and atlas_registration), so no pixel can be assigned to a cortical area.
Both imaging planes give the indicator as GCaMP6f; the paper's Methods and the file's keywords give GCaMP6s (CamKII-tTA x TRE-GCaMP6s).
The raw file's imaging planes state an imaging rate of 15 Hz; the timestamps give 31.2 Hz per channel (32.03 ms intervals), and the Methods give 30 Hz.
The dandiset's keywords and description name "CNTNALP2", which is neither the gene of the paper and the files (Nrxn1a) nor a correct spelling of Cntnap2.

The wheel series state that counter-clockwise is positive, but trials whose choice is labelled counter_clockwise turn the wheel with negative velocity (95.5% of them 0.1 to 0.3 s after movement onset). The choice labels agree with the rewards, so the sign convention of the wheel or of the labels is misdescribed.
The wheel movement onset is described as the first movement after the go cue, but 151 of 899 onsets precede the go cue (by up to 0.18 s).
The ROI motion energy series give the ROI position in pixels but not the body part it covers; the paper's model uses whisker-pad and body motion energy.
The SVD spatial components cover the whole 540 x 640 frame with no brain mask, and the corners of the frame carry large values in stimulus-evoked maps.
The dandiset has no published version; only the draft exists, so no version can be cited or pinned.
The paper's analysis code is to be made public on publication. The encoding code it links (churchlandlab/chiCa) implements the model for single-cell data in another task, not the widefield analysis.

In the Figure 3 legend the correlation panel is labelled (E) twice and (D) is missing, the correlation panel's legend says the KO minus WT matrix shows reduced inter-regional correlations while the Results say correlations are increased, and the legend of panel C describes variance difference maps, as does panel E.

attempts.paper_title: Three-dimensional spatial selectivity of hippocampal neurons during space flight
attempts.entry_title: Place cells during space flight on the Neurolab mission (Knierim et al. 2000)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Knierim, McNaughton and Poe (2000) that can be tested on dandiset 001754, which holds sorted units, task epochs, rate maps and spike-time positions of three rats recorded before and during the Neurolab shuttle mission. It tests spatial selectivity on the Escher staircase in flight, spatial information in flight against preflight, and the stability of place fields across two sessions. The paper is not open access; claims come from its abstract, its figure titles and the dandiset's description. There is no EEG in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Knierim et al. (2000) from dandiset 001754

outcomes.statement: Hippocampal neurons recorded on the space shuttle form a robust spatial code on the three-dimensional Escher staircase track in weightlessness.
outcomes.source: Abstract; dandiset description ("Place cells eventually demonstrated normal spatially specific firing")
outcomes.notes: The third verification round agreed with the change from partially_reproduced to not_reproduced. On flight day 9, 12 of 25 Rat1 units (0.48) have spatial information above the 95th percentile of 500 circular-shift shuffles on the Escher staircase (binomial p = 6.9e-10 against 0.05), and 3 of 28 Rat2 units (0.107, p = 0.16). By the criterion Rat1 is above chance but below 0.5 and Rat2 is not above chance, so neither the reproduced nor the partially reproduced rule is met. With spikes at the lost position given a neighbouring position, as in the first version, Rat1 had 13 of 25 (0.52), which gave partially_reproduced. Rat1 FD9 is close to the bound. 6 units have p between 0.01 and 0.1, repeats with 2000 shuffles and five other seeds give 11 or 12 of 25 (0.44 to 0.48), and the run of 200 shuffles in the data check, with the same lookup, gives 13 of 25 (0.52); across these seven runs the count is 11 to 13 of 25, on both sides of 0.5, so the outcome for Rat1 is not robust. The outcome follows the pre-specified run of 500 shuffles, with which the five repeats of 2000 shuffles agree. Rat2 FD9 gives 2 or 3 of 28 in every repeat. Shifted spikes are dropped for lack of a position more often in Rat2's ES epochs (median 0.307 on FD9) than in Rat1's (0.074), but a count-matched variant gives the same counts for Rat2. Rat2's units are not selective with the shared position trace in any window, and Rat1's units are selective in Rat2's FD4 ES epoch (6 of 15), so the trace in Rat2's epochs may not be Rat2's position; the files do not name the animal tracked. On flight day 4, 10 of 20 Rat1 units, 0 of 16 Rat2 units, and 10 of 16 and 1 of 19 Rat3 units in its two ES epochs are significant. In MC epochs 0 to 2 units per session are significant. The "three orthogonal surfaces" part of the abstract is tested apart, and blocked.
deviations: The paper's Methods were not available; the selection (50 spikes at a known position), the 32 x 32 binning, the shuffle and the thresholds are common choices fixed in the claims file.

Occupancy is the original analysis's occupancy map for the epoch, and shuffled spikes take the nearest position sample within 0.25 s, as the dandiset gives position only at spike times. A spike whose nearest sample is the lost position is dropped.
Robust is read as at least half of the units significant in each flight day 9 session.
Rat2's flight day 9 session is judged although whose position the trace holds in it could not be established.

outcomes.statement: The spatial code covers each of the three orthogonal surfaces of the Escher staircase.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds one two-dimensional pixel position per time from one camera. Nothing in the files or the dandiset metadata describes the camera's view or the track layout, and the conversion code describes the ES track only as a three-dimensional track with 90 degree yaw and pitch turns and the position as video tracker pixel coordinates (its lines are printed in the notebook), so pixels cannot be assigned to the three surfaces. The NASA record of the study (OSD-968) says position was recorded with two synchronised cameras (printed in the notebook); a second view is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: In flight, spatial information content of place cells is comparable to preflight levels.
outcomes.source: Dandiset description (not checked against the paper's text)
outcomes.notes: Flight day 9 ES rate maps (64, Rats 1 and 2) have a median spatial information of 1.385 bits/spike against 1.448 for preflight ES maps (53); two-sided Mann-Whitney p = 0.45, difference -0.064 bits/spike, ratio 0.96. Per rat, CEL-named maps only, maps with a peak of 1 Hz or more, MC maps, all flight maps, bins with 5 or more occupancy counts (p = 0.44) and information adjusted for rate x occupancy (p = 0.45), all give p of 0.20 or more. Rate x occupancy is proportional to the spike count in the flight maps (about 22 per spike) and is assumed to be so in the preflight maps, where it cannot be checked. Information falls with the spike count (Spearman rho -0.252 over all ES maps). Rat1's compared sessions have similar counts and Rat2's do not (median unit spikes 359 and 352 preflight, 437 and 205 on FD9; median rate x occupancy 7862 and 7628 against 9105 and 5226), so Rat2's FD9 maps rest on fewer spikes, which by sampling bias raises their spatial information. The rate maps are smoothed with an unstated kernel, so no shuffle-corrected value could be computed. The dandiset description says preflight was recorded on a flat rectangular track, so this may compare different apparatus. Rat2's FD9 ES maps have a median of 1.343 bits/spike although only 3 of its 28 units are significant against shuffles, so the rate maps' spatial information does not show that Rat2's cells were selective.
deviations: The source is the dandiset's description of the paper's findings, not the paper's text.
The paper's test is unknown; a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test at 0.05 was fixed in advance.

findings.statement: The Rat1 and Rat2 files of each flight day hold the same position trace (98.6 to 98.8% of samples at common timestamps within 2 pixels), presented as each rat's position. Rat1's units are spatially selective with it, Rat2's are not in any window, and Rat1's units are also selective in Rat2's flight day 4 ES epoch. Each file samples the trace at its own units' spike times, and the files do not name the animal the tracker followed. Whose position the trace is during Rat2's task epochs is not stated and could not be established.
Position is given only at spike times (taken from the spike files), so occupancy cannot be computed from the files' position, and the preflight files have no position at all.

The dandiset description says the preflight recordings were made on a flat rectangular track, but the preflight files label their epochs ES (Escher staircase) and MC (Magic Carpet) and hold ES and MC rate maps, as the flight files do. Which apparatus the preflight epochs were recorded on is not stated in the files.

The rate-map `source_file` names are Windows 8.3 short names (ESCELL~1 to ~4, then hashed names such as ES2BC0~1), so `cell_number`, read from the ~N suffix, is not a cell number. It equals the cluster id of the best-matching unit in 84 of 211 unit-epochs, and the rate maps cannot be linked to units as the table's description says. The long names are in the NASA archive (OSD-968), whose description names files like BL2.cell5.
The rate maps are smoothed (in the median well-matched map, 91% of the bins with a positive rate hold no spike of the unit), and the kernel is not stated.

Rate maps use -999 for unvisited bins, which the column description (rate in Hz) does not state. The tracker's lost position (0, 255), 5 to 12% of position samples, is counted in the original occupancy maps (bin [63, 0], up to 19% of an occupancy map in flight).

Eight rate maps are identical copies of another map in the same file, some stored under a different tetrode (for example Rat1 FD4 TT1 and TT11 ESCELL~1, and four maps of Rat2 FD4 under TT13, TT19 and TT22).

Units merge per-epoch spike files that share a tetrode and cluster id; nothing states that a cluster id names the same neuron in different epochs. The unit table lacks the `session_type` and `source_file` columns the conversion's README lists, so a unit's spikes cannot be traced to their spike file.
The dandiset's description reports normal theta and sharp waves and ripples in the hippocampal EEG, but no EEG is in the dandiset.

Spike times are given to 10 ms in five files and to 1 ms or finer in three; 2 to 15% of within-unit intervals are zero, in every epoch type and not mainly in overlapping epochs; their cause is not resolved. In the Rat1 flight day 4 file two baseline epochs overlap (2525 to 3390 s and 2720 to 3390 s).
The age is "/" for every subject, and the position's pixel scale and camera view are not described.

attempts.paper_title: Three-dimensional spatial selectivity of hippocampal neurons during space flight
attempts.entry_title: Place cells during space flight on the Neurolab mission (Knierim et al. 2000)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Knierim, McNaughton and Poe (2000) that can be tested on dandiset 001754, which holds sorted units, task epochs, rate maps and spike-time positions of three rats recorded before and during the Neurolab shuttle mission. It tests spatial selectivity on the Escher staircase in flight, spatial information in flight against preflight, and the stability of place fields across two sessions. The paper is not open access; claims come from its abstract, its figure titles and the dandiset's description. There is no EEG in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Knierim et al. (2000) from dandiset 001754

outcomes.statement: Hippocampal neurons recorded on the space shuttle form a robust spatial code on the three-dimensional Escher staircase track in weightlessness.
outcomes.source: Abstract; dandiset description ("Place cells eventually demonstrated normal spatially specific firing")
outcomes.notes: On flight day 9, 10 of 25 Rat1 units (0.40) have spatial information above the 95th percentile of 500 circular-shift shuffles on the Escher staircase (binomial p = 1.6e-7 against 0.05), and 2 of 28 Rat2 units (0.071, p = 0.41). By the criterion Rat1 is above chance but below 0.5 and Rat2 is not above chance, so neither the reproduced nor the partially reproduced rule is met. Repeats with 2000 shuffles and five other seeds give 10 or 11 of 25 for Rat1 and 2 of 28 for Rat2, and the run of 200 shuffles in the data check gives 10 and 2; 5 Rat1 units have p between 0.01 and 0.1. The outcome is the same as in 001754-knierim-2000-01, which recorded 12 of 25 for Rat1 (11 to 13 over seven runs); on the earlier version's files the notebook gives 11 or 12 of 25 for Rat1 and 2 or 3 of 28 for Rat2 over five seeds. Every real spike has a sample at its own time in both versions; the draft's trace adds samples at the other rat's spike times in each window, so shifted spikes find a sample more often and the shuffles change. Shifted spikes are now dropped about as often in Rat2's FD9 ES epoch (median 0.058) as in Rat1's (0.060), against 0.306 to 0.307 and 0.074 to 0.075 on the earlier version's files, and a count-matched variant gives 12 of 25 (0.48) for Rat1 and 2 of 28 for Rat2. With each unit's spikes replaced by a Poisson train of the same mean count, 9 of 122 flight ES units are significant (0.074, binomial p = 0.16 against 0.05), and 12 of 125 (0.096, p = 0.023) when each spike is moved to its nearest position sample, which reproduces the real drop rates; per session the false-positive fraction is 0 to 0.21, and in the judged sessions 0.160 and 0.154 for Rat1 and 0.037 and 0.214 for Rat2. Against these fractions Rat1's 10 of 25 is still above chance (p = 0.0035 and 0.0026) and Rat2's 2 of 28 is not (p = 0.28 and 0.99), so the outcome is the same, though the criterion's 0.05 is below the false-positive fraction of some sessions. With each unit's real train reversed in time within its epoch, which keeps its bursts and changes in rate and breaks its relation to the position, 2 of 122 flight ES units are significant (1 of 25 in Rat1's FD9 session, 0 of 27 in Rat2's), and Rat3's ES1 trains against the ES2 trace and the reverse give 0 of 16 and 0 of 19, so with real temporal structure the test is conservative. A unit's 95th percentile of the shuffles is nearly the same for its reversed train (Spearman rho 0.995), 1.7 to 2.3 times that of a Poisson train of the same count per session, and higher the fewer 10 s periods hold its spikes (rho -0.874 with the effective fraction of 10 s bins filled) and the fewer spikes it has (rho -0.601); the two explain 80% of its variance on a log scale. Rat2's FD9 units are the most clumped (median 0.145 of the bins, against 0.190 to 0.358 in the other sessions) and have the highest median 95th percentile (3.572). The test has less power for such units, and its power was not measured, so a low fraction, Rat2's especially, is weak evidence against a spatial code; the criterion's rule decides the outcome. The trace moves as a tracked animal would in Rat2's windows (median step 0.50 pixels and path length 33.0 pixels per second in its FD9 ES window), and units of neither rat are selective in any MC window (0 to 2 of 11 to 32), so neither settles whose position it is. Rat2's units are not selective with the trace in any window (1 of 16 and 2 of 28 in their own ES epochs, 0 of 15 and 0 of 41 in Rat1's), and Rat1's units are selective in Rat2's FD4 ES epoch (10 of 15), so the trace in Rat2's epochs may not be Rat2's position; the files say it is taken to be, and that the source does not name the animal tracked. On flight day 4, 11 of 20 Rat1 units, 1 of 16 Rat2 units, and 11 of 16 and 1 of 19 Rat3 units in its ES1 and ES2 epochs are significant. In MC epochs 0 to 2 units per session are significant. The "three orthogonal surfaces" part of the abstract is tested apart, and blocked.
deviations: The paper's Methods were not available; the selection (50 spikes at a known position), the 32 x 32 binning, the shuffle and the thresholds are common choices fixed in the claims file.

Occupancy is the original analysis's occupancy map for the epoch, and shuffled spikes take the nearest position sample within 0.25 s, as the dandiset gives position only at spike times. A spike whose nearest sample is the lost position is dropped.
Robust is read as at least half of the units significant in each flight day 9 session.
Rat2's flight day 9 session is judged although whose position the trace holds in it could not be established.

outcomes.statement: The spatial code covers each of the three orthogonal surfaces of the Escher staircase.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds one two-dimensional pixel position per time from one camera. The draft's position reference frame says the camera view and the pixel size on the apparatus are not recorded in the source files, nothing in the files or the dandiset metadata describes the track layout in the image, and the conversion code at the new commit describes the ES track only as a three-dimensional track with 90 degree yaw and pitch turns (its lines are printed in the notebook), so pixels cannot be assigned to the three surfaces. The NASA record of the study (OSD-968) says position was recorded with two synchronised cameras (printed in the notebook); a second view is not in the dandiset. Same outcome as in 001754-knierim-2000-01.

outcomes.statement: In flight, spatial information content of place cells is comparable to preflight levels.
outcomes.source: Dandiset description (not checked against the paper's text)
outcomes.notes: Flight day 9 ES rate maps (64, Rats 1 and 2) have a median spatial information of 1.385 bits/spike against 1.448 for preflight ES maps (53); two-sided Mann-Whitney p = 0.45, difference -0.064 bits/spike, ratio 0.96. The main test's maps and numbers are the same as in 001754-knierim-2000-01, and so is the outcome. Per rat (p = 0.25 and 0.88), maps with archived names containing CEL (0.43), maps with a peak of 1 Hz or more (0.89), MC maps (0.92), all flight maps (0.12), bins with 5 or more occupancy counts (0.44) and information adjusted for rate x occupancy (0.37) all give p of 0.12 or more. Rate x occupancy is proportional to the spike count in the flight maps (about 22 per spike) and is assumed to be so in the preflight maps, where it cannot be checked. Information falls with the spike count (Spearman rho -0.226 over all ES maps). Rat1's compared sessions have similar counts and Rat2's do not (median unit spikes 359 and 352 preflight, 437 and 205 on FD9; median rate x occupancy 7862 and 7628 against 9105 and 5226), so Rat2's FD9 maps rest on fewer spikes, which by sampling bias raises their spatial information. The rate maps are smoothed with an unrecorded kernel, so no shuffle-corrected value could be computed. The dandiset description says preflight was recorded on a flat rectangular track, so this may compare different apparatus, and Rat2's preflight file shares no tetrode with its flight files. Rat2's FD9 ES maps have a median of 1.343 bits/spike although only 2 of its 28 units are significant against shuffles, so the rate maps' spatial information does not show that Rat2's cells were selective. Over the 124 tested flight ES units, the rate maps of units significant against shuffles have a higher median than the others (1.855 against 1.076, p = 9.0e-7), but Rat2's 26 non-significant FD9 units have a median of 1.283, close to the preflight 1.448. The bootstrap 95% interval of the FD9 minus preflight median difference is -0.425 to 0.312 bits/spike (-29% to +22% of the preflight median); for Rat1 alone it is -0.750 to 0.543 (p = 0.25). The test has no equivalence margin, so a drop of up to 29% of the preflight median (40% for Rat1 alone) is not excluded, and the result shows only that no difference was detected.

The paper's test is unknown; a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test at 0.05 was fixed in advance.

outcomes.notes: Flight day 4 ES rate maps (104, Rats 1 to 3) have a median of 1.177 bits/spike against 1.441 preflight (98); one-sided Mann-Whitney p = 0.024, below the criterion's 0.05 (ratio 0.82). This differs from 001754-knierim-2000-01 (not_reproduced, 107 maps, p = 0.055) because the draft leaves out every copy in the groups of identical maps, and three Rat2 FD4 ES maps that the first attempt counted once each (7.583 bits/spike each, mean rate below 0.001 Hz) are no longer in the dandiset. On the earlier version's maps the test gives p = 0.055 with all 107 distinct maps and p = 0.024 with the 104 that are in the draft, so the outcome rests on whether those three maps are counted. The FD4 median is lower in each rat (ratios 0.65 to 0.88), significantly only for Rat1 (p = 0.032). The test passes with maps of peak rate 1 Hz or more (p = 0.0095), over bins with 5 or more occupancy counts (p = 0.023) and with information adjusted for rate x occupancy (p = 0.0011), and not with maps whose archived names contain CEL (p = 0.073) or with MC maps (p = 0.060). Rat1's and Rat2's FD4 maps have fewer spikes than preflight, so sampling bias works against the claim. FD4 against FD9 for Rats 1 and 2 gives 1.081 against 1.385 (p = 0.095); spike-based information minus the shuffle mean is 0.025 against 0.211 for Rats 1 and 2 (p = 0.13) and 0.232 against 0.211 with Rat3 (p = 0.31). The spike-based fraction of significant units is 24 of 71 on FD4 and 12 of 53 on FD9 (p = 0.94), so the spike-based measures do not show lower selectivity on flight day 4. Without Rat2, whose position trace could not be attributed, Rats 1 and 3 give 1.242 against 1.510 (p = 0.035), on the draft and on the earlier version alike, as the three left-out maps are Rat2's.

outcomes.notes: In Rat3's two flight day 4 ES epochs, the 15 units with 50 or more spikes in each have a median rate-map correlation of 0.537 (range -0.107 to 0.849), above the 95th percentile of 1000 re-paired medians (0.102, p = 0.001) and above 0.5; 8 of 15 exceed 0.5. attempts.paper_title: CalMS21 - Caltech Mouse Social Interactions (Sun et al., 2021)
attempts.entry_title: CalMS21 mouse social behavior dataset (Sun et al. 2021)
attempts.description: Tests the claims of Sun et al. (2021), the paper describing the CalMS21 dataset of resident-intruder pose and behavior annotations, on dandiset 001878, which holds one CalMS21 sequence (Task 1 test sequence mouse071) with its video, and on the full dataset deposited on CaltechDATA. It checks the format, identities and annotations of the dandiset's sequence, links it to the deposit, and tests the dataset's counts and label fractions. The model benchmarks are not run.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Sun et al. (2021) from dandiset 001878 and the CalMS21 deposit

outcomes.statement: Each frame holds seven MARS keypoints (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base) for each of two mice, the resident (mouse 0) and the intruder (mouse 1), in pixel coordinates of a 1024 x 570 image, at 30 Hz, with a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each keypoint.
outcomes.source: Section 3 and Figure 3; Appendix C (data format); Appendix D.1
outcomes.notes: The file holds 14 keypoint series named for the seven parts of the resident and the intruder, in pixels, at 30 Hz, with every coordinate inside the 1024 x 570 image (x 5.0 to 991.2, y 9.0 to 563.3). The confidence field is present for every keypoint but all 333,340 values are NaN, so the confidence part of the claim fails.
deviations: Judged on the one CalMS21 sequence in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Mouse 0, the resident, is the black C57Bl/6J mouse, and mouse 1, the intruder, is the white BALB/c mouse.
outcomes.source: Appendix C; Appendix B (Collection Process); Appendix D.1
outcomes.notes: In 746 of 794 sampled frames (every 30th) the body centres are at least 60 px apart; in all of them the 12 px patch on the resident is darker than the one on the intruder (median grey level 46.4 against 250.9). With 8 and 24 px patches the fractions are 0.997 and 1.000, with separations of 30 and 120 px 0.999 and 1.000, and 1.0 in every minute.
deviations: The coat colour test (grey level of the video at the body centre) was chosen here; the paper states the identities without a test.

outcomes.statement: Task 1 frames are annotated by one annotator (annotator id 0) with exactly one label per frame from the vocabulary attack 0, investigation 1, mount 2 and other 3.
outcomes.notes: The catalogue holds attack 0, investigation 1, mount 2 and other 3; the bouts give the annotator as "CalMS21 annotator 0"; the 170 bouts tile the session from 0 to 793.67 s with no gaps, so all 23,810 frames have exactly one label. The session has no attack bouts.

outcomes.statement: The source videos of Task 1 are released, recorded at 30 Hz and 1024 x 570 pixels.
outcomes.notes: The video is 1024 x 570, h264, at 30 frames per second with 23,810 frames, equal to the pose. Its motion energy correlates best with the pose speed at lag 0 (r = 0.754, falling to 0.19 and 0.26 at 15 frames either way). It is 184,059,454 bytes against 964,451,532 for CaltechDATA's mouse071_task1_annotator1.mp4, so it was re-encoded; the two were not compared frame by frame.

outcomes.statement: Close investigation, attack and mount are behaviors in which the resident is in close contact with the intruder; other frames include the animals apart.
outcomes.notes: Median distance from the resident's nose to the nearest intruder keypoint is 21.4 px in 4,679 investigation frames and 15.0 px in 2,894 mount frames, against 376.0 px in 16,237 other frames (differences -354.6 and -361.0 px, 95% block bootstrap intervals -408.9 to -295.2 and -413.6 to -303.8, with blocks of contiguous session time). The centroid distance gives -307.2 and -355.5 px, with intervals excluding 0, and each half of the session gives the same order. Attack is absent from the session, so the attack part of the statement is untested.
deviations: The paper defines the behaviors in words; the distance measure, the comparison with other frames and the bootstrap were chosen here.
One session, with no attack frames.

outcomes.statement: Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
outcomes.notes: 657 of 23,810 frames (2.8%) have a body length outside the session's quartiles widened by 3 IQR. In the closest 10% of frames (centroid distance at most 66.4 px) the fraction is 0.131 against 0.016 elsewhere (difference 0.115, 95% interval 0.064 to 0.179). In the fastest 10% (at least 389 px/s) it is 0.010 against 0.030 (difference -0.020, interval -0.033 to -0.008), the reverse of the claim. Both directions hold at 5% and 20% and with a factor of 1.5. With the speed taken as the running median of the larger speed per frame, the fast difference is -0.020 (interval -0.033 to -0.008) at 10% and -0.011 (interval -0.025 to 0.001) at 20%. Error fractions by label are 0.045 (investigation), 0.105 (mount) and 0.009 (other), so a hunched posture in mount could give real outliers. Checked against the MARS confidence of the same frames, flagged close frames have a lower confidence than unflagged close frames (median 0.574 against 0.657, difference -0.082, interval -0.107 to -0.050), and in each of eight flagged close frames drawn at random and shown with the video, at least one segment visibly runs across the other mouse or the background (judged by eye). The flags in close frames therefore mark mostly tracking errors, though the share of real postures among them is not measured.
deviations: The dandiset has no confidence values, so pose errors are counted with an anatomical proxy chosen here; the paper gives no measure of pose error.
The thresholds for close and fast frames were chosen here.

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's CalMS21 sequence is the CalMS21 Task 1 test sequence mouse071, with the same keypoints, confidence scores and frame annotations.
outcomes.source: Appendix C; CaltechDATA record 10.22002/D1.1991, file task1_classic_classification.zip
outcomes.notes: Matched by name to task1/test/mouse071_task1_annotator1 on CaltechDATA. Both have 23,810 frames; every keypoint coordinate is identical (largest difference 0 px), while swapping the mice or the axes gives differences of about 895 px. The frame labels from the bouts agree with the CaltechDATA annotations on all 23,810 frames (4,679 investigation, 2,894 mount, 16,237 other). CaltechDATA's confidence scores (0.030 to 0.980, all finite) are NaN in the dandiset. The same recording is also deposited on CaltechDATA as the Task 3 training sequence task3/groom/train/mouse002_task3_groom.

outcomes.statement: Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly, as shown by the MARS confidence scores.
outcomes.notes: The mean confidence per frame (CaltechDATA scores, matched frame by frame) is lower in the closest 10% of frames (median 0.649 against 0.740, difference -0.091, 95% interval -0.107 to -0.074), most of all for the intruder (-0.149 against -0.031 for the resident). In the fastest 10% of frames it is higher (0.751 against 0.732, difference 0.018, interval 0.012 to 0.025), the reverse of the claim. Both hold at 5% and 20%. The confidence correlates with the body-length error flags of pose-errors-close-fast (point-biserial r = -0.366). With the speed taken as the running median of the larger speed per frame, the fast difference is 0.018 (interval 0.012 to 0.025). The link holds in full, so the match of scores to frames is exact.
deviations: Confidence is a proxy for pose error; the paper gives no measure.
The confidence scores come from CaltechDATA, as the dandiset's are missing.

outcomes.statement: Task 1 has 70 training sequences with 507,738 frames and 19 test sequences with 262,107 frames.
outcomes.notes: The training file holds 70 sequences with 507,738 frames and the test file 19 with 262,107, as reported. Annotation lengths equal the frame counts of the scores in every sequence, and the frame counts of the keypoints and the scores agree in all 574 sequences of the deposit.

outcomes.statement: Task 2 has, for annotators 1 to 5, 6 training sequences each with 139,112, 135,623, 107,420, 108,325 and 92,383 frames, and 13, 6, 4, 4 and 20 test sequences with 286,810, 150,919, 77,079, 76,174 and 364,007 frames.
outcomes.notes: 19 of 20 counts match exactly. Annotator 1's training set has 139,122 frames where Table 5 gives 139,112 (10 frames, 0.007%); its six sequences match. The six sequences have the same frame counts in scores, keypoints and annotations; the paper gives no per-sequence counts, so the sequence that holds the 10 frames is not known. Annotator ids in the metadata agree with those in the keys.

outcomes.statement: Task 3 has, for approach, disengaged, grooming, intromission, mount attempt, sniff face and white rearing, 3, 2, 2, 1, 4, 3 and 2 training sequences with 20,624, 35,751, 45,174, 19,200, 46,847, 19,244 and 36,181 frames, and 25, 1, 13, 10, 12, 47 and 1 test sequences with 126,468, 19,088, 156,664, 55,218, 85,836, 251,793 and 17,939 frames.
outcomes.notes: All 28 counts match Table 5.

outcomes.statement: In the Task 1 training set, 2.76% of frames are labelled attack, 28.9% investigation, 5.64% mount and 62.7% other.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the training split, investigation, mount and other are within half a unit of the last reported digit; attack is 14,039 of 507,738 frames, 2.765009%, 0.005009 from 2.76 against a tolerance of 0.005. It rounds to 2.77 and truncates to the reported 2.76. All four are within 10% of the reported values. Reading (b), training and test, gives 3.46, 27.00, 7.85 and 61.68% and does not match.
deviations: The tolerance of half a unit of the last digit is tighter than the protocol's default of 10%, because these are percentages of a fixed file; under the default the claim would be reproduced.

outcomes.statement: The five Task 2 annotators label different fractions of frames as other, investigation, mount and attack (annotator 1 60.0, 20.6, 16.2 and 3.2%; annotator 2 65.5, 25.8, 3.4 and 5.3%; annotator 3 68.9, 13.5, 9.5 and 8.1%; annotator 4 75.2, 11.6, 4.5 and 8.7%; annotator 5 69.5, 26.4, 1.0 and 3.0%).
outcomes.notes: Under the training split with the class order of the Task 1 pie (other, investigation, mount, attack), all 20 percentages are within 0.05 of the figure's values; the best assignment of classes gives the same 20. The closest case is annotator 1 attack, 4,517 of 139,122 frames (3.2468%, 0.047 from 3.2), which would stay within 0.05 with up to 4 more attack frames. Training and test together match 1 of 20 under either class reading.
deviations: The Task 2 pies carry no class names; the order was read from the Task 1 pie, and the alternative reading (best assignment) was listed before the analysis. Both match.

outcomes.statement: In Task 3 the behaviors occupy 3.25% (approach), 1.47% (disengaged), 14.0% (groom), 19.3% (intromission), 0.90% (mount attempt), 4.74% (sniff face) and 9.29% (white rearing) of frames.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the training split, all seven are within tolerance. Training and test together give values outside 10% for five of seven (for example groom 7.36%).

outcomes.statement: The unlabeled set has 282 videos and about 6 million frames; the dataset holds over 1 million annotated frames, over 70 hours of tracked poses and over 10 hours of frame-by-frame annotation.
outcomes.notes: The unlabeled set has 282 sequences and 5,952,058 frames (55.1 h), counted the same in the keypoints and the scores. Annotated frames are 769,845 (7.1 h) in Task 1, 3,243,734 (30.0 h) over all labelled sets, and 2,273,674 (21.1 h) with each recording counted once; tracked pose including the unlabeled set is 62.2, 85.2 and 76.2 h. So the three "over" statements (1 million annotated frames, 10 hours of annotation, 70 hours of pose) hold under readings (b) and (c) and none holds under reading (a).
deviations: The paper does not say which sets its totals cover; three readings were listed before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: On Task 3, classifier performance depends on the percentage of frames in which a behavior is observed and on its average bout duration, with shorter bouts giving lower performance.
outcomes.notes: Across the seven behaviors the baseline F1 of Table 10 rises with the percentage of labelled frames (Spearman 0.786, exact one-sided p = 0.024 on the training split; 0.929, p = 0.003 on the test split) and with mean bout length, but the latter is not significant (0.321, p = 0.249; 0.607, p = 0.083). With the task programming model's F1 the bout-length correlations are 0.536 (p = 0.118) and 0.679 (p = 0.055). The direction of both parts of the statement holds; only the frequency part is significant with seven behaviors.
deviations: The paper states the dependence without a test; the correlation and the permutation test were chosen here, using the paper's published F1 scores with frequencies and bout lengths computed from the data.

outcomes.statement: Among baseline architectures trained on Task 1, the 1D convolutional network performs best (F1 0.793, MAP 0.856), ahead of fully connected (0.659), LSTM (0.675) and self-attention (0.610) models.
outcomes.notes: Needs the four baseline networks trained on Task 1. The paper gives some settings (input window, skip factor, the ranges searched) and refers to the project code for the rest, but the code at gitlab.aicrowd.com/aicrowd/research/mab-e/mab-e-baselines did not answer, with or without the sandbox, and no copy was found in Software Heritage or on GitHub; the web archive holds its landing page only. The data are public on CaltechDATA. Training five runs of each network was also not attempted within the time limit.

outcomes.statement: Adding task programming features learned from the unlabeled set raises Task 1 F1 from 0.793 to 0.829, and the challenge's top entry reaches 0.864.
outcomes.notes: Needs the baseline network (code unavailable, see table1-architectures) and the challenge's top entry, whose code is not linked. The task programming code (GitHub neuroethology/TREBA) and precomputed features on CaltechDATA are public, but without the baseline classifier the comparison cannot be repeated.

outcomes.statement: On Task 2 the fine-tuned baseline reaches an annotator-averaged F1 of 0.754, 0.774 with task programming features and 0.809 for the top entry, and all models do better on annotators 1 and 2 than on 3, 4 and 5.
outcomes.source: Table 3 and Table 9; Section 4.3 and Appendix G.2
outcomes.notes: Needs the fine-tuned baseline and the top entry; the baseline code is unavailable (see table1-architectures) and the top entry's code is not linked.

outcomes.statement: On Task 3 the baseline reaches a behavior-averaged F1 of 0.338 (0.328 with task programming features, 0.319 for the top entry), far below Tasks 1 and 2.
outcomes.notes: Needs the fine-tuned baseline with per-behavior learning rates hand-tuned on a validation set, and the top entry; neither's code is available (see table1-architectures).

outcomes.statement: Many prediction errors of the baseline models fall around the boundaries between behaviors.
outcomes.notes: Needs the baseline model's predictions; its code is unavailable (see table1-architectures), so the claim depends on a blocked claim. The predictions are also not deposited in either archive (data_missing).

outcomes.statement: The annotator embedding learned by the top Task 2 entry places annotators 3 and 4 close to each other and apart from annotators 1, 2 and 5.
outcomes.notes: Needs the trained top entry's annotator embedding; the entry's code is not linked and the paper describes the model only in outline. The learned matrix is also not deposited in either archive (data_missing).

findings.statement: The MARS confidence scores, which CalMS21 distributes with every keypoint, are missing from the dandiset's CalMS21 file; the confidence field of all 14 pose series is present but all 333,340 values are NaN. CaltechDATA's copy of the same sequence has them (0.03 to 0.98).

For CalMS21 the dandiset holds one sequence, the Task 1 test sequence mouse071, out of 574 sequences on CaltechDATA. Its description presents a collection of datasets and does not say that only one CalMS21 sequence is included or why this one was chosen.

The behavior catalogue (CalMS21_ethogram) has an empty definition for attack, investigation, mount and other, though the paper defines the three behaviors (Appendix D.2) and states that annotations refer to behaviors initiated by the resident.

The two mice are stored as one subject with strain C57BL/6, sex unknown and age P0D/; the intruder's strain (BALB/c) and the residents' sex (male) are known from the paper but not recorded, and which series belongs to the black or white mouse is given only by the series names.
The session start time is 2024-01-01T00:00, a placeholder; CalMS21 gives no recording dates.

The `centroid_speed` series, and the bout columns mean_speed, peak_speed and immobility_fraction that reduce it, are the speed of the mean of all 14 keypoints, which is the midpoint of the two mice, not the speed of either animal. The description ("the pose centroid, mean over keypoints") does not make this clear.

The dandiset's mouse071 video (184 MB) is a re-encoding of CaltechDATA's (964 MB). It has the same frame count, size and rate, and its motion follows the pose at lag 0, but the dandiset does not say it was re-encoded.

The dandiset links the CalMS21 dataset DOI (10.22002/D1.1991) as IsDerivedFrom, but not the paper that describes the dataset and its benchmarks (arXiv 2104.02710, NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks).

On CaltechDATA, 574 CalMS21 sequences hold 450 distinct recordings (identical keypoints over the whole sequence). 93 of the 109 Task 3 test sequences are Task 1 training recordings, five Task 1 test recordings (mouse071 among them) appear as six Task 3 training sequences, and four Task 2 recordings are in the training set of one of annotators 3 and 4 and the test set of the other. The paper describes each sequence as an independent observation and does not mention the overlap, and the CaltechDATA readme says that training and test sets are split by animal identity.

The paper's datasheet says the dataset does not include the raw videos, while Section 3.1 says all source videos of Task 1 are released, and the deposit holds them. The datasheet also gives the licence as CC-BY-NC-SA, while the CaltechDATA record and the dandiset give CC-BY 4.0.
Table 5 gives 139,112 training frames for Task 2 annotator 1; the deposited file holds 139,122. The other 47 counts of Table 5 match.

The baseline code the paper links (gitlab.aicrowd.com/aicrowd/research/mab-e/mab-e-baselines) is not reachable and no archived copy of the repository was found; the code of the challenge's top entries is not linked. The paper leaves the architectures' settings to that code, so none of the benchmark results can be repeated.

verifications.reviewed: The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file (commit cf06231).
